Systems Perspective 13.1: ResNet-50 across the serving spectrumSystems insight: It is tempting to read table 2 as one model deployed three ways. That reading is misleading: the cloud and mobile tiers share the ResNet-50 graph but use different precision and runtimes, while the TinyML tier cannot run ResNet-50 at all and substitutes an architecture designed for its constraints. Treating these as one model hides the work that makes each deployment possible.






When traffic exceeds what a single machine can handle, cloud and data center deployments that run multiple replicas of the same model require an additional infrastructure layer: the load balancer. Production serving systems place load balancers between clients and model servers.
A serving load balancer performs three functions. First, request distribution routes incoming traffic to available model replicas using algorithms such as round-robin or least-connections; routing away from slow or saturated replicas directly curbs tail latency. Second, health monitoring verifies replica readiness by inspecting both process liveness and model initialization state, confirming that weights are loaded and warmup passes are complete before admitting traffic. Third, deployment support enables progressive rollouts by shifting traffic gradually between model versions rather than cutting over abruptly.


↪ Shadow, canary, and blue-green release strategies that build on this traffic shifting are developed in Model deployment.
On a single machine running several model instances, such as several Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) Runtime sessions, the serving framework and the operating system queue requests without a separate balancer; a dedicated balancer becomes necessary once replicas span machines, and its distribution algorithms belong to that distributed setting. This chapter therefore plans capacity one node at a time. The unit of capacity is the sustained model throughput of one node, and the queueing analysis in section 1.5 determines the utilization at which that node can no longer meet its latency target and a second replica must be added behind the balancer.
Whether a deployment runs one replica or many, each replica must turn an irregular stream of requests into work its accelerator can execute efficiently. That conversion is the job of the inference server’s internal architecture.

Inside each replica, production serving confronts an impedance mismatch at the system boundary. User requests arrive stochastically, bursting milliseconds apart and then falling silent for seconds, whereas accelerator compute engines demand steady streams of uniform, dense batches to saturate memory bandwidth and functional units. Bridging this gap requires a specialized serving architecture that decouples network ingress from execution scheduling, absorbing arrival bursts and packing irregular inputs into dense batches without violating latency SLOs.


An inference server3 (such as NVIDIA Triton or TensorFlow Serving) functions as a specialized runtime scheduler that manages concurrency, device memory, and data movement between host CPUs and accelerator devices. Rather than invoking model execution synchronously upon request arrival, the server pipelines incoming requests through dedicated subsystems that isolate client network handling from accelerator compute. Every request traverses a multi-stage runtime pipeline designed to maximize hardware throughput while bounding queuing latency. Figure 4 diagrams the six stages of this pipeline, tracing how incoming client queries traverse network ingress and request buffering queues before the dynamic batcher stages them downward to the inference runner and the hardware accelerator.

This architecture orchestrates four primary responsibilities: concurrency management, request transformation, model lifecycle management, and execution scheduling.
First, the server manages concurrency. Serving engines employ asynchronous event loops (such as epoll or kqueue) and worker thread pools to handle thousands of concurrent client TCP connections without stalling accelerator execution pipelines. Decoupling network I/O from compute ensures that slow client transfers or network stalls do not starve the accelerator of ready work.
Second, the server executes request transformation. It decodes serialized network payloads into contiguous, aligned memory buffers matching the tensor layout required by the underlying execution engine. For example, four-dimensional vision tensors typically adopt NCHW4 or NHWC formats. On modern accelerators, matrix multiplication units (such as Tensor Cores) load 8- or 16-element channel vectors using coalesced memory transactions that favor channels-last (NHWC) layout. If the execution kernel requires a different physical layout, the server must materialize that layout. Calling torch.permute merely creates a view with reordered strides; an explicit memory copy or transpose kernel must physically reorder the data in memory. Because such materialization performs zero arithmetic (\(\ArithmeticIntensity\approx 0\) FLOP/byte), memory traffic and launch overhead dominate its cost. A device-local conversion consumes device memory bandwidth, whereas conversions across the host-device boundary consume PCIe bandwidth.
4 NCHW and NHWC (tensor memory layouts): These acronyms encode the dimension order of 4D image tensors: N (batch), C (channels), H (height), and W (width). In a contiguous NCHW tensor, each channel plane is contiguous; in NHWC, channels for one spatial position are adjacent. Optimized kernels may favor either layout, and a semantic mismatch can scramble values even when the element count is correct. Serving code should therefore make both dimension meaning and any physical-layout conversion explicit.Third, the server governs model lifecycle management. The runtime establishes the CUDA context before allocating device memory (VRAM) and streaming weights onto the accelerator. It pins host memory buffers for direct memory access (DMA) transfers and executes representative warmup passes to trigger deferred compilation and memory allocation before admitting live client traffic. While enterprise model registries, canary rollouts, and rollback policies belong to cluster-level operations (ML Operations), the serving engine governs local state: validating that active model instances are warmed, resident in accelerator memory, and ready for dispatch.
Fourth, the execution scheduler coordinates the transition between request buffering and accelerator execution by implementing dynamic batching (section 1.7). For weight-dominated inference at batch size \(\BatchSize=1\), streaming parameters from HBM can limit execution before the arithmetic units reach peak throughput. Grouping \(\BatchSize\) requests into a concurrent batch amortizes the byte transfers of reading model weights across all \(\BatchSize\) inputs, increasing the arithmetic intensity (\(\ArithmeticIntensity= \Operations/\DataVolume\)).
To balance individual request latency against batch compute efficiency, the scheduler tunes queue residency using a batching window (or timeout threshold). Setting the batching window to zero removes deliberate batch formation delay, but requests can still wait for an available worker. An immediately dispatched small batch may also expose too little work to use the accelerator efficiently. Conversely, setting a bounded window (such as 2 to 5 ms) allows the scheduler to buffer arriving requests until either the queue reaches a target batch size or the timeout expires. The window bounds deliberate formation delay; waiting for a busy worker is a separate resource-queue delay. Batching trades that formation time for greater weight reuse and potentially higher service capacity, while total latency includes both waits and execution.



As accelerator kernels undergo aggressive compilation (via TensorRT, TorchDynamo, or custom kernels), device execution time often drops below a single millisecond, and the host-side cost of ingesting, transporting, and deserializing payloads becomes the dominant term in end-to-end latency (the serving tax itemized in section 1.4.2.1).


Machine learning payloads differ fundamentally from conventional web API payloads: they consist of multi-dimensional arrays of floating-point numbers (such as image tensors, dense embedding vectors, or token sequence logits). While text-based JSON is ubiquitous in web services, serializing dense numerical arrays into text incurs severe CPU and memory penalties. Serialization overhead manifests because JSON parsers must scan every byte sequentially, validate syntax, allocate heap nodes, and invoke string-to-float conversion routines (such as strtod). Each 32-bit float expands from 4 raw bytes into 7 to 15 ASCII characters including punctuation. Furthermore, raw binary data (such as compressed JPEG or raw image bytes) requires Base64 encoding to travel within JSON strings, imposing a 33 percent size inflation before parsing begins.


↩︎ Clipper’s decomposition of serving latency, in which serialization rivals model execution, is established in End-to-end vs. component latency.
5 Protocol Buffers (Protobuf): Protobuf uses a predefined schema (from a .proto file) to encode structured data into a compact binary format (Protocol Buffers Authors 2026). Because the schema carries field names and types, the wire payload need not repeat them as JSON does. Its wire format is still not identical to a C++ object’s in-memory layout, so it requires a parsing step and does not provide the same direct zero-copy access pattern that FlatBuffers targets.
Protocol Buffers Authors. 2026. Overview: Protocol Buffers.
6 FlatBuffers: The “flat” in the name describes the design: the binary buffer can serve as the serialized representation and the data structure being read, avoiding a separate parsing or unpacking phase for supported access patterns (FlatBuffers Authors 2026). For ML inference, this can enable zero-copy access to tensor metadata—the serving system reads tensor shapes and offsets directly from the buffer rather than allocating a second object representation.
FlatBuffers Authors. 2026. FlatBuffers Documentation.
Binary serialization formats, such as Protocol Buffers5 and FlatBuffers,6 bypass this text translation tax. Float arrays transmit directly as packed IEEE 754 byte streams with zero ASCII conversion and zero Base64 framing. Furthermore, FlatBuffers organizes serialized records with internal relative offsets, enabling zero-copy deserialization: the serving application reads tensor dimensions, data types, and byte offsets directly out of the network receive buffer without allocating an intermediate object graph on the heap.



Transport protocol selection governs connection life cycles and socket multiplexing. Conventional REST APIs typically deploy HTTP/1.1 with JSON payloads. HTTP/1.1 clients commonly use multiple persistent TCP connections for concurrency. Establishing each connection incurs handshake and, for HTTPS, TLS costs, but keep-alive reuse amortizes setup across requests. HTTP/1.1 also suffers from request-level head-of-line blocking, because responses on a single connection must return in request order. While REST APIs can adopt HTTP/2 or binary encodings, the combination of HTTP/1.1 and JSON creates significant socket overhead and CPU parsing contention when serving high-throughput tensor workloads.
In contrast, gRPC (gRPC Remote Procedure Call)7 pairs HTTP/2 transport with Protocol Buffers serialization. HTTP/2 establishes a single long-lived TCP connection and multiplexes hundreds of concurrent request and response streams simultaneously using binary framing. This architecture multiplexes concurrent streams over a persistent connection and removes HTTP-level response-order blocking (a lost TCP packet can still stall every stream on the connection, which HTTP/3 addresses by moving to QUIC), while Protobuf enforces strongly typed contracts and serializes binary tensor payloads efficiently. Consequently, gRPC is the standard protocol for internal microservice communication in model serving clusters, where low latency, compact wire payloads, and bidirectional token streaming are primary design criteria.
7 gRPC (gRPC remote procedure call): The gRPC framework pairs HTTP/2 transport with an interface definition language and message format, most commonly Protocol Buffers (gRPC Authors 2026). The relevant serving advantage is the combination of typed contracts, persistent multiplexed connections, streaming support, and compact binary messages. The size and latency benefit over REST/JSON depends on payload shape, client/server implementation, and whether serialization is a meaningful share of the end-to-end latency budget.
gRPC Authors. 2026. Introduction to gRPC.
A concrete payload comparison quantifies how the serialization format alters wire footprint and host CPU parsing overhead.

Napkin Math 13.1: JSON vs. Protobuf serializationConsider a request payload containing 1,000 floating point numbers (for example, an embedding vector).

JSON: Uses ~9 KB on the wire. Requires ~50 μs to parse.
Protobuf: Uses ~4 KB on the wire. Requires ~5 μs to parse.

Math: Switching one request to the binary payload saves 50 μs − 5 μs = 45 μs of parse time. For this illustrative system processing 10,000 requests per second, the savings compound to 10,000 \(\times\) 45 μs = 0.45 s of CPU time reclaimed every wall-clock second, which is 45 percent of one core freed from serialization overhead alone.
Systems insight: This 10× scenario gain makes gRPC/Protobuf, FlatBuffers, or another binary protocol a strong candidate for high-throughput internal microservices when serialization is a visible part of the latency budget.


Architectural selection is governed by system constraints. REST over HTTP/1.1 remains practical for public-facing edge gateways where broad client compatibility and human-readable debugging take precedence over raw wire efficiency. Within cluster boundaries, gRPC over HTTP/2 with binary serialization can reduce overhead when high query volume or tensor serialization consumes a significant share of the host CPU budget; its streaming support also suits incremental token responses.
Protocol selection and process architecture establish the structural skeleton of an inference server. Evaluating actual operational performance, however, requires tracing how latency accumulates as individual requests traverse each stage of this runtime pipeline.

For dynamic inference systems, the serving inversion established in section 1.1 creates a latency budget that shapes system design (Gujarati et al. 2020). A serving system with second-scale per-request latency may miss many interactive SLOs, even if it achieves excellent throughput.
8 Tail latency: Unlike averages, percentile latencies reveal the performance impact of system outliers common in ML serving, such as model cache misses or garbage collection pauses. These rare, high-latency requests can disproportionately harm user satisfaction and business outcomes. Because the magnitude is workload-specific, services validate percentile targets (p95, p99) against their own users and SLOs.Relevant metrics expand from aggregate throughput and mean latency to the latency distribution. Mean and p50 describe the center, while p95 and p99 expose the slow tail. If mean latency is 50 ms but p99 is two seconds, the p99 threshold is 40× the mean, so about 1 percent of requests are at or beyond two seconds. Whether that tail matters depends on the service and its users, which is why percentile targets should come from the SLO rather than convention.8
Managing these percentile constraints requires decomposing the total allowed response time into a latency budget that allocates time across each processing phase, the serial accounting that the latency budget principle (\(\ref{pri-latency-budget}\)) states formally.

Definition 13.2: Latency budget
Latency budget is the time allocated to request stages under an end-to-end deadline; the SLO also specifies the required completion quantile.

Significance: It acts as a zero-sum constraint system where any milliseconds consumed by serialization or network overhead directly reduce the latency budget (\(\EndToEndRequestLatency\)) available for model inference.
Distinction: A latency SLO couples a deadline (for example, \(<50\text{ ms}\)) with a completion quantile (\(\text{p99}\) or \(\text{p99.9}\)). A service-level indicator (SLI) is the measured quantity used to evaluate that objective. Missing an internal SLO consumes reliability margin; crossing an external SLA threshold may trigger the remedies defined by the contract. Tail latency spikes can stem from queueing, batch formation, cache state, interference, or data movement.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that the “model” has the entire budget. In the illustrative breakdown in table 3, the remainder is consumed by host preprocessing and data movement (JPEG decode, resize, normalization, and PCIe transfer), while upstream network and serialization taxes (table 5) consume further margin.



Every serving request decomposes into three phases that each consume part of the latency budget. Preprocessing transforms raw input such as image bytes or text strings into model-ready tensors. Inference executes the model computation. Postprocessing transforms model outputs into user-facing responses.



Inference is one slice of the latency budget; preprocessing rivals it.
Accelerating model execution alone yields diminishing returns when host-side preprocessing and response formatting consume the majority of the latency budget—an immediate manifestation of Amdahl’s law. As hardware compilers compress accelerator kernel runtimes into sub-millisecond durations, host-device coordination and memory transfers emerge as the primary latency bottlenecks.



Dissecting where latency accumulates requires independent instrumentation across each pipeline boundary. In visual inference, for example, aggregate request duration conflates CPU-bound image decompression, host-to-device PCIe transfers, tensor execution across accelerator cores, and classification score deserialization. Isolating these distinct phases reveals the true bottleneck, preventing misdirected optimization efforts on kernels that account for only a fraction of total response time.

Barroso, Patterson, and colleagues identified a critical gap in how computer systems handle latency across time scales (Barroso et al. 2017). Nanosecond-scale stalls (such as cache misses) are hidden by hardware instruction-level parallelism, while millisecond-scale delays (such as disk I/O or network RPCs) are hidden by operating system thread context switching. Operations in the microsecond range (1–100 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)) fall into an awkward gap: they are too long to spin-wait on a CPU core without wasting compute cycles and power, yet too short for the operating system to context-switch to another thread without paying scheduling overheads that exceed the wait time itself.

Barroso, Luiz, Mike Marty, David Patterson, and Parthasarathy Ranganathan. 2017. “Attack of the Killer Microseconds.” Communications of the ACM 60 (4): 48–54. https://doi.org/10.1145/3015146.
Serving infrastructure operates directly in this killer microseconds regime. Using the representative ranges in table 5, serialization at 50–500 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\), dispatch at 10–50 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\), and data copy at 100–500 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) are each individually small, but for a 5 ms inference service, these named microsecond-scale overheads collectively consume about 3.2 percent to 21 percent of the latency budget before network and queuing delays are counted. No single overhead justifies optimization in isolation, yet together they determine whether the system meets its SLO.
Tackling this compound overhead demands systematic architectural intervention across the software-hardware interface. When microsecond delays accumulate across serialization, kernel dispatch, and memory copies, isolated optimizations to individual functions yield negligible improvements. Instead, high-performance serving runtimes eliminate boundaries altogether: employing zero-copy memory buffers between networking and execution runtimes, maintaining persistent CUDA streams to bypass driver dispatch latencies, and migrating preprocessing kernels directly onto the accelerator to avoid intermediate host-device transfers.




Input resolution represents an operational control that couples host preprocessing overhead directly to accelerator inference latency. While model architectures are often evaluated at fixed resolutions, the serving runtime must ingest variable client inputs and rescale them before kernel execution. In convolution-dominated vision networks, floating-point operations scale quadratically with spatial dimensions (\(\mathcal{O}(H \cdot W)\)), whereas static costs—such as weight streaming from accelerator memory and kernel launch overheads—remain invariant. Varying input resolution therefore shifts the operational arithmetic intensity across the roofline boundary: compute-bound stages slow down quadratically as pixel count expands, whereas memory-bound stages scale with activation memory footprint.

Different deployment contexts impose distinct resolution requirements shaped by their dominant constraints. A mobile application may accept lower resolution (\(224{\times}224\)) when latency and battery life outweigh marginal accuracy gains. Some medical-imaging workloads use \(512{\times}512\) or higher when diagnostic detail warrants the additional compute. A perception pipeline may use lower resolution over a wide field and high-resolution crops for fine-grained recognition. A public API can instead normalize arbitrary uploads to a fixed contract or select among validated resolution profiles. Adaptive resolution is useful only when the selection policy and every chosen profile preserve the task’s quality requirements.



Adaptive resolution lets production systems select resolution dynamically based on content. One approach runs a lightweight classifier at \(128{\times}128\) to categorize content type, then selects task-appropriate resolution with documents at \(512{\times}512\), landscapes at \(224{\times}224\), and faces at \(384{\times}384\). In this illustrative scenario, the policy provides 1.4× throughput improvement with 99.2 percent accuracy retention vs. fixed high resolution. This pattern trades preprocessing cost from running the lightweight classifier for inference savings on the main model.
Resolution sets the cost of the stages before the model. The stage after it is usually far cheaper, but it still crosses the device boundary and spends host CPU time, so it belongs on the same budget.




The request lifecycle ends with postprocessing, which transforms raw accelerator output tensors into structured application responses. This stage straddles the physical boundary between the accelerator and the host CPU. Because client applications cannot consume device memory buffers directly, output tensors must cross the interconnect (typically a PCIe bus) to reach host memory. How the serving engine partitions computation across this boundary dictates whether postprocessing completes in microseconds or stalls the entire serving pipeline.


Classification models emit unnormalized logits across the label space. Converting these numerical scores into actionable predictions requires reduction, filtering, and calibration. The simplest reduction is argmax selection, which extracts the index of the highest logit. Thresholding discards predictions below an empirical certainty cutoff, returning predictions only when the model meets a target precision. When applications require ranked alternatives, top-\(\TopClassCount\) extraction selects the \(\TopClassCount\) largest scores alongside their class indices. Probability calibration scales raw scores (for example, through temperature scaling) so that output confidence scores reflect empirical accuracy.
Executing reduction operations on the accelerator can reduce host-device transfer volume when the saved transfer cost outweighs the device execution and launch overhead. Performing softmax, argmax, or top-\(\TopClassCount\) selection in device memory prunes the payload before it crosses the PCIe bus. In ResNet-50 classification, for example, running top-\(\TopClassCount\) on the GPU reduces the transfer payload from 1,000 float32 logits (4,000 bytes) to five values and five integer indices. For ResNet-50 image classification, listing 1 traces this execution path from GPU tensor operations to host CPU label lookup and response formatting.



Listing 1: ResNet-50 Postprocessing: Normalizes raw logits into probabilities, extracts top-\(\TopClassCount\) predictions, and formats the API response.


# Normalize raw logits into probabilities
# Input: logits tensor of shape (1, 1000), one score per ImageNet
# class
probs = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)  # Normalize to sum=1 on GPU

# Extract top-5 predictions for multi-class response
# topk returns (values, indices) sorted by probability
top5_probs, top5_indices = probs.topk(5)  # GPU operation
top5_probs = top5_probs.squeeze(0).tolist()
top5_indices = top5_indices.squeeze(0).tolist()

# Map class indices to human-readable labels
# imagenet_labels: list of 1000 class names from synset mapping
labels = [imagenet_labels[i] for i in top5_indices]  # CPU lookup

# Format response with predictions and metadata for API contract
response = {
    "predictions": [
        {"label": label, "confidence": float(prob)}
        for label, prob in zip(labels, top5_probs)
    ],
    "model_version": "resnet50-v2.1",  # Client-side version tracking
    "inference_time_ms": 5.2,  # Observability for latency monitoring
}



In listing 1, total postprocessing time is approximately 0.1 ms, negligible compared with preprocessing and inference. The GPU handles the normalization and top-5 reduction, so the subsequent .tolist() call transfers only tens of bytes across PCIe. However, .tolist() forces a synchronous device-to-host copy, blocking the host thread until the GPU stream finishes. In high-throughput pipelined servers, such synchronization barriers must be scheduled carefully to avoid stalling the CPU thread while it feeds subsequent requests. Fitting a calibration mapping is an offline task; applying a simple fitted mapping online is usually inexpensive, but it is valuable only when downstream decisions require confidence scores whose empirical meaning has been validated.



Production systems package predictions to satisfy application-level API contracts. These contracts govern JSON serialization schemas, floating-point formatting, error codes, and fallback defaults when thresholding rejects all candidates. In Python-based runtimes, repetitive JSON serialization and string allocation can consume unexpected host CPU cycles under heavy concurrency, turning a microsecond-scale formatting step into a CPU bottleneck. High-throughput servers address this by delegating serialization to native C++ runtimes or binary protocols like Protocol Buffers. Response metadata, including model version and inference execution time, completes the payload to enable downstream observability.
Characterizing postprocessing closes the individual request’s latency budget. However, analyzing these stages strictly in isolation assumes sequential evaluation, where each transaction completes its entire lifecycle before subsequent work begins.




Executing each request in lockstep isolation leaves specialized accelerators heavily underutilized. Because network termination, payload preprocessing, neural network evaluation, and response serialization bind on distinct physical subsystems—host network interfaces, CPU cores, PCIe interconnects, and accelerator matrix units—strict serial processing forces the accelerator into idle bubbles while the host prepares incoming tensors. The central systems objective is to maximize the accelerator’s duty cycle—the proportion of wall-clock time spent actively executing arithmetic kernels—without violating request tail-latency deadlines. Serving runtimes achieve this through request pipelining, overlapping asynchronous host preprocessing of forthcoming queries with concurrent accelerator execution on previously staged batches.


↩︎ Asynchronous host-accelerator transfer and double buffering mechanisms are established in Transfer optimization.


Figure 5 sequences execution across CPU preprocessing and GPU inference to demonstrate how request pipelining recovers lost compute capacity. In serial execution (A), each request must complete its entire lifecycle (Network \(\rightarrow\) CPU Preprocessing \(\rightarrow\) GPU Inference \(\rightarrow\) Postprocessing) before the next request begins, leaving the GPU idle for more than 50 percent of wall-clock time. Pipelining concurrent requests (B) overlaps CPU preprocessing of upcoming requests with active GPU inference on earlier inputs, eliminating the idle bubbles and maximizing accelerator duty cycle.






Figure 5: Request Pipelining: Pipelining hides latency by overlapping independent operations across different hardware resources. In pipelined execution (B), the CPU processes the next request’s data while the GPU executes the current request’s inference. This can increase accelerator duty cycle and throughput without changing the model.



Pipelining relies on non-blocking hardware queues and asynchronous execution streams. Instead of blocking until a GPU kernel completes, the host CPU thread enqueues memory transfers and kernel launches into an accelerator stream and immediately begins preprocessing the next incoming request. The accelerator’s DMA engine and compute cores execute those queued operations independently, overlapping host preprocessing with device execution.



System efficiency here measures accelerator duty cycle rather than the fraction of peak arithmetic throughput or bandwidth achieved. In equation 2, compute time is the union of useful kernel-active intervals on each resource, summed across resources; overlapping kernels on one GPU are not counted twice. \[\text{System Efficiency} = \frac{\sum \KernelActiveTime}{\text{Wall Clock Time} \times \text{Resource Count}} \tag{2}\]
If a ResNet-50 request takes 10 ms total (5 ms GPU, 5 ms CPU), a serial system achieves only 50 percent efficiency. With at least two requests in flight in a sustained stream, duty cycle can approach 100 percent after pipeline fill if the CPU keeps up with the GPU. A finite pair still pays pipeline fill and drain time, and stochastic service must retain enough capacity headroom to meet its tail-latency objective. If the CPU is too slow to feed the GPU, the system becomes CPU-bound, and further model optimization provides zero throughput gain; this is the Amdahl ceiling of section 1.4.2 seen from the throughput side. Hardware upgrades tighten it, because accelerator compute throughput has grown far faster than CPU single-thread performance across successive generations. A system that was compute-bound on an older accelerator may become CPU-bound after a hardware upgrade, not because preprocessing got slower but because the model got dramatically faster while the CPU did not.

When arrival streams fluctuate, queuing theory formalizes how contention for shared physical resources (accelerator execution queues, host-to-device PCIe transfers, and memory buses) degrades latency distributions. Its governing laws explain why seemingly well-provisioned inference services experience sharp, nonlinear latency explosions as utilization approaches capacity.


Capacity planning begins by determining system concurrency: given an expected arrival rate and measured mean response time, an engineer must calculate how many concurrent requests reside in the system at any instant. This calculation determines how much memory must be reserved for request buffers and activation states before deciding how many accelerators to provision. Little’s Law resolves this concurrency question by relating mean in-system population to throughput, while queuing models predict how response times degrade as utilization nears saturation. Together, they provide the quantitative framework for capacity planning.


↪ The derivation of Little’s Law from conservation of requests is developed in Little's Law.

Systems Perspective 13.3: Notation alert: L vs. latencyClassical queueing texts write Little’s law with single letters for the in-system count and the time in system; this book writes \(\RequestConcurrency\) for the count and \(\RequestTimeInSystem\) for the time, because the classical count letter would collide with the loss \(\LossFunction\) and with the iron law’s fixed-latency term \(\Latency\). In queuing theory, \(\RequestTimeInSystem\) denotes the response time or time in system per request; queue-only waiting time is \(\QueueWaitTime\). Here, \(\RequestConcurrency\) denotes the average in-system request count, \(\ArrivalRate\) the arrival rate, \(\ServiceRate\) the service rate of a server that handles one request at a time, and \(\ServingUtilization=\ArrivalRate/\ServiceRate\) the serving utilization. The subscripts distinguish queueing notation from the degradation equation’s \(\FittedSensitivity\) sensitivity parameter and keep serving utilization from occupying bare \(\Glyph{\rho}\). Section 1.7.2 adds the few symbols that batching needs.


Formulated by John D. C. Little, Little’s law9 establishes an exact relationship among three macroscopic metrics in any stable queuing system: \[\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \cdot \RequestTimeInSystem \tag{3}\] where \(\RequestConcurrency\) is the average number of requests residing in the system, \(\ArrivalRate\) is the arrival rate (requests per second), and \(\RequestTimeInSystem\) is the average time each request spends from arrival to completion.
9 Little’s law: John D. C. Little (1961) proved that \(\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \RequestTimeInSystem\) holds for stable long-run averages over consistent system boundaries, regardless of arrival distribution, service distribution, or scheduling discipline; this universality anchors ML capacity planning: the formula requires no Poisson-arrival or exponential-service assumption. It does require well-defined long-run averages and consistent definitions of arrival rate, time in system, and population.Little’s law holds regardless of the arrival distribution, service-time distribution, or scheduling discipline; it requires only that the system is stable and that requests are neither created nor destroyed internally. For an inference service targeting 1000 QPS with a mean response time of 50 ms, Little’s law dictates the average in-flight request population that host memory buffers and worker threads must sustain.

Napkin Math 13.2: Little's Law capacity sizingProblem: How many requests are in the system on average at 1,000 QPS?
Math: Little’s Law gives \(\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \RequestTimeInSystem\), so average population equals throughput multiplied by mean time in system.
Given:

Arrival rate \((\ArrivalRate)\), equal to throughput in a stable system: 1,000 QPS.
Mean time in system \((\RequestTimeInSystem)\): 50 ms (0.05 s).

Math: \(\RequestConcurrency\) = 1,000 QPS \(\times\) 0.05 s = 50 concurrent requests on average
Systems insight: The system holds 50 requests on average across batch and queue state. That population is a memory and concurrency requirement, not a limit on the accelerator. A server whose GPU executes at most 32 requests per batch can still sustain this load, because the requests not currently executing wait in host memory; service rate, queueing behavior, and the tail distribution, not the population itself, determine whether the load is feasible.


Because equation 3 binds these three variables, constraining any two dictates the third. If an inference service averages 10 ms per request \((\RequestTimeInSystem = 0.01 \text{ s})\) and holds 50 concurrent requests on average \((\RequestConcurrency = 50)\), the sustainable arrival rate must be \(\ArrivalRate = \RequestConcurrency / \RequestTimeInSystem = 5000\) requests per second. Conversely, if host memory limits concurrency to an average of 10 requests while average time in system remains 10 ms, the system cannot exceed a throughput of 1,000 requests per second without dropping traffic.



Little’s Law describes average system inventory under steady-state conditions, but it does not reveal how latency behaves as traffic approaches system capacity. The M/M/1 queuing model (in Kendall’s notation: Markovian, that is Poisson, arrivals; Markovian, that is exponential, service times; and one server) quantifies the headroom required to prevent latency collapse (Harchol-Balter 2013).10 For a system with Poisson arrivals and exponential service times, equation 4 gives the average time in system: \[\RequestTimeInSystem = \frac{1}{\ServiceRate- \ArrivalRate} = \frac{\text{service time}}{1 - \ServingUtilization} \tag{4}\] where \(\ArrivalRate\) is the arrival rate, \(\ServiceRate\) is the service rate (requests per second the server can handle), and \(\ServingUtilization = \ArrivalRate/\ServiceRate\) is the utilization (the fraction of time the server is busy).
10 M/M/1 queue: Queuing theory originated with Agner Krarup Erlang’s 1909 analysis of the Copenhagen Telephone Exchange, where call arrivals were modeled as memoryless (Poisson). The M/M/1 model’s exponential service-time assumption introduces more variance than many fixed-shape ML inference workloads exhibit. At the same utilization and mean service time, its mean queueing wait is twice the M/D/1 value; the ratio for total response time approaches two only as utilization becomes high. This comparison makes the model useful for planning against a deterministic-service baseline; it does not establish a bound for arbitrary production traffic.11 Super-linear latency divergence: The planning knee often appears well before full saturation; in the M/M/1 mean response-time equation, \(\RequestTimeInSystem = \frac{1/\ServiceRate}{1-\ServingUtilization}\), where \(\ServingUtilization = \ArrivalRate/\ServiceRate\) is utilization. The \((1-\ServingUtilization)^{-1}\) term diverges as \(\ServingUtilization \to 1\): at \(\ServingUtilization = 0.7\), mean response time is already 3.3\(\times\) the base service time; at \(\ServingUtilization = 0.9\), it is 10\(\times\). The exact operating limit is a policy and workload choice, but trying to stretch a latency-sensitive queue toward saturation creates disproportionate latency growth.Because the denominator contains \(1 - \ServingUtilization\), latency grows nonlinearly as utilization approaches unity.11 Small incremental increases in traffic near saturation trigger severe backpressure and queuing delays.
The standard M/M/1 formulation assumes exponentially distributed service times. For compiled neural networks processing fixed-size batches and static tensor dimensions, execution times are nearly constant, making an M/D/1 queue a tighter model of mean queuing delay. The analysis here retains the M/M/1 model because it yields closed-form solutions and predicts greater mean queueing delay than M/D/1 under matched arrival rate and mean service time. In production environments, variable input lengths, dynamic batch formation, CPU preprocessing, and key-value cache lookups introduce runtime variance that quickly breaks deterministic assumptions.12

A single serving node forms the atomic building block of inference infrastructure. Analyzing single-node queuing dynamics under \(\KendallMarkovianCode/\KendallMarkovianCode/1\) assumptions exposes the fundamental headroom requirements and saturation thresholds of the hardware pipeline before deploying at scale. Rigorous node profiling determines whether service-time bottlenecks stem from accelerator compute saturation, dynamic batching window delays, host preprocessing overheads, or memory allocator locks. Once single-node performance and queueing knee boundaries are established, accommodating higher aggregate request volumes shifts the architectural focus to horizontal replication and traffic dispatch.
When ingress traffic exceeds single-node capacity, the architecture scales out horizontally by distributing incoming queries across a fleet of identical serving replicas positioned behind a load balancer. The \(\KendallMarkovianCode/\KendallMarkovianCode/\QueueServerCount\) queuing model extends single-server theory to \(\QueueServerCount\) parallel workers, illustrating how centralized request pooling buffers stochastic arrival bursts more effectively than isolated single-server queues. In practice, achieving theoretical tail-latency gains across a replicated cluster depends critically on dispatch policies (such as least-loaded routing or power-of-two-choices), input-dependent service time variance, and per-replica headroom margins. Furthermore, horizontal replica scaling remains architecturally distinct from distributed model parallelism: horizontal replication duplicates complete model instances across independent nodes to process disjoint queries concurrently without inter-node synchronization, whereas model parallelism shards a single large model across accelerators linked by high-bandwidth fabrics (such as NVLink) to evaluate an individual query cooperatively.



Production SLOs typically specify percentile targets (p95, p99) rather than averages because tail latency determines user experience for the slowest requests (Dean and Barroso 2013).
The M/M/1 model that produced the mean in equation 4 also yields the full latency distribution, and the tail follows from it. Total request latency (queue wait plus service) is exponentially distributed with cumulative distribution function \(\ResponseTimeDistributionFunction(\RequestResponseTime) = 1 - e^{-\RequestResponseTime/ \RequestTimeInSystem}\), where \(\RequestTimeInSystem = \frac{\text{service time}}{1 - \ServingUtilization}\) is that mean response time. To derive the 99th percentile latency (p99), we solve for the time \(\RequestResponseTime_{99}\) where 99 percent of requests have completed (\(\ResponseTimeDistributionFunction(\RequestResponseTime_{99}) = 0.99\)): \[1 - e^{-\RequestResponseTime_{99}/\RequestTimeInSystem} = 0.99 \implies e^{-\RequestResponseTime_{99}/\RequestTimeInSystem} = 0.01 \implies -\frac{\RequestResponseTime_{99}}{\RequestTimeInSystem} = \ln(0.01) = -\ln(100) \approx -4.605\] Solving for \(\RequestResponseTime_{99}\) and substituting the mean latency \(\RequestTimeInSystem\) yields the governing expression for tail latency: \[\TailRequestLatency\approx \frac{\text{service time}}{1 - \ServingUtilization} \cdot \ln\left(\frac{1}{1 - 0.99}\right) \approx \frac{4.6 \cdot \text{service time}}{1 - \ServingUtilization} \tag{5}\]
Mean latency masks tail contention: at 70 percent utilization, average latency is only 3.3 times service time, while p99 latency reaches 15.3 times service time \((4.6/0.3 \approx 15.3)\). For deterministic-service models such as M/D/1, tail values require numerical calculation rather than a simple universal multiplier, but the core systems reality remains: evaluating a serving cluster by average latency conceals severe tail degradation.


Dean and Barroso’s analysis reveals why tail latency becomes critical as systems scale beyond single machines (Dean and Barroso 2013). When requests fan out to \(\FanoutBackendCount\) parallel backends (querying an ensemble of models, searching sharded embedding indices, or parallelizing pipeline stages), the overall user request completes only when the slowest sub-task finishes. If sub-task completion events are independent and each has a 99 percent probability of finishing within latency threshold \(\LatencySlo\), the probability that all \(\FanoutBackendCount\) backends finish within \(\LatencySlo\) is \((0.99)^\FanoutBackendCount\). For a fan-out of \(\FanoutBackendCount= 10\), only \(0.99^{10} \approx 90.4\%\) of requests meet the target; at \(\FanoutBackendCount= 100\), that probability drops to \(0.99^{100} \approx 36.6\%\), meaning nearly two-thirds of user requests experience a tail delay. This “tail at scale” effect makes controlling single-node tail variance essential for overall system performance.
Before exploring software mitigations like hedging, systems engineers must first provision sufficient accelerator capacity to satisfy tail-latency SLOs under peak load. Applying the M/M/1 tail-response-time model to a ResNet-50 deployment makes the provisioning workflow concrete.

Napkin Math 13.3: ResNet-50 capacity planningConsider designing a ResNet-50 serving system with these requirements:

Queue-plus-GPU p99 subbudget: 50 ms
Peak expected traffic: 5,000 QPS
GPU service time (batch one, the chapter’s reference ResNet-50 profile): 5 ms

Step 0: Define the modeled request boundary. The worker model covers waiting for the GPU and the GPU forward pass only. This scenario allocates 50 ms to that portion of the request and separately assumes a combined 18 ms upper bound for network transit, serialization, preprocessing, transfer, and postprocessing. The end-to-end deadline must accommodate both allowances. A 50 ms end-to-end deadline would instead require subtracting the outside-worker allowance before applying the queue model; the arithmetic below would no longer apply. An outside-stage mean or p99 cannot substitute for the stipulated combined upper bound.
Step 1: Find safe utilization. From equation 5, \(\TailRequestLatency\approx\) 4.6 \(\times\) service time / \((1 - \ServingUtilization)\). Setting \(\TailRequestLatency\leq 50\) ms with 5 ms service time gives \(\ServingUtilization \leq 1 - (4.6 \times 5\,\mathrm{ms})/50\,\mathrm{ms} = 0.54\) (54 percent maximum utilization). This is an M/M/1 p99 estimate under the stated arrival and service assumptions. The mean-wait comparison with M/D/1 does not establish a conservative bound on production p99; a load test must validate the tail.
Step 2: Calculate required service rate. \(\RequiredServiceRate = 5,000\,\mathrm{QPS} / 0.54 = 9259.3\,\mathrm{req}/\mathrm{s}\)
Step 3: Determine GPU count. In this M/M/1 model, the single-GPU rate is 200 req/s.
GPUs needed = 9259.3 req/s / 200 req/s = 46.3 → 47 GPUs
This single-GPU rate is the batch-1 service rate. Each request holds the GPU for the full service time, which keeps the M/M/1 model closed-form. Dynamic batching (section 1.7) amortizes fixed overhead across requests and raises the per-GPU rate several-fold, so a batched deployment may need fewer GPUs after its own latency distribution is validated; section 1.11.3 compares the two regimes.
Step 4: Add headroom for variance. This scenario adds 30 percent headroom for traffic spikes and variance: final count = 47 \(\times\) 1.3 = 61.1, rounded up to 62.
Step 5: Verify fault tolerance. The 30 percent headroom addresses traffic variance, but production systems also need fault tolerance. With 62 GPUs, losing one leaves 61 GPUs handling 5,000 QPS. The postfailure utilization is 5,000 QPS / (200 req/s \(\times\) 61) = \(41.0\%\).
This remains well below the 54 percent safe utilization threshold, confirming N+1 redundancy is satisfied. For stricter fault tolerance requirements, N+2 redundancy (tolerating two simultaneous failures) would require 49 GPUs under the same safe-utilization threshold, or about 64 GPUs if the 30 percent headroom must remain after two simultaneous failures.
Result: Under the batch-1 M/M/1 assumptions, 62 V100 GPUs supply the modeled queue-plus-GPU capacity for 5,000 QPS within the 50 ms p99 subbudget, including one failed replica. End-to-end acceptance still requires validating the tail under load and the separately reserved outside-worker allowance.


The queuing analysis explains the capacity planning approach detailed in section 1.11.3 and connects directly to the MLPerf Server scenario. Server defines that scenario as Poisson arrivals scored by throughput against a tail-latency target. A Server result is therefore valid only when the run satisfies its percentile-latency constraint; otherwise, the target QPS must be reduced and the run repeated.




Eliminating all sources of latency variability is often impractical. Production systems instead employ techniques that tolerate variability while still meeting SLOs (Dean and Barroso 2013; Dean 2012). For one serving node, the first distinction is between an isolated straggler and overload. Racing an isolated slow request can reduce its latency when spare capacity exists; duplicating work on an overloaded accelerator deepens the queue. Admission control and graceful degradation instead limit how much work the node accepts.

When the node is overloaded, racing requests only exacerbates queue depth by injecting duplicate work. The system must instead protect the latency of admitted requests through graceful degradation or admission control. Graceful degradation returns lower-fidelity results to preserve throughput: classification pipelines fall back to cached approximations, generative models truncate decoding lengths, and model ensembles evaluate only a subset of members. Dynamically reducing active ensemble members shortens the service time \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) of each batch of \(\BatchSize\) requests, which increases the effective service rate \(\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize) = \BatchSize/\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) and lowers utilization \(\ServingUtilization = \ArrivalRate / \EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize)\) toward a workload-appropriate operating point with more headroom, as illustrated by figure 1, trading a controlled accuracy reduction for SLO survival instead of an uncontrolled latency collapse. Admission control enforces an even stricter boundary: when the ingress queue exceeds a designated threshold, the server immediately rejects excess queries with HTTP 503 status codes rather than admitting work doomed to violate its latency deadline.
Setting this rejection threshold requires accounting for the work ahead of the arriving request. Consider a warmed, isolated worker that serves requests sequentially in first-in-first-out (FIFO) order, without batching or preemption. Assume known upper bounds on each request’s service time and on every remaining stage outside the worker, including the response path. Subtract time already spent since the request began from its end-to-end latency allowance, then subtract the remaining outside-worker bound and the arriving request’s service bound. The result is its waiting allowance. The worker’s outstanding-work bound is the sum of the current request’s residual service bound and the service bounds of queued requests. Admission passes the deadline screen only when that sum fits within the waiting allowance; a negative allowance rules out admission even to an idle worker. A request-count limit approximates this comparison only when service costs are sufficiently uniform.
Suppose the outstanding work exceeds the full model’s waiting allowance but fits the allowance obtained with a validated, faster model that is already resident and warmed. The server can admit the request through that fallback if its prediction quality meets the application’s minimum requirement. Shortening the new request’s service time frees waiting allowance, but does not remove work already queued ahead of it. If neither acceptable model fits, rejection avoids spending accelerator time on a result that would arrive too late. Rejection reduces availability, while fallback can reduce prediction fidelity; both outcomes must be counted alongside latency so that shedding difficult requests does not make the service appear successful merely by shrinking its measurement population.
The deadline screen is a deterministic bound only under the stated service, isolation, and scheduling assumptions. Mean service time or a per-stage p99 cannot replace those upper bounds. Variable input lengths, batch formation, and shared memory-bus contention require empirical calibration against the joint request-latency distribution. Completed-request tails must be reported together with rejection rates and fallback quality over offered traffic. Adaptive admission control can tighten the admissible backlog as measured tail latency approaches the SLO, but neither a fixed queue count nor the simplified screen certifies a production p99 target.
An optional extension beyond the local admission decision concerns races across replicas and protection against fan-out delays. For an isolated straggler replica, the system can race the slow path. Under hedging, when a request has not completed within the expected time, the system sends a duplicate request to another server.13 The client uses whichever response arrives first and cancels the other. For ML serving, this means maintaining multiple model replicas and routing slow requests to alternative replicas. With a stable latency distribution, a threshold set at the historical 95th percentile triggers duplicates for about 5 percent of requests; correlated slowdowns can raise that fraction and make hedging amplify overload instead of reducing the tail.
13 Hedging: The term is borrowed from finance, where an offsetting bet reduces risk; here, the redundant request is a bet against a slow server. This is not free: for ML systems, the losing hedged request may still occupy accelerator time if inference has already launched, because ordinary GPU kernels are not cheaply canceled mid-execution. Thus, a hedging policy must budget duplicate work as well as the latency benefit.Cancellation before dispatch prevents a losing copy from consuming accelerator time; cancellation after dispatch may only discard its result. A race therefore needs spare capacity and a duplicate-work budget, even when only a small fraction of requests trigger it.
Tied requests make the same race more aggressive by placing the request in multiple server queues simultaneously, with coordination that cancels the other copies once one server begins processing. This avoids waiting to detect a slow response before hedging and can reduce queuing delay when multiple ready replicas are available. It also creates duplicate queue entries, so the coordination mechanism must cancel losing copies before they consume scarce accelerator time.
Fan-out systems need a different intervention point because one slow backend can stall the entire distributed request. Canary requests first send the request to a small subset of one to two servers.14 If these return within expected time, the system sends to the remainder. If the canary is slow, the system can retry elsewhere or use cached results before committing to the full fan-out. The technique turns a potential tail-latency amplification problem into an early warning signal.
14 Canary: Named for the coal mine practice (early 1900s–1980s) of using birds whose high metabolic rate made them sensitive to toxic gases before concentrations became lethal to humans. In ML serving, canary requests serve the same early-warning function for fan-out queries: by testing 1–2 backends before committing to the full fan-out, the system detects slow or failing replicas before a single straggler stalls the entire distributed inference request—a critical protection when fan-out width means tail latency grows with the maximum of all backend response times. Canary deployments borrow the name for a different mechanism, exposing a new model version to a small slice of traffic.The same duplicate-work constraint applies to retries across a fleet. A cascading failure occurs when all replicas experience simultaneous overload. If upstream load balancers retry rejected requests at other replicas that are also overloaded, retry traffic amplifies the overload. Coordinated load shedding addresses this by sharing load information across replicas, enabling system-wide decisions about which requests to accept. When global load exceeds capacity, replicas collectively reject the same fraction of requests rather than each rejecting independently and triggering retries.
Replicas or streams on one machine can also race requests, but sharing an accelerator or memory bus can correlate their slowdowns and exhaust the same headroom. The local admission decision remains the foundation; fleet coordination is an extension of it. Production frameworks may use shortest-job-first or deadline-aware scheduling rather than FIFO, changing which queued work lies ahead of an arrival and requiring a corresponding admission analysis (Harchol-Balter 2013).

Checkpoint 13.2: Queuing and SLO headroom
Latency SLOs are not enforced by fast inference alone; they are enforced by headroom.

If a faster fallback fits behind the outstanding work, what quality and availability conditions distinguish admitting it from rejecting the request? Why would substituting measured mean times invalidate the deterministic bound?

Queuing theory and tail-tolerance policies govern the steady-state processing of requests. They presuppose, however, that serving instances are already initialized and that incoming data matches offline training assumptions. Both preconditions frequently fail during cold starts, auto-scaling surges, and silent feature corruption.

Steady-state queuing optimizations offer little protection when a serving cluster fails to initialize properly or emits degraded predictions. In a representative deployment, a newly provisioned replica needs 35 seconds before it can answer its first request, most of them spent compiling a TensorRT engine, while a subtle PIL-to-OpenCV preprocessing discrepancy silently bleeds five percentage points of classification accuracy. The two failures sit at opposite ends of a replica’s life. Skew corrupts every prediction a correctly running replica makes, so it is prevented by keeping training and serving transformations identical. Cold start delays the moment a new replica becomes useful, so it is controlled by how weights are loaded, cached, and shared across the models that occupy one machine.


A model that performed well during validation may silently degrade when deployed. This phenomenon, training-serving skew, represents one of the most subtle failure modes in production ML because it is invisible to latency monitoring and exception tracking (Sculley et al. 2015; Baylor et al. 2017). The consistency requirement belongs to the data pipeline; serving is where a violation surfaces. Because the divergence is measurable on identical inputs without labels (principle \(\ref{pri-training-serving-skew}\)), it is also one of the most preventable.

Definition 13.3: Training-serving skew
Training-serving skew is the distributional divergence between the training and inference environments caused by inconsistent logic or state.

Significance: It violates the consistency imperative and can cause silent accuracy degradation when the transformation functions differ \((\TrainingTransformFunction(\RawPipelineInput) \neq \ServingTransformFunction(\RawPipelineInput))\).
Distinction: Unlike data drift (which is an external shift in the environment), training-serving skew is an internal failure of the engineering stack.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that skew is “found” by looking for errors. In reality, it is invisible to exceptions: the system runs perfectly and the latency is low, but the predictions are statistically wrong.



Training-serving skew: Diagnosis and prevention catalogs the skew categories and the method that detects each. The serving-specific manifestation of skew is preprocessing divergence: the real-time inference pipeline processes raw data differently than the batch training pipeline, a common failure mode when training uses Python/Pandas while serving uses C++/Java or optimized inference servers. Unlike data drift, this divergence is internally introduced and often preventable through shared transformations, parity tests, and careful engineering.

Example 13.5: ResNet-50: Image preprocessing skewScenario: ResNet-50 vision serving models experience silent prediction accuracy degradation between offline training and online serving pipelines.
Diagnosis: The serving pipeline implemented C++/OpenCV preprocessing (cv2.INTER_LINEAR, BGR order) while training used Python/PIL (PIL.BILINEAR, RGB order, different normalization constants).
Systems lesson: Preprocessing divergence causes silent training-serving skew without raising runtime exceptions. Standardizing data transformation pipelines across training and serving environments prevents input distribution corruption.





Even with mathematical parity guaranteed between training and serving pipelines, a newly provisioned serving instance cannot process queries until its state is instantiated across hardware memory hierarchies (Romero et al. 2021). This initialization latency, known as cold start, dictates system responsiveness during deployments, autoscaling events, and failure recovery.

Definition 13.4: Cold start
Cold start is the initialization latency incurred when instantiating a new model replica.

Significance: It represents the fixed cost of state hydration (loading weights, compiling graphs), which can take seconds or minutes, effectively blocking the system’s ability to scale elastically in response to traffic bursts.
Distinction: Unlike inference latency \((\InferenceLatency)\), which is a per-request cost, cold start is an initialization cost paid when a replica or model instance is created, including deployment, scale-out, recovery, and on-demand model loading.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that cold start is “just loading weights.” In reality, it includes graph compilation and memory allocation, which can often take longer than the bandwidth-limited data transfer itself \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)\).



Total cold-start latency compounds across distinct physical operations along the critical initialization path. First, weight loading transfers serialized parameters from persistent storage across the network or host I/O subsystem into host memory, and ultimately across the PCIe bus into GPU HBM. Graph compilation lowers the framework computational graph into device-specific machine code, executing kernel fusion and auto-tuning matrix multiplication kernels for the specific accelerator architecture. Memory allocation reserves device memory arenas for activation scratchpads and intermediate buffers. Finally, warmup15 execution issues synthetic inferences to populate kernel caches, prime framework memory allocators, and force lazy initialization before live traffic arrives.
15 Warmup: Borrowed from just-in-time (JIT) compilation, where initial executions compile hot paths into optimized machine code; for ML serving, warmup inferences trigger CUDA kernel compilation, cuDNN algorithm auto-tuning, and memory pool allocation that frameworks defer until first use. Without warmup, the first live request absorbs all of this setup and can be orders of magnitude slower than steady state. During autoscaling events, this means new replicas can violate SLOs for their first several seconds of traffic.16 CUDA (compute unified device architecture): NVIDIA’s parallel computing platform (Nickolls et al. 2008), named for its goal of unifying diverse GPU shader models into a single general-purpose architecture. Before CUDA, GPU programming required disguising computations as graphics operations. The CUDA context—the data structure tracking memory allocations, loaded kernels, and device state—is the runtime’s per-process gateway to GPU resources; in serverless or rapidly scaling serving systems, context creation and lazy module loading can become visible parts of cold start latency (NVIDIA 2026a).

Establishing a CUDA context16 represents the first fixed cost on the device initialization timeline. Before launching any GPU kernel or allocating device memory, the runtime must instantiate a driver-level context: an internal control structure that manages virtual address spaces, loaded kernel binaries, and hardware event queues. Creating this context requires synchronous communication with the kernel-mode driver and allocates tens to hundreds of megabytes of device memory for bookkeeping. The 0.3–0.5 s range in table 8 reflects a typical data center environment; while CUDA lazy loading defers kernel module loading to shorten this initial pause, it merely defers that latency penalty to the first executed inference (NVIDIA 2026a).
In multi-process serving deployments where multiple worker processes share a single accelerator, replicating individual CUDA contexts wastes both memory capacity and initialization time. CUDA Multi-Process Service (MPS)17 coordinates concurrent work from multiple client processes, reducing scheduling overhead when individual processes underuse the device (NVIDIA 2026d). Its isolation behavior depends on the architecture. Pre-Volta clients shared a GPU address space; Volta clients retain separate GPU address spaces and contexts while their kernels can execute concurrently. Separate address spaces do not provide hard fault containment: a fatal GPU fault can affect other clients sharing the affected GPU, so the serving design must budget for correlated replica failures.
17 CUDA MPS (multi-process service): MPS creates a control daemon that allows CUDA work from different processes to overlap on the GPU, which can improve utilization and reduce context-switching overhead when processes individually underuse the accelerator (NVIDIA 2026d). For multi-model serving, MPS can help replicas share GPU streaming multiprocessors efficiently. The trade-off is fault isolation: clients share MPS-managed GPU state, so hardware partitioning with Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) provides stronger isolation at the cost of fixed partition granularity.

Without warmup, the first live request absorbs deferred JIT compilation, driver memory allocation, and kernel launch overhead. A request with a steady-state execution time of 5 ms can stall for 500 ms during an unmitigated cold start, violating strict SLOs. Controlling this initialization overhead requires systematic selection among storage, memory, and runtime loading strategies.



Different loading strategies trade off cold start duration against serving performance and memory efficiency. The simplest approach, full loading, reads the entire model into memory before serving begins. This maximizes inference speed since all weights are immediately available, but extends cold start duration and limits model size to available memory. The approach is appropriate when cold start latency is acceptable and models comfortably fit in memory.
Memory mapping offers an alternative by mapping model files into the process address space and faulting pages in on access. It can reduce eager copying and shorten apparent startup, but a dense model will eventually touch nearly all of its weights, so deferred page faults can move loading latency into early requests. Selective benefit is greater for sparsely accessed components or model repositories that load subsets on demand; latency-sensitive services still prefault or warm the pages needed on the request path.
A third strategy, lazy initialization, defers compilation and allocation until first use. This minimizes startup time but shifts latency to the first request. Production systems often combine lazy initialization with synthetic warmup requests to trigger initialization before real traffic arrives.



Production systems cache model weights at the infrastructure level to reduce cold start for common deployment scenarios. One approach, container image embedding, bundles model weights directly in the container image. This produces a single deployment artifact and eliminates network fetches at startup, but creates large images (often 10–50 GB) that slow container pulls and consume registry storage. This approach works best for models that rarely update.
For organizations with many models and frequent updates, a shared filesystem (EFS, GCS FUSE) containing versioned model weights provides a more flexible alternative. Multiple replicas can read the same artifacts without baking each version into a container. Updates still require an explicit, atomic version switch and rollout; allowing files to change underneath live replicas would undermine reproducibility. The trade-off is that network latency affects cold start and filesystem availability becomes a critical dependency.
When cold start latency is critical for high-traffic models, node-local SSD caching prepopulates local SSDs on inference nodes with frequently-used models. This approach provides fast loading from Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) drives at several GB/s without network dependency, but requires cache management to handle model updates and capacity limits. Infrequent updates favor container embedding, frequent updates favor shared filesystems, and performance-critical deployments benefit from local caching with background refresh.



Production systems often serve multiple models from a single machine, whether different model versions for A/B testing, ensemble components, or entirely different models sharing infrastructure. GPU memory becomes the limiting resource, requiring careful management strategies.
Three strategies address multi-model memory management. Time-multiplexing loads one model at a time and swaps based on request routing: this approach is simple but introduces swap latency. Memory sharing partitions GPU memory among models, limiting concurrent execution count but enabling more models to remain resident. Model virtualization, as implemented by frameworks like Triton, separates model lifecycle from application code through model repository and control APIs for loading, unloading, and versioning models (NVIDIA 2024b, 2026c, 2026b). The choice depends on request patterns: if models receive traffic evenly, concurrent loading works; if traffic is bursty and model-specific, time-multiplexing with explicit preloading reduces average latency while maximizing GPU utilization.

When multiple models or multiple instances of the same model must run concurrently on a single GPU, the hardware must partition resources between them. NVIDIA’s Multi-Instance GPU18 technology enables hardware-level isolation, dividing an A100 into up to seven independent GPU instances, each with dedicated memory and compute resources (NVIDIA 2026e). MIG is available on A100, A30 (up to four instances), H100, H200, and newer data center GPUs. For older GPUs such as V100 or T4, CUDA stream scheduling permits overlapping or time-multiplexed work without hardware partitioning. The choice depends on whether consistent latency with MIG or maximum utilization with shared streams is the priority.
18 MIG (multi-instance GPU): Introduced with NVIDIA’s A100 (NVIDIA Corporation 2020) and documented across supported data-center GPUs (NVIDIA 2026e), MIG partitions a single physical GPU into independent instances, each with dedicated compute and memory resources; unlike software sharing (MPS or time-slicing), MIG provides hardware-level isolation between partitions. The trade-off is granularity—partitions must follow fixed profiles, so resources cannot be divided arbitrarily. For multi-model serving, MIG reduces noisy-neighbor risk on shared hardware, while per-model SLO guarantees still depend on scheduler policy, load, and the selected partition profile.

When the aggregate size of all models exceeds GPU memory capacity, the serving system must swap models between host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) and device memory (VRAM) on demand. This introduces a new latency component determined by the PCIe bus bandwidth.
For a 10 GB model on PCIe Gen4 x16 (32 GB/s theoretical bandwidth), loading takes at least 312.5 ms before deserialization, graph setup, or warmup. This raw transfer latency dwarfs a tight service-level objective such as a 50 ms deadline by more than \(6\times\), rendering on-demand model swapping unviable on the interactive request path.



Model loading lands far outside a tight serving SLO.
To accelerate this transfer path, systems keep the weights in pinned memory (page-locked host RAM). The GPU’s DMA copy engines require the source pages to stay at fixed physical addresses for the whole transfer, but ordinary heap memory is pageable, and the operating system may relocate or swap its pages at any time. A transfer from a pageable buffer therefore takes two stages: the CPU first copies the data into a pinned staging buffer, and the DMA engine then moves that buffer across PCIe. Allocating model weights with cudaHostAlloc removes the CPU staging copy; achieved bandwidth still depends on transfer size, memory locality, and contention. What serving adds is a capacity trade-off. Pinned memory cannot be paged out or reclaimed by the OS under memory pressure, so every pinned model holds its share of physical host RAM until it is released. High-throughput serving systems therefore pin active model weights and I/O ring buffers while leaving standby model checkpoints in pageable memory.

Once a model is loaded, warmed up, and producing predictions consistent with training, request grouping becomes the next optimization lever. Dynamic batching directly governs the balance between hardware efficiency and tail latency in queuing formulations.

Consider a representative ResNet-50 classifier on a V100 GPU operating at batch size one. Each forward pass streams the model’s weights from high-bandwidth memory to serve a single image and issues dozens of small kernels whose fixed launch cost is paid once per image, leaving neither weight traffic nor launch overhead shared across inputs. During each batch-1 forward pass, the GPU achieves only 15 percent compute execution efficiency (the fraction of streaming multiprocessor execution pipelines active during kernel execution), despite processing requests continuously at 200 images per second. Processing 32 images at once reaches 95 percent active compute efficiency and 1,280 images per second, a 6.4\(\times\) throughput improvement on identical hardware, because the loaded weights are reused across inputs in on-chip memory, amortizing both memory bandwidth demands and kernel launch overheads. This in-kernel execution efficiency must not be confused with serving utilization: a single worker processing batch 1 at 200 requests per second is 100 percent busy in queueing terms (\(\ServingUtilization = 1.0\)) with zero spare serving capacity, yet uses its internal arithmetic pipelines at only 15 percent efficiency. Batching19 is the primary lever for improving serving economics, but its operational constraints differ sharply between training and serving (Crankshaw et al. 2017). Training batches maximize throughput by grouping hundreds or thousands of samples together with no constraint on individual sample latency. Serving batches must balance accelerator saturation against individual request deadlines, ensuring that no early-arriving input waits excessively for a batch to form. An inference server resolves this tension through dynamic batching, adjusting batch size at runtime to match incoming request arrivals.
19 Batch: From Old French bache (a quantity baked at one time), entering computing in the 1950s for jobs processed together without human interaction. The ML serving usage preserves the original trade-off: grouping requests amortizes fixed costs (kernel launch, weight movement) across multiple inputs, but an online request may wait for a batch to form. Training can use batches of hundreds or thousands when memory permits; serving batch sizes range from one to much larger values depending on the model, arrival rate, and latency SLO.

Definition 13.5: Dynamic batching
Dynamic batching is the ML serving optimization that trades latency for throughput under stochastic arrival patterns.

Significance: By buffering requests into a batching window, the scheduler amortizes fixed overheads \((\Latency)\) across multiple inputs, pushing the system away from the memory-bound regime \((\Bandwidth)\) toward the compute-bound regime \((\PeakRate)\).
Distinction: Unlike fixed-size serving batches, dynamic batching adjusts the realized batch size at inference time according to arriving traffic, a timeout, and a maximum-batch limit.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that batching “always helps.” In reality, there is a latency-throughput Pareto frontier: if the batching window is too large, the increased queuing delay may violate the system’s SLO before the throughput gains are realized.





For workloads that underuse the device at small batches, increasing batch size can improve efficiency (Shen et al. 2019). A single request can leave compute units idle when its operations expose too little parallel work or weight reuse; large spatial operations and smaller accelerators may already run efficiently at batch one. Batching amortizes fixed costs across multiple requests and enables parallel execution across the batch dimension.

Shen, Haichen, Lequn Chen, Yuchen Jin, Liangyu Zhao, Bingyu Kong, Matthai Philipose, Arvind Krishnamurthy, and Ravi Sundaram. 2019. “Nexus: A GPU Cluster Engine for Accelerating DNN-Based Video Analysis.” Proceedings of the 27th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 322–37. https://doi.org/10.1145/3341301.3359658.
20 Kernel (GPU): CUDA borrowed this term from operating systems circa 2007 because GPU functions represent the computational “core” of parallel algorithms. Unlike OS kernels that run continuously, GPU kernels are discrete units of parallel work launched by the CPU, so each one carries a host-side launch cost that serving pays per request unless batching or graph capture amortizes it.Two fixed costs dominate at small batch sizes. Kernel launch overhead20 is the time for the CPU to prepare and submit work to the GPU. The number of launches depends on graph lowering and fusion rather than the layer count: the CPU must assemble kernel parameters, copy them to GPU-accessible memory, and signal the GPU to begin execution. This overhead is typically 5–20 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) per kernel, independent of batch size. For an illustrative ResNet-50 execution with fifty kernel launches, this range contributes 250–1000 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) per inference. At batch size 1, this overhead may exceed the actual compute time; at batch size 32, the same overhead is amortized across thirty-two images. Weight loading reads model parameters from GPU memory (VRAM) to the compute units. In a weight-streaming approximation, batch size 1 reads the weights for one image; batch size 32 reuses that weight stream across thirty-two images, increasing weight-only operational intensity by 32\(\times\). Activation traffic, caches, and workspace determine the executed operation’s full intensity. Measuring batching efficiency on a concrete model quantifies how these fixed costs amortize in practice.
