Continuous batching and chunked prefill keep decode batches full and their cadence steady, but at small batch each generated token still pays for one full weight stream. Speculative decoding31 attacks that bound directly. A small draft model proposes several tokens, and the target model verifies the whole proposal in one parallel pass, so a single weight stream can yield more than one accepted token. Evaluated T5-XXL workloads achieved roughly 2–3\(\times\) speedups (Leviathan et al. 2023), though the gain depends on how often the target model accepts the draft.
Keeping decode batches full, however, shifts the primary serving bottleneck to memory management. Because transformer generation appends attention states at every step, the KV cache for each active request grows dynamically in accelerator HBM. When sequences of varying lengths share memory, contiguous allocation produces severe external fragmentation. If a completed 100-token sequence releases its cache, an arriving 150-token request cannot occupy that freed memory because it requires a larger contiguous address range. Over time, physical memory fractures into small, noncontiguous gaps, preventing new sequences from launching even when total unallocated capacity appears sufficient. Together with the over-reservation of contiguous allocators, this memory fragmentation can waste 60 to 80 percent of KV-cache memory in naive implementations (Kwon et al. 2023), severely limiting the concurrent batch size that determines serving throughput.





PagedAttention recovers the KV-cache waste of contiguous allocation.
32 PagedAttention: The name directly references OS virtual memory paging, first implemented on the Atlas computer at Manchester (1962) to solve the same class of allocation problem—programs needed more memory than physically available, and contiguous allocation wasted space (Kilburn et al. 1962). Introduced at SOSP 2023, PagedAttention applies this six-decade-old abstraction to GPU KV-cache memory: the evaluated earlier serving systems wasted 60 to 80 percent of KV-cache memory due to fragmentation and over-reservation. In that evaluation, PagedAttention reduced waste to under 4 percent, enabling 2–4\(\times\) higher throughput on the same hardware (Kwon et al. 2023).
Kilburn, Tom, David B. G. Edwards, Michael J. Lanigan, and Frank H. Sumner. 1962. “One-Level Storage System.” IRE Transactions on Electronic Computers EC-11 (2): 223–35. https://doi.org/10.1109/TEC.1962.5219356.

Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, and Ion Stoica. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165.
PagedAttention,32 introduced in vLLM, resolves this fragmentation by applying operating system virtual memory paging to accelerator memory (Kwon et al. 2023). In static contiguous allocation, reserving maximum sequence length memory up front causes internal waste, while freed regions may be too small or poorly placed to satisfy a new contiguous reservation. Instead of allocating one contiguous region per sequence, PagedAttention divides the KV cache into fixed-size blocks mapped through a block table. A sequence’s cache can therefore occupy noncontiguous physical blocks. When a sequence completes, its blocks return to a free pool for reuse. Rather than copying noncontiguous blocks into a temporary contiguous buffer before computing attention, a specialized PagedAttention CUDA kernel traverses the block table directly, staging noncontiguous blocks into on-chip SRAM during query-key multiplication. By eliminating external fragmentation and bounding internal waste to each sequence’s last, partially filled block, PagedAttention reduced KV-cache waste below 4 percent in the reported evaluation and enabled substantially higher batch concurrency on the same accelerator hardware (Kwon et al. 2023).
Paging decides where cache blocks live; it does not reduce how many blocks each sequence needs, and that number grows with every generated token.




The KV cache33 is a stateful memory structure that grows with sequence length. Prefill creates cache entries for every prompt token, and each decoded token adds another entry, so a request’s footprint is set by its prompt length plus the number of tokens it has generated so far. Summed across concurrent variable-length sequences, this dynamic state can exceed the model weights and dominate available accelerator memory, which is why the remaining memory levers either reuse cache state across requests or move it off the accelerator.
33 KV cache (key-value cache): To avoid redundant work, the system caches the Key and Value vectors from previous tokens, which remain valid throughout generation. This design choice causes the dynamic memory growth described in the text, because the cache grows linearly with every generated token, making memory management a primary constraint. For a 70-billion-parameter-class model with grouped-query attention, the FP16 KV cache is about 0.33 MB per token per sequence; grouped-query attention (GQA), used in Llama-family models such as Llama 3, shares key/value heads across multiple query heads, reducing the cache relative to full multi-head attention (Dubey et al. 2024). A batch of 32 requests at an 8,000-token context therefore requires roughly 80 GB just for KV cache, several times larger still without grouped-query or multi-query attention.
Dubey, Abhimanyu, Abhinav Jauhri, Abhinav Pandey, Abhishek Kadian, et al. 2024. The Llama 3 Herd of Models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.21783.


Many requests carry identical prefixes, and recomputing their cache entries wastes both prefill compute and memory. Prefix caching stores the KV states of common instruction prefixes (such as a 2,000-token system prompt or a shared retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) context), allowing independent requests to reuse the prefill result for an identical prefix. For \(\SharedPrefixRequestCount\) requests sharing a prefix of \(\SharedPrefixLength\) tokens, the avoided prefill work is roughly \((\SharedPrefixRequestCount-1)\SharedPrefixLength\) token steps, subject to cache hits, eviction, and implementation overhead. For multi-turn conversations, the same principle lets a subsequent turn process only the new suffix after reusing compatible prior state.
When the aggregate KV cache exceeds GPU VRAM, systems can employ KV cache offloading. This strategy spills inactive or low-priority context windows to host CPU RAM or NVMe SSD, freeing VRAM for active generation. The reload cost is bounded below by bytes moved divided by PCIe or NVMe bandwidth, before software overhead and queueing are added. Offloading therefore prevents OOM failures and enables larger context windows, but it also creates affinity, invalidation, and hot-decode latency risks that must be budgeted explicitly. Distributed parallelism, which splits one request across multiple devices or machines, is a further lever that belongs to large-scale systems.




Prefix reuse and offloading both assume that the next turn of a conversation reaches the replica that holds its cache. Session affinity, routing successive requests from a client to the same physical replica, arises whenever serving state resides in local accelerator memory rather than being reconstructed on every invocation. In conversational models, this resident state is dominated by the KV cache. When turn \(\ConversationTurnIndex\) executes on a replica, that replica’s HBM retains the projected keys and values across all prior prompt and generation tokens. Routing turn \(\ConversationTurnIndex+1\) to a different replica discards that local memory footprint, forcing the new node to recompute the entire prefix sequence from scratch. This redundant prefill consumes memory bandwidth and tensor-core cycles that would otherwise advance active decode iterations, directly inflating time-to-first-token.
A parallel physical constraint governs personalized serving using fine-tuned Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules: small per-user adapters, each a pair of low-rank matrices whose product is added to a frozen base weight matrix. While base-model weights remain pinned in device HBM, individual user adapters must be dynamically staged into memory. If incoming requests for a user scatter across multiple replicas, each node must repeatedly transfer adapter tensors over the host-to-device PCIe bus or fetch them across the network, displacing other active working sets in memory. Stateful preprocessing pipelines, such as tokenizer vocabularies and per-session normalization state, impose the same penalty, requiring redundant CPU-side allocations and cache rebuilds whenever execution moves across node boundaries.


↩︎ Products of two low-rank matrices, and the storage and memory traffic they save relative to a full matrix, are established in Low-rank factorization.
Fleet routing is an optional extension of this local state-reuse constraint. Strict affinity creates a direct conflict with dynamic batching. Continuous batch schedulers maximize accelerator throughput by packing concurrent requests into unified matrix multiplications, raising operational arithmetic intensity in proportion to batch size (\(\ArithmeticIntensity\propto \BatchSize\)). When requests are pinned to designated replicas, the scheduler’s pool of batchable candidates fragments across the cluster. A replica assigned to an idle or low-concurrency user session must either process underfilled batches, collapsing arithmetic intensity back into the memory-bandwidth-bound regime, or stall waiting for affinity-matched tokens. To prevent this collapse in utilization, production routers use soft affinity. Under soft affinity, the ingress gateway prioritizes the cache-holding replica when capacity allows, but sheds requests to alternate nodes when local queue delays exceed the physical latency required to transfer adapter weights or recompute prefix tokens.

Systems Perspective 13.8: LLM serving: Beyond the fundamentalsEach LLM serving technique answers one of two physical limits. The first is the decode bound, in which every generated token pays for a full weight stream at small batch: continuous batching keeps decode batches full so each stream serves many sequences, chunked prefill keeps prompt processing from stalling that stream, and speculative decoding extracts more than one accepted token per stream. The second is the KV cache, which grows with sequence length and batch size and often exceeds the weights themselves; PagedAttention, prefix caching, offloading, and session affinity decide where it lives and how much of it can be reused. Weight-only quantization (such as INT4 weights with FP16 activations), the precision lever of section 1.8.2 applied to the weight stream, addresses both at once, because it shrinks the bytes streamed per token and frees capacity for cache (Lin et al. 2024).
These LLM-specific optimizations build directly on core serving mechanics: queueing models govern scheduling timeouts, batching dynamics determine throughput-latency curves, and reduced precision bounds memory traffic. Advanced treatments extend these mechanics to multi-tenant prefix sharing across fleets and multi-node tensor-parallel execution.



Napkin Math 13.5: The energy cost of a chatProblem: How much energy does an H100-backed chat service spend per generated token and for a response with 500 tokens?
As LLMs scale, joules per token becomes a first-class operational metric alongside latency. Assuming the H100 draws its 700 W thermal design power (TDP), this scenario estimate follows from throughput and power (Choquette 2023):

Throughput: 114 concurrent requests \(\times\) 8 tokens/s per request ≈ 912 tokens/s.
Power: 700 W (GPU) + 300 W (Host/Overhead) = 1000 W.
Energy per token: 1000 W / 912 tokens/s ≈ 1.0965 J/token

Systems insight: Under these assumptions, a response of 500 tokens consumes ≈ 548.2 J.

For comparison, charging a smartphone consumes ≈ 40000 J.
Boiling a cup of water consumes ≈ 100000 J.

The primary way to reduce J/token is to increase hardware utilization and eliminate redundant compute. If the GPU sits at 10 percent utilization due to poor batching, it still draws ~300 W and the host adds 300 W, causing energy per token to rise to 6.6 J/token (approximately 6× the baseline). Architectural optimizations like prefix caching also skip the energy-intensive prefill phase for shared context, directly reducing the energy footprint of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and chat applications. The serving lesson is that efficiency is not only a latency or cost metric; it also determines how much energy each useful token consumes.


Every lever so far takes the number of tokens a request generates as given. Reasoning models make that number a choice.

Systems Perspective 13.9: Looking ahead: Spending more compute per queryFixed-output serving minimizes latency (\(\EndToEndRequestLatency \to 0\)) for a fixed amount of work per request. Some inference-time-compute systems instead deliberately spend more computation per query to improve answer quality, generating intermediate reasoning or search tokens before the visible answer. The optimization target then expands to include answer quality, and every extra reasoning token pays the decode costs this section derived: one more step of decode work at the batch’s cadence, one more KV-cache entry held until the response ends, and its share of the joules per token. Answer quality now trades directly against TPOT, cache capacity, and energy per query.

Every LLM serving optimization ultimately decides how many sequences share each weight stream and how much accelerator memory each sequence holds. The chat-energy calculation showed that the same sharing sets the joules spent per useful token: each decode step streams the weights once for the whole active batch, so a well-filled batch divides that energy across sequences. These per-token bounds describe one accelerator. Deciding how many accelerators a service needs, and what each generated token costs, requires carrying them, together with the fixed-output results of the earlier sections, into capacity planning and unit economics.

Batching, precision tuning, kernel fusion, graph compilation, and the LLM levers that decide how many sequences share each weight stream can reduce latency, increase capacity, or lower the cost of a completed inference. Production deployment, however, requires answering a fleet-level question: how many machines, of what type, and at what total cost. A team that has raised a V100’s ResNet-50 throughput several-fold through batching still needs to know whether a few V100s or several times as many lower-cost T4s yield lower cost for its 5,000 QPS target while meeting the same SLO. Serving infrastructure cost grows with sustained request volume (Zhang et al. 2019), while training cost follows its own dataset, model, and optimization budget. The bitter lesson sharpens this asymmetry. The methods that win are the ones that scale, so successive models grow larger, and while training pays for that scale once, serving pays for it on every request. The multi-order-of-magnitude price collapse charted in figure 2 adds market pressure on top. As public API token prices plunge from thirty dollars per million tokens to several cents, infrastructure efficiency becomes the decisive factor in operational viability.

The cost per inference divides the allocated serving cost by the number of completed inferences that satisfy the service objective. The numerator can include provisioned CPU or accelerator time, memory capacity, data transfer, storage, and orchestration. At high utilization, useful throughput spreads that provisioned cost across many requests. At low utilization, paid capacity sits idle, so the same hourly bill is divided among fewer successful inferences. Applying the framework to ResNet-50 shows how hourly price and sustained valid throughput combine into a unit cost.



Hardware selection for model serving presents an asymmetric trade-off between nominal hourly lease rates and parallel execution efficiency. While specialized GPU instances incur hourly costs that exceed commodity CPU instances by integer multiples, their massively parallel matrix units deliver throughput gains that can reduce the effective cost per completed query by an order of magnitude. The economic crossover point between general-purpose CPUs and dedicated accelerators is governed by arithmetic intensity, batchability, and the strictness of the latency deadline.
Host CPU execution is economically optimal for lightweight models with modest parameter counts, applications with relaxed latency thresholds (hundreds of milliseconds), and workloads characterized by low or unpredictable query density where dedicated accelerator capacity sits idle. Conversely, GPU acceleration dominates when models feature dense tensor operations, when service-level objectives require sub-tens-of-milliseconds response times, and when sustained traffic volumes enable dynamic batching to amortize kernel launch and memory streaming overheads.
Beyond steady-state costs, startup time affects scaling economics. Instance launch, image pull, driver initialization, model loading, compilation, and warmup can make accelerator replicas slower to become ready than CPU replicas, although exact times depend on the platform and deployment artifact. If traffic rises faster than useful capacity can come online, latency SLOs can fail despite sufficient eventual capacity.
When accelerator replicas have a long readiness delay, predictive scaling or a warm pool may be more reliable than purely reactive scaling. For a model that runs acceptably on both device types, a hybrid design can use always-on accelerator capacity for baseline load and CPU overflow for spikes, trading a different unit cost and latency profile for faster reserve capacity. Whether this GPU+CPU hybrid works depends on model compatibility and identical output semantics across runtimes.

Systems Perspective 13.10: The physics of token generation

Recall the energy-movement principle quantified in Energy Cost of Moving vs. Computing on a 32-Bit Value: moving a bit is 100–1,000\(\times\) more expensive than computing on it. In the decode phase, this law determines the physical “cost per word.” 
Physics: For batch-one decode with INT4 weights, the weight-dominated arithmetic intensity is approximately \(2\) FLOPs per parameter divided by \(0.5\) byte per parameter, or \(4\) FLOPs/byte. This is far below the H100 ridge point, so the modeled step is memory-bandwidth bound. Larger decode batches reuse the weight stream across sequences and raise arithmetic intensity (Pope et al. 2023). The batch-one bandwidth floor is captured in equation 17: \[ \DecodeTokenTimeFloor\approx \frac{\DataVolume}{\AcceleratorMemoryBandwidth}  \tag{17}\]
Implication: Every token generation pays an energy cost to move model weights from HBM into compute registers. For comparison with the case study’s H100, on an A100 80 GB (2.04 TB/s HBM2e), the same model has a theoretical weight-streaming floor of approximately 1.97 ms per token. When decode remains bandwidth-bound, adding more compute cores yields little latency improvement; faster memory (Physics), smaller models (Algorithm), or better batching and cache management change the bound.




The model processes the 1,000-token prompt in parallel. Assuming 40 percent of peak compute efficiency during prefill, the model-side TTFT estimate is 41.9 ms, comfortably within the 200 ms SLO and leaving the remaining budget for network ingress, tokenization, and queueing.



The model generates 256 tokens sequentially. At batch one, this phase is memory-bandwidth bound: each step streams the 4 GB weight tensor from VRAM. A batched step amortizes that stream across its active sequences.
Dividing the 4 GB weight tensor by the 3.35 TB/s bandwidth yields the theoretical floor: \(\DecodeTokenTimeFloor\approx\) 1.2 ms. Adding an assumed per-layer dispatch overhead gives a modeled TPOT of 1.57 ms. This dispatch overhead reflects the cumulative cost of launching 8–10 discrete GPU kernels (RMSNorm, RoPE, projections, attention, multilayer perceptron (MLP)) across each of the model’s 32 layers. At batch size one, launching $$250–300 small kernels adds several milliseconds of CPU-GPU submission and driver overhead, which serving engines mitigate by capturing the decode graph into a single CUDA Graph. Generating all 256 tokens therefore takes 256 tokens \(\times\) 1.57 ms = 0.40 s.




With 4-bit weights occupying 4 GB, the remaining ~81.9 GB is available for the KV cache and runtime workspace. Each token requires approximately 0.131 MB of FP16 KV cache in the 8-billion-parameter Llama 3 configuration; while AWQ compresses weights to 4 bits, it leaves the KV cache in 16-bit precision. This per-token footprint derives directly from the architecture: storing 16-bit Key and Value tensors across \(\LayerCount=32\) layers with \(\KvHeadCount=8\) grouped-query attention heads of dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension=128\) requires \(2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2\text{ bytes} = 131{,}072\text{ bytes} \approx 131\text{ KB}\) per token per sequence, cutting cache volume to one-fourth that of standard 32-head multi-head attention. Dividing the 77.3 GB reserve by that per-token cost yields capacity for ≈ 0.6 million tokens, so at 1,256 tokens the GPU can hold a concurrent batch size of ~469 requests.



Consider a representative H100 SXM5 rental cost of approximately $3/hour and an assumed isolated prefill rate of 10,000 prompt tokens/s. Dividing that rate by the 1,000-token prompt gives the prefill request capacity. For this calculation, each completed request counts both prompt and generated output tokens, totaling 1,256 tokens. Multiplying the limiting request rate by this token count and the seconds in an hour gives 45.2 million tokens/hour; dividing the hourly rental cost by that throughput gives $0.066/million tokens.
The comparison also converts KV residency into a request rate by dividing the resident request count by the modeled time to complete prefill and decode. It assumes that all those resident requests can advance at the modeled per-request pace, which is an optimistic concurrency assumption rather than a measured decode capacity. Under these assumptions, isolated prefill supplies the smaller rate and sets the displayed cost floor. Shared prefill/decode contention, batched decode timing, runtime workspace, and SLO-qualified throughput determine whether the service realizes that rate; memory fit alone does not establish it.
The resulting cost floor is a bound for this workload. A load experiment must supply the missing service capacity before the same arithmetic can price an accepted deployment configuration.

For large language models, memory capacity (the size of the unallocated VRAM dedicated to the KV cache) determines maximum concurrent residency, while prefill compute and decode bandwidth determine realized token throughput and cost under a specific traffic mix. Memory bandwidth bounds low-batch decode latency; larger batches amortize parameter movement and shift the limit toward compute or KV-cache traffic.
Physical constraints govern serving economics across the entire stack: latency budgets partition into prefill and decode phases, queueing theory dictates batch sizing and capacity headroom, and memory bandwidth bounds decode throughput. Misinterpreting these interactions leads directly to the operational fallacies and pitfalls that follow.

Serving inverts training priorities in ways that violate intuitions from batch processing. The nonlinear relationship between utilization and latency, the hidden costs of preprocessing, and the silent failure modes of training-serving skew cause violated SLOs, wasted optimization effort, and accuracy degradation invisible to standard monitoring.

Fallacy: Reducing model inference latency proportionally reduces user-perceived latency.
Engineers who optimize model inference expect proportional improvement in user-perceived latency, but serving systems introduce latency sources absent from offline benchmarks. Under load, queuing delay dominates: equation 4 shows that at 80 percent utilization with 5 ms service time, average wait time is 20 ms before inference even begins. Reducing inference from 5 ms to 2 ms changes service time but also shifts utilization from 80 percent to 32 percent, reducing queuing wait from 20 ms to 0.9 ms, a 21.2× queuing improvement that dwarfs the 3 ms inference gain.
This nonlinear interaction between inference speed and queuing behavior produces an apparent paradox: the system-level speedup (25 ms → 2.9 ms, or 8.5×) far exceeds the model-level speedup (5 ms → 2 ms, or 2.5×). At first glance, this superlinear improvement appears to contradict Amdahl’s law, which states that total system speedup is strictly bounded by the enhanced execution fraction. However, the fixed-fraction Amdahl calculation holds other stage costs unchanged; serving is a dynamic queueing system. Average queue waiting time scales nonlinearly with server utilization: \(\QueueWaitTime \propto \frac{\ServingUtilization}{1 - \ServingUtilization}\), where \(\ServingUtilization = \ArrivalRate \cdot \BatchServiceTime(1)\) for unbatched service. When kernel optimization cuts service time \(\BatchServiceTime(1)\), it does not merely accelerate execution; it simultaneously lowers server utilization \(\ServingUtilization\). Pulling utilization away from saturation collapses queue waiting times nonlinearly. Kernel optimizations thus pay a compound dividend: shortening compute time and annihilating the queue. Conversely, profiling inference latency in isolation without modeling arrival load conceals the primary driver of user-perceived performance.


Pitfall: Running serving infrastructure at high utilization to maximize cost efficiency.
Teams target 90 percent utilization to minimize idle capacity. In production, latency degrades nonlinearly as utilization approaches capacity. Equation 4 shows that at 90 percent utilization, average time in system reaches 10× service time. Moving from 70 percent to 90 percent utilization cuts modeled infrastructure cost by 22.2 percent but triples average latency. For a 5 ms inference service, modeled p99 latency rises from ~76.7 ms to ~230 ms under the M/M/1 assumptions. In this scenario, operating at 60 to 70 percent utilization preserves substantially more latency headroom than 90 percent. A production target must instead be selected from the measured arrival process, service-time distribution, SLO, failure reserve, and cost objective.


Fallacy: Training accuracy guarantees serving accuracy.
Engineers assume identical model weights preserve validation-set performance. In production, preprocessing differences can shift inputs outside the training distribution. Section 1.6.1 explains how resize interpolation, numerical precision, and feature timing can create skew despite identical weights. Validation accuracy holds only over the population it sampled (principle \(\ref{pri-verification-gap}\)), and a serving path that transforms inputs differently presents the model with a different population. The illustrative scenario here drops from 95 percent to 90 percent, a 5 percentage-point loss; these values are not a reported production incident. Production systems require consistent preprocessing and task-quality monitoring because latency and exception checks cannot detect this failure.


Pitfall: Using average latency to evaluate serving system performance.
Engineers monitor average latency because it trends smoothly and is simple to compute. An average, however, cannot show whether the percentile named by an SLO is failing. As section 1.5.4 demonstrates, at 70 percent utilization with 5 ms service time, average latency is 16.7 ms but the modeled p99 reaches 76.7 ms, a 4.6× gap invisible to mean-based monitoring. Services therefore report the relevant latency distribution and SLO percentile rather than the mean alone.


Fallacy: Larger serving batches always improve throughput without affecting latency SLOs.
Engineers maximize batch size assuming GPU saturation improves cost efficiency under production load. In serving systems, however, batching introduces a latency-throughput trade-off governed by queuing dynamics absent from offline benchmarks. Accumulating requests into larger batches increases wait time for early arrivals: an oldest-request window of 10 ms can add up to 10 ms of formation wait if the batch-size trigger does not fire first. Waiting for an available worker can add further delay; the combined distribution determines p99 latency. In the representative ResNet-50/V100 scenario in section 1.7.5, increasing batch size from 16 to 32 improves throughput only 12 percent but nearly doubles per-batch inference time from 14 ms to 25 ms, and variable input sizes within a batch can create padding overhead that wastes compute on padding tokens. Section 1.7.4 shows why, for tight p99 targets, larger batch sizes can violate SLOs when batch formation delay plus increased per-batch inference time exceeds the latency budget. Serving batch optimization requires jointly tuning batch size, batch timeout, and concurrency against latency SLOs under realistic traffic patterns, not maximizing throughput in isolation.


Pitfall: Calibrating quantized models with unrepresentative data.
Teams may calibrate with a convenient sample even when it does not represent the supported deployment distribution. Post-training quantization determines INT8 scale factors from activation ranges in calibration data, so representative coverage matters. The illustrative scenario here drops from 76.1 percent to 72.9 percent, a 3.2 percentage-point loss; it is not a reported production incident. Effective quantization requires calibration and validation on data representative of the inputs the service is expected to handle.


Fallacy: Cold start latency only matters for the first request.
Engineers optimize steady-state latency assuming most requests hit warm instances. Cold starts can compound during traffic spikes, deployments, and recovery. In this illustrative scenario, 10 instances each require 30 s of compilation, totaling 300 instance-seconds; parallel warming makes capacity useful after about 30 s. The assumed cold-request latency is 500 ms versus 5 ms at steady state.


Pitfall: Scaling without a warm-pool or staged-loading budget.
Autoscaling policies that count only steady-state replicas underestimate the capacity needed during traffic spikes and deployments. Serving systems need warm pools (pre-initialized spare replicas), staged model loading, or admission control so that new replicas become useful before user requests depend on them. The budget should include compilation, weight loading, cache initialization, and health-check time, because those steps determine whether scale-out adds capacity or adds another source of tail latency.

Serving moves a validated model into an operating workload. Online requests add a latency distribution, queueing, traffic variability, and failure reserve to the throughput concerns familiar from training. Little’s Law relates stable long-run population, arrival rate, and response time; M/M/1 supplies an intentionally simple model of nonlinear latency growth near saturation. Neither replaces measurement, but together they turn headroom and capacity into explicit hypotheses that a load test can validate.
Effective serving optimization measures the complete request path rather than model inference alone. Protocol and serialization choices matter when transport is a visible fraction of the budget; preprocessing matters when it feeds an accelerator too slowly; batching matters only when arrivals and the SLO permit waiting. Training-serving skew adds a different failure mode: the service can remain fast and error-free while inconsistent transformations silently change its predictions.
The chosen deployment paradigm changes the feasible request path. A cloud API may use dynamic batching under a measured arrival process, synchronized sensors impose a frame deadline, and a single-stream mobile workload may choose batch one to protect responsiveness and energy. The MLPerf scenarios provide standardized approximations of these shapes; production design still begins with the service’s own traffic, hardware, and objective.
Node-level optimization connects the model’s operations to the machine that executes them. Profiling reveals whether compilation, kernel fusion, precision, locality, serialization, or loading actually binds the request path. Gains matter only when they survive production input shapes, accuracy checks, and latency variation. Token-streaming language models stretch the whole toolkit at once. Latency splits into time to first token and time per output token, batching must reschedule at every generated token, and the KV cache, not arithmetic, bounds how many requests can share an accelerator. Capacity planning converts that valid throughput into replica count and unit cost, while the Llama 3 case study in section 1.11.4 separates calculable capacity bounds from the load experiment needed to establish valid throughput. A faster kernel that neither reduces provisioned capacity nor improves the SLO has not produced an economic gain.

Key Takeaways: Inverting every training priority

Serving is latency economics: Training rewards throughput over long runs, but serving spends a fixed per-request budget across serialization, preprocessing, queuing, inference, postprocessing, and the network. Optimizing only model latency misses the stages users actually wait on.
Utilization turns into waiting: In the chapter’s M/M/1 approximation, average time in system rises from 5\(\times\) service time at 80 percent utilization to 10\(\times\) at 90 percent. Headroom keeps modest traffic surges from becoming SLO failures.
Fast models reveal pipeline taxes: Once inference is fast, image decode, tokenization, and other preprocessing can dominate total latency. The binding optimization becomes the request path, not the neural network kernel.
Batching follows traffic, not habit: Poisson-modeled web arrivals can use dynamic batching, synchronized sensors need aligned batches, and single-stream mobile workloads may have little batching opportunity. A useful window converts available latency slack into throughput without violating the SLO.
Skew breaks accuracy without errors: Resize methods, color-channel order, normalization constants, or feature definitions that differ between training and serving can change the model’s effective input distribution. Shared transformations, parity tests, and production-slice monitoring reduce this risk.
Runtime choices become infrastructure bills: Precision, graph compilation, kernel fusion, and serving runtime translate directly into replica count and cost per inference. Quantization and specialized runtimes can materially reduce required serving capacity when they preserve accuracy and fit the target hardware.
LLM serving is memory management: Decode often reads weights from VRAM for every generated token, so token latency is bandwidth-bound unless batching changes the constraint. KV-cache layout, PagedAttention, continuous batching, precision, and runtime choice determine both concurrency and cost per token.



Training is judged by useful work completed; an online service is judged by whether requests meet their latency objective. Each stage spends against the same envelope: serialization, preprocessing, the queue, the model, and the response. Data determines input size and arrival shape, the algorithm determines compute and state, and the machine determines service rate and movement costs. Queueing couples all three nonlinearly, so a system within budget at moderate traffic can breach it after a small surge. Serving engineering therefore allocates the budget across the request path, preserves headroom for variability and failure, and verifies that the required fraction of requests finishes before the deadline, which is the latency budget principle (\(\ref{pri-latency-budget}\)) in operational form.

What’s Next: From fast to still correctThis chapter evaluates the request path under a specified workload: latency within budget, headroom preserved, and useful throughput converted into cost. Those performance checks do not establish whether the answers are still right. Training-serving skew showed that a service can stay fast and error-free while its predictions change, and drift produces the same silence when the world moves rather than the pipeline. ML Operations widens the unit of concern from request-path performance to the model’s operating lifetime. Monitoring tracks prediction quality alongside system health, feature stores and model registries keep serving aligned with training, and staged rollout with rollback lets a replacement model reach users without turning a bad release into an outage.

Maximum-throughput greedy allocation, which concentrates all incoming traffic onto a single primary replica until its memory is completely saturated before spilling over.

Answer: Tail at scale means a fan-out request inherits the slowest participating subrequest, so a small per-node tail probability can become a much larger end-to-end tail probability when many backends must all finish. Under the independence and shared-threshold assumptions, the probability that at least one of 50 leaves misses the target is \(1 - (0.99)^{50} \approx 39.5\%\). The practical implication is that single-node p99 performance is not enough when a user request depends on many parallel backends.
Learning Objective: Calculate fan-out tail-latency amplification in distributed multi-server inference architectures.
True or False: Hedged requests (speculative backup requests) reduce p99 tail latency by sending identical duplicate requests to multiple servers simultaneously for every incoming query upon arrival, without incurring any additional cluster compute overhead.
Answer: False. Hedging trades extra work for a chance to avoid stragglers, so it can add compute and queueing load rather than being free. Practical policies usually trigger duplicates only after a request looks slow relative to a reference distribution, but the extra load is not fixed: correlated slowdowns, traffic level, and cancellation behavior determine whether hedging helps or hurts.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the trade-offs and operational mechanics of hedged requests for tail-latency mitigation.
Order the following overload-handling workflow for a serving system from first diagnosis to final verification: (1) choose a mitigation that fits the current bottleneck and SLO trade-off, such as admission control, graceful degradation, or a batching change, (2) measure arrival rate, service time, queue depth, and observed tail latency, (3) identify the binding constraint from those measurements, such as overload, queue growth, or service-time inflation, (4) validate the chosen policy under representative load and confirm it improves SLO compliance.

An inference node modeled as an \(M/M/1\) queue has an average execution service time of \(T_{\text{svc}} = 10\text{ ms}\). If the arrival rate increases such that system utilization \(\rho\) increases from \(50\%\) (\(\rho = 0.5\)) to \(90\%\) (\(\rho = 0.9\)), what happens to the mean total response time \(W\)?

\(W\) increases linearly from 10 ms to 18 ms.
\(W\) increases nonlinearly from 20 ms to 100 ms (\(5\times\) increase).
\(W\) decreases from 20 ms to 11.1 ms due to batching efficiency.
\(W\) remains fixed at 10 ms because service time is independent of arrival rate.

At \(\rho = 0.5\), this gives \(\frac{10\text{ ms}}{0.5} = 20\text{ ms}\); at \(\rho = 0.9\), it gives \(\frac{10\text{ ms}}{0.1} = 100\text{ ms}\). So utilization rises by \(1.8\times\), while mean response time rises by \(5\times\) because the dependence is reciprocal rather than linear.

Redeploy the cluster on 50 dedicated GPU nodes running continuous batching 24/7.
Quantize all models to 1-bit weights to fit all 50 models into GPU L2 cache simultaneously.
Maintain a tiered memory cache (storing active models in GPU VRAM and inactive models in host pinned DRAM), using asynchronous PCIe DMA transfers to swap weights into VRAM on demand with an LRU eviction policy.
Compress all models into a single shared zip archive on remote S3 and download the entire archive over HTTP on each incoming request.

Why can increasing batch size during deep learning inference improve hardware throughput on modern GPUs for weight-streaming workloads, and when does that improvement stop paying off on a Roofline model?

Batching converts all floating-point operations into integer bitshifts, bypassing GPU ALUs entirely.
Batching reduces the total parameter count of the neural network by sharing weights across batch samples.

Timeouts dispatch the request rather than dropping it, a batch of 1 does not imply peak utilization, and the configured timeout prevents indefinite waiting.

The model compiler will fail to generate valid GPU assembly code and reject the weights.
The server’s physical power consumption will double due to misaligned integer registers.
The dynamic batcher will permanently lock its batch size to 1.

In a CPU-based model serving deployment, how do vector extensions like Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) or Vector Neural Network Instructions (VNNI) accelerate inference throughput compared to standard scalar x86 execution?
Answer: Scalar execution handles only a small number of values per instruction, while vector and matrix extensions let the CPU apply one instruction across many elements or tiles at once. In practice, optimized runtimes combine these instructions with cache-aware tiling so matrix multiplies and convolutions move through the CPU more like dense blocks than isolated scalar operations. The practical consequence is much higher arithmetic throughput per socket for supported data types, especially when the data layout and kernel implementation are tuned to feed those units efficiently.

nvidia-smi measures fan speed and ambient temperature rather than compute kernel activity.
The GPU memory clock is automatically halved during Nsight Systems tracing.
The CPU is running at 100% duty cycle, which forces nvidia-smi to report false GPU metrics.
nvidia-smi reports the fraction of sampled time with one or more kernels active on the GPU, not how efficiently those kernels used the compute units.

That is why detailed traces and hardware counters are needed to distinguish ’GPU active’ from ‘GPU doing useful compute efficiently.’ Fan speed, profiler-induced clock halving, and CPU duty cycle are not the explanation here.

In Large Language Model (LLM) serving, how do the computational and hardware characteristics of the Prefill phase fundamentally differ from the Decode phase?

Prefill processes tokens autoregressively one by one and is memory-bandwidth bound, whereas Decode processes all output tokens simultaneously and is compute-bound.
Prefill processes all prompt tokens concurrently in parallel matrix multiplications and is often more compute-intensive, whereas Decode generates one token per step autoregressively and at low batch sizes is often memory-bandwidth bound due to repeated weight and KV-state movement.
Prefill operates exclusively on host CPU DRAM, whereas Decode runs on GPU Tensor Cores.
Prefill latency scales quadratically with batch size, whereas Decode latency is strictly independent of sequence length and KV-cache size.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Prefill handles the whole prompt together, so it uses larger parallel matrix operations and typically has higher arithmetic intensity than decode. Decode then generates output step by step, and at low batch sizes often becomes limited by repeatedly moving model weights and KV state through memory rather than by raw compute. The autoregressive behavior belongs to decode, not prefill. Both phases usually run on the accelerator, and TTFT includes more than just the prefill kernel time in a full serving path.

Calculate the total memory footprint (in bytes) required to store the KV cache for a batch of \(B = 16\) requests, each with an active context length of \(S = 2\text{,}048\) tokens, for a model with \(L = 32\) transformer layers, \(H_{\text{kv}} = 8\) key-value attention heads (Grouped-Query Attention), head dimension \(D_{\text{head}} = 128\), stored in FP16 precision (\(P = 2\text{ bytes}\)).

Substituting gives \(2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 \times 2048 \times 16 = 4{,}294{,}967{,}296\) bytes. That is exactly \(4\ \text{GiB}\), or about \(4.295\ \text{GB}\) in decimal units. This is the KV-cache payload only; allocator overhead and runtime workspace would add more memory in a real serving system.

**Order the step-by-step execution cycle of Speculative Decoding for accelerating LLM inference:


Target model runs a single parallel forward pass over the draft candidate tokens to compute verification logits
Draft model (a lightweight autoregressive model) generates \(K\) candidate tokens sequentially
Engine appends the accepted tokens to the KV cache and advances the generation context
Verification logic compares the draft tokens with the target model’s verification results and accepts a prefix of them**

Answer: The correct order is: (2) Draft model (a lightweight autoregressive model) generates \(K\) candidate tokens sequentially, (1) Target model runs a single parallel forward pass over the draft candidate tokens to compute verification logits, (4) Verification logic compares the draft tokens with the target model’s verification results and accepts a prefix of them, (3) Engine appends the accepted tokens to the KV cache and advances the generation context. The sequence matters because the target model cannot verify tokens before the draft proposes them, and the engine should not advance the live context until verification decides which proposed tokens are accepted. Swapping verification and context advancement would commit unverified state and break correctness.
Learning Objective: Sequence the high-level workflow of speculative decoding from draft generation through verification and context update.

True or False: Speculative decoding speeds up serving regardless of draft-model quality, because the target model always verifies multiple tokens in parallel.
Answer: False. Speculative decoding helps only when the draft model is cheap enough and its proposed tokens are accepted often enough to offset the extra draft-and-verify work. If acceptance is low, the system can spend more time running two models than it saves through parallel verification.
Learning Objective: Evaluate how draft-model cost and acceptance rate determine whether speculative decoding improves LLM serving performance.
In a multi-turn conversational AI system with extensive system prompts (e.g., 2,000 tokens of instructions and few-shot examples shared across thousands of user sessions), what serving optimization eliminates redundant prefill compute across requests?

Linear Attention Approximation, which drops system prompt tokens entirely from the attention window.
Static Graph Compilation, which hardcodes user inputs directly into the weight tensors.
Prefix Caching (e.g., RadixAttention), which stores the KV-cache states of common prompt prefixes in memory and reuses them across queries matching the prefix.
Speculative Quantization, which quantizes prompt tokens into 1-bit binary representations during the decode phase.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Prefix caching stores KV states for a compatible shared prefix so later requests with that same prefix can reuse the prefill result instead of recomputing it. This can cut TTFT substantially for the cached portion, though any uncached suffix still has to be processed normally. Dropping prompt tokens changes model behavior, static graph compilation does not reuse dynamic KV state, and 1-bit prompt quantization is not the mechanism described here.
Learning Objective: Apply prefix caching to reduce repeated prefill work for shared prompt prefixes in conversational serving.
Contrast traditional request-level dynamic batching with iteration-level continuous batching (as introduced in Orca and vLLM) for Large Language Model (LLM) serving. Why is request-level batching severely inefficient for autoregressive generation?
Answer: In request-level batching, batch membership stays fixed while requests decode, so short generations that finish early cannot immediately free their slots for unrelated waiting work. In continuous batching, the scheduler can admit or remove sequences at iteration boundaries, which uses capacity more efficiently when output lengths vary. For example, if one reply ends after 20 tokens while another runs for 500, a fixed request-level batch leaves part of the batch underused until the long sequence advances far enough. The practical consequence is lower throughput and longer waits for queued requests unless the runtime can reschedule state across iterations.
Learning Objective: Compare request-level dynamic batching with iteration-level continuous batching for autoregressive LLM serving and explain why variable output lengths make fixed batch membership inefficient.
True or False: PagedAttention resolves the primary memory waste in LLM KV-caching by allocating key and value states in non-contiguous, fixed-size physical memory blocks managed via a virtual page table, eliminating both internal fragmentation from over-allocation and external memory fragmentation.
Answer: False. PagedAttention removes the need for one large contiguous KV-cache allocation and greatly reduces external fragmentation, but it does not eliminate internal waste entirely: each sequence can still leave one partially filled final block. Its benefit is reducing fragmentation enough to raise usable concurrency, not making memory waste literally zero.
Learning Objective: Explain how PagedAttention reduces KV-cache fragmentation and identify the remaining source of memory waste.

Provisioning 16 to 20 replicas is an illustrative way to preserve headroom so the system can keep meeting its latency target when real conditions deviate from the forecast. For example, if one zone loses capacity or traffic spikes above the expected peak, the extra replicas absorb the shock instead of pushing every remaining node immediately to its limit. The practical consequence is that capacity planning is a resilience decision, not just a division problem.
Learning Objective: Justify why mission-critical serving clusters provision reserve capacity beyond forecast peak demand.
True or False: For an 8-billion-parameter LLM with 32 layers, 8 KV heads, and head dimension 128, deployed in FP16 precision with a 16 GB weight footprint on an 80 GB GPU, serving long-context requests with batch size \(B = 8\) and context length \(S = 32\text{,}768\) tokens causes the KV cache to exceed the static weight footprint of the model itself.
Answer: True. For this specific architecture, each token per sequence needs \(2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131{,}072\) bytes, which is \(128\ \text{KiB}\), to store both Keys and Values in FP16. At \(B = 8\) and \(S = 32{,}768\), the KV-cache payload is \(131{,}072 \times 32{,}768 \times 8 = 34{,}359{,}738{,}368\) bytes, which is \(32\ \text{GiB}\) or about \(34.36\ \text{GB}\) in decimal units. That exceeds the 16 GB weight footprint, showing how long contexts can make dynamic KV memory dominate static weights.
Learning Objective: Compare dynamic KV-cache growth against static model weights for a specified LLM architecture, batch size, and context length.
An engineer serves an 8-billion parameter LLM on a GPU with 2 TB/s of High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) bandwidth. Assume the model weights are 16 GB in FP16, the decode step effectively streams those 16 GB of weights from HBM each token at batch size \(B = 1\), and ignore KV-cache traffic and compute time. What is the theoretical hardware-bandwidth lower bound on Time Per Output Token (TPOT)?

\(8.0\text{ ms}\) (\(\text{TPOT} = 16\text{ GB} / 2\text{,}000\text{ GB/s}\))
\(0.8\text{ ms}\) (\(\text{TPOT} = 1.6\text{ GB} / 2\text{,}000\text{ GB/s}\))
\(80.0\text{ ms}\) (\(\text{TPOT} = 160\text{ GB} / 2\text{,}000\text{ GB/s}\))
\(0.08\text{ ms}\) (\(\text{TPOT} = 16\text{ MB} / 2\text{,}000\text{ GB/s}\))

Answer: The correct answer is A. Under the stated assumption that one decode step streams 16 GB of weights from HBM and the device provides an idealized 2 TB/s = 2,000 GB/s of bandwidth, the transfer-time floor is \(16\text{ GB} / 2{,}000\text{ GB/s} = 0.008\text{ s} = 8.0\text{ ms}\). That makes 8 ms a lower bound from weight movement alone in this simplified case. The smaller and larger numbers come from unit or arithmetic mistakes, and the setup intentionally ignores KV-cache traffic, compute, and other overheads.
Learning Objective: Calculate a bandwidth-only lower bound on LLM decode TPOT from model size and HBM bandwidth.
When LLM decode at small batch sizes is dominated by moving model weights rather than by arithmetic throughput, why can INT4 weight-only quantization (e.g., AWQ or GPTQ) reduce Time Per Output Token (TPOT), and what limits the gain even if INT4 compute kernels provide no higher FLOP/s than FP16 Tensor Cores?
Answer: At small batch sizes, decode is often dominated by moving model weights rather than by raw arithmetic throughput. Weight-only INT4 quantization cuts the raw weight payload by about \(4\times\) relative to FP16, so the memory system has fewer bytes to fetch each decode step even if the math units themselves are not any faster. For an 8B model, that can mean reading something closer to 4 GB of quantized weights instead of 16 GB of FP16 weights per step, excluding metadata and dequantization overhead. The practical consequence is lower TPOT when weight traffic is the bottleneck, although the realized gain is usually less than \(4\times\) once KV traffic, dequantization, launch overhead, and kernel details are included.
Learning Objective: Explain why weight-only quantization can speed up memory-bound LLM decode even without increasing raw compute throughput.

Self-Check: Answer

A team attempts to maximize hardware cost efficiency by targeting 95% steady-state utilization \(\rho\) across their production serving queue. Why is this strategy a dangerous engineering pitfall?

High utilization permanently erases model weights from GPU memory registers.
In stochastic serving systems, queue waiting times grow asymptotically toward infinity as utilization approaches 100%, causing minor traffic fluctuations to trigger massive tail-latency spikes and widespread SLO breaches.
Running above 90% utilization forces the operating system to switch from 64-bit to 32-bit execution mode.
Modern GPUs automatically shut down power when utilization exceeds 80% for more than 10 seconds.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Here \(\rho\) means arrival rate divided by service capacity in the serving queue, not a coarse GPU busy counter. In queueing models, waiting time grows sharply as \(\rho\) approaches 1, so a system run near 95% has very little headroom for burstiness or service-time variation. That makes p99 latency fragile even if average load looks efficient. The other answers invent hardware or OS behaviors unrelated to the chapter’s queueing argument.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why operating a serving queue near saturation creates tail-latency risk even when average utilization looks cost-efficient.
True or False: Evaluating an online serving system using mean (average) latency is sufficient for capacity planning, because if the average latency is well below the SLA target, user-facing requests are guaranteed to experience good performance.
Answer: False. Average latency conceals extreme tail outliers (p95, p99, p99.9) where requests experience severe queueing delays. In modern microservice architectures where a user query fans out to dozens of downstream models in parallel, the slowest component determines overall user latency, meaning a low average latency can co-exist with a large fraction of users experiencing SLA violations.
Learning Objective: Justify why tail-latency metrics (p99/p99.9) must be used over mean latency for evaluating online serving systems.
Why is the assumption that ‘cold-start latency only affects the very first request’ a critical fallacy in autoscaling serverless or Kubernetes-based serving environments with bursty traffic?
Answer: During a burst, new replicas may spend time loading weights, initializing runtimes, or warming caches before they can accept traffic, so cold start reduces usable capacity exactly when demand is rising. Requests usually are not sent to replicas that are still unready, but they still suffer indirectly by waiting longer on the already-live replicas or in upstream queues. For example, if traffic doubles before new GPU pods finish becoming ready, p99 latency can spike across many users even though no request is intentionally routed to an uninitialized instance. The practical consequence is that cold start is a fleet-level capacity problem, not just a first-request problem.
Learning Objective: Analyze how cold-start delays amplify tail latency during autoscaling events by withholding new capacity during bursts.
An engineering team increases the dynamic batch size on their vision model serving nodes from 8 to 64. Offline peak throughput doubles, and production traces show batch-formation wait time grew sharply after the change. User-facing p99 latency violations then increase by 40%. What fallacy explains this outcome?

Model weights become corrupted when executed with batch sizes greater than 16.
GPU Tensor Cores disable INT8 acceleration when batch size exceeds 32.
High batch sizes reduce arithmetic intensity on the GPU Roofline model.
The fallacy that larger serving batches always improve throughput without affecting latency; early-arriving requests can spend too much of the latency budget waiting in the batcher before execution.

Answer: The correct answer is D. The added trace detail matters: if batch-formation wait rose sharply, the doubled offline throughput did not come for free in the online path. Larger batches can improve hardware efficiency, but they also make early arrivals wait longer before execution, and that extra waiting can dominate p99 latency even when the per-batch compute is efficient. The corruption, universal Tensor Core cutoff, and reduced-arithmetic-intensity explanations do not match the serving mechanism described here.
Learning Objective: Evaluate how batch-formation delay can turn an offline throughput win into an online p99 latency regression.
Describe the pitfall of ‘Calibrating quantized models with unrepresentative data,’ and explain how it can lead to silent production failure despite passing offline validation checks.
Answer: PTQ calibration chooses quantization ranges from the activation statistics seen in the calibration set. If that data is cleaner or from a different domain than production traffic, the resulting scales may clip important live activations or represent them too coarsely, degrading prediction quality without causing crashes or latency alarms. The failure can stay hidden if offline validation used similarly unrepresentative data, because both calibration and evaluation would miss the same production patterns. The practical consequence is that quantized models need calibration and quality checks on data that matches the real serving distribution as closely as possible.
Learning Objective: Explain how unrepresentative calibration and evaluation data can hide quantization-induced production accuracy failures.

Self-Check: Answer

Which core architectural takeaway summarizes the fundamental difference between machine learning model training and online production model serving?

Training optimizes single-query tail latency under fixed memory bounds, whereas serving optimizes long-run epoch throughput across distributed cluster networks.
Training requires specialized graph compilers and quantization, whereas serving relies exclusively on uncompiled Python eager execution.
Training is time-to-quality optimization over long data runs, whereas online serving is latency-constrained economics that allocates a per-request time budget across the entire pipeline and reserves headroom against nonlinear queueing collapse.
Training runs on integer-only microcontrollers, whereas serving runs exclusively on floating-point supercomputers.

Answer: The correct answer is C. The chapter’s serving inversion is that training usually optimizes throughput over long runs, while online serving must satisfy per-request latency targets under variable demand. Serving therefore budgets time across ingress, preprocessing, queueing, model execution, and response handling, while preserving headroom so queueing delay does not explode near saturation. The other choices either reverse the roles, invent exclusivity around toolchains, or make absurd hardware claims.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the chapter’s serving inversion: throughput-oriented training versus latency-budgeted production serving.
True or False: In a fixed serial production-serving pipeline, if upstream preprocessing, transport serialization, and downstream postprocessing remain unchanged and there is no queueing feedback effect, optimizing only the neural network accelerator kernel execution time yields diminishing returns.
Answer: True. In a fixed end-to-end request path, speeding up only the model leaves the other stages unchanged, so they consume a larger share of total latency and limit further gains. This is the serving version of Amdahl’s law: once inference shrinks, preprocessing, serialization, queueing, or postprocessing can become the dominant bottleneck.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why end-to-end serving performance depends on the whole request path, not just accelerator kernel time.
Summarize how memory management—specifically KV-cache allocation, paging, and precision—can constrain throughput and concurrency in Large Language Model (LLM) serving.
Answer: LLM serving is constrained by both memory bandwidth and memory capacity: low-batch decode often spends much of its time moving weights and KV state, while the KV cache also grows linearly with context length and concurrent requests until it limits how many sessions fit on the GPU. Paging schemes such as PagedAttention reduce fragmentation and let the runtime use that capacity more effectively, while lower-precision weights or KV representations reduce raw bytes moved or stored. For example, a large context with many active sessions can hit the KV-capacity limit long before compute saturates, forcing smaller batches or shorter contexts. The practical consequence is that serving throughput depends as much on memory layout and byte volume as on peak compute throughput.
Learning Objective: Explain how memory bandwidth, KV-cache capacity, paging, and precision jointly constrain LLM serving throughput and concurrency.

title: Model Serving
text:
Architecture stack focus for this chapter.
Why does serving change the optimization priorities that made training successful?
Training and serving pursue fundamentally opposing operating objectives. Training maximizes aggregate throughput across homogeneous, scheduled batches and extended runs, whereas serving must evaluate individual, heterogeneous requests under strict latency deadlines. Training amortizes hardware initialization and weight streaming across millions of examples; serving pays a distinct tax on every incoming query, where microsecond-level inefficiencies accumulate into operational liabilities. A system processing one billion requests daily converts a single millisecond saved per transaction into more than eleven days of recovered machine time every twenty-four hours.
This operational divergence explains why architectures that train efficiently often falter in production. An online serving system operates within an uncompromising end-to-end latency budget. Delays in network ingress, serialization, input preprocessing, queueing, and response postprocessing directly diminish the execution window allocated to the model itself. When non-inference stages consume the bulk of the budget, aggressive kernel optimizations yield negligible improvement to the user. Furthermore, a prediction that arrives after an interactive client has timed out possesses zero utility, regardless of its mathematical accuracy.
Serving is therefore more than an isolated latency challenge; it is a systems capacity problem under stochastic, uncontrolled traffic. Request arrival rates oscillate between diurnal peaks and troughs, forcing systems to preserve operational headroom for sudden demand surges and hardware failures. Capacity provisioned solely for average load collapses under peak traffic, whereas capacity provisioned for peak demand sits idle and costly throughout off-peak hours. Evaluating an ML model ultimately moves beyond whether it computes correct outputs in isolation to whether it sustains reliable, low-latency execution under production variability. In D·A·M terms, serving is where the trained algorithm meets unpredictable live data within the machine’s strict latency budget, causing all three constraints to bind simultaneously on every incoming request.

Learning Objectives

Explain serving inversion from training throughput to per-request latency, headroom, and tail behavior
Decompose request latency across serialization, preprocessing, inference, queuing, postprocessing, and network overhead
Apply queueing laws and simple queue models to plan capacity against percentile latency targets
Diagnose training-serving skew and cold starts from mismatched preprocessing, model loading, or cache behavior
Select batching, load shedding, autoscaling, and runtime strategies for traffic patterns and latency budgets
Evaluate LLM serving bottlenecks using token latency, KV-cache memory, and continuous batching constraints
Calculate cost per inference from precision, hardware utilization, replica count, and runtime throughput

title: Model Serving
text:
In a benchmark run, a load generator decides when each request arrives. Production traffic has no such scheduler. Model serving must sustain the operating targets that benchmarking evaluated under specified conditions while live traffic tests that operating envelope continuously, so measurement remains part of the service’s lifecycle. In offline training, systems maximize aggregate throughput by packing large batches to amortize weight transfers from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and saturate matrix arithmetic units. In online serving, requests arrive stochastically from independent clients and must return within strict service-level objectives (SLOs). The primary engineering priority therefore inverts from long-run throughput to per-request latency. This serving inversion restructures the balance of terms in the iron law of ML systems (\(\Time = \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency\)). When an application cannot delay requests to assemble large batches, it must process small batches or individual inputs (\(\BatchSize=1\)). For weight-dominated operations, small batches reduce arithmetic intensity and can shift execution from compute-bound matrix multiplications toward memory-bandwidth-bound transfers (\(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\)). Simultaneously, the latency term \(\Latency\) expands beyond microsecond accelerator kernel launches to include network transit, request serialization, and host orchestration, often becoming the binding constraint on end-to-end response time.


↩︎ The additive and pipelined formulations of the iron law of ML systems are established in Iron Law of ML Systems.
The D·A·M taxonomy clarifies how this inversion reshapes each layer of the system. In the data layer, the constraint shifts from total dataset volume to the arrival rate, payload freshness, and variable sequence dimensions of live queries. In the algorithm layer, execution becomes strictly forward-only: backpropagation state and optimizer memory vanish from the accelerator, but dynamic input shapes introduce runtime execution variability into previously static operator graphs. In the machine layer, the operating target shifts from maximum hardware utilization to headroom. While offline training treats an idle accelerator as wasted capital, online serving treats near-saturation as an operational hazard. Because request arrivals follow stochastic distributions, queue lengths and waiting times diverge nonlinearly as utilization approaches 100 percent. Maintaining adequate headroom preserves the spare capacity needed to absorb transient traffic spikes without violating tail-latency percentiles. Serving therefore optimizes completed requests under a strict latency deadline rather than steady-state hardware occupancy.
Meeting that latency deadline governs how engineering teams partition the end-to-end serving stack. A request’s latency budget encompasses three sequential stages: host-side ingress and preprocessing (network termination, payload deserialization, and tokenization or feature transformation), accelerator kernel execution, and downstream postprocessing. Any millisecond consumed by unoptimized feature retrieval or queueing delays directly subtracts from the execution time allocated to the neural network itself. Consequently, the central engineering task in model serving is deciding which operations must remain on the synchronous request path, which tasks can be offloaded to asynchronous background pipelines, and how much headroom the system must reserve before tail-latency guarantees collapse under load.

Self-Check: Question

When transitioning a deep learning model from training to an online serving environment, how does the system constraint in the D·A·M (Data-Algorithm-Machine) taxonomy fundamentally shift regarding machine utilization and algorithm state?

Machine utilization must be maximized at 100% to amortize capital costs, while the algorithm continues parameter backpropagation during request serving.
Machine capacity must maintain operational headroom below saturation to prevent tail-latency queueing collapse, while the algorithm’s weights remain fixed for a deployed version.
Machine allocation switches from accelerators to general-purpose CPUs exclusively, while the algorithm dynamically modifies its architecture per incoming user payload.
Machine throughput replaces latency as the primary operational constraint, while data volume shifts from live request streams to historical offline batches.

True or False: In online model serving, the latency term (\(L_{\text{lat}}\)) in the iron law of ML systems must encompass external factors such as network round-trip time, request serialization, and system orchestration, rather than solely the accelerator kernel execution time.
Explain why achieving high average throughput during offline benchmarking does not guarantee that an online serving system will satisfy its tail-latency Service-Level Objective (SLO) during production traffic spikes.
