Streaming traffic correlates arrivals through sensor synchronization, making batch size and deadline externally fixed. At the opposite end of the spectrum, interactive mobile and edge applications process one request stream at a time, leaving no opportunity to batch independent queries. The MLPerf SingleStream scenario captures this sequential-serving shape. Here, the optimization target shifts from a synchronization budget under a frame deadline to per-request latency and energy consumption under a rigid thermal envelope. For the smartphone vision pipeline modeled below, the primary engineering objective is not batch formation, but minimizing per-phase latency and energy dissipation.



Cloud services often emphasize fleet cost and latency; mobile serving adds three closely coupled constraints. The first is an energy budget that throughput alone does not capture, because each inference consumes battery. In the modeled pipeline, 2.98 mJ at 22 FPS draws about 66 mW for the inference path alone, before camera, display, ISP, and OS overhead add to that total in a full photo app. Thermal throttling can compound this limit when sustained system power reaches a device-specific thermal boundary. Memory constraints close the set because the model shares RAM with the application and operating system. Reload time depends on device storage, runtime, and model state; quantization and memory-mapped loading (section 1.6.3) can reduce footprint and startup work but do not eliminate those dependencies.

The contrast is workload- and hardware-specific, but it shows why a mobile accelerator designed for single-stream execution can operate efficiently without the batches used to amortize a large server GPU.


These physical constraints make edge serving optimization fundamentally different from data-center optimization. Rather than maximizing aggregate batch throughput, the objective is to sustain real-time execution within a tight thermal and battery envelope without triggering hardware throttling or starving foreground applications of system memory.



Traffic-adaptive batching adjusts the batching window as queue depth and request rate change. Table 17 relates the four MLPerf scenarios to representative deployment contexts and common batching strategies.
These scenarios are benchmark abstractions rather than deployment prescriptions. The operative batching policy must still follow the service’s current concurrency, deadline, and power constraints.

The examples developed here (cloud API traffic under the Server scenario, grouped sensor inputs motivated by MultiStream, and throughput-dominated pipelines under Offline inference) all decide how requests share the accelerator. None of them decides how efficiently the accelerator executes each batch once it forms. The same batch of the same model can run several times faster or slower depending on the engine that compiles and schedules its kernels and on the number format it computes in, and those choices are the next lever.

Checkpoint 13.3: Batching and traffic patterns
Batching is the primary lever for serving economics, but the optimal strategy depends on context.

Throughput-latency trade-off: Explain why batch size 32 achieves 6\(\times\) higher throughput than batch size 1, yet a production system with a 20 ms SLO might still choose batch size 8.
Wait vs. compute: Given an end-to-end latency budget, can you separate batch formation, waiting for an available worker, and batch service time \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\)? Which wait does a batching timeout control?
Dynamic vs. static batching: Describe why static batching fails under variable traffic arrival rates, and how dynamic batching with an adaptive time window resolves queue starvation.
Traffic pattern matching: Map deployment scenarios (cloud API, autonomous vehicle, mobile edge) to corresponding MLPerf scenarios, identifying the batching strategy suited to each operational constraint.
Adaptive windows: For a desired expected batch count, explain why higher traffic permits a shorter formation window. How would you check whether the realized batches can keep up with arrivals, and what must a load test verify before accepting the configuration?
When not to batch: Name a latency target, runtime limitation, or memory condition under which a batching window of zero is the right configuration.




Self-Check: Question

Why can increasing batch size during deep learning inference improve hardware throughput on modern GPUs for weight-streaming workloads, and when does that improvement stop paying off on a Roofline model?

Batching converts all floating-point operations into integer bitshifts, bypassing GPU ALUs entirely.
Batching reduces the total parameter count of the neural network by sharing weights across batch samples.
Batching eliminates PCIe bus data transfer overhead by generating synthetic input tensors on the device.
Batching increases arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte of memory accessed) by reusing loaded weight matrices across multiple input samples, shifting the workload toward the compute ceiling until another limit or saturation is reached.

What is the operational impact on latency and batch efficiency?

Requests are automatically dropped because the queue fails to reach the maximum batch size of 32 within 50 ms.

title: Model Serving
text:
Dynamic batching and request scheduling dictate how inferences are grouped and queued, but an underlying execution engine must evaluate the resulting tensor operations on physical hardware. The latency budgets established in section 1.4.1 and the batching gains of section 1.7 are achievable only if the runtime maps operations efficiently to accelerator execution units and memory hierarchies. The inference runtime, the software layer that orchestrates tensor operations and manages hardware resources, can materially change latency and throughput for an unchanged model architecture. Runtime engineering consists of two phases: selection chooses the execution engine, and configuration tunes that engine for the target model, hardware, input shapes, and latency distribution.


Engine selection begins with the binding system constraint rather than the framework used during training. When deployment velocity and framework compatibility dominate, PyTorch and TensorFlow models can serve directly through their native runtimes without an intermediate compilation pass. This preserves support for dynamic Python control flow and custom training operators, though Python interpreter overhead, Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) contention, and non-contiguous memory allocations can restrict production throughput. To alleviate interpreter overhead while maintaining framework compatibility, serialized graph representations—such as torch.export and TensorFlow SavedModel (with TorchScript supporting legacy deployments)—capture deterministic operator graphs for ahead-of-time graph optimization and multi-threaded C++ runtime execution. Nevertheless, framework-native runtimes prioritize developer expressiveness and broad operator coverage, whereas specialized inference engines trade that generality for targeted graph transformations and reduced execution overhead.


When cross-hardware portability is the binding constraint, ONNX Runtime22 provides an intermediate, hardware-agnostic execution layer (Microsoft 2024). Models export to the ONNX format, after which ONNX Runtime applies target-independent graph optimizations and delegates subgraphs to hardware-specific execution providers. This architecture enables single-format deployment across CPUs, GPUs, and custom accelerator application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs).
22 ONNX Runtime: Microsoft’s inference engine acts as a hardware abstraction layer: the same ONNX model can run on CPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, or custom accelerators through pluggable execution providers. ONNX Runtime applies graph optimizations such as constant folding, redundant-node elimination, and kernel fusion. Performance relative to a tuned target-specific engine such as TensorRT depends on the workload, execution provider, and hardware.
Microsoft. 2024. ONNX Runtime: Cross-Platform Inference and Training Machine-Learning Accelerator. GitHub.
Portability still demands profiling operator placement across execution boundaries. If an operation is unsupported by the preferred execution provider, placement depends on the configured provider order and available implementations. A CPU fallback can introduce host-accelerator transfers and synchronization that erode the expected latency advantage; if no provider supports the operation, execution may fail. Profiling must therefore verify provider assignment and operator coverage across the entire graph, not merely confirm that the exported artifact executes without errors.



When latency budgets or serving costs bind more tightly than portability, specialized engines such as TensorRT23 for NVIDIA GPUs and OpenVINO24 for Intel hardware optimize graphs specifically for target microarchitectures (NVIDIA 2024a; Intel Corporation 2026; Chen et al. 2018). Rather than maintaining portable abstractions, these compilers specialize kernels directly to the hardware’s register files, cache hierarchies, and matrix execution units.
23 TensorRT: An NVIDIA inference compiler and runtime that optimizes models ahead of time for a specific microarchitecture (such as Hopper or Blackwell) (NVIDIA 2024a). Requiring a target-specific build phase allows the compiler to generate fused kernels, select microarchitecture-specific Tensor Core execution paths, and optimize memory layouts (such as NC/32HW32). The resulting nonportable engine reduces per-request execution latency and minimizes the accelerator count needed to satisfy a target throughput.
NVIDIA. 2024a. NVIDIA TensorRT: Programmable Inference Accelerator.
24 OpenVINO (open visual inference and neural network optimization): An Intel-oriented inference toolkit that converts, optimizes, and runs models across Intel CPU, GPU, and NPU targets (Intel Corporation 2026). Specializing for direct hardware execution departs from the portable execution guarantees of general-purpose frameworks, enabling the compiler to emit architecture-tuned vector instructions (such as AVX-512 or AMX) and exploit low-precision integer execution units. While speedups depend on the specific operator mix and target processor, this specialization can make CPU or edge serving economically viable for latency-sensitive models.
Intel Corporation. 2026. OpenVINO Documentation.

Chen, Tianqi, Thierry Moreau, Ziheng Jiang, Lianmin Zheng, Eddie Q. Yan, Haichen Shen, Meghan Cowan, et al. 2018. “TVM: An Automated End-to-End Optimizing Compiler for Deep Learning.” Proceedings of the 13th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI ’18), 578–94.
25 Layer fusion: Analogous to loop fusion in compiler optimization, where adjacent loops over the same array are combined to reduce memory traffic. Kernel fusion applies the same principle to GPU operations: sequential kernels that write and re-read intermediate tensors from HBM are merged into a single kernel that can keep data in registers.Layer fusion25 is kernel fusion (also called operator fusion) applied when the engine is built. For the convolution \(\to\) batch normalization \(\to\) ReLU block fused in Kernel fusion, the serving compiler performs that folding once, at engine build time, because batch normalization is a fixed affine transform once training ends. It first folds the linear batch normalization parameters directly into the convolution weights and bias (\(\FusedConvolutionWeight = \frac{\NormalizationScaleVector}{\BatchNormRunningStandardDeviation} \WeightMatrix\) and \(\FusedConvolutionBias = \frac{\NormalizationScaleVector}{\BatchNormRunningStandardDeviation}(\BiasVector- \BatchNormRunningMean) + \NormalizationShiftVector\), where \(\BatchNormRunningMean\) is the per-channel running mean and \(\BatchNormRunningStandardDeviation\) denotes the square root of the sum of running variance and the numerical stabilizer used at inference and \(\NormalizationScaleVector\) and \(\NormalizationShiftVector\) are the learned scale and shift), eliminating the normalization operation entirely. The compiler then fuses the convolution and the subsequent ReLU into a single kernel: thread blocks read the input feature map from HBM once, compute matrix multiply-accumulate operations in registers and shared memory, evaluate the ReLU activation directly in registers, and write only the final activated result back to HBM.


↩︎ Kernel fusion, which merges adjacent operations so intermediates stay in registers and on-chip memory instead of round-tripping through HBM, is established in Why execution strategy matters: The memory wall.
Kernel auto-tuning benchmarks and selects the optimal algorithm for each operation on the target microarchitecture. A single 2D convolution can be evaluated through direct convolution, GEMM transformation (im2col), Winograd minimal filtering (efficient for small \(3 \times 3\) filters), or Fast Fourier Transforms (efficient for large spatial filters), alongside dozens of tile-size variations. Because the winning strategy depends on filter dimensions, batch size, and the accelerator’s register and shared memory capacity, the compiler benchmarks candidate implementations against target hardware and caches the lowest-latency kernel, trading ahead-of-time compilation time for predictable serving latency.
These optimizations produce substantial speedups over an untuned framework-native baseline, but they require explicit graph compilation and may restrict dynamic tensor dimensions. The illustrative runtime comparison that follows quantifies one such optimization spectrum.

This optimization-compatibility trade-off governs engine selection. Higher specialization can improve hardware efficiency for supported operations and shapes but increases deployment complexity, restricts dynamic control flow, and may introduce numerical deviations from the training baseline. The engineering choice depends on latency budgets, operational constraints, and how frequently model architectures evolve.
Once an execution engine is selected, configuration tunes its resource allocation to the hardware envelope. For CPU inference, thread pool sizing must match physical core topologies: undersubscription leaves execution units idle, while oversubscription induces CPU cache thrashing, OS scheduling latency, and lock contention across non-uniform memory access (NUMA) domains. For accelerators, static memory preallocation creates fixed-size activation workspaces during initialization, eliminating runtime memory allocations (cudaMalloc) and page-table faults from the latency-critical request path. Execution provider priority determines which hardware backend handles each operator subgraph, while graph optimization levels balance build times against constant folding and algebraic simplification. Production deployments must benchmark these configurations across full latency distributions (p50, p99) rather than relying on framework defaults.




On NVIDIA V100 GPUs, Tensor Cores accelerate FP16 matrix operations, whereas INT8 computations execute on standard integer ALUs (via DP4A vector instructions). In an illustrative serving scenario, transitioning a ResNet-50 model from FP32 to INT8 triples inference throughput while sacrificing less than 0.4 percentage points of top-1 accuracy. This dynamic establishes a direct coupling between numerical precision and infrastructure economics. At the serving layer, precision engineering introduces operational constraints: calibration data fidelity, layer sensitivity under live inputs, and dynamic precision dispatch.


↩︎ The quantization techniques this selection draws on, from numerical formats through calibration and quantization-aware training, are established in Quantization and Precision.


For memory-bandwidth-bound operations, reducing precision raises throughput by cutting the byte volume transferred across the memory bus. Equation 15 gives the bandwidth-only upper bound from precision reduction: \[
\frac{\text{Throughput}_{\text{INT8}}}{\text{Throughput}_{\text{FP32}}} = \frac{32}{8} = 4\times \text{ (theoretical maximum)}
\tag{15}\]
Actual speedup depends on the compute-to-memory ratio, operator mix, hardware instruction throughput, and matrix alignment, falling below the bandwidth-only bound whenever arithmetic throughput or memory alignment binds. Low-precision kernels achieve peak arithmetic efficiency only when matrix dimensions align with the accelerator’s warp-level execution tiles (for example, multiples of 8 or 16 elements). When dimensions do not align with hardware tiles, libraries such as cuBLAS and cuDNN pad tensors or fall back to slower execution paths. The precision trade-offs for a standard vision model illustrate how these theoretical limits manifest in practice.


↩︎ Tensor Core tile architectures and their matrix-dimension alignment constraints are established in Tensor Cores.

INT8 operations achieve their speedup by using DP4A vector single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) instructions on the standard integer CUDA cores, hence Tensor Core utilization is marked N/A. Precision selection is constrained by layer sensitivity, calibration data, and runtime policy. Not all layers tolerate reduced precision equally. The uniform quantizer of Quantization and Precision bounds the error each layer must absorb. For a scalar uniform \(\QuantizationBitWidth\)-bit quantizer over the calibrated range \([\ClippingRangeLowerBound,\ClippingRangeUpperBound]\), the step size (scale) \(\QuantizationScale\) and within-range rounding-error bound in equation 16 are \[\QuantizationScale= \frac{\ClippingRangeUpperBound-\ClippingRangeLowerBound}{2^\QuantizationBitWidth-1}, \qquad |\QuantizationRoundingError| \leq \frac{\QuantizationScale}{2} \tag{16}\] for values that are not clipped. Values outside the calibrated range are clipped and incur additional saturation error. Layer-level output or task error depends on activation distributions and downstream sensitivity, so it must be measured rather than inferred from a universal norm law. This mechanism explains why first convolutional and final classification layers are commonly retained at FP16, while intermediate layers tolerate INT8. Initial layers process low-dimensional raw inputs (such as 3 RGB channels) before representations expand into overcomplete feature spaces that can absorb quantization noise, whereas final classification layers produce raw logits where small numerical perturbations directly shift decision boundaries and alter top-\(1\) predictions.
Post-training quantization adds a data dependency. The calibration dataset determines the clipping thresholds \([\ClippingRangeLowerBound, \ClippingRangeUpperBound]\) and scale factors \(\QuantizationScale\) used for INT8 conversion, requiring it to match the statistical profile of live serving traffic rather than arbitrary training or validation splits. A calibration-serving distribution mismatch causes excessive clipping or underflow, degrading end-to-end task accuracy, an operational pitfall analyzed in section 1.12.
Production serving architectures can elevate precision from a static compilation setting into a dynamic runtime policy. When request queues are shallow and the system operates with ample latency headroom against its service level objective (SLO), the engine can dispatch requests at FP16 to maximize task accuracy. During traffic spikes that threaten queue saturation, the engine can dynamically downcast execution to INT8 to preserve latency bounds. Similarly, requests that yield low classification confidence under INT8 can be selectively re-evaluated at FP16. This dynamic dispatch operationalizes adaptive quality-latency trade-offs under fluctuating request arrival rates.
Precision selection carries direct infrastructure sizing consequences: under an illustrative \(3\times\) saturated-throughput improvement, 10 GPUs at INT8 offer the same aggregate saturated capacity as 30 GPUs at FP32. Equal capacity does not establish equal queueing latency; service-time distributions, batching policy, and failure reserve must still satisfy the same SLO. Precision engineering is therefore an infrastructure sizing discipline, directly coupling numerical representation to cluster capital expense and energy consumption. Yet configuring the runtime and numerical bit width addresses only the model level; achieving low-latency serving in production requires optimizing the host-to-device boundaries within the physical server node itself.

Self-Check: Question

An ML systems team is deploying a transformer-based ranking model on NVIDIA data center GPUs. They consider running the raw PyTorch model in eager Python mode versus compiling the model into an optimized NVIDIA TensorRT engine. Which graph-level serving optimization is TensorRT designed to apply more aggressively than an unoptimized eager execution path?

TensorRT automatically converts the supervised classification task into an unsupervised reinforcement learning policy.
TensorRT trains additional adapter layers during live request serving to adapt to data drift.
TensorRT eliminates all GPU memory usage by running inferences exclusively in the CPU instruction cache.
TensorRT performs aggressive vertical and horizontal operator fusion (e.g., combining Conv/MatMul, BiasAdd, and Activation into a single kernel), reduces redundant memory round-trips, and selects hardware-tuned kernels.

Why can quantizing a model’s weights and activations from FP16 to INT8 for GPU serving increase throughput, what limits the gain, and what role does Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) calibration play in preserving accuracy?
True or False: In deep neural network quantization, when sensitivity evaluation identifies particular layers as unusually vulnerable to precision loss, preserving those layers in FP16/FP32 while quantizing the remaining bulk layers to INT8/INT4 can preserve model accuracy in mixed-precision serving.
When deploying models to edge devices with Apple Silicon (such as iPhones and iPads), developers export models to the ____ framework to take full advantage of the dedicated Apple Neural Engine (ANE) hardware accelerator.
When calibrating an INT8 quantized model using Post-Training Quantization (PTQ), what is the primary danger of using a synthetic or unrepresentative calibration dataset (e.g., ImageNet validation images for a medical endoscopy model)?

The activation dynamic ranges and outlier distributions in production may be misrepresented by the calibration dataset, causing clipping of real-world features or overly coarse quantization scales that degrade serving accuracy.
The model compiler will fail to generate valid GPU assembly code and reject the weights.
The server’s physical power consumption will double due to misaligned integer registers.
The dynamic batcher will permanently lock its batch size to 1.

title: Model Serving
text:
Consider an image classification service where the compiled neural network forward pass takes only 0.8 milliseconds in a standalone benchmark, yet real-world request latency approaches 15 milliseconds at the network boundary. Profiling the physical host reveals that input JPEG decoding consumes 8 milliseconds of CPU time, serialized PCIe host-to-device transfers stall the accelerator queue for 4 milliseconds, and individual kernel launches suffer 2 milliseconds of driver synchronization bubbles. The isolated model benchmark masked every physical bottleneck on the host server.
Runtime selection and precision tuning operate at the model level, determining what computation runs and what numerical format it uses. Between the model graph and the silicon, however, lies an execution layer encompassing graph compilation, bus transfers, and CPU-accelerator coordination. Node-level optimization targets this complete end-to-end request path on concrete hardware, eliminating overhead between the network socket and accelerator execution units across four primary physical boundaries:

Graph-to-kernel boundary: Translating computation graphs into numerous fine-grained kernel launches incurs driver serialization overhead and forces intermediate tensors through device HBM. Graph compilers fuse adjacent operations into composite kernels that preserve intermediate activations in on-chip SRAM or register files.
Host-accelerator boundary: Accelerators sit idle when the host processor fails to enqueue work ahead of execution. Unpipelined copies across host-device interconnects (such as PCIe) and blocking synchronization calls stall accelerator compute pipelines.
CPU execution boundary: Host preprocessing pipelines and CPU-based inference degrade when executed through interpreted scalar code rather than vectorized SIMD instruction units and NUMA-local memory allocations, and when operating-system noise preempts the threads that feed the accelerator.
Storage and deserialization boundary: Initializing serving replicas requires streaming weight tensors from persistent storage into host memory. Formats requiring recursive object deserialization bottleneck CPU execution, creating cold-start latency spikes that impede autoscaling.

Each boundary represents a distinct physical constraint where execution stalls on memory bandwidth, bus transit, or control overhead rather than peak arithmetic throughput.


Specialized inference engines (section 1.8) outperform eager framework baselines because serving environments provide static execution topologies and bounded input-shape profiles. When operator sequences and tensor dimensions are fixed before incoming requests arrive, compilers shift optimization costs from runtime query processing to offline deployment preparation.
When the trace reveals intermediate-memory traffic or repeated launch overhead, a candidate intervention is kernel fusion, applied by the engines of section 1.8.1.2 across the whole graph. Its serving payoff is largest on chains of elementwise operations, such as the bias add and activation that follow a convolution. These operations perform \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) arithmetic per byte transferred, so separate kernels can spend substantial time writing and reading global-memory intermediates instead of performing arithmetic; cache behavior determines the traffic that reaches HBM or GDDR. Fusion keeps those intermediates in registers or shared memory (SRAM), cutting memory traffic and amortizing kernel launch overheads over larger computational blocks.
Static execution graphs also enable compile-time constant folding. In model serving, model parameters are immutable. Compilers evaluate subexpressions composed entirely of static weights and constants prior to deployment. The batch-normalization folding shown above for the convolution block is the canonical case. It eliminates the normalization layer’s kernel launches and associated memory traffic entirely, removing computational work from every live request without altering mathematical outputs.
Memory planning applies structural optimization to memory layout rather than arithmetic. Reactive allocation during request processing triggers framework allocator locks, heap searches, and operating system page table modifications. In a static graph, tensor lifetimes are known deterministically from input to output. The runtime compiler calculates exact buffer offsets ahead of time, allowing intermediate tensors with nonoverlapping lifetimes to reuse the same physical memory arena. This precalculated buffer reuse bounds total memory consumption, prevents memory fragmentation, and eliminates runtime allocation stalls.
Beyond memory planning and kernel fusion, static execution paths can use CUDA Graphs to amortize host submission overhead across a captured sequence. In standard eager execution, launching an accelerator operation from Python or a serving runtime requires the host CPU to perform substantial bookkeeping: verifying tensor memory addresses, validating dimensions, selecting device kernel variants, and writing a hardware command descriptor into the driver’s memory-mapped ring buffer. Each submission pays the 5–20 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) of host launch work quantified in section 1.7.1. Total submission cost depends on the executed kernel count, not the number of layers: a decode step launching 8 to 10 sub-kernels across each of 32 transformer layers can accumulate several milliseconds of host submission work. At small batch sizes, this dispatch latency can exceed the time the accelerator silicon takes to execute the actual tensor math, leaving compute units starved of work. CUDA Graphs circumvent this host bottleneck: during an initial warm-up execution, the driver captures the entire sequence of kernel launches, memory bindings, and inter-kernel dependencies into a static execution graph. During live inference, the host CPU dispatches the captured graph with a single driver invocation (illustratively \(\sim 5\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\), depending on the graph, driver, and hardware). The accelerator then schedules its constituent kernels while respecting their dependencies, reducing repeated host submission work without eliminating device execution costs.

Systems Perspective 13.6: Compilation timing trade-offJust-in-time compilation defers graph optimization until the runtime engine observes concrete input shapes and execution paths. This runtime visibility enables aggressive kernel specialization for dynamic control flow and variable sequence lengths, but it injects compilation overhead directly into the serving path, generating multi-second latency spikes on early requests.
Ahead-of-time compilation executes graph analysis, kernel fusion, and hardware-specific auto-tuning prior to deployment. Pre-building removes the covered compilation work from the request path, but weights, device contexts, allocations, and representative execution paths still require loading and warmup. The compiled engine remains constrained to its supported shape profiles and may require padding or multi-profile compilation to accommodate dynamic input sizes.








Noisy neighbors stretch identical forward passes unevenly, widening the tail.
Compilation fixes what the accelerator executes; it does not control how steadily the host feeds it. An inference server does not execute in a dedicated vacuum. On a single host, the operating system multiplexes hardware across background telemetry daemons, logging agents, and kernel worker threads. When these unisolated processes contend for execution resources, they intermittently preempt the inference pipeline. These noisy neighbors are a primary source of latency jitter, where the physical time required to execute identical forward passes fluctuates unpredictably. This contention inflates 99th percentile (p99) tail latency even when average hardware utilization remains low. Resource contention thus widens tail latency through service-time variance, a physical degradation distinct from the queuing-delay accumulation along the saturation knee plotted in figure 1.
Reducing performance variability requires controlling interference from the operating system’s default time-sharing heuristics. Serving systems such as Clockwork demonstrate that deep neural network (DNN) inference execution times can be predictable down to sub-millisecond tolerances under their controlled workload and hardware conditions (Gujarati et al. 2020). CPU affinity (thread pinning) establishes the baseline compute boundary by binding inference worker threads to designated physical cores. Without pinning, the OS scheduler periodically migrates threads between cores, losing access to warm private L1 and L2 cache contents and requiring lines to be refetched from shared L3 cache or DRAM. On multi-socket architectures, thread migration across NUMA boundaries is even more penalizing: accesses to memory left on the previous socket cross inter-socket interconnects, adding tens of nanoseconds of latency per transaction. Pinning threads to specific cores and binding their memory allocations to local NUMA nodes reduces migration-related cache misses and remote-socket memory traffic.

Gujarati, Arpan, Reza Karimi, Safya Alzayat, Wei Hao, Antoine Kaufmann, Ymir Vigfusson, and Jonathan Mace. 2020. “Clockwork: Predictable and Scalable DNN Inference in the Cloud.” USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI), 443–62.
Even with pinned CPU cores, memory access latency remains vulnerable to the virtual memory subsystem. Under host memory pressure, the kernel can page inactive address ranges out to disk. When the CPU touches a paged-out address, execution can stall for milliseconds while the page returns to DRAM. Host buffers used for PCIe DMA also need resident, registered backing pages during the transfer. Memory locking (mlock) instructs the kernel to pin specified virtual address ranges into physical host RAM, preventing page eviction for host-resident weights, input staging buffers, and offloaded key-value (KV) cache blocks. This removes eviction-related page faults at the cost of host memory flexibility; locked pages remain resident until unlocked, while cache misses and memory contention can still delay access. Because mlock operates strictly on host page tables, it does not apply to accelerator HBM, which is allocated directly by the accelerator driver.
Beyond scheduled processes, asynchronous hardware interrupts introduce another source of sub-millisecond preemption. When a network interface card (NIC) receives packet bursts, it triggers hardware interrupt requests (IRQs) that force the handling CPU core to immediately suspend user-space execution and process kernel interrupt handlers. If the OS routes these interrupts to cores running the inference engine’s submission loop, the CPU pauses command dispatch to the accelerator. Because GPUs process short inference layers in microseconds, even brief CPU submission stalls drain the accelerator’s hardware command ring buffer, causing pipeline bubbles where compute units sit idle waiting for the next kernel descriptor. Interrupt shielding restricts IRQ affinities to dedicated housekeeping cores, reducing preemption of the GPU dispatch thread by those device interrupts.
Isolating physical cores, locking host memory, and shielding interrupt lines reduce specific sources of operating system noise. The resulting service-time distribution still needs measurement under the intended load. Isolation makes the host a predictable partner that feeds the accelerator; when deployment constraints or workload profiles preclude dedicated accelerators, the host becomes the executor itself, and vectorization and the memory hierarchy govern execution speed.



Deploying inference on CPUs remains practical for lightweight models, sparse or bursty request streams that cannot saturate an accelerator, and applications where host-to-device transit latency dominates total computation time. Modern server CPUs26 (such as Intel Xeon and AMD EPYC) integrate wide SIMD vector registers and matrix accelerators (including AVX-512 and AMX). General-purpose Python interpreters and scalar implementations leave these execution units idle. Specialized runtimes such as OpenVINO map neural network operators to optimized microkernels that tile matrix operations across L1/L2 caches and use packed fused multiply-add (FMA) instructions (Intel Corporation 2026).
26 SIMD: From Michael Flynn’s 1966 taxonomy of computer architectures, SIMD enables one instruction to operate on multiple data elements simultaneously. Intel’s AVX-512 can process sixteen FP32 values in a 512-bit vector, while AMX adds matrix tile operations. The attainable fraction of peak depends on data type, matrix shape, memory behavior, and implementation, but optimized vector kernels provide multiple-fold speedups over scalar execution.The NUMA boundaries that thread pinning respects matter more when the CPU itself runs the model. Memory controllers are physically distributed across CPU sockets and linked by coherent interconnects (such as Intel UPI or AMD Infinity Fabric). Accessing memory attached to a remote socket incurs substantially higher latency and lower bandwidth than local channel access. An inference server must maintain NUMA awareness: worker threads must be pinned to dedicated physical cores, and the weight tensors and request buffers those threads touch must reside in memory nodes local to that socket. Because model weights, at hundreds of megabytes to tens of gigabytes, routinely exceed per-socket L3 cache capacities, every forward pass streams weights from main RAM. Mismatched socket allocations force continuous weight streaming across the slower inter-socket interconnect, creating severe tail-latency degradation.
For lightweight models evaluated at batch size one, a CPU frequently outperforms a discrete GPU. When an accelerator processes an isolated request, the fixed overhead of transferring inputs across the host PCIe bus (several microseconds), driver queue serialization, and kernel launch overhead (5–20 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) per kernel) can easily surpass the arithmetic execution time. The CPU processes the request directly in local cache without bus transfers or driver queue delays. Determining the operational crossover requires empirical measurement across model architecture, arithmetic intensity, batch size, and latency constraints.



Autoscaling systems operate as closed-loop controllers that provision or deprovision serving replicas in response to traffic demand. During demand surges, cold-start latency (section 1.6.2) governs how rapidly new replicas become ready to serve traffic. For multi-gigabyte models, cold-start duration is heavily dominated by streaming serialized model weights from persistent storage into host memory. The architectural choice of serialization format determines whether this stage is bounded by storage read bandwidth or by CPU parsing overhead.
Legacy PyTorch checkpoints loaded via torch.load() package weights within a zip archive containing pickle-encoded object metadata. Deserializing a pickle file forces the CPU to interpret a stream of serialization opcodes sequentially, allocating individual Python objects (dictionaries, metadata wrappers, and tensor headers) and potentially copying tensor bytes into newly allocated memory. Restricted loading modes reduce arbitrary code execution risks, while memory-mapped options can avoid some eager copies. Whether parsing or storage dominates depends on the checkpoint, loading path, and hardware.
A tensor-oriented format27 bypasses interpreter-driven object construction. Safetensors organizes checkpoints with a lightweight header containing tensor metadata followed by contiguous, uncompressed tensor byte buffers aligned to memory boundaries. Because the on-disk binary layout mirrors the in-memory array layout, the runtime uses memory mapping (mmap(2), introduced in section 1.6.3) to map file blocks directly into the process’s virtual address space. Virtual memory pages fault into host RAM on demand or are prefetched sequentially by the operating system, reducing Python object reconstruction and avoiding eager user-space tensor copies on the mapped path. On systems with discrete accelerators, transferring these tensors across PCIe or NVLink is still required before computation begins, but memory-mapped host loading can reduce CPU reconstruction costs without eliminating page faults, storage reads, or device initialization.
27 Safetensors: The name emphasizes safety: unlike unrestricted pickle deserialization, the format does not encode executable Python objects (Hugging Face 2026). It stores tensors as contiguous raw bytes with a small header and supports memory-mapped loading. In the local benchmark example, that path is 10× faster than the compared PyTorch checkpoint path; the result is workload- and storage-specific and does not include transfer to a discrete accelerator.
Hugging Face. 2026. Safetensors Documentation.

Example 13.13: Loading speed: Safetensors vs. PickleScenario: A serverless inference replica loads a 5 GB model checkpoint during cold-start scaling events.
Diagnosis: PyTorch torch.load() (Pickle) requires CPU object reconstruction, taking 15 s to initialize. Safetensors memory-mapping bypasses CPU parsing, loading weights in 1.5 s (10× faster).
Systems lesson: Tensor-oriented, memory-mapped formats can reduce CPU reconstruction and eager-copy overhead during cold start. Storage throughput, page faults, runtime initialization, and accelerator transfer still remain in the scale-out budget.





Optimization without empirical measurement degrades into speculative trial and error. The duty-cycle metric defined in equation 2 helps locate idle intervals, but active time alone does not measure arithmetic efficiency or prove adequate queueing headroom. The objective is useful throughput that meets the latency SLO. Timeline profilers, such as PyTorch Profiler and NVIDIA Nsight Systems (nsys), make this objective actionable by recording concurrent CPU threads, OS runtime calls, memory transfers, and GPU hardware queues along a synchronized timeline.
Effective trace analysis proceeds bottleneck-first from hardware utilization back toward application logic:

Idle compute bubbles: White space on the GPU execution track indicates hardware starvation. Compute warps idle while waiting for the host CPU to complete request preprocessing (e.g., tokenization or image decoding), page faults during on-demand weight paging, or blocking inter-thread synchronization.
Kernel launch fragmentation: A sequence of micro-kernels, each executing in under 5–10 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\), suggests launch overhead as a candidate. Host launch timing and gaps between device kernels reveal whether submission starves the GPU; if so, graph capture or legal fusion may help.
Interconnect transfer stalls: Synchronous MemcpyHtoD blocks on the primary CUDA stream indicate unpipelined host-to-device data movement. Overcoming this stall requires allocating page-locked (pinned) host memory and executing asynchronous transfers on dedicated copy streams to overlap bus transit with concurrent accelerator execution on preceding requests.


Example 13.14: The profiling loopScenario: An inference serving node exhibits high p99 tail latency despite low average GPU compute utilization.
Diagnosis: Timeline profiling (Nsight Systems/PyTorch Profiler) reveals large idle gaps between tiny GPU kernels caused by CPU host-side preprocessing bottlenecks and kernel launch overhead.
Systems lesson: Serving node optimization requires empirical timeline profiling. Iteratively identifying trace bottlenecks (kernel launch overhead, host-device copy stalls) guides targeted optimizations like kernel fusion and pinned memory.


Table 20 summarizes representative node-level optimization techniques alongside their primary target metrics and engineering costs. The table serves as a decision matrix rather than an exhaustive checklist: engineering effort should be directed exclusively to the row that addresses the binding bottleneck identified on the measured execution trace.

This diagnostic hierarchy ensures engineering resources address structural bottlenecks along the entire request path rather than applying isolated micro-optimizations. A four-level audit checkpoint structures this prioritization from external service boundaries down to device kernels.

Checkpoint 13.4: The optimization hierarchy
Optimizing inference follows the request path from the outside in across four structural levels:

System budget: Partition the end-to-end latency budget between network transit, host application processing, queueing delay, and kernel execution using distributed tracing tools to verify compliance.
Application level: Determine whether the arrival stream and latency budget permit batching, and test whether the gain in service capacity outweighs formation and resource-queue waiting.
Model level: If dispatch or operator placement binds the request path, evaluate a compatible compiled engine or graph configuration and recheck quality across supported input shapes.
Kernel level: Where intermediate traffic or launch overhead is measured, assess legal fusion candidates and verify their numerical behavior and end-to-end benefit.



Systematically eliminating node-level bottlenecks lets every provisioned server operate near its physical efficiency limit. Every workload so far, however, has treated a request as one completed prediction. That assumption belongs to the service-time and batching models developed here, which it simplifies, rather than to the MLPerf scenarios, which do not require fixed-size outputs. The fastest-growing category of serving workloads violates this assumption entirely. Large language models generate outputs token by token, with each token depending on every previous one. A single request may produce hundreds or thousands of tokens over seconds of elapsed time, yet must feel responsive from the first token onward. The shift from fixed-output to variable-length, streaming-output serving reopens each tool developed so far, from the latency budget to the runtime.

Self-Check: Question

Why can loading model weights from modern safetensors format provide faster startup times than some legacy PyTorch checkpoint paths?

In a CPU-based model serving deployment, how do vector extensions like Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) or Vector Neural Network Instructions (VNNI) accelerate inference throughput compared to standard scalar x86 execution?
To reduce OS scheduler thread migration and cross-socket memory bus contention on multi-socket CPU serving nodes, engineers bind worker threads to specific processor cores and local memory nodes using the ____ utility.
Order the iterative steps of an end-to-end performance profiling workflow for diagnosing an inference serving bottleneck:

True or False: In Ahead-of-Time (AOT) graph compilation, operator fusion is restricted to combining adjacent layers of the exact same mathematical type (e.g., fusing two consecutive Conv2D operations).
When profiling a GPU inference server under high load, an engineer sees nvidia-smi report 95% utilization.gpu, but a detailed profile over the same period shows low achieved FLOP rate and many kernels stalled on memory or synchronization. What best explains the discrepancy?

nvidia-smi measures fan speed and ambient temperature rather than compute kernel activity.
The GPU memory clock is automatically halved during Nsight Systems tracing.

nvidia-smi reports the fraction of sampled time with one or more kernels active on the GPU, not how efficiently those kernels used the compute units.

title: Model Serving
text:
Large language models (LLMs) make three properties far more prominent than in fixed-output serving: autoregressive generation28 (each token depends on all previous tokens, making output inherently sequential), variable-length output (response length is unknown at request time, complicating fixed-batch assumptions), and stateful memory (the key-value cache grows with each generated token, creating dynamic memory pressure). Each property strains a different tool from the preceding sections: sequential generation splits the latency budget into phases, unknown output length breaks fixed-batch scheduling, and the growing cache makes memory capacity, not arithmetic, the limit on concurrency. The p50, p95, and p99 metrics used for classification serving still matter, but they apply separately to the initial prompt processing and to the subsequent token generation. The same principles of queuing theory, batching trade-offs, and latency budgets remain applicable; LLM serving adds domain-specific techniques atop them.
28 Autoregressive: From Greek auto- (self) and Latin regressus (a going back)—the output “regresses” on itself; George Udny Yule introduced autoregressive models in 1927 for analyzing sunspot cycles. In language modeling, each output token conditions on all previously generated tokens, creating a serial dependency that prevents the parallelism exploited during training. Decode is often weight-bandwidth-bound at small batches; larger batches amortize the weight stream and can shift the bottleneck toward compute or KV-cache traffic (Pope et al. 2023).
Pope, Reiner, Sholto Douglas, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Jacob Devlin, James Bradbury, Jonathan Heek, Kefan Xiao, Shivani Agrawal, and Jeff Dean. 2023. “Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference.” Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems (MLSys) 5: 606–24.

↩︎ Prefill, small-batch autoregressive decode, and the KV cache that every decode step reads are established in Small-batch autoregressive decoding: The memory bandwidth wall.






Prefill and low-batch decode often face different resource limits.
Generative models produce a stream of tokens rather than a single output tensor. This streaming nature requires dedicated LLM performance metrics that reflect the transition from prefill (processing the prompt and populating its KV cache) to decode (generating output). Two key measures are time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT), which capture responsiveness and average generation pace. Per-gap inter-token latency (ITL) measures the distribution of pauses between individual streamed tokens; TPOT instead averages the post-first-token interval across an output.

Definition 13.6: LLM performance metrics
LLM performance metrics separate initial responsiveness from the cadence of streaming autoregressive generation.

Significance: They decompose user-perceived latency into time to first token (TTFT) (whose prefill work is often compute-bound) and time per output token (TPOT) (whose decode work is often bandwidth-bound at small batches).
Distinction: Unlike fixed-output metrics (for example, end-to-end latency), LLM metrics measure the fluidity of generation, acknowledging that the user experience depends on the rhythm of token arrival.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that a low TTFT means a fast model. In reality, a model can have a fast TTFT but a sluggish TPOT (if the memory wall \((\Bandwidth)\) is the bottleneck), leading to a frustrating user experience where the answer starts quickly but “stutters” thereafter.



These metrics capture distinct aspects of the user experience, so interactive services often set separate targets for TTFT, TPOT or ITL, and aggregate throughput.

Systems Perspective 13.7: LLM serving latency targetsInteractive LLM services usually need separate SLOs for responsiveness, generation fluidity, and fleet throughput. The following values are illustrative targets rather than universal requirements:

TTFT: \(<\) 500 ms (for a 1000-token prompt)
TPOT: \(<\) 50 ms (equivalent to ~20 tokens/s, faster than human reading speed)
Throughput: \(>\) 1000 tokens/s aggregate across active serving replicas

A single “latency” number therefore hides the prefill/decode split. TTFT is the blank-screen budget, TPOT is the reading-flow budget, and aggregate service throughput, measured as tokens/s summed across active serving replicas, determines whether those targets hold under shared load.





Meeting per-token latency (TPOT) targets depends on more than raw accelerator memory bandwidth: the discrete sampling algorithm executed at each step governs both output distribution and host-accelerator synchronization. Generative inference relies on decoding algorithms that negotiate an explicit trade-off among token diversity, sequence quality, and runtime overhead.
The simplest approach, greedy decoding, selects the token with the highest predicted logit at each step, requiring a single forward pass per token. While computationally efficient, greedy selection frequently produces repetitive degeneration because it cannot recover from early sub-optimal choices. Beam search preserves multiple candidate hypotheses across generation steps, pruning low-scoring sequences at each iteration; this exploration improves sequence-level coherence but scales computational work and KV-cache footprint linearly with beam width. Stochastic sampling incorporates parameterized entropy: temperature scaling modulates logit sharpness, while top-\(\TopTokenSampleCount\) and top-\(\NucleusProbabilityMass\) nucleus sampling truncate the vocabulary distribution to restrict sampling to high-probability subsets (Holtzman et al. 2020). The serving cost of any strategy depends on its kernel implementation and the sequence length distribution that continuous batching must absorb.

Holtzman, Ari, Jan Buys, Li Du, Maxwell Forbes, and Yejin Choi. 2020. “The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration.” Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2020).
Interactive LLM services commonly return tokens as they are produced rather than waiting for complete generation. This streaming response transforms the user experience: a two-second total generation feels responsive when tokens stream continuously, but feels broken when users stare at a blank screen for two seconds. Streaming requires infrastructure support for incremental responses and client-side rendering. The latency profile shifts accordingly: TTFT determines when output starts appearing (responsiveness), while TPOT determines the perceived generation speed (fluidity). Once generation streams token by token, the serving unit changes from one fixed-output prediction to a stateful sequence whose length is unknown when it is admitted and whose memory footprint grows on every step. The unknown length breaks the fixed-batch scheduling developed for fixed-output models, and the growing state turns accelerator memory into the next constraint.



An autoregressive request finishes only when it emits an end-of-sequence token, so its length is revealed one step at a time. Extending the request-level dynamic batching of section 1.7 to an entire generation cycle keeps batch membership fixed until every sequence finishes. When sequence lengths vary, this static commitment degrades accelerator efficiency. If one sequence in a batch of eight finishes after ten tokens while others require 100 tokens, 90 percent of the compute and memory bandwidth allocated to that sequence slot is wasted on padding tokens or masked dummy operations while awaiting the slowest sequence (Yu et al. 2022).
29 Continuous batching: Also called “iteration-level batching” (Yu et al. 2022) and, in NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM, “in-flight batching” (NVIDIA 2026f); the distinction is scheduling granularity. Traditional batching commits to a fixed batch for an entire generation sequence (potentially hundreds of iterations), while continuous batching reschedules at every token-generation step—analogous to preemptive OS process scheduling vs. run-to-completion. This finer granularity reduces the waste from variable-length sequences, where a batch slot occupied by a completed sequence sits idle until all other sequences finish.
Yu, Gyeong-In, Joo Seong Jeong, Geon-Woo Kim, Soojeong Kim, and Byung-Gon Chun. 2022. “Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models.” 16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 22), 521–38.

NVIDIA. 2026f. NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM.
Continuous batching29 (also called iteration-level batching) eliminates this idle-slot tax by rescheduling batch composition at each decoding iteration (Yu et al. 2022; Kwon et al. 2023). Rather than committing to a static batch that persists across hundreds of forward passes, the serving engine re-evaluates batch membership at every token-generation step. When a sequence emits its end-of-sequence token, the scheduler immediately reclaims that execution slot, admitting an arriving request into the batch for the subsequent forward pass. Active sequences continue decoding without interruption, maintaining high accelerator utilization across variable-length workloads.
Serving runtimes such as vLLM30 and TensorRT-LLM improve throughput via two mechanisms: reclaiming wasted compute from completed sequences and shortening queue wait times for new arrivals (Kwon et al. 2023; NVIDIA 2026f). However, admitting new requests dynamically creates a systems collision between prompt prefill and token decoding. Long-prompt prefill often exposes high arithmetic intensity and can occupy the GPU for tens of milliseconds. Low-batch decoding often has less weight reuse and is memory-bandwidth bound, advancing one token per active sequence at a time. When an engine executes a prefill in the same iteration as active decodes, the ongoing decode streams stall, causing severe spikes in inter-token latency. Sarathi-Serve resolves this interference through chunked prefill and stall-free batching (Agrawal et al. 2024). By splitting long prompts into fixed-size chunks (e.g., 512 tokens) and co-scheduling a single chunk alongside active decode requests per step, the scheduler limits the prefill work admitted per iteration, reducing interference with active decodes; measured iteration times determine the resulting token cadence.
30 vLLM (virtual large language model (LLM)): An open-source serving system that enables continuous batching via its PagedAttention algorithm (Kwon et al. 2023). Inspired by OS virtual memory, this technique reduces the severe KV-cache fragmentation and reservation waste that constrains static batching. By keeping KV-cache waste low, vLLM can serve larger effective batches on the same hardware.
Agrawal, Amey, Nitin Kedia, Ashish Panwar, Jayashree Mohan, Nipun Kwatra, Bhargav S. Gulavani, Alexey Tumanov, and Ramachandran Ramjee. 2024. “Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve.” 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24), 117–34.
31 Speculative decoding: A small “draft” model generates \(\DraftTokenCount\) candidate tokens autoregressively; the large target model then verifies the proposed block in parallel (Leviathan et al. 2023). Parallel verification is possible because the draft model guesses all \(\DraftTokenCount\) candidate tokens in advance. Rather than generating sequentially, the target model evaluates the entire \(\DraftTokenCount\)-token block in a single causal-attention forward pass—acting like a compute-bound mini-prefill—which replaces \(\DraftTokenCount\) memory-bandwidth-bound matrix-vector operations with one parallel matrix-matrix evaluation. When the draft model’s proposals are accepted at rate \(\DraftAcceptanceRate\), effective throughput can scale with the number of accepted tokens per verification step. This breaks the serial autoregressive bottleneck at the runtime layer, not the architecture layer.
Leviathan, Yaniv, Matan Kalman, and Yossi Matias. 2023. “Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 19274–86.
Continuous batching and chunked prefill keep decode batches full and their cadence steady, but at small batch each generated token still pays for one full weight stream. Speculative decoding31 attacks that bound directly. A small draft model proposes several tokens, and the target model verifies the whole proposal in one parallel pass, so a single weight stream can yield more than one accepted token. Evaluated T5-XXL workloads achieved roughly 2–3\(\times\) speedups (Leviathan et al. 2023), though the gain depends on how often the target model accepts the draft.
Keeping decode batches full, however, shifts the primary serving bottleneck to memory management. Because transformer generation appends attention states at every step, the KV cache for each active request grows dynamically in accelerator HBM. When sequences of varying lengths share memory, contiguous allocation produces severe external fragmentation. If a completed 100-token sequence releases its cache, an arriving 150-token request cannot occupy that freed memory because it requires a larger contiguous address range. Over time, physical memory fractures into small, noncontiguous gaps, preventing new sequences from launching even when total unallocated capacity appears sufficient. Together with the over-reservation of contiguous allocators, this memory fragmentation can waste 60 to 80 percent of KV-cache memory in naive implementations (Kwon et al. 2023), severely limiting the concurrent batch size that determines serving throughput.





PagedAttention recovers the KV-cache waste of contiguous allocation.
32 PagedAttention: The name directly references OS virtual memory paging, first implemented on the Atlas computer at Manchester (1962) to solve the same class of allocation problem—programs needed more memory than physically available, and contiguous allocation wasted space (Kilburn et al. 1962). Introduced at SOSP 2023, PagedAttention applies this six-decade-old abstraction to GPU KV-cache memory: the evaluated earlier serving systems wasted 60 to 80 percent of KV-cache memory due to fragmentation and over-reservation. In that evaluation, PagedAttention reduced waste to under 4 percent, enabling 2–4\(\times\) higher throughput on the same hardware (Kwon et al. 2023).
Kilburn, Tom, David B. G. Edwards, Michael J. Lanigan, and Frank H. Sumner. 1962. “One-Level Storage System.” IRE Transactions on Electronic Computers EC-11 (2): 223–35. https://doi.org/10.1109/TEC.1962.5219356.

Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, and Ion Stoica. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165.
PagedAttention,32 introduced in vLLM, resolves this fragmentation by applying operating system virtual memory paging to accelerator memory (Kwon et al. 2023). In static contiguous allocation, reserving maximum sequence length memory up front causes internal waste, while freed regions may be too small or poorly placed to satisfy a new contiguous reservation. Instead of allocating one contiguous region per sequence, PagedAttention divides the KV cache into fixed-size blocks mapped through a block table. A sequence’s cache can therefore occupy noncontiguous physical blocks. When a sequence completes, its blocks return to a free pool for reuse. Rather than copying noncontiguous blocks into a temporary contiguous buffer before computing attention, a specialized PagedAttention CUDA kernel traverses the block table directly, staging noncontiguous blocks into on-chip SRAM during query-key multiplication. By eliminating external fragmentation and bounding internal waste to each sequence’s last, partially filled block, PagedAttention reduced KV-cache waste below 4 percent in the reported evaluation and enabled substantially higher batch concurrency on the same accelerator hardware (Kwon et al. 2023).
Paging decides where cache blocks live; it does not reduce how many blocks each sequence needs, and that number grows with every generated token.




The KV cache33 is a stateful memory structure that grows with sequence length. Prefill creates cache entries for every prompt token, and each decoded token adds another entry, so a request’s footprint is set by its prompt length plus the number of tokens it has generated so far. Summed across concurrent variable-length sequences, this dynamic state can exceed the model weights and dominate available accelerator memory, which is why the remaining memory levers either reuse cache state across requests or move it off the accelerator.
33 KV cache (key-value cache): To avoid redundant work, the system caches the Key and Value vectors from previous tokens, which remain valid throughout generation. This design choice causes the dynamic memory growth described in the text, because the cache grows linearly with every generated token, making memory management a primary constraint. For a 70-billion-parameter-class model with grouped-query attention, the FP16 KV cache is about 0.33 MB per token per sequence; grouped-query attention (GQA), used in Llama-family models such as Llama 3, shares key/value heads across multiple query heads, reducing the cache relative to full multi-head attention (Dubey et al. 2024). A batch of 32 requests at an 8,000-token context therefore requires roughly 80 GB just for KV cache, several times larger still without grouped-query or multi-query attention.
Dubey, Abhimanyu, Abhinav Jauhri, Abhinav Pandey, Abhishek Kadian, et al. 2024. The Llama 3 Herd of Models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.21783.


Many requests carry identical prefixes, and recomputing their cache entries wastes both prefill compute and memory. Prefix caching stores the KV states of common instruction prefixes (such as a 2,000-token system prompt or a shared retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) context), allowing independent requests to reuse the prefill result for an identical prefix. For \(\SharedPrefixRequestCount\) requests sharing a prefix of \(\SharedPrefixLength\) tokens, the avoided prefill work is roughly \((\SharedPrefixRequestCount-1)\SharedPrefixLength\) token steps, subject to cache hits, eviction, and implementation overhead. For multi-turn conversations, the same principle lets a subsequent turn process only the new suffix after reusing compatible prior state.
When the aggregate KV cache exceeds GPU VRAM, systems can employ KV cache offloading. This strategy spills inactive or low-priority context windows to host CPU RAM or NVMe SSD, freeing VRAM for active generation. The reload cost is bounded below by bytes moved divided by PCIe or NVMe bandwidth, before software overhead and queueing are added. Offloading therefore prevents OOM failures and enables larger context windows, but it also creates affinity, invalidation, and hot-decode latency risks that must be budgeted explicitly. Distributed parallelism, which splits one request across multiple devices or machines, is a further lever that belongs to large-scale systems.




Prefix reuse and offloading both assume that the next turn of a conversation reaches the replica that holds its cache. Session affinity, routing successive requests from a client to the same physical replica, arises whenever serving state resides in local accelerator memory rather than being reconstructed on every invocation. In conversational models, this resident state is dominated by the KV cache. When turn \(\ConversationTurnIndex\) executes on a replica, that replica’s HBM retains the projected keys and values across all prior prompt and generation tokens. Routing turn \(\ConversationTurnIndex+1\) to a different replica discards that local memory footprint, forcing the new node to recompute the entire prefix sequence from scratch. This redundant prefill consumes memory bandwidth and tensor-core cycles that would otherwise advance active decode iterations, directly inflating time-to-first-token.
A parallel physical constraint governs personalized serving using fine-tuned Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules: small per-user adapters, each a pair of low-rank matrices whose product is added to a frozen base weight matrix. While base-model weights remain pinned in device HBM, individual user adapters must be dynamically staged into memory. If incoming requests for a user scatter across multiple replicas, each node must repeatedly transfer adapter tensors over the host-to-device PCIe bus or fetch them across the network, displacing other active working sets in memory. Stateful preprocessing pipelines, such as tokenizer vocabularies and per-session normalization state, impose the same penalty, requiring redundant CPU-side allocations and cache rebuilds whenever execution moves across node boundaries.


↩︎ Products of two low-rank matrices, and the storage and memory traffic they save relative to a full matrix, are established in Low-rank factorization.
Fleet routing is an optional extension of this local state-reuse constraint. Strict affinity creates a direct conflict with dynamic batching. Continuous batch schedulers maximize accelerator throughput by packing concurrent requests into unified matrix multiplications, raising operational arithmetic intensity in proportion to batch size (\(\ArithmeticIntensity\propto \BatchSize\)). When requests are pinned to designated replicas, the scheduler’s pool of batchable candidates fragments across the cluster. A replica assigned to an idle or low-concurrency user session must either process underfilled batches, collapsing arithmetic intensity back into the memory-bandwidth-bound regime, or stall waiting for affinity-matched tokens. To prevent this collapse in utilization, production routers use soft affinity. Under soft affinity, the ingress gateway prioritizes the cache-holding replica when capacity allows, but sheds requests to alternate nodes when local queue delays exceed the physical latency required to transfer adapter weights or recompute prefix tokens.

Systems Perspective 13.8: LLM serving: Beyond the fundamentalsEach LLM serving technique answers one of two physical limits. The first is the decode bound, in which every generated token pays for a full weight stream at small batch: continuous batching keeps decode batches full so each stream serves many sequences, chunked prefill keeps prompt processing from stalling that stream, and speculative decoding extracts more than one accepted token per stream. The second is the KV cache, which grows with sequence length and batch size and often exceeds the weights themselves; PagedAttention, prefix caching, offloading, and session affinity decide where it lives and how much of it can be reused. Weight-only quantization (such as INT4 weights with FP16 activations), the precision lever of section 1.8.2 applied to the weight stream, addresses both at once, because it shrinks the bytes streamed per token and frees capacity for cache (Lin et al. 2024).
These LLM-specific optimizations build directly on core serving mechanics: queueing models govern scheduling timeouts, batching dynamics determine throughput-latency curves, and reduced precision bounds memory traffic. Advanced treatments extend these mechanics to multi-tenant prefix sharing across fleets and multi-node tensor-parallel execution.



Napkin Math 13.5: The energy cost of a chatProblem: How much energy does an H100-backed chat service spend per generated token and for a response with 500 tokens?
As LLMs scale, joules per token becomes a first-class operational metric alongside latency. Assuming the H100 draws its 700 W thermal design power (TDP), this scenario estimate follows from throughput and power (Choquette 2023):

Throughput: 114 concurrent requests \(\times\) 8 tokens/s per request ≈ 912 tokens/s.
Power: 700 W (GPU) + 300 W (Host/Overhead) = 1000 W.
Energy per token: 1000 W / 912 tokens/s ≈ 1.0965 J/token

Systems insight: Under these assumptions, a response of 500 tokens consumes ≈ 548.2 J.

For comparison, charging a smartphone consumes ≈ 40000 J.
Boiling a cup of water consumes ≈ 100000 J.

The primary way to reduce J/token is to increase hardware utilization and eliminate redundant compute. If the GPU sits at 10 percent utilization due to poor batching, it still draws ~300 W and the host adds 300 W, causing energy per token to rise to 6.6 J/token (approximately 6× the baseline). Architectural optimizations like prefix caching also skip the energy-intensive prefill phase for shared context, directly reducing the energy footprint of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and chat applications. The serving lesson is that efficiency is not only a latency or cost metric; it also determines how much energy each useful token consumes.


Every lever so far takes the number of tokens a request generates as given. Reasoning models make that number a choice.

Systems Perspective 13.9: Looking ahead: Spending more compute per queryFixed-output serving minimizes latency (\(\EndToEndRequestLatency \to 0\)) for a fixed amount of work per request. Some inference-time-compute systems instead deliberately spend more computation per query to improve answer quality, generating intermediate reasoning or search tokens before the visible answer. The optimization target then expands to include answer quality, and every extra reasoning token pays the decode costs this section derived: one more step of decode work at the batch’s cadence, one more KV-cache entry held until the response ends, and its share of the joules per token. Answer quality now trades directly against TPOT, cache capacity, and energy per query.



Checkpoint 13.5: LLM serving fundamentals
LLM serving introduces constraints absent from traditional model serving.

TTFT vs. TPOT: Contrast the distinct user experiences captured by TTFT and TPOT, explain why long-prompt prefill often exposes more arithmetic intensity than low-batch decode, and convert a 50 ms TPOT target into its tokens-per-second equivalent.
Continuous batching and PagedAttention: Contrast static batching waste under variable sequence lengths against iteration-level scheduling, and explain how PagedAttention eliminates external fragmentation in the KV cache and bounds internal waste to a single partially filled block per sequence.
Memory wall: Explain why adding compute units yields negligible latency improvement when token generation is bandwidth-bound, and identify how higher-bandwidth memory, model quantization, or batching alters the operating regime.
Prefix caching and offloading: Explain how caching key-value activations for shared prompt prefixes eliminates redundant prefill compute, and evaluate the latency trade-offs that govern offloading KV caches to host system memory.
Joules per token: Explain why energy consumption scales with generated sequence length, and how low hardware utilization inflates the energy cost per useful token.



Every LLM serving optimization ultimately decides how many sequences share each weight stream and how much accelerator memory each sequence holds. The chat-energy calculation showed that the same sharing sets the joules spent per useful token: each decode step streams the weights once for the whole active batch, so a well-filled batch divides that energy across sequences. Unlike fixed-output inference, LLM energy also grows with response length. Carbon accounting additionally requires an emissions factor and a defined boundary. These per-token bounds describe one accelerator. Deciding how many accelerators a service needs, and what each generated token costs, requires carrying them, together with the fixed-output results of the earlier sections, into capacity planning and unit economics.

Self-Check: Question

In Large Language Model (LLM) serving, how do the computational and hardware characteristics of the Prefill phase fundamentally differ from the Decode phase?

Prefill processes tokens autoregressively one by one and is memory-bandwidth bound, whereas Decode processes all output tokens simultaneously and is compute-bound.
Prefill processes all prompt tokens concurrently in parallel matrix multiplications and is often more compute-intensive, whereas Decode generates one token per step autoregressively and at low batch sizes is often memory-bandwidth bound due to repeated weight and KV-state movement.
Prefill operates exclusively on host CPU DRAM, whereas Decode runs on GPU Tensor Cores.
Prefill latency scales quadratically with batch size, whereas Decode latency is strictly independent of sequence length and KV-cache size.

Calculate the total memory footprint (in bytes) required to store the KV cache for a batch of \(B = 16\) requests, each with an active context length of \(S = 2\text{,}048\) tokens, for a model with \(L = 32\) transformer layers, \(H_{\text{kv}} = 8\) key-value attention heads (Grouped-Query Attention), head dimension \(D_{\text{head}} = 128\), stored in FP16 precision (\(P = 2\text{ bytes}\)).
Order the step-by-step execution cycle of Speculative Decoding for accelerating LLM inference:


Target model runs a single parallel forward pass over the draft candidate tokens to compute verification logits
Draft model (a lightweight autoregressive model) generates \(K\) candidate tokens sequentially
Engine appends the accepted tokens to the KV cache and advances the generation context
Verification logic compares the draft tokens with the target model’s verification results and accepts a prefix of them


True or False: Speculative decoding speeds up serving regardless of draft-model quality, because the target model always verifies multiple tokens in parallel.
In a multi-turn conversational AI system with extensive system prompts (e.g., 2,000 tokens of instructions and few-shot examples shared across thousands of user sessions), what serving optimization eliminates redundant prefill compute across requests?

Linear Attention Approximation, which drops system prompt tokens entirely from the attention window.
Static Graph Compilation, which hardcodes user inputs directly into the weight tensors.
Prefix Caching (e.g., RadixAttention), which stores the KV-cache states of common prompt prefixes in memory and reuses them across queries matching the prefix.
Speculative Quantization, which quantizes prompt tokens into 1-bit binary representations during the decode phase.

Contrast traditional request-level dynamic batching with iteration-level continuous batching (as introduced in Orca and vLLM) for Large Language Model (LLM) serving. Why is request-level batching severely inefficient for autoregressive generation?
True or False: PagedAttention resolves the primary memory waste in LLM KV-caching by allocating key and value states in non-contiguous, fixed-size physical memory blocks managed via a virtual page table, eliminating both internal fragmentation from over-allocation and external memory fragmentation.
