Implementation decisions—device placement, batch size, compilation mode—cascade through execution, differentiation, and abstraction layers simultaneously. When systems treat the framework as an opaque mathematical interpreter rather than a hardware-aware scheduler, these interactions trigger launch starvation, memory fragmentation, and throughput collapse.

Systems Perspective 7.6: The three problems in actionIn D·A·M terms, the single training step exposes how the framework balances algorithm and machine:

Execution (Machine scheduling): Eager mode preserves imperative line-by-line debugging at the cost of per-kernel launch and dispatch latency.
Differentiation (Algorithmic graph): Reverse-mode automatic differentiation retains intermediate forward activations in HBM to compute exact vector-Jacobian products in reverse topological order.
Abstraction (Hardware portability): Unified tensor APIs decouple model code from heterogeneous silicon, dispatching identical operations to cuBLAS, oneMKL, or XLA HLO kernels.

Resolving the friction among these dimensions requires matching operator granularity to hardware rooflines: fusing operations to eliminate memory round-trips, scaling batches to amortize launch latency, and structuring tensors to saturate accelerator execution pipelines.


Balancing execution models, differentiation overhead, and hardware abstractions creates a high-performance execution engine when applied correctly. Yet because these mechanisms interact below the surface of standard Python APIs, engineers frequently rely on simplistic assumptions carried over from general-purpose programming. Examining where these assumptions break down reveals the subtle traps that derail real-world framework deployments.

Framework selection involves subtle trade-offs where intuitions from conventional software engineering fail. The memory wall, kernel fusion constraints, and deployment target diversity create pitfalls that waste engineering effort and cause production systems to miss latency targets.

Fallacy: All frameworks provide equivalent performance for the same model architecture.
Engineers assume that ResNet-50 yields identical performance across frameworks since the mathematics is the same, forgetting that performance is an emergent property of algorithm-machine co-design. In production, implementation matters. Compiled execution can improve supported eager workloads, and hardware-specialized inference engines such as TensorRT or TVM can reduce latency relative to untuned eager baselines when conversion is clean. The difference arises from kernel fusion depth, graph optimization strategies, memory access patterns, precision support, and backend libraries that vary between frameworks. Organizations that assume equivalence can miss latency service level agreements and require costly last-minute framework migrations.


Pitfall: Choosing frameworks based on popularity rather than project requirements.
Engineers assume the most popular framework works for any project. In reality, deployment constraints dominate. A mobile runtime such as ExecuTorch or TensorFlow Lite and a microcontroller runtime such as TensorFlow Lite Micro make different assumptions about memory allocation, operator coverage, and hardware delegates; the former targets phones with GB-scale memory, while the latter often targets devices with hundreds of KB of RAM, commonly below 256 KB for small TinyML deployments. Teams that prototype edge applications without checking the final runtime can face memory bloat that exceeds device capacity or a late framework migration after development completes. Evaluate deployment targets per section 1.8 before selecting a training framework.


Fallacy: Framework abstractions eliminate the need for systems knowledge.
Engineers assume high-level APIs handle all optimization automatically. The Roofline Model proves otherwise. Element-wise operations such as ReLU perform little arithmetic per byte moved, so memory traffic and launch overhead can dominate even on accelerators with abundant compute. Section 1.3.1 explains how this imbalance can leave compute resources idle. Engineers must identify the limiting resource before choosing fusion, batching, layout, or precision optimizations.


Pitfall: Ignoring vendor lock-in from framework-specific formats.
Engineers assume framework migration is straightforward since models are “just math.” Converting TensorFlow SavedModel to PyTorch can require rewriting custom operations, validating numerical equivalence across large test suites, and retraining when operations lack exact equivalents. ONNX (section 1.8) improves portability, but custom operators, dynamic shapes, and backend-specific optimizations can still require manual work. Organizations that ignore this during initial framework selection face costly migrations when deployment requirements change or better frameworks emerge.


Fallacy: Training framework choice is independent of production infrastructure.
Engineers assume training framework choice is independent of deployment infrastructure. In practice, framework-infrastructure mismatches can impose substantial operational overhead. Some serving stacks provide atomic model swaps, while others require a process or container restart unless the deployment architecture adds version routing around them. Some frameworks and runtimes expose monitoring hooks directly; others require custom instrumentation. The lesson is to evaluate the complete deployment stack during framework selection, including serving infrastructure, monitoring, and operational tooling.



↪ Model versioning, staged release strategies, and serving integration that a framework’s deployment path must support are operationalized in Model deployment.

Pitfall: Increasing batch size without modeling activation memory.
Engineers assume that if memory is available, larger batches always improve throughput. Larger mini-batches can amortize fixed dispatch overhead, but they also scale the activation memory that must remain live during training. A 7-billion-parameter model in FP16 consumes 14 GB, leaving 71.9 GB on an 80 GB A100 before accounting for other training state. Increasing batch size from 8 to 32 quadruples the batch-dependent activation footprint; materialized transformer attention scores add a large \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) term in sequence length that makes each sample expensive. The resulting memory pressure can trigger recomputation strategies whose additional work reduces throughput despite the larger batch. Teams that blindly maximize batch size can achieve lower throughput than smaller batches that avoid these memory management pathways; Gradient-based optimization methods formalizes the throughput target.



↪ How activation memory grows linearly with batch size and caps the batch that fits in accelerator memory is developed in Mini-batch processing.

Fallacy: Compilation overhead is negligible.
Engineers assume compilation overhead is a one-time cost that pays off quickly. The hypothetical values in table 3 assign ResNet-50 higher compiled throughput and a compile window of 15 s to 30 s per graph change. Under those assumptions, timed with the table’s inference throughputs (a training loop would add backward work but pay the same recompilation cost), a 10,000-image experiment with 10 code changes completes in 6.9 s in eager mode and 304.7 s in compiled mode, including recompilation overhead. The compiled workflow is therefore about 44.2× slower in this illustrative rapid-prototyping scenario. Teams that enable compilation during rapid prototyping can waste time waiting for recompilations that negate throughput gains.


Pitfall: Using one execution policy for exploration and production.
The right framework mode depends on the loop. During exploration, eager execution and small tests shorten feedback by avoiding repeated graph captures and recompilations. During production serving or long training runs, compilation can amortize setup across many requests or samples. The deciding factors are workload duration and stability: compilation pays when graph structure and shapes recur, whereas changing control flow or input shapes can invalidate cached artifacts and restart the amortization. Teams should choose the policy from measured iteration latency and steady-state throughput. One policy for both phases either slows research iteration or leaves production throughput unused.

Machine learning frameworks solve three core systems challenges that make deep learning tractable on modern hardware. The first is execution: deciding when and how operations run. Frameworks balance the trade-off between eager evaluation for interactive debugging and graph execution for whole-program compilation, while modern hybrid approaches such as torch.compile capture graphs dynamically without sacrificing the Python control loop. The second is differentiation: computing gradients automatically. Frameworks implement reverse-mode automatic differentiation that applies the chain rule across compositions of operations, constructing an autograd tape or backward graph of vector-Jacobian products while making the required forward values available through retention or recomputation. This primitive makes training large models feasible through a single loss.backward() call. The third is abstraction: targeting heterogeneous hardware from a unified interface. Frameworks provide multi-dimensional tensor abstractions, intermediate representations, and runtime dispatch systems that bridge high-level model definitions to optimized device kernels across CPUs, GPUs, TPUs, and custom accelerators.
These challenges are linked through the iron law of ML systems (Iron Law of ML Systems): execution strategy affects dispatch latency \((\Latency)\), differentiation adds arithmetic and memory traffic \((\DataVolume)\), and abstraction influences hardware utilization efficiency \((\EfficiencyHw)\). These are diagnostic emphases, not exclusive assignments, since fusion changes both launches and traffic while differentiation changes both work and live storage. Workloads with little reuse are frequently memory-bandwidth bound (\(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\)). Frameworks mitigate this memory wall through kernel fusion, which merges compatible element-wise operations to keep intermediates in registers or on-chip SRAM instead of round-tripping through global memory. The separate capacity limit yields to selective recomputation, which trades additional floating-point operations \((\Operations)\) for lower peak activation memory.

Key Takeaways: The layer between math and hardware

Every framework solves three problems: Execution dictates runtime dispatch, differentiation computes gradients, and abstraction targets heterogeneous hardware. TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX make distinct infrastructure wagers across these axes, from static graph capture to dynamic tracing and functional transformations, and those wagers are architectural commitments that outlast API syntax.
The memory wall drives optimization: Accelerator compute capacity has outpaced memory bandwidth, making off-chip data movement a recurring bottleneck. Kernel fusion and lower-precision layouts can reduce the memory traffic term (\(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\)), while selective recomputation primarily reduces peak activation storage by adding work.
Compilation must amortize setup cost: The compilation continuum principle in equation 2 quantifies when runtime speedup offsets compilation overhead. While dynamic workloads favor eager execution, repeatedly executed graphs benefit from JIT or ahead-of-time compilation, where the dispatch overhead law (equation 4) demonstrates that small operations gain disproportionately when host launch overhead (\(\Latency\)) is reduced.
Module abstractions automate state management: Automatic parameter registration, mode-dependent execution (training versus inference), and hierarchical state serialization enable multi-billion-parameter model updates in a single optimizer step across diverse hardware backends.
Deployment constraints should drive selection: Specialized runtimes trade operator coverage, static memory allocation, and compilation latency against stringent hardware budgets. The gap between server-class accelerator memory and microcontroller SRAM requires evaluating the downstream deployment target before committing to a development framework.



A framework presents itself as an ergonomic programming interface, yet its true role is translating mathematical graphs into physical hardware operations. That translation determines the work, traffic, and overhead paid under the iron law of ML systems (principle \(\ref{pri-iron-law}\)). Eager execution prioritizes developer iteration at the cost of host dispatch latency (\(\Latency\)), while graph compilation trades upfront optimization time to reduce avoidable global memory traffic (\(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\)) through fused kernels. Automatic differentiation adds backward work and traffic (\(\DataVolume\)), with checkpointing trading retained activation storage against recomputed arithmetic (\(\Operations\)). What appears to be an API convenience is therefore a standing systems commitment: a framework respects physical limits while determining how much avoidable work and data movement the implementation performs.

What’s Next: From control room to power plantFrameworks are the software substrate that translates abstract architectures into executable kernels. Computational graphs, autograd tapes, and kernel dispatch pipelines are the control room instruments: they give engineers visibility into and control over the training process. This chapter traced a single training step through that machinery. A training run repeats that step many thousands or millions of times, and every budget decision the machinery exposes is still unmade, including which activations to checkpoint when memory runs short, how large a batch the hardware allows, and at what point a single device stops being enough. Model Training is where those bills come due. It opens with why training costs orders of magnitude more than inference, then budgets memory, time, and cost for real training runs and shows how far one machine can go before scaling out.

In the chapter’s small-operation scenario, each eager op pays host dispatch and launch work while the device kernels themselves are very short, so end-to-end time is driven more by repeated host overhead than by arithmetic or memory throughput. Execute the forward pass while registering operations and saving required activation tensors on the autograd tape
Accumulate calculated parameter gradients into the .grad attributes of leaf parameters
Compute the scalar loss \(\mathcal{L}\) from model outputs and ground truth targets
Traverse the GradFn DAG backward, applying operation-specific Vector-Jacobian Products (chain rule)**

Loss calculation: Produces the scalar objective value \(\mathcal{L}\).


Gradient seed initialization: Sets the root adjoint \(d\mathcal{L}/d\mathcal{L} = 1.0\).


Backward DAG traversal: Evaluates Vector-Jacobian Products along reverse-linked nodes.


Gradient accumulation: Writes computed gradients to leaf parameter .grad buffers.

Kernel dispatch: CPU enqueues compute operation onto the CUDA stream.

Because the dynamic class hierarchy in the framework leaks memory between layers
Because repeated host-side dispatch and kernel-launch overhead for many small operations can dominate when the device kernels themselves are short

Answer: The correct answer is D. In that hypothetical profile, many short kernels separated by host dispatch gaps would support an overhead-bound diagnosis: even if compute and memory lower bounds are small, eager execution can still spend substantial time issuing many separate operations. The chapter’s peak-rate lower bounds and dispatch-cost assumptions motivate this explanation, but by themselves they do not constitute an observed profile. The network answer does not fit a single-device step, and the thermal-throttling and memory-leak explanations are not the chapter’s modeled source of overhead.
Learning Objective: Analyze why small model training steps on fast accelerators can be overhead-bound rather than limited by raw compute or memory bandwidth
Contrast the arithmetic intensity of a matrix multiplication (MatMul) with an element-wise activation such as ReLU, and explain how their performance bottlenecks can differ on modern GPUs depending on shape and execution conditions.
Answer: A matrix multiplication typically reuses its operands many times, so it performs much more arithmetic per byte moved than an element-wise activation does. By contrast, ReLU does very little computation for each value it reads and writes; in the chapter’s simplified example it is about \(0.125\) FLOP/byte, which makes bandwidth and launch overhead loom large. A MatMul can therefore move toward a compute-bound regime when its shapes are favorable, while ReLU often stays memory- or overhead-sensitive because there is so little work per byte. The practical implication is that compilers often target ReLU-like chains with fusion, whereas large matrix multiplies are more often optimized through kernel quality, layout, and precision choices.
Learning Objective: Compare the arithmetic intensity and likely bottlenecks of matrix multiplication versus element-wise activation under the roofline model
**Order the complete sequence of computational and system phases occurring inside a framework during a single standard training iteration:
Loss calculation: The criterion function evaluates the scalar training loss \(\mathcal{L}\)
Backward pass: Autograd traverses the reverse tape, executing Vector-Jacobian Products and populating .grad buffers
Optimizer step: The optimizer reads .grad values and updates parameter tensors in-place using the optimization algorithm
Forward pass: The model executes layer operations and records the dynamic autograd tape
Gradient reset: optimizer.zero_grad() clears or sets .grad buffers to None**
Answer: The correct sequence is 5 -> 4 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3:



Gradient reset: Clears accumulated gradients from previous iteration (zero_grad()).


Forward pass: Evaluates layer activations and builds the autograd tape.


Loss calculation: Computes scalar objective \(\mathcal{L}\).


Backward pass: Traverses tape backward to compute parameter gradients.


Optimizer step: Updates model weights using computed gradients and momentum/decay state.

Learning Objective: Order the operational phases of a standard deep learning training step


During the backward pass of a training step, why is memory traffic often higher than in the forward pass even when the amount of arithmetic work is of the same order?
Answer: Backward computation often has to revisit saved forward values, combine them with upstream gradients, and write out new gradients, so more tensors are read and written during the pass. For example, a layer may need the saved forward input plus the incoming gradient to produce both weight gradients and propagated gradients. In the chapter’s two-layer MLP, backward evaluates three GEMMs because the raw input needs no gradient; its traffic follows the operands and results of those products plus the activation and loss derivatives, rather than a universal multiplier of forward traffic.
Learning Objective: Analyze why the backward pass often incurs higher memory traffic than the forward pass

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A research team exploring architecture modifications runs experiments where model code changes every 10 training steps. When they enable JIT graph compilation (torch.compile), total training time increases by 5\(\times\) compared to standard eager mode. What systems principle explains this performance degradation?

Compilation incurs a large upfront compilation latency (\(T_{\text{compile}}\)); if graph structures or tensor shapes change frequently, the compilation cost cannot be amortized across executions (\(N_{\text{steps}} \times (T_{\text{eager}} - T_{\text{compiled}}) < T_{\text{compile}}\)), making repeated recompilation slower than eager execution
Compiled kernels run at half the floating-point clock frequency of eager kernels on NVIDIA GPUs
JIT compilers disable GPU hardware acceleration when running short training scripts
Dynamic graph compilation automatically converts all FP32 operations to 64-bit double precision

Answer: The correct answer is A. Compilation provides execution speedups by generating optimized fused kernels, but compiling incurs an upfront cost (\(T_{\text{compile}}\), often seconds to minutes); if frequent code or shape changes trigger continuous recompilation without sufficient execution steps to amortize the setup overhead, total runtime will be significantly worse than eager mode. GPU clock frequency is identical for compiled and eager kernels. JIT compilers do not disable GPU acceleration. JIT compilers preserve data types and do not convert FP32 to double precision.
Learning Objective: Calculate and analyze compilation break-even thresholds under frequent model recompilation
Explain why choosing a framework based on community popularity or GitHub stars rather than binding deployment constraints is a severe engineering pitfall for edge and embedded ML projects.
Answer: Popularity says little about whether a runtime matches the deployment contract. Edge phones, embedded Linux devices, and microcontrollers impose very different limits on memory allocation, operator support, packaging, and hardware acceleration, so a framework that is convenient for cloud training may still be a poor fit for the target runtime. For example, a mobile runtime such as ExecuTorch is solving a different deployment problem from TensorFlow Lite Micro, which is built for far tighter memory budgets and fixed-allocation execution. The practical consequence is that teams who optimize for ecosystem buzz instead of target constraints can reach the end of development with a model that cannot run acceptably on the actual device.
Learning Objective: Explain why popularity is an insufficient criterion for framework selection in constrained deployment environments
True or False: Because standard neural network architectures (like ResNet-50 or Transformers) have identical mathematical definitions, any two frameworks running the same model on identical GPU hardware will produce identical throughput.
Answer: False. Execution throughput depends on framework compiler quality, kernel fusion depth, memory layout decisions (NCHW vs. NHWC), dispatch overhead efficiency, and backend library optimizations (e.g. cuBLAS vs custom Triton kernels), leading to substantial performance variations across frameworks for identical mathematical architectures.
Learning Objective: Critique the fallacy that identical model mathematics implies identical framework runtime performance

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

How do the three framework problems (Execution, Differentiation, Abstraction) connect to the iron-law-style performance terms emphasized in the chapter?

Execution controls dataset size, differentiation controls network latency, and abstraction controls cloud pricing
All three problems affect only the floating-point precision of weights
Execution affects differentiation, while abstraction has no measurable systems consequence
Execution strongly shapes launch and dispatch overhead, differentiation changes work and the forward information or memory traffic needed for backward, and abstraction influences how effectively computation is lowered onto hardware

Answer: The correct answer is D. The chapter ties framework design back to physical performance terms by showing that execution strategy changes how much avoidable launch and dispatch overhead the system pays, differentiation changes both the extra work of backward computation and the live forward information or traffic required to support it, and abstraction affects how well kernels, layouts, and placements map to hardware. The key idea is diagnostic rather than exclusive: these associations are useful for reasoning, but mechanisms such as fusion can affect both traffic and launch count. The other answers either collapse the framework into unrelated business quantities or deny the chapter’s central claim that abstraction choices materially shape runtime efficiency.
Learning Objective: Synthesize how execution, differentiation, and abstraction connect to the main iron-law performance terms
Summarize why the memory wall—rather than raw floating-point arithmetic capacity—has become a major driver of framework compiler innovations such as kernel fusion and activation checkpointing.
Answer: Framework compilers focus on the memory wall because many workloads are limited more by data movement than by available arithmetic throughput. Kernel fusion helps by reducing intermediate reads and writes, keeping compatible values on chip instead of sending them repeatedly through slower memory. Activation checkpointing addresses a different pressure point: saved-state capacity during training, trading extra recomputation for a smaller live-memory footprint, with its effect on traffic depending on the recomputation path.
Learning Objective: Explain why the memory wall drives framework compiler optimizations like kernel fusion and activation checkpointing
True or False: An ML framework can eliminate the physical constraints imposed by the iron law of performance if an engineer writes clean, high-level declarative Python code.
Answer: False. A framework can reduce avoidable work, traffic, or launch overhead through better compilation and runtime choices, but it cannot bypass the underlying limits of hardware bandwidth, latency, memory capacity, or compute throughput.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the systems reality that framework abstractions reduce avoidable costs but do not eliminate physical limits

title: The dispatch tax: Python overhead vs. GPU reality
text:
Architecture stack focus for this chapter.
Why does the framework silently constrain every decision that comes after it?
Model equations do not execute themselves. A framework translates an architecture into work that hardware can run, and that translation is not neutral. It decides when operations execute, what intermediate state training retains, how memory is allocated, and which deployment targets can use the resulting artifact. These choices shape more than speed. They also determine what can be debugged directly, what the compiler can optimize, and whether the same model survives the path from a research environment to a production runtime. The same model expressed through two execution paths can differ in speed or memory use by several times, a gap that no amount of model tuning recovers when the framework hides the structure a compiler needs. The abstractions that make experimentation convenient therefore create long-lived commitments. Once a project accumulates checkpoints, modules, data loaders, serving formats, and team expertise around a framework, changing it becomes a system migration rather than a library substitution, measured in engineer-months rather than afternoons. A framework well suited to rapid exploration can expose too little structure for efficient deployment, while a constrained execution path can sacrifice the flexibility needed during discovery. Because execution, differentiation, and abstraction meet in the same software layer, a local convenience can become a downstream performance or portability constraint. The engineering question is not which framework is universally best, but which trade-offs the workload, team, and target machine can afford to make fixed. Understanding frameworks is therefore about reasoning through those system choices rather than learning transient API syntax, which changes with each release while the underlying trade-offs persist. In D·A·M terms, the framework mediates algorithm-machine co-design by turning algorithmic intent and data representation into executable work under machine constraints.

Learning Objectives

Explain how frameworks mediate algorithm-machine co-design through execution, differentiation, and hardware abstraction
Compare execution strategies using dispatch overhead, compilation cost, and deployment constraints
Analyze backward saved-state requirements and explain the storage and recomputation consequences of a supplied activation-checkpointing policy
Implement module abstraction patterns for parameter discovery, mode behavior, serialization, and hooks
Calculate training-step FLOPs, memory traffic, and dispatch overhead to identify fusion and layout bottlenecks
Select TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, or edge runtimes based on model, hardware, team, and deployment requirements

title: The dispatch tax: Python overhead vs. GPU reality
text:
Network Architectures ended by treating architecture selection as a contract with the hardware. A convolutional neural network (CNN) commits the system to spatial locality and weight reuse, and a transformer commits it to attention, matrix multiplications, activation state, and memory traffic. Those commitments fix what work exists. The framework is the layer that decides how that work reaches the machine. A few calls such as logits = model(tokens), loss = criterion(logits, targets), and loss.backward() hide billions of floating-point operations across memory hierarchies, gradients through millions of parameters via automatic differentiation, thousands of GPU kernel launches, and gigabytes of intermediate state. The API looks simple because the framework is acting as a compiler for the silicon contract.
The gap between what and how is wide. A transformer’s attention mechanism requires coordinating computation across memory hierarchies and accelerator cores in patterns where naive implementations can run one to two orders of magnitude slower than optimized ones because of uncoalesced memory accesses (scattered reads the hardware cannot merge into wide memory transactions) and repeated round-trips to high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Implementing these operations from scratch for every model would make deep learning economically infeasible. ML frameworks exist to bridge this gap by lowering abstract model graphs into hardware-aligned execution pipelines that maximize compute unit utilization while minimizing off-chip memory traffic.
A framework is to machine learning what a compiler is to traditional programming. A C compiler translates human-readable code into optimized machine instructions, managing register allocation, instruction scheduling, and memory layout. An ML framework translates high-level model definitions into hardware-specific execution plans, managing kernel fusion, memory reuse, and device placement. The correspondence is operational rather than figurative: modern frameworks incorporate optimizing compilers (such as Accelerated Linear Algebra (XLA) or TorchInductor) that lower graph representations directly to target machine code.
Every ML framework, regardless of API or design philosophy, must solve three core problems. The first is the execution problem: deciding when and how computation runs. A framework can execute operations immediately as written (eager execution1) or first construct a computational graph2 (a record of operations and their data dependencies, developed in section 1.3.2) to optimize before launching device kernels (graph execution). This choice determines the fundamental trade-off between interactive debugging and whole-program compiler optimization.
1 Eager execution: This mode executes each operation immediately, which enables direct debugging with standard tools but sacrifices the global view needed for graph-level optimizations. Without capturing a larger region of computation, an eager runtime cannot fuse across that region or preplan its memory, leaving workload-dependent optimization opportunities for compilers such as torch.compile.2 Computational graph: Optimizing before executing is the design choice that separates graph execution from eager execution. Capturing the program as a data structure lets a framework fuse compatible operations into fewer GPU kernels before execution, reducing launch overhead and intermediate memory traffic. The engineering cost of this visibility is that the executed program differs from the source code, making debugging harder, a trade-off every graph-based framework must justify against the performance gain.With an execution strategy in place, the framework must solve the differentiation problem: computing gradients automatically. Because gradient-based training requires derivatives of a scalar loss with respect to millions or billions of parameters, manual calculus is impossible at scale. Frameworks implement automatic differentiation by registering derivative rules across supported operator compositions, chaining vector-Jacobian products while managing numerical precision and the memory overhead of intermediate activations retained for backward passes.


↩︎ Reverse-mode automatic differentiation and computational graph traversal for gradient computation are established in Gradient computation and backpropagation.

Tillet, Philippe, H. T. Kung, and David Cox. 2019. “Triton: An Intermediate Language and Compiler for Tiled Neural Network Computations.” Proceedings of the 3rd ACM SIGPLAN International Workshop on Machine Learning and Programming Languages, 10–19. https://doi.org/10.1145/3315508.3329973.
The third problem is hardware abstraction: targeting diverse hardware from a single interface. The same model definition should be expressible across CPUs, GPUs, Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), and mobile accelerators, even though each target presents distinct memory hierarchies, instruction sets, and interconnect bandwidths. Within the GPU domain, framework ecosystems increasingly expose custom-kernel languages such as Triton (Tillet et al. 2019), allowing developers to write high-performance, block-level kernels without hand-crafting low-level CUDA or device assembly.
These three problems are tightly coupled: the execution model dictates when differentiation data structures are recorded, while the hardware abstraction layer determines which graph transformations can be lowered to silicon. Unifying execution, differentiation, and hardware abstraction under physical machine constraints requires evaluating frameworks through the governing equation of machine learning performance.

Systems Perspective 7.1: The ML compilerIn the context of the iron law of ML systems (principle \(\ref{pri-iron-law}\)), a framework is a compiler for the silicon contract (principle \(\ref{pri-silicon-contract}\)).
The “source code” is the model architecture (the \(\Operations\) term). The framework’s job is to take this high-level mathematical specification and compile it into a series of hardware-specific kernel launches that:

Minimize data movement \((\DataVolume)\) through techniques such as kernel fusion.
Maximize utilization \((\EfficiencyHw)\) by matching operations to specialized hardware units such as Tensor Cores.
Minimize overhead \((\Latency)\) through efficient asynchronous dispatch and graph capture.

Choosing a framework therefore also chooses the compiler that determines hardware efficiency. Read against the three framework problems, execution strategy bears most directly on \(\Latency\), differentiation on \(\DataVolume\) (and on the operation count \(\Operations\)), and abstraction on \(\EfficiencyHw\). These are emphases rather than exclusive assignments, since fusion, for example, cuts both launches and traffic, and the chapter uses this one mapping throughout. The formal definition below makes that compiler role precise and separates frameworks from numerical libraries such as NumPy.



Definition 7.1: Machine learning frameworks
Machine learning frameworks are software systems that translate high-level mathematical model definitions into hardware-optimized execution plans by managing the computational graph, automatic differentiation, kernel dispatch, and memory allocation across the hardware hierarchy.

Significance: Frameworks shape every iron law term that the model itself does not fix: the bytes moved \((\DataVolume)\), the hardware efficiency achieved \((\EfficiencyHw)\), and the fixed overhead paid \((\Latency)\). Compiler-backed kernel fusion, for example, can eliminate writes and subsequent reads of intermediate values between compatible operations. Fusing a matrix multiplication, bias add, and rectified linear unit (ReLU) changes how the same mathematics reaches hardware without changing the model.
Distinction: Unlike a numerical library such as NumPy, which normally evaluates each operation as it is called, an ML framework can capture or defer execution to analyze a larger computational graph and apply cross-operation optimizations: kernel fusion, memory layout transformations, and parallel scheduling. Those optimizations require visibility beyond separately dispatched operations.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that frameworks are interchangeable API wrappers. Framework choice determines which compiler paths are available. PyTorch can recover graph-level optimization from eager code through torch.compile(), while TensorFlow and JAX commonly rely on XLA-backed compilation paths that lower operations to target hardware. Moving from eager execution to a compiler path can change throughput materially, but the gain depends on model structure, shapes, operator support, and hardware.



An ML framework translates logical intent into physical execution under the constraints of the iron law, deciding how to partition computation across memory hierarchies, when to trade numerical precision for throughput, and how to schedule operations so that whichever term dominates (data movement \(\DataVolume\), arithmetic computation, or launch latency \(\Latency\)) is minimized. The framework is where the governing physics developed throughout this book becomes executable code.
Automating this machinery—recording operation graphs, allocating gradient buffers, traversing dependencies in reverse, and dispatching hardware kernels—did not happen all at once. Execution, differentiation, and abstraction emerged sequentially as responses to scaling bottlenecks in earlier numerical tools, creating a four-decade historical progression from hand-tuned assembly routines to compiled graph runtimes.

Self-Check: Question

A team reports that their model executes correctly on CPU but produces mismatched tensor shapes and silent numerical corruption when switched to a GPU backend because some operators silently default to a different memory layout (such as NCHW versus NHWC). Which of the three fundamental framework problems does this failure most directly expose?

The hardware abstraction problem, because one unified model interface must preserve consistent semantic behavior, memory layouts, and numerical contracts across diverse hardware backends
The execution problem, because the operators were evaluated eagerly instead of being captured into a static graph
The differentiation problem, because the backward pass failed to propagate gradients through non-contiguous strides
A data engineering pipeline defect unrelated to framework runtime responsibilities

Explain how viewing an ML framework as a compiler for the silicon contract—rather than merely a numerical library like NumPy—changes an engineer’s expectations regarding framework selection and optimization under the systems iron law.
True or False: Two frameworks that expose nearly identical user-facing Python tensor APIs and target the same GPU hardware will necessarily provide equivalent graph-level operator fusion and ahead-of-time compilation capabilities.
An engineering organization chose a specialized research framework for rapid prototyping, only to discover later that the framework lacks export paths to their production edge accelerators, requiring months of manual re-implementation. Applying the chapter’s infrastructure-commitment principle, what is the key systems insight?

Framework choice is easily reversible because weight arrays can be loaded into any runtime with zero engineering overhead
Framework selection functions as a durable infrastructure commitment whose reversal cost compounds across model checkpoints, serving runtimes, CI/CD pipelines, and hardware access
The primary failure was selecting an overly compact model architecture that failed to saturate edge accelerator memory
Hardware abstraction layers eliminate all differences between training frameworks and production inference engines

title: The dispatch tax: Python overhead vs. GPU reality
text:
In 1979, writing a matrix multiplication in Fortran that used the hardware efficiently required deep knowledge of cache lines, register scheduling, and vector units. By 2016, a single line of Python (torch.matmul(A, W)) could dispatch to a highly optimized implementation without the programmer knowing the details of the silicon. That compression of effort did not happen in one step; it accumulated across four decades of abstraction, each layer solving a bottleneck that made the previous generation impractical for scaling. The result is a ladder of abstraction where each rung automates what the rung below exposed.
The first rung established reusable hardware primitives (1979–1992). The original Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (BLAS)3 standardized low-level linear-algebra operations (Lawson et al. 1979), while LAPACK4 (Bai et al. 2006) built higher-level numerical factorizations and eigensolvers on top of that foundation. Naive nested loops fail to exploit memory hierarchies: without cache tiling and register blocking, memory bandwidth saturates long before arithmetic units reach peak throughput. BLAS and LAPACK solved this hardware-primitive bottleneck by establishing stable interfaces that let numerical software delegate compute-heavy operations such as matrix multiplication (C = A @ B)5 to vendor libraries tuned for specific cache line sizes, single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) widths, and register files, rather than requiring hand-written assembly for every target architecture.
3 BLAS (basic linear algebra subprograms): The 1979 API specification that forms the bottom rung of the ladder described here; it standardized a fixed set of Fortran-callable vector operations, separating the public routine names from the machine-specific implementation decisions beneath them. Every framework above it inherits the broader version of this bargain: call a standard linear-algebra primitive from any language and let a tuned vendor library target the silicon. For modern general matrix multiply (GEMM) on NVIDIA GPUs, that tuned path is cuBLAS rather than the 1979 BLAS specification itself (NVIDIA 2024a).
NVIDIA. 2024a. cuBLAS: CUDA Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms.

Lawson, Charles L., Richard J. Hanson, David R. Kincaid, and Fred T. Krogh. 1979. “Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms for Fortran Usage.” ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software 5 (3): 308–23. https://doi.org/10.1145/355841.355847.
4 LAPACK (linear algebra package): Extends BLAS by providing a standard API for higher-level routines (SVD, eigendecomposition, least-squares) that vendors implement with chip-specific code layered on top of fast GEMM kernels. This layered design is the architectural pattern every ML framework inherits: high-level operations delegate downward to hand-tuned primitives, so a vendor-optimized LAPACK call can execute over 10\(\times\) faster than a naive implementation without the framework author writing a single line of hardware-specific code.
Bai, Zhaojun, James Demmel, Jack Dongarra, Julien Langou, and Jenny Wang. 2006. “LAPACK.” In Handbook of Linear Algebra. Chapman; Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/9781420010572-75.
5 GEMM: The matrix-matrix primitive behind C = A @ B. Hardware vendors hand-tune GEMM for their specific chips because dense layers, attention projections, and convolution lowering all rely on matrix multiplication, making this one routine a performance floor for many frameworks above it on the ladder. Its high arithmetic intensity makes GEMM the operation most able to approach peak compute throughput, while small or misaligned shapes often fall back to much lower utilization.6 NumPy (numerical Python): In 2005, Travis Oliphant unified two competing Python array libraries (Numeric and Numarray) into a single package, giving the scientific computing community one BLAS-backed array standard at the moment it needed to scale. The “vectorization” contract this created (write logic in Python, execute loops in C/Fortran via BLAS) became the design template for every ML framework that followed: PyTorch tensors and TensorFlow arrays are direct descendants, extending the same \(\TensorAxisCount\)-dimensional array abstraction to GPUs. Python’s role in ML infrastructure inherits much of its shape from this consolidation decision.
Harris, Charles R., K. Jarrod Millman, Stéfan J. van der Walt, Ralf Gommers, Pauli Virtanen, David Cournapeau, Eric Wieser, et al. 2020. “Array Programming with NumPy.” Nature 585 (7825): 357–62. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2649-2.
The second rung introduced unified array abstractions to unlock developer velocity (2005–2006). NumPy6 addressed the productivity barrier of low-level languages by wrapping BLAS and LAPACK in high-level Python (Harris et al. 2020). Under NumPy’s strided array model, Python manages control flow and tensor metadata (shape, strides, and data type), while the underlying C runtime dispatches vector and matrix loops across contiguous memory buffers. This vectorization contract—orchestrating high-level algorithmic intent in an interpreted language while delegating inner loops to compiled native routines—became the architectural template for scientific and numerical computing.
The third rung automated gradient computation (2007–present). Deep learning frameworks such as Theano,7 TensorFlow (Abadi et al. 2016), and PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019) solved the scalability limits of manual differentiation. While numerical packages required practitioners to derive and implement analytical backpropagation gradients by hand—a process error-prone and unmanageable for deep networks—modern frameworks turned automatic differentiation over computational graphs into a core runtime primitive. By capturing operations in a directed acyclic graph during the forward pass, these frameworks automatically construct the backward graph to evaluate vector-Jacobian products, transforming the calculus of the chain rule into automated reverse-mode execution. That automation let the bitter lesson operate at the pace of research. Once a new architecture no longer needed a hand-derived backward pass, general methods that scale with computation could be tried as quickly as their forward functions could be written.
7 Theano: Developed at the Montreal Institute for Learning Algorithms (MILA) under Yoshua Bengio starting in 2007, Theano was an early and influential Python framework that compiled symbolic mathematical expressions into optimized CPU and GPU code via computational graphs (Bergstra et al. 2010; Team et al. 2016). It demonstrated that a Python-defined computation graph could be compiled for GPU execution without requiring the researcher to write CUDA code. Mila ended active development of Theano in 2017 (Mila 2026).
Bergstra, James, Olivier Breuleux, Frédéric Bastien, Pascal Lamblin, Razvan Pascanu, Guillaume Desjardins, Joseph Turian, David Warde-Farley, and Yoshua Bengio. 2010. “Theano: A CPU and GPU Math Compiler in Python.” Proceedings of the Python in Science Conference 4: 18–24. https://doi.org/10.25080/majora-92bf1922-003.

Team, The Theano Development, Rami Al-Rfou, Guillaume Alain, Amjad Almahairi, Christof Angermueller, Dzmitry Bahdanau, Nicolas Ballas, et al. 2016. “Theano: A Python Framework for Fast Computation of Mathematical Expressions.” arXiv Preprint.

Mila. 2026. Open Source Software.

↩︎ The bitter lesson, that general methods which exploit growing computation outlast hand-engineered approaches, is established in The Bitter Lesson.

Figure 1 sequences these numerical computing milestones across four decades (1979–2018), charting the shift from assembly-tuned BLAS and LAPACK routines to NumPy vectorization, symbolic graph capture in Theano and TensorFlow, dynamic dispatch in PyTorch, and functional transformation in JAX.






Figure 1: Computational Library Evolution: A timeline of numerical computing milestones spanning 1979 to 2018. Each era automates what the layer below exposed—from BLAS and LAPACK hardware routines to NumPy vectorized syntax and graph-based automatic differentiation in modern frameworks—trading low-level transparency for developer velocity.



Each generation abstracted away details that consumed engineering effort in the previous one, yet each abstraction introduced new trade-offs. BLAS hid assembly-level optimization but fixed the interface. NumPy hid memory management but required manual differentiation. Modern frameworks hide gradient computation but introduce a choice among execution models. The deeper pattern is that every abstraction hides details by preserving a contract about shape, dtype, device, and sometimes units; when that contract becomes implicit, correct components can still compose into a wrong system.

War Story 7.1: The interface that forgot its units (1999)Context: NASA’s Mars Climate Orbiter depended on ground software, spacecraft software, navigation teams, and contractor interfaces all agreeing on the physical meaning of exchanged values (Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board 1999).
Mechanism: Ground software supplied by Lockheed Martin computed thruster impulse in English units (pound-force seconds), while JPL navigation software consumed the values assuming SI units (newton-seconds)—a 4.45\(\times\) implicit unit mismatch.
Impact: On September 23, 1999, the spacecraft was lost after entering occultation. Its corrected 57 km periapsis, rather than the planned 226 km, was judged too low for survival.
Response: The board recommended unit-consistency checks, specification audits of transferred data, and stronger end-to-end verification of ground software.
Systems lesson: Framework abstractions are valuable because they carry contracts: shape, dtype, device placement, and physical units. If those contracts are implicit, two pieces of correct code can still compose into a wrong system. ML frameworks hit this whenever tensor memory layouts (such as channels-first NCHW [\(\text{Batch} \times \text{Channels} \times \text{Height} \times \text{Width}\)] vs. channels-last NHWC [\(\text{Batch} \times \text{Height} \times \text{Width} \times \text{Channels}\)]), quantization scale factors, or physical feature units differ across pipeline stages, producing plausible outputs that quietly corrupt downstream inference.



Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board. 1999. Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board Phase i Report. National Aeronautics; Space Administration.
Preventing these silent mismatches requires checking contracts somewhere between writing code and running it. A framework can check them as each operation executes, when the failing line and its intermediate values are directly visible, or before execution, when a captured graph can be validated and optimized as a whole. When those checks and optimizations happen is the execution problem. It is the first framework design choice because runtime dispatch and graph capture determine not only the debugging experience but also what optimizations automatic differentiation and hardware mapping can subsequently exploit.
