title: Deployment Paradigm Framework
text:
Given a recommendation engine or wake-word detector, the workload question is which term will bind first on the target hardware. The central analytical tool for answering that silicon-contract question is the iron law of ML systems from Iron Law of ML Systems, restated here in the same notation because every tier in this chapter is analyzed through it. For a serialized execution path, equation 4 adds three costs: \[\Time= \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency \tag{4}\]
Equation 4 decomposes total latency into three terms: data movement \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)\), compute \((\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))\), and fixed overhead \((\Latency)\). For an inference path that executes these stages sequentially, their times add. A single request can also contain overlapping work, so its latency must follow the actual dependencies. In production systems, however, tasks are processed continuously as a stream, and the analysis shifts from single-task latency to identifying which term limits the system. The answer depends on the workload, its execution conditions, and the deployment hardware. A workload is compute bound when its compute term \(\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)\) exceeds its data term \(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\), and memory bound in the reverse case. A model that is compute bound during training may become memory bound during inference; a system that runs efficiently in the cloud may hit power limits on mobile devices. Batch size is one lever that moves a workload between these regimes. Larger batches reuse each loaded weight across more inputs, shifting a memory-bound kernel toward compute-bound behavior, at the price of a larger working set and a longer service time per batch. In pipelined production serving, hardware concurrency alters this linear sum: faster stages hide behind whichever subsystem saturates first.


The iron law quantifies the cost of each term; the bottleneck principle identifies which term governs system throughput. In a pipelined ML workload, identifying the system bottleneck matters because speeding a nonlimiting stage does not increase ideal steady-state throughput while the slowest stage remains unchanged. Modern accelerators use pipelined execution to overlap data movement with computation: while the accelerator computes on batch \(\BatchIndex\), the memory system prefetches batch \(\BatchIndex+1\). Once the pipeline fills, different requests occupy different stages. Under ideal overlap, the slowest stage sets the interval between completions, although each request still traverses its dependent stages. Equation 5 extends the pipelined form from Iron Law of ML Systems with one more overlapped stage, \(\IoTransferTime\), the time to transfer data over a storage or network link. Here the left-hand side is the steady-state time per completed task, with fixed overhead treated as nonoverlapped; equality requires ideal overlap of the other stages: \[ \PipelinedExecutionTime\ge \max\left(\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}, \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}, \IoTransferTime\right) + \Latency  \tag{5}\]

\(\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}\) (Memory): Time to move data between memory and processor.
\(\frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}\) (Compute): Time to execute calculations.
\(\IoTransferTime\) (I/O): Time to move data over a storage or network link (including offloading to a remote server).
\(\Latency\) (Overhead): Fixed latency (kernel launch, runtime overhead).

When a system is memory bound \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth > \Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))\), faster processors \((\PeakRate)\) do not raise ideal pipeline throughput while memory remains the slowest stage, just as widening a highway cannot help traffic constrained by a narrow bridge. Shortening a sequential compute stage can still reduce an individual request’s latency. Engineers must identify the dominant term before optimizing. The iron law quantifies the cost of each ingredient; the bottleneck principle identifies the speed of the assembly line. As a rule of thumb, use the additive form in equation 4 for a single task’s serialized path, and the max form in equation 5 for an ideally overlapped continuous stream. Actual dependencies determine which stages can overlap.



The bottleneck principle reduces optimization to identifying the dominant constraint for a given workload. The answer depends on all three D·A·M axes at once: the data a request carries, the algorithm’s arithmetic and memory demands, and the machine that executes it. Different deployment environments create different bottlenecks along these axes, so the same model family can require different engineering when it moves from a cloud server with terabytes of memory to a microcontroller with kilobytes. Classifying workloads by what binds them first yields four workload archetypes.5 These are not model categories; they are recurring physical bottlenecks that determine which engineering moves can help. Two of them are named by the iron law’s own terms. The other two are bound by preconditions the time equation assumes are already met, that the working set fits in memory and that the energy budget can pay for the run, which is why a capacity or energy limit can decide feasibility before any term of equation 4 is evaluated.
5 Workload archetype: A classification of ML workloads by their dominant bottleneck, either a term of the iron law or a memory-capacity or energy precondition it assumes is met, rather than by their model family. The distinction matters because the optimization strategy differs fundamentally: a compute-bound workload benefits from faster arithmetic \((\PeakRate)\), while a bandwidth-bound workload benefits from wider memory buses or fewer bytes moved through reuse, fusion, compression, or lower precision. Misidentifying the archetype wastes optimization effort on the wrong term of the iron law, as when teams add accelerator FLOP/s to a memory-bound inference pipeline and obtain little improvement while memory transfer remains dominant.The first split, between the two iron-law terms, separates arithmetic-bound systems from data-movement-bound systems. A compute beast performs many calculations per byte loaded, so progress comes from higher arithmetic throughput, better utilization, and more parallel execution; large neural-network training is the canonical case. A bandwidth hog, by contrast, waits on dense weight or activation movement, so wider memory buses and better data reuse matter more than additional peak FLOP/s; autoregressive text generation illustrates this regime.
The second split covers workloads where the binding constraint is not a term of the time equation at all. Sparse scatter workloads are dominated by irregular table lookups and poor cache locality, so memory capacity, access latency, and communication shape performance in recommendation systems with massive embedding tables. Tiny constraint workloads face the opposite envelope: energy per inference and memory footprint, not raw speed, determine whether always-on sensing can run at all.

Lighthouse 2.1: Five reference workloads
Lighthouse models put the iron law into practice introduced five lighthouse models by the system bottleneck each isolates (Lighthouse Models as Reference Workloads); table 2 pairs each with a representative workload archetype and deployment paradigm. The classifications describe operating regimes: batched image processing can emphasize arithmetic, single-request text generation can emphasize weight transfers, and a large recommendation table can exceed local memory capacity. Changing batch size, model size, or hardware can change the binding constraint. The two perspectives on MobileNetV2 align under this principle. The introduction classified MobileNetV2 under latency and power because those physical limits defined its design envelope. In table 2, it illustrates an efficient vision workload operating in a compute-bound regime when its convolutional stages sustain arithmetic saturation, but with operations sized down to fit mobile thermal and energy envelopes. Whether arithmetic throughput or memory bandwidth ultimately binds MobileNetV2 on a specific device depends on target hardware balance, precision, and batching, as the roofline analyses in section 1.3 demonstrate. Lighthouse Roster: Model Biographies provides full architectural details and model biographies.



Table 2: Five Lighthouse Models: Recurring workloads used throughout the book to ground the iron law in concrete practice. Each lighthouse pairs an archetype (Compute Beast, Bandwidth Hog, Sparse Scatter, Tiny Constraint) with the deployment paradigm where it predominantly runs, illustrating a distinct resource constraint under representative execution conditions.

These archetypes map onto deployment paradigms. Large-scale compute beasts (training) and sparse scatter workloads gravitate to cloud data centers; compact vision workloads operating in efficient compute-bound regimes such as MobileNetV2 can fit mobile and edge devices; bandwidth hogs run in the cloud unless a smaller model fits locally; and tiny constraint workloads belong on microcontrollers.
The archetypes become concrete once each lighthouse is given its cost. The image classifier ResNet-50 spends approximately 8.2 GFLOP per image on 25.6 million parameters, which occupy 102.4 MB at FP32 (He et al. 2016). That regular, compute-dense structure makes it the canonical benchmark for hardware accelerator performance.

He, Kaiming, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, and Jian Sun. 2016. “Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition.” 2016 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 770–78. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2016.90.

Radford, Alec, Jeffrey Wu, Rewon Child, David Luan, Dario Amodei, and Ilya Sutskever. 2019. Language Models Are Unsupervised Multitask Learners. OpenAI.

Touvron, Hugo, Thibaut Lavril, Gautier Izacard, Xavier Martinet, Marie-Anne Lachaux, Timothée Lacroix, Baptiste Rozière, et al. 2023. “LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2302.13971.

Pope, Reiner, Sholto Douglas, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Jacob Devlin, James Bradbury, Jonathan Heek, Kefan Xiao, Shivani Agrawal, and Jeff Dean. 2023. “Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference.” Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems (MLSys) 5: 606–24.
The language models GPT-2/Llama exemplify autoregressive text generation (Radford et al. 2019; Touvron et al. 2023). These models generate text one token at a time. Because multi-billion parameter models exceed on-chip cache, weights reside in external memory; generating text token-by-token for one request at a time forces the processor to stream the weights across the memory bus for each token with little reuse across inputs (1.5 billion parameters for GPT-2, 7 billion–70 billion parameters for Llama). This sequential access pattern creates an autoregressive bottleneck that shapes serving cost (Pope et al. 2023).


↪ Continuous batching and KV-cache paging, the runtime mechanisms that serve token-by-token generation, are developed in Continuous batching.

Naumov, Maxim, Dheevatsa Mudigere, Hao-Jun Michael Shi, Jianyu Huang, Narayanan Sundaraman, Jongsoo Park, Xiaodong Wang, et al. 2019. “Deep Learning Recommendation Model for Personalization and Recommendation Systems.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1906.00091.
The recommendation lighthouse, DLRM, represents the embedding-heavy recommendation workload behind large-scale “You might also like” systems (Naumov et al. 2019). It maps users and items to embedding vectors stored in tables that can exceed 100 GB of embeddings, making memory capacity rather than computation the binding constraint.
The mobile lighthouse, MobileNetV2, performs the same image classification task as ResNet-50 while cutting its computation by 13.7× (Sandler et al. 2018). It gets there by restructuring the image-filtering layers, splitting each expensive filtering step into two much cheaper ones (depthwise separable convolutions). That reduction makes it a candidate for real-time inference within a smartphone’s 3–5 W envelope; the implementation and workload determine whether it meets the deadline.

Sandler, Mark, Andrew Howard, Menglong Zhu, Andrey Zhmoginov, and Liang-Chieh Chen. 2018. “MobileNetV2: Inverted Residuals and Linear Bottlenecks.” 2018 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 4510–20. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2018.00474.

↪ How depthwise separable convolutions factor one filtering step into two cheaper ones is developed in Efficient architectures: Depthwise separable convolutions.

Zhang, Yundong, Naveen Suda, Liangzhen Lai, and Vikas Chandra. 2017. Hello Edge: Keyword Spotting on Microcontrollers.

The TinyML lighthouse, keyword spotting (KWS), represents the always-on sensing archetype. KWS systems detect short trigger phrases with compact models built for resource-constrained microcontrollers (Zhang et al. 2017). The lighthouse workload has approximately 200K parameters, about 200 KB at INT8 (stored in flash), placing it in the kilobyte-memory, milliwatt-budget TinyML regime.
A smart doorbell, a TinyML scenario that recurs through later chapters alongside the five lighthouses, applies the same always-on pattern to vision. A visual wake-word model, a small classifier that answers only whether a person is in view, runs on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, the TinyML platform of table 4. Its feasibility is screened in two levels, storage first and latency second. At level 1, the 0.5 MB of 16-bit weights occupy 11.9 percent of the 4 MB flash. Passing this storage check does not establish complete memory fit, because intermediate results and runtime state must also fit in SRAM, the two-tier split that section 1.7.1 develops. Level 2 applies the iron law. The model needs 25 MFLOP per frame, and the microcontroller sustains about 0.25 GFLOP/s at this precision, so compute takes 100 ms; about 1 ms of fixed overhead brings the total to 101 ms. That estimate clears the scenario’s canonical 200 ms budget; sensor acquisition and any data movement omitted by the estimate must still be checked. A more responsive chime with a 50 ms budget changes the verdict without changing the model, and figure 2 plots that tightened case. Each bar is demand over supply, so flash stays far below the saturation line while latency reaches 202 percent of its budget. Storage was never the constraint that decided feasibility; latency is.














Figure 2: Smart Doorbell Constraint Scorecard: Each bar is demand over supply, so the dashed line marks the point where a level is exactly saturated. The model occupies a small fraction of the ESP32-S3’s 4 MB flash budget (Level 1: PASS), but its 101 ms latency (25 MFLOP of compute plus fixed overhead) is twice a tightened 50 ms budget for a responsive chime (Level 2: FAIL), even though it clears the scenario’s canonical 200 ms budget.



The range in compute requirements and memory footprints explains why no single deployment paradigm fits all workloads. A keyword spotter can operate with roughly 20 MFLOP per inference and about 200 KB of INT8 weights, while ResNet-50 requires about 8.2 GFLOP per image and roughly 102.4 MB of FP32 weights. The reference DLRM example already reaches 100 GB, and Meta has demonstrated scaling recommendation models to 100 TB using embedding offloading (Park et al. 2024). Language models add a bandwidth-dominated regime: billions of parameters streamed repeatedly from memory during autoregressive inference.

When analyzing ML system performance, when should an engineer apply the additive form of the iron law (\(T = \frac{D_{\text{vol}}}{\text{BW}} + \frac{O}{R_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{hw}}} + L_{\text{lat}}\)) versus the bottleneck principle’s max form (\(T_{\text{pipelined}} \ge \max\left(\frac{D_{\text{vol}}}{\text{BW}}, \frac{O}{R_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{hw}}}, T_{\text{IO}}\right) + L_{\text{lat}}\))?

Use the additive form when batch size is greater than 128, and the max form when batch size equals 1.

title: Deployment Paradigm Framework
text:
The iron law and workload archetypes gain practical meaning when matched against real hardware. The single-node stack connects the application’s requirements to the software that executes the work and the hardware limits beneath it.


Connecting workload requirements to hardware limits requires an architectural model of the single-node stack, which refines the machine side of the D·A·M taxonomy for one host while data and algorithm enter through workload requirements. At the top of the stack, the application defines the mission through a training-throughput or inference-latency target. The ML framework translates model code into executable operations. The operating system, drivers, and runtime coordinate resources and transfers between host memory and accelerator memory. The hardware itself, defined by HBM capacity, memory bandwidth, intra-node interconnects such as NVLink that connect accelerators, and compute throughput, sets the physical limits, with the memory wall as a recurring constraint.


↪ How an ML framework turns model code into executed operations, eagerly or through a captured graph, is developed in Three execution strategies.
The hardware layer fixes the terms on offer to any model: a memory bandwidth \((\Bandwidth)\), a peak compute rate \((\PeakRate)\), and a fixed overhead \((\Latency)\). The silicon contract names the bargain struck over these terms. The hardware offers them, and the workload and its execution conditions determine which resource limits progress first. This chapter works with the hardware’s half, asking which term a given platform makes scarce; the model architecture’s half, the wager on which resource to saturate, is stated as a principle (\(\ref{pri-silicon-contract}\)) once model architectures enter the book. The stack helps locate where a constraint enters: the application sets the deadline, the software determines how work reaches the hardware, and the hardware limits how quickly that work can execute.


↩︎ The iron law of ML systems and its decomposition of end-to-end latency are established in Iron Law of ML Systems.



The match proceeds from coarse to fine. The coarse test asks whether an operation can fit inside the latency budget at all. The fine test asks which hardware resource limits the operations that do fit, and its answer depends on system balance, the ratio of peak compute throughput to memory bandwidth and I/O capacity on a given platform.
Operation latencies supply the coarse test, and they turn latency-vs-throughput trade-offs into decisions through concrete numbers. They span roughly eight orders of magnitude, from about a nanosecond for an on-chip cache hit or a single accelerator multiply, through milliseconds for one mobile vision inference, to tens or hundreds of milliseconds for a cross-region network call. Numbers to Know collects the memory-hierarchy and network round-trip anchors along with illustrative application latency budgets. The span matters because of one strict rule: an operation with latency \(> \CompletionDeadline\) cannot appear on the critical path of a system whose latency budget is \(\CompletionDeadline\) ms.6
6 Critical path: The longest sequential chain of dependent operations in a pipeline. The decision rule in the triggering sentence is strict: if a 200 ms cross-region network call appears anywhere on the critical path, a system with a 100 ms total budget is guaranteed to fail regardless of how fast every other stage runs. Model inference need not be the longest stage; preprocessing and postprocessing can dominate, making the critical path longer than model execution alone suggests.

In this example, batching moves the workload from the memory-bound side toward the compute ceiling.

With the critical path settled, system balance decides which resource limits the operations that remain. Roofline analysis classifies bottlenecks by comparing a workload’s arithmetic intensity, the operations performed per byte moved (FLOP/byte) that the memory wall made decisive, against the hardware machine balance point \((\PeakRate / \Bandwidth)\), the ridge point introduced with the iron law in Iron Law of ML Systems. The framing is informal here; The Roofline model develops the model, defining arithmetic intensity formally and deriving the ridge point that separates the memory-bound and compute-bound regimes. In that framing, the same ResNet-50 model can shift from compute-bound training behavior at high batch sizes to more memory-sensitive single-image inference at batch=1. Deployment paradigm selection must account for this shift.
The batch-size shift is one instance of a broader change between execution phases, in which physical constraints reconfigure all three D·A·M axes at once. Training updates model weights from batches of examples; serving applies fixed weights to new inputs. Table 3 contrasts typical training and latency-sensitive serving demands; cloud serving can also batch requests for throughput.



Table 3: D·A·M \(\times\) Phase: The same model imposes starkly different demands on Data, Algorithm, and Machine depending on whether the system is training or serving. When bottlenecks shift unexpectedly, check which phase is currently being optimized.

A quantitative comparison applies this analysis to ResNet-50 inference on a high-end data center accelerator and a mobile neural processing unit (NPU). Treat these as point-in-time hardware anchors: the arithmetic is about compute rate, memory bandwidth, and batch size.

Napkin Math 2.1: ResNet-50 on cloud vs. mobile
Problem: Is ResNet-50 inference compute bound or memory bound on (a) a high-end data center accelerator (an NVIDIA A100) and (b) a flagship mobile NPU?
Given (from lighthouse models):

ResNet-50: 8.2 GFLOP per inference, 25.6 million parameters (102.4 MB FP32, 51.2 MB FP16)

Analysis:
(a) Cloud data-center accelerator (batch=1, FP16)
The analytical model assumes 56.3 MB moved per inference, including weights and activation traffic. This is a modeled transfer volume, not the stored parameter footprint; reuse and runtime choices can change it.

Peak compute: 312 TFLOP/s (FP16)
Memory bandwidth: 2.04 TB/s
Compute time: \(\IronLawComputeTime\) = \(\frac{8.20 \times 10^{9}}{3.12 \times 10^{14}}\) = 0.026 ms
Memory time (weights plus activations): \(\IronLawMemoryTime\) = \(\frac{5.63 \times 10^{7}}{2.04 \times 10^{12}}\) = 0.028 ms
Result: Bottleneck = Memory (1.1× slower than compute)
Ridge point: \(\PeakRate/\Bandwidth\) = 312 TFLOP/s ÷ 2.04 TB/s ≈ 153 FLOP/byte.
Analysis: Arithmetic intensity = \(\frac{8.20 \times 10^{9}}{5.63 \times 10^{7}}\) = 146 FLOP/byte, just below the ridge point, so the workload is memory bound; above the ridge it would be compute bound. For single-image inference, the low batch size yields limited reuse, explaining why even high-throughput accelerators can be memory bound at batch = 1. Both times use peak rates (efficiency \(\EfficiencyHw = 1\) and full bandwidth), so they are lower bounds; because this workload sits close to the ridge, the efficiencies a real kernel achieves decide which term dominates in practice.

(b) Mobile: Flagship NPU (batch=1, INT8)
At INT8, the analytical model assumes 28.2 MB moved per inference, including weights and activation traffic. The INT8 weight footprint below is only one component of that transfer volume.

Peak compute: ~35 TOPS (INT8)—representative of modern mobile NPUs
Memory bandwidth: ~51.2 GB/s (LPDDR5)
Model size: 25.6 MB (INT8 quantized)
Compute time: \(\IronLawComputeTime\) = \(\frac{8.20 \times 10^{9} \text{ INT8 ops}}{3.50 \times 10^{13} \text{ INT8 ops/s}}\) = 0.23 ms
Memory time (weights plus activations): \(\IronLawMemoryTime\) = \(\frac{2.82 \times 10^{7}}{5.12 \times 10^{10}}\) = 0.55 ms
Result: Bottleneck = Memory (2.3× slower than compute)

Systems insight: Under these peak-rate assumptions, both platforms are memory bound for single-image inference. The A100’s faster memory bandwidth (2.04 TB/s vs. 51.2 GB/s = 39.8×) gives roughly 19.9× lower modeled memory-transfer time under the stated FP16 and INT8 traffic assumptions; this ratio is not a measured end-to-end inference speedup. This explains why byte-reduction and lower-precision techniques can beat simply buying more peak FLOP/s for deployment.
ResNet-50 becomes compute bound when batching and data reuse raise computation per byte moved above the hardware balance point, \(\ArithmeticIntensity > \PeakRate/\Bandwidth\), where \(\ArithmeticIntensity = \Operations/\DataVolume\). With ideal reuse during batched inference, each weight is transferred across the memory bus once and used across all \(\BatchSize\) samples in the batch. This amortizes the weight transfer over \(\BatchSize\) inputs, increasing the arithmetic intensity until computation time overtakes memory-transfer time. The crossover is architecture- and implementation-dependent because activation traffic, input/output movement, cache reuse, and runtime execution details all change the effective bytes moved per inference.


The four deployment paradigms gain precision when grounded in concrete hardware. Where table 1 defined the paradigms by operating regime, table 4 places one real platform in each and pairs it with the per-device envelope that marks the tier.7 The example-platform and power columns describe complete systems, including a cloud pod, while the tier compute and bandwidth columns describe per-device envelopes. The following spans compare those complete examples, not equivalent individual chips. Memory drops from 128 TB (cloud) to 512 KB (TinyML), a 250 million-fold reduction. Power spans nine orders of magnitude, from about 3 MW for the cloud pod to the TinyML tier’s average-power target of < 1 mW, and hardware cost spans six, from multimillion-dollar clusters to $10 microcontrollers. Together with facility overheads such as power usage effectiveness (PUE),8 these spreads decide which paradigm can serve a workload economically, and they explain why model compression becomes essential as the budget tightens.
7 ML hardware cost spectrum: AI infrastructure spans six orders of magnitude in cost, from $10 microcontrollers to multi-million-dollar accelerator clusters. This million-fold range means deployment paradigm selection is simultaneously a physics decision and an economics decision. Even within individual-device choices, the same accuracy target may be achievable on a low-cost microcontroller only after substantial model reduction, or on an expensive data-center accelerator with a much larger resource budget, with fundamentally different latency, power, and operational cost profiles.8 Power usage effectiveness (PUE): PUE is total facility energy divided by IT equipment energy over the same measurement period. It captures facility overhead, including cooling and power distribution. Even a PUE of 1.06 leaves substantial noncompute power at data-center scale. TinyML does not require dedicated facility cooling, although sensing, communication, conversion losses, and sleep power still contribute to its complete system-energy budget. These device-level costs sit outside PUE.The hardware spectrum turns the bottleneck diagnosis into a fit test. These platforms are products of decades of hardware evolution, from floating-point coprocessors in the 1980s through graphics processors in the 2000s to today’s domain-specific AI accelerators. Here the consequence matters most: each workload must be matched to the tier whose compute, bandwidth, power, and cost envelope it can satisfy.


↪ The progression from floating-point coprocessors to domain-specific AI accelerators is developed in Specialized computing.

Envelope figures mark a paradigm’s typical class rather than a hard ceiling. The DGX Spark sits at the high end of the edge spectrum as a compact workstation example; most edge deployments use far smaller devices. Systems Perspective 2.1: System balance across paradigmsThe last column of table 4 reads each tier through the pipelined bound in equation 5. For cloud and edge the binding constraint is a term of that bound; for mobile and TinyML it is a limit the time equation leaves out, and in every tier the dominant constraint sets the optimization strategy. Compute-bound cloud training rewards higher accelerator utilization and larger batches. Memory-bound large language model (LLM) decode (token-by-token generation) and memory-bound edge inference reward fewer bytes moved, through smaller models, lower precision, and more reuse per loaded weight; a faster accelerator helps them little. Mobile adds an implicit energy term, because battery energy is power integrated over time and heat caps sustained power, so lower precision and duty cycling pay off twice. TinyML faces a precondition before any term applies: weights and code must fit in flash, while activations and runtime state must fit in SRAM. Compact models and low-precision arithmetic help meet those budgets. Bottleneck diagnostic maps each dominant term to the optimizations that work and the ones that are wasted, turning this diagnosis into an action plan.


Each paradigm is therefore an operating envelope with different resource budgets, and moving from warehouse data centers down to microcontrollers traces a physical gradient that trades raw compute throughput for energy and memory efficiency. The four sections that follow walk that gradient one tier at a time, and each asks the same four questions, which the constraint map in each section draws as four branches: which constraint binds, how the system responds, where the paradigm fails, and which workloads fit. Because that structure is shared, each section concentrates on what is distinctive about its tier and on the one or two calculations that decide whether a workload belongs there.

Self-Check: Question

Why is single-image (batch=1) ResNet-50 inference memory-bound on both a high-end cloud accelerator (NVIDIA A100) and a mobile NPU (iPhone 15 Pro)?

ResNet-50 contains dynamic control flow that causes branching stalls on SIMD execution units.
Both platforms lack matrix multiplication coprocessors, forcing scalar CPU execution.
At batch=1, model weights must be loaded from memory once per single image without weight reuse across batch items, keeping arithmetic intensity below each platform’s hardware balance point (\(R_{\text{peak}}/\text{BW}\)).
The activations at batch=1 exceed the total high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and SRAM capacities of both devices.

Why does a convolutional neural network (e.g., ResNet-50) shift from a compute-bound regime during cloud training to a memory-bound regime during single-sample (\(\text{batch}=1\)) edge inference?
An ML service SLA guarantees a total end-to-end response time of 100 ms. The pipeline involves client preprocessing, a cross-region network RPC, model inference, and postprocessing. According to critical path latency principles, why will this system fail if a cross-region network call taking 120 ms is placed on the synchronous critical path?

The ML framework compiler will refuse to lower the graph if network RPC operations are detected.
Cross-region RPCs corrupt the numerical precision of FP16 tensors during serialization.
A cross-region network call reduces the accelerator compute throughput (\(R_{\text{peak}}\)) by half.
The critical path is the longest sequential chain of dependent operations; any single stage exceeding 100 ms guarantees the end-to-end SLA will be breached regardless of how fast all other stages execute.

What is the hardware balance point (or roofline ridge point) of an accelerator, and what does it tell an ML systems engineer about whether a workload will be compute-bound or memory-bound?
For batch-1 LLM decode in the cloud and for most edge inference, the iron-law term that binds first is memory ____ rather than peak compute, so a faster accelerator alone yields little speedup.

title: Deployment Paradigm Framework
text:
Consider the estimated resources needed to train GPT-3:9 3,634.3 PFLOP-days of computation, equivalent to 10,000 V100 GPUs running for approximately 15 days at the reported sustained rate, and about 1.3 GWh of electricity (Patterson et al. 2021). A PFLOP-day is \(10^{15}\) FLOP/s sustained for one day, about \(8.6 \times 10^{19}\) FLOPs, so this total is the same few hundred zettaFLOPs estimated from the model’s parameter and token counts in The deep learning era and the infrastructure bottleneck. At the hardware rates used in that estimate, a smartphone or edge server could not have completed this training run on a practical schedule. It required a data-center-scale cluster with enough aggregate compute, memory, and storage. That bill is the bitter lesson paid in hardware. General methods that improve with computation keep winning, and the computation they consume concentrates wherever power, cooling, and accelerators can be pooled. Cloud ML rests on this proposition. When latency can be tolerated, it offers computational scale that no other paradigm can match.
9 Large language model (LLM) training scale: Only centralized data centers can aggregate enough \(\PeakRate\) for 3,634.3 PFLOP-days training runs (Patterson et al. 2021), but training location does not determine serving location. A trained model or a smaller derived version can later run near users and sensors.
Patterson, David, Joseph Gonzalez, Quoc Le, Chen Liang, Lluis-Miquel Munguia, Daniel Rothchild, David So, Maud Texier, and Jeff Dean. 2021. “Carbon Emissions and Large Neural Network Training.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2104.10350.

↩︎ The bitter lesson, the volume’s account of why compute-scaled general methods keep winning, is established in The Bitter Lesson.
10 Cloud as utility computing: The utility model allows providers to offer a specialized hardware portfolio that many organizations could not economically maintain themselves. This provides direct, on-demand access to the specific architectures required by each workload archetype: dense accelerator pods for compute beasts, HBM-equipped nodes for bandwidth hogs, and high-memory systems with fast interconnects for sparse scatter. A team can rent access to specialized accelerators rather than purchase and maintain the entire installation.
Centralizing these resources under a utility model10 allows providers to assemble specialized accelerator topologies tailored to distinct hardware demands. This infrastructure serves as the natural home for three of the four workload archetypes: compute beast workloads like ResNet training that demand sustained TFLOP/s across thousands of accelerators, bandwidth hog workloads like large language model inference that benefit from TB/s HBM bandwidth, and sparse scatter workloads like recommendation systems that require terabytes of embedding tables and high-bandwidth interconnects for all-to-all communication patterns.
Cloud deployments scale from single-accelerator instances to warehouse-scale clusters, but systems engineering at every one of these scales begins on a single node, with memory bus saturation, PCIe and NVLink bandwidth, and accelerator utilization inside one machine.

Definition 2.1: Cloud ML
Cloud machine learning is the deployment paradigm that trades latency for elastic compute by locating ML workloads in centralized data centers, decoupling computational capacity from the physical location of data sources and users.

Significance: Cloud deployment dominates the \(\PeakRate\) term: a cloud region can pool thousands of accelerators, with access governed by capacity, quotas, and cost. The trade-off is the \(\Latency\) term: a minimum round-trip latency of 10–100 ms (set by the speed of light over continental distances) makes those distant cloud paths infeasible for workloads requiring sub-10 ms response.
Distinction: Unlike edge ML, which prioritizes local response and data locality at fixed \(\PeakRate\), cloud ML prioritizes elastic \(\PeakRate\) at the cost of variable \(\Latency\).
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that cloud ML is “unlimited compute.” In reality, the distance penalty \((\Latency)\) and the ingestion bottleneck \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)\) are physics constraints that no software optimization can eliminate, setting a hard floor on response time for any workload whose data originates outside the data center.



Figure 3 diagrams the cloud computing trade-off across four operational branches, tracing how pooling elastic accelerators and sharding models overcome local capacity ceilings while encountering hard failure boundaries in speed-of-light propagation latency and internet dependence.






Figure 3: Cloud ML Constraint Map: Centralized infrastructure solves the scale problem for compute beasts, bandwidth hogs, and sparse scatter workloads, but it introduces the distance, dependency, privacy, and cost constraints that determine when cloud ML stops being the right deployment target.



Workloads that thrive in this regime (such as asynchronous fraud detection, batch recommendation updates, and large language model pretraining) tolerate this bargain because scale matters more than instantaneous response. When an application requires real-time control, however, network latency stops being an engineering inconvenience and becomes a hard physical barrier. The light-barrier calculation already ruled out a cross-country data center for a 10 ms budget; the sharper question is whether a regional data center, much closer to the machine it protects, fares any better.

Napkin Math 2.2: The distance penaltyProblem: Consider a real-time safety monitor for a robotic arm on a factory floor. The safety logic requires a 10 ms end-to-end response time to prevent injury, so the distance penalty imposed by the light barrier matters. The model runs in a regional cloud data center 1,500 km away, less than half the cross-country distance. Can the safety budget be met?
Physics:

Light in fiber: ~200,000 km/s.
Round-trip propagation: (1,500 km \(\times\) 2)/200,000 km/s = 15 ms.
Result: Round-trip propagation alone requires 15 ms, exceeding the 10 ms end-to-end budget by 5 ms before the model performs any inference.

Systems insight: The specified regional cloud path misses the budget on propagation alone and is therefore infeasible. Running the model beside the arm removes that remote propagation term, but the complete local sensing, inference, and control path must still be checked against the deadline.




Cloud ML concentrates computational resources at physical dimensions no local device approaches. TPU supercomputer designs organize thousands of specialized accelerator chips into data-center-scale systems that deliver PFLOP/s-to-EFLOP/s reduced-precision throughput (Jouppi et al. 2023), orders of magnitude beyond the edge and mobile rows of table 4.
11 Tensor processing unit (TPU): An application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) designed for operations common in ML, especially matrix multiplication. PFLOP/s-to-EFLOP/s figures describe aggregated TPU systems rather than one chip. Specialization trades general-purpose flexibility for workload-dependent efficiency; its advantage over a GPU depends on the model, numerical format, and systems being compared (Jouppi et al. 2023).
Jouppi, Norm, George Kurian, Sheng Li, Peter Ma, Rahul Nagarajan, Lifeng Nai, Nishant Patil, et al. 2023. “TPU v4: An Optically Reconfigurable Supercomputer for Machine Learning with Hardware Support for Embeddings.” Proceedings of the 50th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1145/3579371.3589350.
Figure 4 captures the physical reality of warehouse-scale infrastructure, showing aisles of liquid-cooled racks packed with thousands of interconnected TPU accelerator chips11 and dense optical cabling bundles that draw megawatts to sustain exaFLOP-scale matrix throughput. That physical scale is what makes training on hundreds of terabytes of data practical.


↪ How training extends beyond a single node across distributed workers is developed in Scaling beyond a single node.






Figure 4: Cloud Data Center Scale: Dedicated accelerator facilities aggregate thousands of specialized TPU chips in liquid-cooled racks to deliver exaFLOP-scale matrix throughput. This centralized infrastructure makes large-scale model training and high-throughput serving viable, but incurs megawatt-scale power consumption and speed-of-light network distance penalties. Image source: (Pichai 2023).


Pichai, Sundar. 2023. Introducing Gemini: Our Largest and Most Capable AI Model.


Centralization also changes how models are served and governed. Cloud APIs make trained models accessible worldwide across mobile, web, and IoT platforms. Shared infrastructure enables engineering teams to collaborate with unified version control, while pay-as-you-go pricing models12 convert upfront capital expenditure (CapEx) into usage-based operational expenditure (OpEx) that scales with demand.
12 Pay-as-you-go pricing: A cloud economic model where users pay for billable allocated accelerator-hours rather than hardware owned. Idle time can still be billed while an instance remains allocated; busy utilization alone does not determine the charge. Sustained allocation can cost more than amortized on-premises hardware, but table 5 illustrates only a partial budget under stated assumptions, not a matched total-cost crossover.Scale does not make the cloud universally superior. The data-gravity principle (\(\ref{pri-data-gravity}\)) explains why. Shipping a dataset of size \(\DataVolume\) over a network link of bandwidth \(\NetworkBandwidth\) takes \(\DataVolume/\NetworkBandwidth\), a time that grows with the data, while shipping the computation (a model and its code) costs roughly the same however much data waits at the other end. As data volume grows, moving the data to a remote cluster therefore eventually costs more than moving the computation to the data. Napkin math: The physics of data gravity works through the transfer arithmetic, and the edge section applies the same comparison to a single request under a deadline. The deployment paradigm is dictated by the binding physical constraint, not by the largest available throughput.



For latency-sensitive workloads, the distance penalty is the cloud’s most consequential cost, and network jitter makes it unpredictable as well as large. Three further costs follow from centralization: the exposure of data the cloud must receive, spending that scales with use, and dependence on the network.
Privacy and security pose additional boundaries for cloud deployment. Transmitting sensitive data to remote data centers expands the disclosure surface and complicates regulatory compliance. Organizations handling data subject to regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)13 or the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)14 must select, document, and maintain safeguards appropriate to the data, system, and applicable legal duties. Privacy-preserving approaches can reduce how much sensitive data leaves its original environment, but they complement rather than replace infrastructure controls.
13 GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation): Article 17 provides a right to erasure when specified grounds apply (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016). For an ML system, an erasure request requires tracing where the person’s data persists across source stores, derived features, logs, caches, and model artifacts. Retraining may be one remediation, but the regulation does not prescribe retraining every model that encountered the data.
European Parliament, and Council of the European Union. 2016. Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016. Official Journal of the European Union.
14 HIPAA: The Security Rule requires regulated entities to implement reasonable and appropriate administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic protected health information, including access and audit controls (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 2005). The rule is technology-neutral and does not mandate confidential-computing enclaves; concrete controls and their performance overhead depend on the system’s risk analysis and implementation.
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. 2005. “Summary of the HIPAA Security Rule.”
15 Total cost of ownership (TCO): Quantifies the gap between sticker price and true system cost by including all direct and indirect costs (power, cooling, labor) over a system’s lifetime, trading upfront capital expense (CapEx) against recurring operational expense (OpEx). For an on-premises GPU, the purchase price is only one component of the three-year TCO, alongside operating costs.Cost management introduces operational complexity because cloud infrastructure converts upfront hardware procurement into continuous operational expenses. Comparing paradigms by raw accelerator hourly rates obscures the cumulative expenses of network egress, persistent storage, and managed orchestration. Sound architectural evaluation demands total cost of ownership (TCO)15 analysis, trading initial capital expenditure against recurring operational maintenance across the system’s operational lifecycle.
A vision system serves 1M daily inferences at ResNet-50 scale (10 ms latency, 100 KB response). The TCO16 analysis begins with an illustrative budget spanning 3 years. It includes the listed components rather than a complete, matched TCO. Cloud operating labor, edge redundancy, installation, and failure recovery are not priced, and comparable capacity and availability have not been established. The 4 instances are a provisioning choice (redundancy and headroom for traffic peaks), not a throughput requirement. Table 5 itemizes the annual GPU, network, load-balancer, and observability costs of this fixed-capacity cloud implementation under public list pricing, and table 6 itemizes the corresponding hardware, power, cooling, network, and DevOps labor costs of an on-premises edge-server implementation.

Napkin Math 2.3: Cloud vs. edge annual budgetsProblem: Under the partial accounting boundaries itemized in table 5 and table 6, which implementation has the lower estimated annual budget over 3 years?
Math: The question is the annual cost at this operating point, so the comparison in equation 6 is the gap between the two annual totals: \[\text{Annual cost gap} = \text{Cloud annual budget} - \text{Edge annual budget} \tag{6}\]
At 1M inferences/day, the gap is ~$35,288/year − ~$21,610/year = ~$13,678/year. Almost all of the cloud bill is provisioned capacity rather than use. At 10 ms per request the day’s traffic needs only about 2.8 GPU-hours of the 96 provisioned, about 2.9 percent utilization. Only egress scales with traffic.
Result: The listed edge budget costs about 38.8 percent less at this operating point. Because the fixed cloud pool alone already costs more than the listed edge budget, no traffic level under this fixed provisioning and partial accounting makes the cloud cheaper; a genuine break-even analysis would need cloud capacity that scales with demand.
Systems insight: The listed edge budget is dominated by labor (~$15,000 ÷ ~$21,610/year ≈ 69.4 percent), not hardware. Organizations without existing DevOps capacity should factor in the full cost of maintaining on-premises infrastructure.


Beyond the direct bill, unpredictable usage spikes complicate budgeting and call for automated monitoring and cost governance. Network dependency, the last of the three costs, creates an availability hazard: any connectivity disruption between clients and the data center immediately degrades or halts service. Proprietary cloud APIs compound the dependency with vendor lock-in, creating software portability friction when migrating workloads across providers. Even so, centralized infrastructure remains uniquely suited to consumer applications that require elastic capacity at global scale.



Cloud ML’s computational advantages manifest most visibly in consumer-facing applications that require massive scale. Virtual assistants like Siri and Alexa illustrate the hybrid architectures that characterize modern ML systems: wake-word detection can run on dedicated sub-milliwatt-to-milliwatt hardware directly on the device, enabling always-on listening without continuously activating the main processor; initial speech recognition can run on-device for privacy and responsiveness; and complex natural language understanding and generation can use cloud infrastructure for access to larger models and broader knowledge.
Economics drive this architecture as much as latency. Attempting to process voice interactions for billions of devices entirely in the cloud runs into both an economic and an infrastructure ceiling. Quantifying the voice assistant wall shows both limits at once.

Napkin Math 2.4: The voice assistant wallProblem: In this illustrative capacity scenario, 1B voice assistant devices (smartphones, smart speakers, earbuds) each issue 20 queries/day after the wake word. Detecting the wake word itself in the cloud would require every microphone to stream audio continuously. What load would cloud-side detection impose, and what load remains in the cloud once detection moves on device?
Cloud-side detection: First, the always-listening path that local detection removes.

Audio streaming: Every device streams audio continuously (16 kHz, 16-bit), about 32 KB/s each. Across 1 billion devices the aggregate is 32 TB/s, and each stream would also need its own continuously running detector.
Cloud cost: ~$0.50/device/year → 1B devices = $500,000,000/year. Economically prohibitive under these assumptions for a free feature.
TinyML alternative: 0.1–1 mW local wake-word detection, <$0.01/device/year. If each post-wake query uploads about 5 s of audio, local detection cuts the audio leaving each device by about 860×.

Residual cloud load: Second, the post-wake queries the hybrid design still serves in the cloud. Even with local wake-word filtering, the residual query volume—1 billion devices generating 20B queries/day at ~200 ms per query—still requires substantial centralized accelerator capacity (~1,111,111 GPU-hours per day).
Five parameters determine the required cluster capacity:

Query volume: 1 billion devices \(\times\) 20 queries/day = 20B queries/day.
GPU demand: Each query requires ~200 ms of GPU time. Total: 1,111,111 GPU-hours/day.
Scenario capacity: A data-center equivalent provisioned with 10,000 GPUs provides 240,000 GPU-hours/day.
Average requirement: ~4.6 dedicated data centers just for voice inference.
Peak reality: Queries cluster in waking hours (~4.5× peak-to-average), requiring ~20.8 data centers at peak.

Systems insight: Detecting the wake word in the cloud would require streaming every microphone continuously, about 32 TB/s across a billion devices, before a single user query is answered. Local detection reduces each device’s upload to its post-wake queries, 20 queries/day of a few seconds each. The residual post-wake load is still large, tens of data centers at peak, but it is bounded by what users actually ask, and it is the load the hybrid design deliberately keeps in the cloud to use a larger language model than the local device can support.


The voice assistant pipeline illustrates a core systems principle: constraints drive hierarchical architecture. Partitioning the pipeline into an on-device wake-word filter and a cloud-based language model relieves both the client’s energy limit and the data center’s capacity limit.
Large-scale recommendation engines demonstrate the cloud bargain in a memory-capacity-bound form. DLRM-style systems17 map millions of users and items to dense vectors through embedding tables that routinely exceed terabytes in aggregate, far beyond any single accelerator. The tables are sharded across pooled host and accelerator memory, and distributed lookups and training updates place heavy demands on the cluster interconnect.
17 Deep learning recommendation model (DLRM): Meta’s 2019 architecture that exemplifies the sparse scatter archetype. Embedding-heavy recommendation models have been scaled to 100 TB by combining accelerator-memory caches with larger host memory (Park et al. 2024). At that scale, memory capacity and communication \(\Bandwidth\) can constrain execution more than raw \(\PeakRate\). These demands motivate specialized cluster designs where memory, not arithmetic, is the scarce resource.
Park, Intaik, Ehsan Ardestani, Damian Reeves, Sarunya Pumma, Henry Tsang, Levy Zhao, Jian He, et al. 2024. “Toward 100TB Recommendation Models with Embedding Offloading.” 18th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems, 841–43. https://doi.org/10.1145/3640457.3688037.

↪ The memory-capacity bounds and sparse gather patterns of high-cardinality embedding tables are developed in Sparse Architectures: Recommendation Systems.

These applications trade latency for scale, accepting remote-path delay in exchange for computational resources that cannot be supplied locally. The trade fails when a latency budget drops below what the remote path permits, or when data volumes exceed what networks can carry; computation must then move closer to the data source.

Self-Check: Question

On-device wake-word detection removes the need to stream every microphone continuously to the cloud, so the data-center-count estimate applies to the remaining post-wake queries rather than to constant listening traffic.
Once wake-word detection moves on device, all cloud serving disappears because speech recognition and language understanding no longer need remote models.
The main problem is only that encrypted audio cannot be processed efficiently in cloud accelerators, so local wake detection solves a hardware compatibility issue rather than a traffic-scaling issue.
Wake-word detection on device matters only for privacy; it does not materially change network load because continuous listening traffic and post-wake query traffic are the same scale.

Dedicated server room air-conditioning and cooling overhead

Under GDPR Article 17 (Right to Erasure), when a user requests deletion of their data, an organization is legally mandated to retrain from scratch every ML model that ever encountered that user’s training samples.

title: Deployment Paradigm Framework
text:
The robotic-arm safety monitor in napkin math 2.2 left one option open, running the model beside the arm it protects.18 Moving computation adjacent to the data source removes that remote transmission term from the request path, and edge ML is the paradigm built on that move.
18 Industrial IoT (IIoT): A domain where latency constraints can be set by physical safety rather than user perception. Keeping sensing and the stop decision local removes the long-haul network term but leaves the edge system bounded by its local compute capacity \((\PeakRate)\).Edge ML trades elastic cloud capacity for shorter request paths and local data retention. Sub-100 ms response remains a requirement to verify, rather than a guarantee of proximity. In archetype terms, edge deployment shifts the binding constraint: a bandwidth hog workload that is memory bound in the cloud can become dominated by remote-path latency when offloaded over wide-area links. Under the iron law from equation 5, local execution removes the I/O offload term from the request path, leaving execution time bounded by local compute and memory transfer.

Definition 2.2: Edge ML
Edge machine learning is the deployment paradigm optimized for local response and data locality by locating computation physically adjacent to data sources.

Significance: It circumvents the distance penalty \((\Latency)\) of the cloud, trading elastic scale for a fixed local compute capacity \((\PeakRate)\).
Distinction: Unlike cloud ML, which prioritizes throughput, edge ML prioritizes response deadlines and local data control. Unlike TinyML, edge ML may still use workstation-class accelerators such as general-purpose GPUs (GPGPUs).
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that edge ML refers to a specific hardware class. In reality, it is a location paradigm: it spans from IoT gateways to on-premises servers, unified by physical proximity to the data source.



Real-time deadlines are not the only driver. Data sovereignty and privacy rules can restrict transmitting raw sensor streams across external networks, which places computation on local gateways, industrial PCs, and on-premises servers. Figure 5 partitions this operational bargain across four structural columns, charting how placing compute near sensors and filtering data locally helps meet sub-100 ms response budgets while introducing failure boundaries in fixed node capacity and remote fleet management.






Figure 5: Edge ML Constraint Map: Moving computation near the data removes the network-latency term and reduces bandwidth pressure, but it replaces centralized scale with fixed local capacity, distributed security exposure, and operational complexity across many sites.






Raw edge data can be wider than the network pipe.
19 Internet of things (IoT) data wall: McKinsey estimates that IoT deployments could create trillions of dollars in economic value by 2030, but those deployments depend on continuous sensor streams from devices distributed across homes, factories, farms, vehicles, and infrastructure (McKinsey Global Institute 2021). In many of those settings, the aggregate \(\DataVolume\) from raw streams overwhelms the available uplink budget or latency budget for centralized ingestion, making local edge processing an architectural requirement rather than merely a cost optimization.
McKinsey Global Institute. 2021. The Internet of Things: Catching up to an Accelerating Opportunity. McKinsey & Company.
Sensor ingestion rates above network uplink capacity rule out transmitting the full raw stream.19 Local filtering or compression can reduce the transmitted representation; the complete local and remote paths then determine where inference can meet the application’s requirements.

Napkin Math 2.5: The bandwidth bottleneckProblem: Consider a quality control system for a factory floor with 100 cameras running at 30 FPS with 1080p resolution. Does video streaming become the bandwidth bottleneck, and does edge ML reduce the bandwidth enough to process locally?
Physics:

Raw data rate per camera: 1920 \(\times\) 1080 \(\times\) 3 bytes \(\times\) 30 FPS ≈ 186.6 MB/s.
Total data rate: 100 cameras \(\times\) 186.6 MB/s = 18.7 GB/s.
Cloud transfer exposure: Uploading raw camera feeds is primarily a bandwidth, ingest, storage, and processing problem; per-GB cloud egress charges apply when data is transferred back out of the cloud. If the raw stream were later retrieved at $0.09/GB data-transfer-out pricing, the transfer charge alone would reach $4.4M/month.
Network reality: Even a dedicated 10 Gbps line (1.25 GB/s) cannot carry the load, because the workload demands 14.9× more bandwidth than exists.

Systems insight: Streaming these raw feeds over the stated link is impossible. Local processing or a smaller transmitted representation is required; compression changes the bandwidth calculation but must preserve the information and timing needed for defect detection. If an edge server transmits only defect metadata (1 KB per detection at roughly 20 events/s across the floor), bandwidth falls by about 933,120×.


Saturating an uplink with uncompressed sensor streams demonstrates the bandwidth barrier of centralized ingestion. For battery-powered edge devices (wireless cameras, drones, wearables), the energy cost of wireless communication introduces an even stricter physical ceiling. Offloading adds energy to the time-based analysis of equation 5, so the local-versus-offload decision must weigh joules as well as milliseconds.

Napkin Math 2.6: The energy of transmissionProblem: Should a battery-powered sensor process data locally (on-device NPU inference) or send it to the cloud when the energy of transmission must come out of a fixed battery budget?
Given:

Data \((\DataVolume)\): 1 MB (illustrative payload volume).
Transmission energy \((\TransmissionEnergyPerByte)\): 100 mJ/MB (Wi-Fi/LTE).
Compute energy \((\LocalInferenceEnergy)\): 0.1 mJ/inference (illustrative MobileNetV2 anchor for the neural processing unit alone, excluding the rest of the phone).

Math:

Cloud approach: \(\CloudOffloadEnergy\approx \DataVolume \times \TransmissionEnergyPerByte\) = 1 MB \(\times\) 100 mJ/MB = 100 mJ.
Local approach: \(\LocalInferenceEnergy\approx\) Inference = 0.1 mJ.

Systems insight: Transmitting raw data is 1,000× more expensive than processing it locally. Charging local inference with the whole phone’s energy over the inference window (2.6 mJ, the MobileNetV2 bar charted in figure 6) still leaves transmission 39× more expensive. Even if the cloud had infinite speed \((\Time\approx 0)\), the stated battery budget favors local inference over raw-data transmission. The machine constraint (battery) shapes the deployment choice.


The matched transmission calculation shows why uploading this raw payload spends more device energy than local inference under the stated assumptions. Figure 6 instead supplies energy scale anchors for different tasks and accounting boundaries on a logarithmic scale spanning eight orders of magnitude, isolating the 100,000,000× gap between an always-on TinyML keyword spotting inference (about 10 µJ) and a cloud foundation-model query (about 1 kJ, an order-of-magnitude scenario anchor that includes data-center overhead rather than a measured value). The across-task ratio does not isolate a hardware advantage or establish an offload decision; that decision requires matched local and remote paths for the same task.














Figure 6: Energy per Inference Across Deployment Tiers: An eight-order-of-magnitude energy gap separates always-on TinyML keyword spotting (~10 µJ) from a cloud foundation-model query (~1 kJ) on a log scale. The three vision bars are device-level estimates (the device’s power draw at its modeled utilization over the batch-1 inference window, counting the whole phone, the edge tier’s NVIDIA Jetson embedded GPU module, or the A100 card) from the same analytical model used throughout this chapter; the two endpoints are scenario anchors. The tasks and accounting boundaries differ, so these bars illustrate energy scales rather than a controlled hardware-efficiency or offload comparison.




Systems Perspective 2.2: Reading the energy-per-inference numbersThe logarithmic comparisons plotted in figure 6 combine solver-derived device-energy estimates with separate scale anchors; they are not controlled full-system measurements. Each vision bar counts one device over its batch-1 inference window. The cloud ResNet-50 bar, for example, charges an A100 averaging about ~130 W for 0.57 ms; it excludes the host CPUs, memory, networking, and cooling that bring an entire server to about ~1 kW, so a whole-server accounting of the same request would be several times larger.
The span becomes tangible when measured in a familiar unit of energy, one smartphone battery. The nominal energy stored in a 3.7 V, 3000 mAh battery is equivalent to about 4 billion inferences by the keyword spotter but only about 40 queries to a cloud LLM. The comparison is one of scale only: a cloud query’s energy is spent in the data center, not drawn from the phone. Nor are the keyword-spotting counts elapsed battery life: actual runtime still depends on inference cadence, sleep power, sensing, communication, and the rest of the device.




The decision between local edge processing and remote cloud processing is governed by a bandwidth-latency trade-off. The data locality invariant below is the per-request, deadline-bound form of the data-gravity principle from the cloud section: where data gravity weighs moving a whole dataset against moving the computation, the invariant weighs moving one input against one deadline. Remote execution is infeasible when its complete path violates the service deadline; otherwise, the faster feasible path follows from comparing complete local and remote times.

Definition 2.3: The data locality invariant
The data locality invariant first screens a remote path against the service deadline. The expression below gives a lower bound on complete remote-path time \(\RemotePathTime\); let \(\CompletionDeadline\) denote the deadline, \(\NetworkBandwidth\) offload bandwidth, \(\NetworkLatency\) network latency, and \(\RemotePeakRate\) and \(\RemoteHardwareEfficiency\) the remote compute rate and efficiency: \[\RemotePathTime \ge \frac{\DataVolume}{\NetworkBandwidth} + \NetworkLatency + \frac{\Operations}{\RemotePeakRate \cdot \RemoteHardwareEfficiency}\]
The bound includes input transmission, network round-trip time, and arithmetic execution, but omits remote memory movement, queueing, preprocessing, runtime overhead, and response serialization. If even this lower bound exceeds the deadline, reject the remote path. A bound below the deadline leaves a candidate for complete-path measurement; it does not establish feasibility. Compare complete local and remote times only after each path meets the deadline and its resource constraints. Here, \(\NetworkLatency\) covers propagation, routing, and protocol handshakes; response serialization may be small for a class label but must be included when material.

Significance: The invariant defines a crossover beyond which adding remote compute \((\RemotePeakRate)\) has little effect because transmission dominates the lower bound. The local path is preferred only after its own complete execution time and resource limits are checked.
Distinction: Unlike the iron law, which decomposes one execution path, the locality invariant uses a deadline to reject an idealized remote path, then requires complete-path evidence to choose between the remaining alternatives.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that 5G/6G “solves” locality. While these technologies improve \(\NetworkBandwidth\), they do not remove propagation and protocol latency, so a remote path can still miss a tight service deadline.



The locality formulation also explains what every local tier gains, edge, mobile, and TinyML alike. Local execution removes network transit time (\(\DataVolume/\NetworkBandwidth + \NetworkLatency\)) from the request path, eliminating wide-area network variability. A closed-loop latency guarantee requires validating a bound on the complete local path under its operating conditions, \(\LocalPathTime\le \CompletionDeadline\). Uplink traffic drops from raw sensor bitrates to lightweight event telemetry, relieving congestion and recurring transit charges. Keeping raw sensor data where it is captured shrinks the transmission attack surface, although local processing alone does not guarantee privacy: data at rest still needs access control, and retention and secondary use still need governance. Local inference also continues through wide-area outages whenever local power and sensor links remain functional. Mobile and TinyML inherit all four gains; what distinguishes them is the price each pays for them.
Evaluating a single high-rate sensor frame against a strict frame deadline illustrates the locality crossover in practice.

Napkin Math 2.7: The locality crossoverProblem: Should a drone’s object avoidance system (4K, 60 FPS) offload to the cloud, or does this become a locality crossover?
Given:

Data \((\DataVolume)\): 4K frame ≈ 24.9 MB.
Bandwidth \((\NetworkBandwidth)\): 100 Mb/s cellular uplink.
Remote network and compute response: 110 ms (round-trip + remote compute).
Per-frame completion deadline: 16.7 ms, equal to the frame interval in this illustrative scenario; each avoidance result must be ready before the next frame arrives.

Math:

Transmission time: 24.9 MB \(\times\) 8 bits/100 Mb/s = 1,990.7 ms.
Remote-path lower bound: Transmission + 110 ms remote response = 2100.7 ms, vs. the stated 16.7 ms per-frame deadline.

Systems insight: The remote path misses the stated per-frame deadline, and faster remote compute cannot remove the transmission time. Cloud offload is therefore infeasible under these assumptions; the local path must still be measured to confirm that it meets the deadline.





Edge deployment trades network transit for fixed local capacity. Edge hardware spans a wide power envelope, from 5–50 W embedded modules to site-powered servers drawing hundreds of watts, and its binding limit is the fixed capacity of a site rather than the elastic capacity of a cloud region. Many smaller embedded modules operate within 1–8 GB of memory,20 and their power and board budgets cannot support the wide, high-power interfaces of HBM. They rely on LPDDR or shared system DRAM instead, so memory capacity limits parameter scale and memory bandwidth limits throughput, and fitting modern machine learning models into these bounds requires efficiency techniques that store weights in fewer bits (quantization), remove weights that contribute little (pruning), or train a smaller model to imitate a larger one (distillation). Model footprint, activation buffers, runtime state, and thermal duty cycles all become binding. Operationally, coordinating software updates and model versions across thousands of heterogeneous, physically exposed devices requires specialized deployment pipelines,21 where intermittent links and physical access complicate rollback and failure diagnosis.
20 Embedded edge constraints: Across representative edge envelopes, 1–8 GB can hold roughly 1–8 billion INT8 weights before activations, runtime state, and other buffers, so the memory budget, not a fixed parameter count, sets the ceiling. Sustainable compute is further limited by power, cooling, and duty cycle.21 Edge fleet coordination: Managing thousands of distributed edge devices amplifies coordination problems: intermittent connectivity causes model version drift, hardware heterogeneity requires per-target optimization, and limited remote access can make failed firmware rollbacks require a site visit.
↪ Over-the-air updates, dual-bank rollback, and lightweight fleet telemetry for edge devices are operationalized in Edge AI deployment.

A realistic retail deployment shows how those constraints turn into throughput, hardware, and fleet-cost requirements. Consider a smart retail chain that deploys person detection across 500 stores, each with 20 cameras/store running at 15 FPS. Table 7 cascades the per-store inference rate through the per-frame FLOP count of YOLOv8-nano, a compact object-detection model, to yield the throughput each store must sustain. The 2\(\times\) headroom keeps the device out of saturation when traffic bursts above the average rate.
