Napkin Math 2.8: Edge inference sizingProblem: Given the throughput target in table 7 and the candidates in table 8, which edge accelerator (USB-scale TPU, workstation-class embedded GPU, or general-purpose mini-PC) delivers the required throughput at the lowest estimated three-year hardware-and-power budget?
Math: We screen capacity using an assumed sustained rate rather than the datasheet peak. The scenario’s 50 percent derating plays the role of the efficiency \(\EfficiencyHw\) in the iron law. One Jetson derates from 100 TOPS to 50 TOPS, far above the 5.22 TOPS requirement. One NUC derates to 0.5 TOPS and falls short; meeting the target would take 11 per store, about $2,200,000 of hardware across the fleet. A Coral Dev Board is rated at 4 TOPS peak; the same derating gives 2 TOPS, so the count per store is 5.22 TOPS required ÷ 2 TOPS per board = 2.6 boards, which rounds up to 3 boards/store. This estimate assumes the model’s operations and numerical format are supported and that work can be divided across the boards at the assumed rate.
Over 3 years across 500 stores, the hardware-and-power estimate for that configuration is Hardware $225,000 + Power (0.006 kW \(\times\) 500 \(\times\) 8760 h/year \(\times\) 3 years \(\times\) $0.12/kWh = $9,460.8) = $234,460.8 total vs. a baseline of one dedicated cloud GPU per store, at the same $0.75/hr instance rate as the cloud-versus-edge comparison, of ~$9,855,000. Within this accounting boundary, the other two candidates need no power arithmetic to rank, because the Coral configuration’s hardware-and-power estimate is already below the Jetson fleet’s $300,000 hardware bill and far below a feasible NUC fleet’s. Integration, maintenance, redundancy, and matched cloud operating costs remain outside this comparison.
Result: One Coral alone is undersized under these assumptions, but the sharded configuration with 3 boards/store is a low-cost edge candidate within the hardware-and-power boundary, with an estimated 6 TOPS and about 1.3× lower per-store hardware CapEx than Jetson. Jetson remains the simpler single-device candidate when integration complexity matters more than hardware cost.
Systems insight: Edge sizing is a capacity-and-cost problem, not a device-name problem. The cheapest feasible design may be several small accelerators per site rather than one larger board, but that hardware saving must be weighed against the coordination and maintenance burden of a sharded edge fleet. The estimate narrows the candidates; measurements of the actual model and runtime must establish task quality, throughput, and end-to-end latency before deployment.


Physical exposure compounds these operational challenges. Unlike servers housed in access-controlled data centers, edge hardware deployed across retail floors or public infrastructure is physically accessible to adversaries. This exposure requires hardware-enforced protection mechanisms: secure boot chains to prevent unauthorized firmware modification, encrypted local storage for model weights and intermediate activations, and tamper-evident enclosures. Furthermore, capital expenditures scale linearly with deployment footprint: equipping 1,000 sites with $500–2,000 of edge hardware per site requires $500,000–2,000,000 in upfront CapEx before installation, cabling, and fleet operations. Whether that upfront investment yields a lower total cost of ownership than recurring cloud inference depends on utilization duty cycles, local energy rates, and site maintenance overhead.



Edge applications differ by domain, but each makes a locality argument concrete: the system cannot wait for the network, cannot ship the data, cannot expose the raw signal, or cannot stop during an outage. Autonomous vehicles represent a demanding application because safety-critical perception and control decisions must fit millisecond-scale budgets. Onboard systems process streams from multiple cameras and other sensors through local hardware; a remote cloud path cannot satisfy the tight control loop when its network delay alone exceeds the deadline.
Smart retail environments demonstrate edge ML’s practical advantages for privacy-sensitive, bandwidth-intensive applications. A checkout-free store22 can process feeds from many cameras on local edge servers, tracking customer movements and item selections without continuously transmitting raw video over a wide-area link. This architecture reduces bandwidth demand and transmission exposure, but it does not by itself ensure privacy: retention, access, secondary use, and governance controls still determine the system’s compliance and risk.
22 Checkout-free retail: A store may fuse camera observations with shelf events and transaction state locally, then transmit only selected events or aggregates. The privacy boundary must still include those derived records, because reducing raw-video transport does not determine retention, access, or secondary use.23 Industry 4.0: The fourth industrial revolution integrates ML into the sensor-actuator feedback loop on factory floors. In an illustrative welding-robot scenario, defect detection samples at 60 Hz, giving a 16.7 ms sampling interval; if each response must finish before the next sample, the complete sensing-to-actuation path must fit that deadline. This completion requirement is a scenario assumption; the sampling rate alone does not establish the control deadline or guarantee safe operation.24 Predictive maintenance: Models analyze sensor data such as vibration and temperature to estimate equipment condition and failure risk. Continuous monitoring makes sensing cadence, duty cycle, power, and local storage first-class constraints. Battery-powered nodes may require sub-watt average operation, whereas mains-powered industrial gateways can use a much larger envelope.The industrial IoT23 uses edge ML for applications where millisecond-level responsiveness directly impacts production efficiency and worker safety. Manufacturing facilities deploy edge ML systems for real-time quality control and predictive maintenance.24
Many industrial and retail edge systems are stationary and connected to site power, where a factory edge server drawing hundreds of watts around the clock remains viable. Mobile devices, by contrast, travel with untethered users on strictly bounded battery reserves. When computation moves from stationary infrastructure to an untethered mobile device, battery energy becomes a central constraint alongside latency, and the dominant optimization target shifts from raw execution time to energy per inference.

Self-Check: Question

A manufacturing facility deploys 100 cameras recording uncompressed 1080p video (\(1920 \times 1080 \times 3\text{ bytes/pixel}\)) at 30 FPS. The factory has a dedicated 10 Gbps (~1.25 GB/s) fiber uplink. Why is streaming all raw video to a cloud ML server physically impossible?

The total is only about \(186.6\text{ MB/s}\) because that is the per-camera rate, so the 10 Gbps uplink has ample headroom.
The aggregate is about \(18.7\text{ Gb/s}\) because the camera output should be compared numerically to 10 Gbps without converting bytes to bits, so the link is close enough to be practical.
The aggregate raw video data rate is approximately \(18.7\text{ GB/s}\), which exceeds the \(1.25\text{ GB/s}\) uplink capacity by roughly \(15\times\).
The aggregate raw stream is large, but normal compression assumptions would make it fit within the 10 Gbps uplink in practice.

An autonomous drone navigates at 60 FPS (16.7 ms per-frame budget) capturing uncompressed 4K frames (~24.9 MB per frame). The drone connects via a 100 Mbps uplink to a cloud server whose round-trip latency plus inference time is 110 ms. Applying the data locality invariant, what is the feasibility of offloading this obstacle avoidance system to the cloud?

Feasible, because the cloud GPU computes inference in under 10 ms.
Feasible, provided 5G network slicing is enabled on the drone modem.
Infeasible, solely because cloud servers do not support drone telemetry protocols.
Infeasible, because transmitting a 24.9 MB frame over a 100 Mbps link requires ~2,000 ms, causing even the remote-path lower-bound estimate (~2,110 ms) to violate the 16.7 ms frame deadline by over two orders of magnitude.

Why cannot high-bandwidth wireless networking technologies (such as 5G or 6G) eliminate the need for edge ML in tight real-time control loops (\(<10\text{ ms}\))?
When sizing edge accelerators for a retail store deployment requiring 7.2 TOPS of sustained INT8 throughput, why is it inadequate to select a single accelerator rated at 8 TOPS peak datasheet throughput?
An illustrative 60 Hz industrial control scenario assumes each sensing-to-actuation response must finish before the next sample. Its complete ML control loop latency (\(L_{\text{lat}}\)) must therefore fit within one ____ (about 16.7 ms).

title: Deployment Paradigm Framework
text:
Carrying edge-style locality into a user’s pocket changes which budget binds. A phone must deliver responsive, private inference all day from a pocket-sized battery, inside a thin chassis with no fan to carry heat away.
Mobile ML integrates machine learning directly into smartphones and tablets. It fits workloads where data locality, offline operation, and immediate response matter more than computational scale, such as voice recognition, computational photography,25 health monitoring, and navigation or translation that must keep working without a network, and its battery and thermal envelope suit frequent, short-duration inference rather than sustained heavy computation.
25 Computational photography: Uses ML algorithms (for example, multi-frame fusion, neural denoising) to overcome the physical limits of small mobile camera sensors. This exemplifies the mobile computing trade-off, as a multi-stage pipeline must execute within the user’s perceived shutter delay while adhering to a shared 3–5 W thermal budget.26 Mobile vision model reduction: MobileNet-style architectures reduce the computation in common vision layers while preserving useful accuracy for mobile tasks. The systems point here is that mobile deployment often requires changing the model family, not merely moving the same model to a phone.The mobile environment elevates energy per inference to a primary design constraint: because a phone operates from a finite battery without active cooling, every joule consumed directly erodes device runtime and thermal headroom. While stationary cloud and edge deployments often focus on minimizing latency \(\Time\) under continuous utility or site power, mobile systems must strictly balance total energy (\(\text{Energy} = \text{Power} \times \Time\)) under the power wall described by equation 2, which caps sustained dissipation at 3–5 W. In archetype terms, a compute-heavy workload such as image classification must be transformed into a more compact vision model,26 reducing FLOPs by 13.7× while preserving target accuracy. The shift is qualitative: the design accepts lower peak throughput in exchange for sustainable operation within a 3–5 W thermal envelope.

Definition 2.4: Mobile ML
Mobile machine learning is the deployment paradigm bounded by thermal design power (TDP) and battery energy.

Significance: It is constrained by the few-watt heat dissipation capacity of passive cooling, requiring architectures that prioritize sustained energy efficiency over peak throughput \((\PeakRate)\).
Distinction: Unlike edge ML, which may have active cooling, mobile ML must operate within a personal energy budget. Unlike TinyML, it still provides a rich OS and multi-watt compute capacity.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that mobile ML performance is a fixed value. In reality, it is a time-varying constraint: performance often drops as the device hits its thermal wall, triggering thermal throttling that lowers clock frequencies and reduces the active duty cycle.



Two boundaries close the mobile envelope, and together they push the design toward on-device NPU acceleration and model compression (figure 7). The first is the battery tax, the share of the phone’s finite energy budget that an always-on ML feature spends before the rest of the system runs. The battery limits total energy over time.
Thermodynamics imposes a second boundary that holds even for a plugged-in tablet. Every watt becomes heat, and where a data center removes heat with active cooling, a thin mobile device relies on passive transfer through its chassis and surfaces. This creates the thermal wall, a hard ceiling on sustained power consumption that exists independently of battery capacity.






Figure 7: Mobile ML Constraint Map: On-device processing buys responsiveness, privacy, offline operation, and personalization, but the phone’s shared battery and passive thermal envelope make sustained energy efficiency the binding design constraint.




Napkin Math 2.9: The battery taxProblem: Consider deploying a “real-time” background object detector on a smartphone. The model consumes 2 W of continuous power when active. The phone has a standard 15 Wh battery. Can the feature stay on all day? This is the battery tax that turns battery life into a mobile ML energy-budget constraint.
Physics:

Ideal runtime: \(\frac{15\text{ Wh}}{2\text{ W}}\) = 7.5 hours
Reality: A user expects their phone to last 24 hours. Running this single feature continuously for a day would require 320 percent of the phone’s daily energy budget.

Systems insight: The model cannot simply be “deployed.” A lighter model, duty cycling, or both must reduce the energy demand, so the feature can stay on all day.





Sustained thermal performance falls well below burst peaks.
The distinction matters for engineering decisions: the battery tax is a budget problem, solvable in principle by reducing how often the model runs or by increasing battery capacity. The thermal wall is a physics ceiling. A larger battery cannot raise the maximum sustained wattage a passive chassis can dissipate; duty-cycle and software changes can only reduce heat generation. Sustained operation above the thermal envelope triggers hardware throttling regardless of remaining battery energy. The two constraints therefore attack different points in the iron law: the battery limits total operations per charge (\(\Operations\) integrated over time), while the thermal wall caps the instantaneous rate (\(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw\)) the silicon can sustain.

Napkin Math 2.10: The thermal wallProblem: An unoptimized vision model requires 12 W peak compute. Can it be deployed on a mobile device, or does it hit the thermal wall and the mobile power wall?
Scenario: A mobile system-on-chip (SoC) allows approximately 3 W for passive cooling. Assume the unoptimized model ships anyway. A representative throttling trace for this heavier model (a different and more demanding case than the power-wall example earlier in the chapter) runs in three steps:

Temperature rise: At 12 W, the device temperature rises at approximately 1 °C/s.
Thermal trip: Within 60 s, the hardware reaches the thermal trip point (80 °C), triggering OS throttling.
Throttled throughput: The 100 FPS model suddenly drops to 30 FPS to stay within the thermal envelope.

Math: Assume that a redesign (a lighter architecture running INT8 instead of FP32 arithmetic) cuts active power by an illustrative 4×: 12 W ÷ 4 = 3 W, which lands right at the 3 W passive-cooling ceiling with no headroom to spare. The factor is a scenario input for the whole redesign. Quantization alone shrinks weight storage by that factor but does not cut power proportionally, because switching and leakage energy outside the arithmetic remain.
Systems insight: Even a 4× power reduction does not create thermal headroom; it only just reaches the sustainable limit. Optimization can bring a model down to the thermal ceiling; it cannot raise the ceiling.


The battery and thermal examples establish why mobile deployments demand explicit energy accounting. With the macro-scale energy spectrum across paradigms established in figure 6, the sections that follow examine how mobile systems operate within these tight thermodynamic envelopes.


The mobile row of table 4 gives the hardware envelope: gigabytes of RAM, neural processing units27 delivering tens of TOPS, and 3–5 W of sustained power on a system-on-chip28 that integrates computation and memory to minimize data-movement energy. Memory capacity constrains model footprint and memory bandwidth constrains how quickly weights and activations move, but the battery sets the budget users notice. Adding 1 W of continuous ML processing to a phone that otherwise lasts 24 hours would cut its runtime to roughly 9.2 hours–11.5 hours, depending on a battery capacity of 15 Wh–22 Wh.
27 Neural processing unit (NPU): A dedicated hardware block on a mobile system-on-chip whose circuits are designed for low-precision tensor operations. This specialization can improve energy efficiency relative to CPU execution, helping AI workloads fit within mobile power budgets.28 System-on-chip (SoC): Mobile SoCs integrate CPU, GPU, and NPU cores with caches and memory controllers to reduce data-movement costs. Mobile DRAM is generally off-die, and feasible model size depends on capacity, precision, working memory, bandwidth, and latency.29 Face ID: Apple performs facial matching within the Secure Enclave and encrypts the stored mathematical representations so that they remain available only to that subsystem and do not leave the device (Apple 2024a, 2024b). Apple reports a random false-match probability below 1 in 1,000,000 for one enrolled appearance, with higher probabilities for some populations and configurations. The example shows how local inference and hardware isolation can reduce transmission exposure while supporting low-latency authentication.
Apple. 2024a. Facial Matching Security. Apple Platform Security.

Apple. 2024b. The Secure Enclave. Apple Platform Security.
Mobile adds two gains to those every local tier shares. The first is hardware isolation for the most sensitive inputs: on-device enclaves such as Apple’s Secure Enclave keep biometric matching inside a dedicated subsystem,29 although the strength of any privacy guarantee still depends on the complete system design and threat model. The second is personalization, because models can exploit on-device signals and user context without shipping raw data anywhere. Specialized on-device ML frameworks keep such inference within 5–50 ms user-interface response times.
The price is paid in engineering effort as well as joules. Peak NPU throughput can substantially exceed what the device sustains under prolonged load, device heterogeneity requires multiple model variants, development multiplies across platforms, and app-store review and staged release slow iteration compared with a service its operator controls entirely.



Across mobile applications, the central systems problem is that several short pipelines must share the same battery and thermal budget. Computational photography exemplifies the challenge of running multiple ML pipelines within a thermal envelope. Modern flagships process each photo through multiple ML stages: portrait mode30 uses depth estimation and segmentation, night mode aligns multiple frames with ML-based denoising, and HDR merging, super-resolution, and scene optimization run in sequence. The engineering challenge is not any individual model but the pipeline: these models must share a 3–5 W power budget and complete within the user’s perceived shutter delay, requiring careful scheduling across CPU, GPU, and NPU to avoid thermal throttling.
30 Portrait Mode pipeline: This is not a single model but a sequence of real-time models for depth estimation, segmentation, and rendering. The core engineering problem is managing the pipeline’s aggregate latency and power, not any single model’s performance. The entire pipeline must execute within the user’s perceived shutter delay and share the phone’s 3–5 W thermal budget, forcing scheduling trade-offs across the CPU, GPU, and NPU to avoid throttling.Voice-driven interactions partition work across the same SoC by power tier: wake-word detection runs continuously on a dedicated low-power core, while speech recognition and keyboard prediction wake the higher-power neural processing tiers only when needed.
Health monitoring and augmented reality push mobile ML to its sustained-performance limits. Wearables like Apple Watch process ECG and accelerometer data on-device to reduce data transmission, while AR frameworks demand a 16.7 ms total frame budget at 60 FPS for simultaneous localization, hand tracking, and scene understanding. These applications represent the ceiling of what battery-powered, passively-cooled devices can sustain, and they define the boundary beyond which mobile optimization alone is insufficient.
These successes can create a misleading sense of ease. A common pitfall is deploying desktop-trained models directly to mobile or edge devices without architecture modifications. A desktop ResNet-50 pipeline may require gigabytes once activations, batches, preprocessing buffers, and runtime overhead are included, even though the FP32 weights alone are about 102.4 MB. Such a pipeline, requiring 8.2 GFLOP per inference, cannot run unchanged on a representative low-end edge target with 512 MB of RAM and a 1 GFLOP/s processor. Beyond simple resource violations, desktop-optimized models may use operations unsupported by mobile hardware, assume numerical formats unavailable on embedded systems, or require batch processing incompatible with single-sample inference. Successful deployment demands architecture-aware design from the beginning: model families, arithmetic formats, and implementation choices must all match the target device.


↪ The framework that organizes pruning, distillation, and quantization to fit edge memory budgets is developed in Optimization Framework.
Mobile ML shows that useful intelligence fits within a 3–5 W thermal envelope on battery power. A smartphone still costs hundreds of dollars, carries gigabytes of memory, and needs a daily recharge, and no amount of mobile optimization closes the roughly 10,000-fold memory gap to a device that must cost dollars and run unattended for years. That regime needs a different class of hardware and algorithms.

Self-Check: Question

How do the battery tax and the thermal wall differ as physical constraints on mobile ML systems?

The battery tax is an energy budget problem bounding total operations over time (\(\int \text{Power} \cdot dt\)), whereas the thermal wall is a heat dissipation ceiling bounding instantaneous sustained power (\(\text{Power} \le 2\text{--}5\text{ W}\)) regardless of battery size.
The battery tax applies only to iOS devices, while the thermal wall applies only to Android devices.
The battery tax can be resolved by lowering clock frequency, but the thermal wall requires increasing the clock frequency to finish calculations faster.
The battery tax represents static memory leakage in SRAM, while the thermal wall represents network transmission power in 5G modems.

Why does deploying a mobile computational photography feature (such as Portrait Mode or Night Mode) present a pipeline scheduling challenge rather than a single-model optimization problem?

Mobile cameras can only run one neural network per battery charge cycle.
The feature executes a multi-stage pipeline (depth estimation, semantic segmentation, alignment, and HDR tone mapping) that must all complete within a perceived shutter delay while sharing a 2–5 W thermal budget across CPU, GPU, and NPU.
Computational photography models cannot use quantized INT8 representations due to mathematical rounding artifacts in lens optics.
Camera image signal processors (ISPs) operate asynchronously from the operating system and reject all external ML tensor inputs.

Why does deploying an unoptimized desktop-trained vision model (such as an FP32 ResNet-50 pipeline) directly onto a mobile device frequently fail, even when the model’s FP32 weights (~98 MB) appear smaller than the phone’s total RAM?
Running biometric matching (such as Face ID) inside a dedicated on-device Secure Enclave reduces data disclosure risks by keeping mathematical representations isolated in encrypted hardware, but it does not automatically eliminate all security or privacy risks without rigorous end-to-end system design.
Order the sequence of events that occurs when an unoptimized 12 W deep learning model runs continuously on a passively cooled 3 W smartphone SoC:


The device temperature rises rapidly (e.g., at ~1 °C per second) as power dissipation exceeds passive cooling capacity
The unoptimized model launches at full burst performance (e.g., 100 FPS) drawing 12 W of active compute power
Operating system and hardware thermal controllers engage thermal throttling, reducing clock frequencies and duty cycles
The internal SoC junction temperature reaches the critical thermal trip point (e.g., 80 °C)
Sustained inference throughput drops precipitously (e.g., from 100 FPS to 30 FPS) to stabilize power within the 3 W TDP envelope

title: Deployment Paradigm Framework
text:
Imagine instrumenting every pallet in a warehouse, every cable on a suspension bridge, every beehive in an apiary. To put “eyes and ears” on this many physical objects, tens of thousands to millions, the device must cost dollars, not hundreds of dollars, and measure millimeters, not centimeters. Smartphones are far too expensive and too large; what is needed is ubiquitous sensing at unit costs under ten dollars and physical dimensions measured in millimeters.
TinyML completes the deployment spectrum by pushing intelligence to its physical limits: low-cost, low-power ML on deeply constrained embedded devices (Janapa Reddi et al. 2022). Devices costing under $10 and averaging less than one milliwatt31 of power when duty-cycled make ubiquitous32 sensing economically practical at massive scale; MLPerf Tiny and MCUNet show how such constraints are evaluated and optimized in practice (Banbury et al. 2021; Lin et al. 2020). This is the domain of the tiny constraint archetype, where the optimization objective shifts from maximizing throughput to minimizing energy per inference. With duty-cycled execution, a keyword spotting model consuming about 10 µJ per inference can operate for years on a coin-cell battery, trading model capacity for operational longevity. Figure 8 highlights this integration on an Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense development board, where on-board microphone, motion, and environmental sensors share a single substrate with a low-power microcontroller executing quantized TensorFlow Lite models. The board illustrates integration; its full power draw depends on the sensors, radio, and duty cycle.
31 The 1 mW Threshold: Ambient energy harvesting can power a device indefinitely only when long-term harvested power exceeds the complete system’s average load. Available power varies across sources and environments—solar cells the size of a thumbnail may produce ~10 mW outdoors but ~10 µW indoors, thermoelectric generators on warm pipes ~100 µW, and RF energy from nearby transmitters ~10 µW. This crossover can transform the deployment model from “battery-limited lifetime” to “deploy and forget,” but it depends on the source, environment, and workload.32 Ubiquitous computing: Mark Weiser’s ubiquitous-computing vision imagined computation woven into everyday environments until it receded from direct attention (Weiser 1991). TinyML is one modern path toward that vision: when the cost and power of an intelligent sensor become low enough for mass deployment, the optimization objective shifts from performance (throughput) to power (energy per inference), the central trade-off of the tiny constraint archetype.
Weiser, Mark. 1991. “The Computer for the 21st Century.” Scientific American 265 (3): 94–104. https://doi.org/10.1038/scientificamerican0991-94.






Figure 8: TinyML Hardware Scale: Microcontroller development boards integrate sensors, processing cores, and low-power radios onto a compact substrate, making constrained ML applications accessible for prototyping. Finished sensing devices must budget SRAM, sensor and radio power, inference cadence, and sleep energy to achieve multi-year battery life. Image source: Figure 6 in (Janapa Reddi et al. 2022), licensed under CC BY 4.0.



Operating at this physical scale requires microcontrollers (MCUs)33 that eliminate the power-hungry infrastructure of conventional computing. Mobile and edge processors rely on external dynamic RAM (DRAM), high-speed memory buses, and operating system runtimes that draw hundreds of milliwatts simply to refresh memory cells and toggle bus lines. Many microcontrollers integrate the processor core, non-volatile flash, and static RAM (SRAM) onto a single silicon die, reducing reliance on external memory buses (Banbury et al. 2021; Lin et al. 2020; Janapa Reddi et al. 2022). Eliminating off-chip signaling lets duty-cycled average power fall below a milliwatt and sleep power reach microwatts, although active inference on boards such as the ESP32-S3 still draws tens to hundreds of milliwatts. Other targets, including ESP32-S3 variants, use external flash or additional RAM. On-chip integration still imposes a strict internal-memory ceiling. On-chip SRAM is physically constrained by silicon die area: because each SRAM cell requires six transistors (\(6\text{T}\)), expanding capacity directly inflates manufacturing cost. A TinyML model must therefore execute within tens to hundreds of kilobytes of SRAM, with no virtual memory, paging, or swap space to cushion an overflow. The small keyword-spotting task and low-power hardware place it at the bottom of figure 6; duty cycle also determines its average power.34 Multi-year coin-cell operation additionally requires the complete device load to fit the battery budget.35 Fitting the entire inference pipeline, from sensor acquisition to classification output, into this kilobyte-scale memory footprint requires formalizing the TinyML operating regime.
33 Microcontroller (MCU): A single-chip computer whose design prioritizes minimal cost and power over performance, so memory fit becomes a deployment prerequisite. Many TinyML targets provide only tens to hundreds of kilobytes of on-chip SRAM and no virtual memory; some higher-end microcontrollers can attach external memory. The complete model, activations, and runtime state must therefore fit the memory actually available to the target, often orders of magnitude less than a smartphone provides.
Banbury, Colby, Vijay Janapa Reddi, Peter Torelli, Jeremy Holleman, Nat Jeffries, Csaba Kiraly, Pietro Montino, et al. 2021. “MLPerf Tiny Benchmark.” arXiv Preprint.

Lin, Ji, Wei-Ming Chen, Yujun Lin, John Cohn, Chuang Gan, and Song Han. 2020. “MCUNet: Tiny Deep Learning on IoT Devices.” In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33: Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems 2020, NeurIPS 2020, December 6-12, 2020, Virtual, edited by Hugo Larochelle, Marc’Aurelio Ranzato, Raia Hadsell, Maria-Florina Balcan, and Hsuan-Tien Lin. Curran Associates.

Janapa Reddi, Vijay, Brian Plancher, Susan Kennedy, Laurence Moroney, Pete Warden, Lara Suzuki, Anant Agarwal, et al. 2022. “Widening Access to Applied Machine Learning with TinyML.” Harvard Data Science Review 4 (1). https://doi.org/10.1162/99608f92.762d171a.
34 TinyML energy gap: The figure compares different tasks on different hardware and with different energy accounting boundaries; its ratios do not identify the effect of hardware integration alone. A batch-1 ResNet-50 inference on a cloud accelerator consumes about 75.5 mJ of accelerator energy, while an always-on keyword spotter uses about 10 µJ, a gap of ~7,500×. A cloud LLM query at about 1 kJ widens the gap to 100,000,000×, the span plotted in figure 6.35 Coin-cell deployment: A CR2032 battery (225 mAh at 3 V, ~675 mWh) ideally powers a complete 10–50 µW system for about 1.5–7.7 years. This “deploy-and-forget” operating model drives innovation in intermittent computing, where the device sleeps between inferences to stretch the energy budget across years of unattended operation.
Definition 2.5: TinyML
TinyML is the machine learning domain of always-on sensing constrained by kilobyte-scale memory and milliwatt-scale power.

Significance: It necessitates models whose weights and code fit in flash while activations and runtime state fit in on-chip SRAM, enabling continuous inference on milliwatt power budgets.
Distinction: Unlike mobile ML, which uses multi-watt processors and a full OS, TinyML runs on microcontrollers using bare-metal firmware or a real-time operating system.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that TinyML is just “small models.” In reality, it is an energy-bound paradigm: the primary metric is energy per inference (microjoules), not just the parameter count.



This definition reframes the iron law of ML systems. In terms of equation 5, TinyML imposes a physical memory-capacity precondition that execution time does not capture: the weight footprint \(\WeightMemory\) and activation footprint \(\ActivationMemory\) must stay within memory capacity \(\DeviceMemoryCapacity\). When total memory is measured in kilobytes, model structure and runtime allocation determine feasibility before latency optimization begins, and every avoidable data movement spends part of the energy budget. The objective therefore shifts from raw throughput toward energy per inference and memory fit.
The same four-branch map applies at the bottom of the spectrum (figure 9). Milliwatt budgets and kilobyte memories favor low-precision execution and duty-cycled sleep, and they move the failure boundary away from latency toward compression-driven accuracy loss and risky firmware updates.






Figure 9: TinyML Constraint Map: Milliwatt power and kilobyte memory make always-on sensing economically possible, but those same limits force the model, activations, runtime, and update path to fit a radically smaller engineering envelope.





TinyML devices range from palm-sized developer kits to millimeter-scale chips,36 and their kilobyte memories and milliwatt budgets buy months or years of autonomous operation37 at the price of specialized algorithms, aggressive model compression, and careful systems co-design.
36 TinyML device range: This physical range reflects a direct trade-off between deployment context and computational capability. Millimeter-scale systems prioritize minimal power for single-function, long-duration tasks, whereas palm-sized boards offer more sensing, interfaces, and debugging support at higher cost and power. Development-board size and power therefore should not be treated as limits for a finished TinyML product.37 On-device training constraints: Updating a model requires working memory beyond that needed to apply it, including information retained from the prediction computation to determine parameter changes. Intermediate results can be discarded only after their final use, which often occurs later during training than during inference. With only 256 KB–2 MB RAM, many microcontrollers cannot hold the full training state; specialized methods reduce that state by limiting which parameters change. TinyTL, for example, freezes the weights and updates mainly the biases, so most intermediate activations need not be retained for the update (Cai et al. 2020). Training elsewhere and delivering an updated model is therefore a common design, although constrained local adaptation remains possible.
Cai, Han, Chuang Gan, Ligeng Zhu, and Song Han. 2020. “TinyTL: Reduce Activations, Not Trainable Parameters for Efficient on-Device Learning.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33: 11285–97.
Beyond the locality gains every local tier shares, TinyML changes deployment economics. Removing the radio uplink and the application processor lets per-node unit cost fall to single-digit dollars, which makes dense instrumentation across thousands of physical assets financially viable, and microjoule inference budgets allow multi-year operation on inexpensive coin-cell batteries or on harvested ambient energy.
The trade-offs are just as distinctive. Microcontrollers commonly provide \(10^5\) to \(10^6\) bytes of RAM and enforce a strict two-tier memory partition: static model weights and compiled code reside in non-volatile flash (often a few megabytes), while mutable activations and the runtime buffer (the tensor arena) must fit within the much smaller on-chip SRAM (a few hundred kilobytes at most, such as the ESP32-S3’s 512 KB, and as little as tens of kilobytes on the smallest parts). As a result, peak intermediate activation volume, rather than static parameter storage, is frequently the barrier that prevents a model from executing. The smart doorbell’s level-1 check (figure 2) shows why that check is only a first screen: its weights fill just 11.9 percent of flash, a figure that says nothing about whether its intermediate results fit in SRAM. Embedded development also demands cross-stack co-design: engineers manage memory pools by hand, debug bare-metal firmware without operating-system abstractions, and optimize operator kernels directly for constrained instruction sets.
Operating under these physical bounds introduces unique lifecycle and reliability challenges. An energy-harvesting device can satisfy its long-term average power budget yet fail when stored energy is exhausted before the next harvest. Its duty cycle must therefore respect both energy per inference and the timing of available power. Model quality can also suffer from aggressive quantization and pruning: converting 32-bit floating-point weights to 8-bit integers (INT8) saves memory but can degrade accuracy and robustness on out-of-distribution sensor inputs. Furthermore, post-deployment flexibility is sharply constrained: models are often packaged with firmware, so field updates must account for limited storage, interrupted transfers, and safe rollback. Ecosystem fragmentation38 across microcontroller vendors and ML frameworks creates additional overhead and portability challenges.
38 TinyML ecosystem fragmentation: TinyML spans microcontroller families such as Arm Cortex-M, RISC-V, and Xtensa, each with different instruction sets, memory layouts, kernels, and vendor toolchains; cloud and mobile stacks also vary, but their runtimes usually hide more of this hardware diversity. A model optimized for one microcontroller target may therefore require retuning and revalidation for another, multiplying the engineering cost of multi-device deployment.


The TinyML regime becomes essential when power budgets, unit economics, and physical isolation rule out every higher tier. Wake-word detection is the most familiar case: the always-on detector acts as a power gate that wakes the costlier processors only when a wake phrase is heard.39 Precision agriculture applies the same locality pressure at farm scale. FarmBeats used sensors, cameras, drones, and local gateway processing to reduce raw data movement where connectivity was costly (Vasisht et al. 2017), and TinyML pushes that logic down to sensing nodes that must run under milliwatt budgets.
39 Always-on wake-word detection: A small, specialized model listens for the acoustic signature of a wake phrase and acts as a power gate for the higher-power application processor. The acceptable detector budget depends on the platform, but spending even a few extra milliwatts continuously can materially shorten battery life. The architecture succeeds only when the always-on path consumes far less average power than the components it prevents from waking.
Vasisht, Deepak, Zerina Kapetanovic, Jongho Won, Xinxin Jin, Ranveer Chandra, Sudipta N. Sinha, Ashish Kapoor, Madhusudhan Sudarshan, and Sean Stratman. 2017. “FarmBeats: An IoT Platform for Data-Driven Agriculture.” 14th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 17), 515–29.
Wildlife conservation shows the uplink arithmetic. Solar-powered acoustic sensors identify species on-device and transmit periodic detection summaries rather than raw audio, cutting uplink data from 4.3 GB/day to 400 KB/day, a 10,750× reduction that conserves power in off-grid deployments. Medical wearables apply the same logic to physiological monitoring, where runtime remains bounded by sensor draw, radio power, duty cycle, and sleep energy rather than by the model alone.
These four paradigms form an operational continuum bounded by the speed of light, heat dissipation, and memory signaling. When architecting an ML system, engineering begins by systematically mapping application constraints against these physical boundaries.

Comparing a dedicated TinyML keyword spotting model (~\(10\ \mu\text{J}\) per inference) to a cloud foundation model query (~\(1\text{ kJ}\) per inference), by approximately what factor does energy consumption per inference differ?

Approximately \(100\times\) (2 orders of magnitude)
Approximately \(10{,}000\times\) (4 orders of magnitude)
Approximately \(100{,}000{,}000\times\) (\(10^8\), 8 orders of magnitude)
Approximately \(10^{14}\times\) (14 orders of magnitude)

Why are microcontroller TinyML devices predominantly restricted to inference-only execution rather than full in-situ backpropagation training?

Microcontrollers use flash memory which permanently locks all transistor gates against state changes.
Backpropagation requires double-precision FP64 floating-point arithmetic which is mathematically impossible on 32-bit cores.
The speed of light inside microcontroller silicon is too slow to support backward gradient propagation.
Conventional training retains intermediate results needed for gradient calculations and adds gradient and optimizer state, which can exceed a microcontroller’s working-memory budget.

Why is the 1 mW average power threshold considered a transformative milestone in TinyML system deployment?
Why is it a fallacy to treat TinyML as merely ‘scaled-down mobile ML’ that can be addressed simply by applying standard INT8 post-training quantization?

title: Deployment Paradigm Framework
text:
An architect choosing where to run an ML feature rarely optimizes one dimension. A privacy rule may forbid cloud processing, a latency budget may forbid remote inference, a memory footprint may exceed the mobile device, and a cost target may rule out always-on edge hardware. Cloud, edge, mobile, and TinyML are operating envelopes for those conflicts, so selecting among them requires a unified comparison framework and a structured decision process.


Deployment decisions require evaluating latency-vs-throughput paradigm trade-offs across physical and operational envelopes at once. The resource envelopes are already on the table: table 1 gives each paradigm’s latency, power, and memory regime, and table 4 grounds them in concrete platforms. What those tables leave out are the operational dimensions that decide many real deployments: how the system scales, what it exposes, whether it needs a network, what it costs, and how hard it is to build and ship. Table 9 contrasts the four paradigms along those eight dimensions.



Table 9: Operational Paradigm Comparison: Eight operational dimensions that complement the resource envelopes of table 1 and table 4. Cloud ML scales most easily, while local processing can reduce transmission and centralized-storage exposure without itself guaranteeing privacy; local tiers can operate without a WAN, but real-time response depends on workload and complete-path timing, while development complexity is highest at the two ends of the spectrum. Cost anchors mix recurring service bills with device purchase prices; they are partial illustrations, not a matched lifecycle-cost ranking.

This contrast reflects the fundamental tension between data locality and computational scale. Remote processing expands the network attack surface and requires robust transport encryption and tenancy isolation; local processing confines raw data to the device, mitigating ingress exposure without eliminating physical side-channel risks. The workload archetypes from section 1.2 map directly to these boundaries, with each archetype gravitating toward paradigms that alleviate its primary bottleneck.
Each paradigm shifts engineering complexity to a distinct subsystem. Cloud deployments demand expertise in multi-tenant networking and dynamic cost governance. Edge and TinyML deployments impose local thermal and memory limits while distributing update and maintenance responsibilities across sites. Mobile deployments operate on user-owned hardware, reducing infrastructure purchase costs while introducing platform-specific drivers, operating-system background task limits, and shared energy budgets. None of these categories supplies a workload-independent latency or energy ranking.
A common architectural failure is selecting a deployment target based on model accuracy alone while treating hardware constraints as downstream optimization details. An unquantized model that delivers 99 percent accuracy in an offline evaluation becomes unviable if its memory footprint triggers paging on mobile hardware, or if continuous inference drives thermal throttling within seconds. Physical invariants—memory capacity, thermal dissipation limits, and network transit delay—must serve as early screening criteria before model development begins, pruning invalid deployment targets before training resources are expended.



Before choosing a deployment tier, an engineer must establish whether the feature justifies machine learning at all. Deep neural networks impose a substantial maintenance burden that traditional software avoids. Before committing to any ML architecture, an engineer must evaluate whether a deterministic heuristic can solve the problem at a fraction of the operational cost.

Systems Perspective 2.3: The complexity taxConsider a classification task solvable either by deterministic heuristic rules or by a deep learning pipeline. The heuristic requires fifty lines of code, incurs near-zero compute cost, demands approximately one hour per month to update rules, and fails in ways engineers can read in the code. The ML system may require only fifty lines of model definition, but it introduces roughly 2,000 lines of supporting infrastructure for feature ingestion, telemetry logging, drift monitoring, and GPU driver management, alongside 40 hours per month diagnosing data drift and maintaining pipelines.
An ML model that increases accuracy from 90 percent to 95 percent while introducing a 40\(\times\) expansion in operational maintenance requires an economic comparison. The accuracy and maintenance ratios alone do not establish the return; the value of the avoided errors must justify the additional engineering cost. Machine learning systems engineering focuses on minimizing this overhead through resilient architectures; when the ongoing maintenance cost outstrips the value of marginal statistical gains, deterministic software remains the correct systems choice.


This trade-off reframes model selection as a systems-level optimization spanning physical execution limits, capital expenditure, and the ongoing maintenance of prediction quality. When this complexity tax outweighs the operational value of improved statistical predictions, maintaining an ML deployment actively degrades overall system efficiency.
Systematic paradigm selection relies on a tiered decision framework ordered by how rapidly a constraint invalidates an architecture. The screening hierarchy evaluates four successive gates: regulatory privacy, physical latency, local compute capacity, and lifecycle economics. Privacy leads the order because a legal prohibition on moving data eliminates an option before anything is measured, whereas the latency and compute gates require numbers. Figure 10 formalizes this screening sequence as successive filters on a candidate set. Each gate passes only its survivors to the next.






Figure 10: Deployment Decision Screening: Apply privacy, latency, resource, and cost gates to the remaining candidate set. Every gate retains upstream exclusions. An empty set requires redesign or partitioning; surviving candidates still need complete-path validation.



The flowchart carries a remaining candidate set through all four gates. If regulatory rules or data sovereignty forbid off-device transmission, remote cloud processing stays excluded when compute demand is considered. If a network round-trip lower bound exceeds the deadline, additional remote compute cannot restore that path. Cost compares only the survivors, and an empty set calls for changing the workload or partitioning it across tiers. Passing a lower-bound latency screen still requires complete-path validation. An automotive emergency braking scenario demonstrates how the latency gate binds before compute capacity or cost enter consideration.

Example 2.1: Autonomous vehicle emergency brakingScenario: An autonomous vehicle vision system performs real-time pedestrian detection for emergency braking under a strict 100 ms end-to-end latency budget.
Diagnosis: At 100 km/h, the vehicle covers 2.8 m during the 100 ms budget, so every millisecond of delay is distance traveled before braking begins. The scenario assumes 50–150 ms of network round-trip delay for cloud offload, which consumes half the budget at best and more than all of it at worst before any detection runs. Local object detection on an automotive edge accelerator takes 10–30 ms; at 10 GFLOPs per frame and 30 FPS, that accelerator must sustain 300 GFLOP/s.
Systems lesson: The stated network-delay range cannot guarantee the deadline, so the latency gate excludes that cloud path. The local candidates remain subject to the resource gate: the pedestrian detector must fit memory and sustain the stated frame rate within its power budget. An automotive edge accelerator remains a candidate under these assumptions; its complete sensing-to-braking path still needs validation. Cloud connections can support offline training and telemetry without reentering the emergency decision path.


A completed placement decision needs evidence about the surviving paths as well as grounds for rejecting the others. A factory inspection example supplies that evidence explicitly.

Example 2.2: Completing a placement decisionProblem: A fixed factory camera requires 20 FPS inspection with a 100 ms sensing-to-decision deadline. Raw images must remain on premises. Which feasible deployment has the lowest matched lifecycle cost under the following hypothetical evidence?
Supplied evidence: A rule-based baseline fails the specified missed-defect criterion, while the learned detector meets both the missed-defect and false-alarm criteria on representative inspection data. The proposed mobile and microcontroller variants fail that same quality requirement. Local edge candidates A and B preserve the validated detector and preprocessing. Both have a complete peak working set of 2 GB within an available 4 GB, and each must stay within a 25 W sustained system-power budget.
Under the specified peak load and thermal conditions, the supplied complete-path latency bounds are 80 ms for A and 40 ms for B, including acquisition, preprocessing, queuing, inference, and the inspection decision. Their sustained rates are 25 FPS and 40 FPS, at 10 W and 20 W. Both satisfy the same availability and recovery requirements. Annualized budgets over the same service lifetime, including hardware, power, installation, maintenance, and recovery provisions, are $2,400 for A and $3,600 for B. These supplied bounds and budgets define an instructional scenario, not benchmarks of named products.
Result: Select local edge candidate A. Privacy excludes raw-image cloud offload, task quality excludes the proposed smaller variants, and both edge paths satisfy the timing, throughput, memory, and power requirements. A has the lower matched cost. B’s faster response supplies no required benefit under this specification; a tighter deadline could change the choice.
Systems lesson: The final choice follows from task quality and complete-path evidence, not the tier label or peak compute rate. The decision remains valid within the supplied operating conditions; changes to the input stream, detector, load, or thermal environment require reevaluating the relevant gates.


The completed comparison depends on operational maintainability as well as execution performance. Its matched budgets include obligations that a hardware-only comparison would omit. Deploying a model across thousands of edge nodes or millions of microcontrollers introduces sustained lifecycle overhead: automated firmware updates, out-of-band telemetry, distributed drift monitoring, and hardware failure recovery. An organization equipped for cloud operations may lack the embedded toolchains and physical testing infrastructure required to support edge or TinyML targets at scale.

Checkpoint 2.2: System design
First justify the learned system against simpler baselines; then screen its deployment candidates against the physical and operational constraints.
Decision gates

The baseline: Can you distinguish a rule-based baseline, such as a regular expression, from a simple learned baseline, such as a small model trained on a handful of features, and explain what comparison each provides?
Physical feasibility: If a remote path’s propagation floor exceeds the service deadline, can you reject it and identify which local execution and memory measurements are still needed before choosing an alternative?
The infrastructure cost: What evidence about error consequences and engineering cost is needed to decide whether a five-point accuracy gain (90 to 95 percent) justifies a 40\(\times\) increase in monthly maintenance hours?



The decision framework screens candidate tiers for physical feasibility and then compares their operational costs. If no single tier meets the requirements of the whole pipeline, the next question is which stages can run separately, and what must cross the boundaries between them.

Self-Check: Question

The layers are ordered by how rapidly a hard constraint can completely invalidate an architecture: legal/privacy rules may forbid remote transmission entirely, physical latency limits can make cloud offload impossible, compute demands eliminate undersized devices, and cost compares the remaining feasible survivors.
Privacy is the easiest parameter to optimize in software using compiler flags, whereas cost cannot be calculated until after deployment.

title: Deployment Paradigm Framework
text:
A voice interface can use a microcontroller to listen continuously for a wake word, a phone to transcribe speech, and cloud servers to interpret requests that need a larger model. Each stage has a different task and resource budget. Sending every audio sample to the cloud would add communication and radio costs; asking the microcontroller to perform every stage would exceed its compute and memory capacity. Hybrid architectures divide the pipeline across tiers so that each stage meets its requirements. The division also creates engineering work: deciding what data crosses each boundary and keeping the participating stages consistent. Three integration patterns organize these choices.


The three essential hybrid ML patterns differ by which physical boundary dictates the partition: train-serve split, hierarchical processing, or progressive deployment. Selecting a pattern is an iron-law decision: each stage of computation must execute where its binding term—whether throughput capacity \(\PeakRate\), local latency floor \(\Latency\), or memory capacity—incurs the lowest system penalty.
Under a train-serve split, training executes in centralized data centers while inference runs locally on edge, mobile, or embedded devices. This decoupling resolves the fundamental asymmetry between model optimization and model execution. Training must retain intermediate results and information used to calculate and apply parameter updates, in addition to the model weights. Under common 16-bit mixed-precision training with a standard adaptive optimizer, the weights, their gradients, and the optimizer’s running statistics together occupy about 16 bytes per parameter, roughly 8\(\times\) the 2 bytes per parameter that 16-bit inference weights need, before any batch activations are counted (Memory management develops this accounting). Inference uses the trained weights to compute predictions, sometimes through repeated passes as in token-by-token generation, and must satisfy local latency and privacy constraints. Amortization underpins the economics of this split: the high fixed cost of training is distributed across millions of forward-pass queries served locally without recurring network transmission costs.40
40 Train-serve cost asymmetry: Training usually requires many forward and backward passes, whereas one inference request uses a trained artifact for one or more forward passes. Training is not literally one-time because models may be retrained, and inference cost varies sharply with model size, sequence length, batching, and service overhead. The economic rationale for the split is amortization: repeated use can spread each training cycle’s fixed cost across many served predictions.
↪ Memory accounting for optimizer states, gradients, and activation buffers during training is developed in Memory management.


Definition 2.6: Hybrid ML
Hybrid machine learning is the deployment strategy that distributes an ML pipeline across two or more deployment tiers, assigning each stage according to its latency, compute, data, and operational constraints.

Significance: Hybrid architectures exploit the iron law’s additive structure: the edge tier can reduce \(\Latency\) for time-sensitive preprocessing and inference, while the cloud tier can provide the \(\PeakRate\) needed for training, retraining, and heavy batch inference. The split follows the data locality invariant: compare each stage’s complete local and remote paths, reject paths that miss the service deadline, and then choose among the feasible alternatives.
Distinction: Unlike cloud-only deployment (which accepts the distance penalty for all stages) or edge-only deployment (which accepts limited \(\PeakRate\) for all stages), hybrid ML assigns each pipeline stage to the tier where its binding iron law term is minimized.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that hybrid ML is just “running two models.” In reality, the participating tiers must share synchronized state—feature definitions, model versions, and preprocessing logic—so that their paths produce consistent results. Without this synchronization, training-serving skew emerges at tier boundaries.



Under hierarchical processing, computation cascades across tiers to progressively filter and aggregate data, matching communication volume to available interconnect bandwidth. Sensor streams generated at the physical periphery often exceed wide-area network (WAN) uplink capacity; continuously streaming raw, uncompressed telemetry to a data center saturates network links and wastes radio power. To prevent network saturation, early tiers filter data locally: TinyML microcontrollers run low-power anomaly detectors, edge gateways aggregate and correlate temporal features across multiple sensors, and cloud clusters ingest only anomalous events or aggregated summaries for global analytics. During inference serving, hierarchical processing frequently takes the form of a confidence cascade. A compact, low-latency model on the local device evaluates the input first. If its prediction confidence exceeds a calibrated confidence threshold, the device returns the result immediately, bypassing the network entirely. Only ambiguous or low-confidence inputs trigger a WAN payload transfer to a larger cloud model. The cascade seeks lower median latency at the required task quality, but confident local errors can bypass escalation. Representative evaluation must establish the routed system’s accuracy, error costs, and escalation frequency before accepting that trade-off.
Under progressive deployment, an engineering team derives a family of specialized model variants from a unified architecture or training corpus, tailoring each variant to the memory capacity, arithmetic intensity, and thermal limits of a specific tier. Rather than forcing a single model onto every device, developers produce tier-specific artifacts and evaluate the quality lost or retained as resource demands fall. The compression mechanisms are developed later; the placement decision here depends on whether each artifact meets its task and hardware constraints. For a shared image-classification task, an edge server and a phone can use different members of a model family, each evaluated against the same task requirements and its own resource budget. A voice interface that divides wake-word detection, acoustic processing, and language understanding among tiers instead illustrates hierarchical processing across different tasks. Such a system can also use tier-specific variants within a task, combining the patterns.
With three integration patterns available, selection becomes a constraint-matching problem: choose the pattern whose trade-off profile matches the system’s dominant bottleneck. Table 10 summarizes the trade-off, the conditions that favor each pattern, and the conditions that argue against it.



Table 10: Hybrid Pattern Selection Guide: The trade-off, favoring conditions, and disqualifying conditions for each of the three hybrid integration patterns. Selection matches the pattern’s trade-off profile to the system’s dominant bottleneck.











Pattern
Trade-off
Choose when
Avoid when




Train-Serve Split
Training cost vs. inference latency
Training requires more resources than inference; training data may leave the serving device
Local adaptation cannot wait for remote training and model delivery


Hierarchical Processing
Local autonomy vs. global optimization
Data volume exceeds transmission capacity; decisions needed at multiple timescales
All processing can occur at one tier; network is reliable and fast


Progressive Deployment
Model quality vs. deployment reach
Same model needed at multiple capability levels; graceful degradation required
Model cannot be meaningfully compressed; single deployment target






Production deployments rarely implement these patterns in isolation; complex systems compose them across different phases of the pipeline. An autonomous vehicle, for example, combines progressive deployment to fit specialized vision backbones into its on-board compute envelope, hierarchical processing to arbitrate between immediate millisecond-scale emergency braking on local hardware and multi-second trajectory planning, and a train-serve split that uploads anomalous driving slices to cloud clusters for fleet-level retraining. Privacy-preserving distributed training approaches extend this composition further when raw training data cannot leave client devices for regulatory or privacy reasons. In federated learning, for example, each device trains on its own data and sends only model updates to the cloud for aggregation.



Production hybrid systems coordinate multiple execution tiers through structured interaction channels. Figure 11 diagrams this multi-tier topology across five distinct communication pathways: compiled model artifacts deploy downward from cloud training clusters to edge, mobile, and TinyML inference engines, while raw sensor streams and filtered telemetry propagate upward toward cloud analytics, complemented by peer-to-peer result forwarding and local assist handoffs.






Figure 11: Hybrid System Interactions: Data flows upward from sensors through processing layers to cloud analytics, while trained models deploy downward to edge, mobile, and TinyML inference points. Five connection types (deploy, data, results, assist, and sync) establish a distributed architecture where each paradigm contributes unique capabilities.



Production systems demonstrate these integration patterns by placing each tier boundary at a distinct physical bottleneck:

Industrial defect detection: Assembly lines running at high cycle rates require sub-10 ms deterministic visual inspection. Streaming high-resolution camera frames over WAN to a data center violates inspection deadlines and exhausts factory uplink bandwidth. The system deploys a train-serve split: centralized cloud infrastructure uses multi-accelerator pods to train high-capacity vision models across historical defect databases, then compiles and quantizes runtime weights for factory-floor edge servers and embedded smart cameras. These on-premises accelerators read frames over local buses (a PCIe card slot or a direct camera interface) and execute inference there without external network dependencies. Bounded inspection latency still requires validating the complete local pipeline, including frame acquisition, preprocessing, and inference, under the expected load.
Agricultural monitoring: Deployed across hundreds of hectares, remote soil probes operate on coin-cell batteries or small solar harvesters, communicating over low-power wide-area radios such as LoRa, which carry little data and spend much energy per bit. Streaming continuous moisture and temperature telemetry exhausts battery reserves within days. Hierarchical processing confines high-frequency sampling and basic anomaly detection to TinyML microcontrollers operating in sub-milliwatt power budgets. When anomalies occur, local edge gateways aggregate measurements across spatial clusters of probes, transmitting only compressed, field-level summaries over cellular backhaul to cloud servers responsible for farm-wide irrigation scheduling.
Wearable fitness tracking: A battery-powered smartwatch must keep its always-on sensing path averaging under \(1\text{ mW}\) to preserve battery life. The system employs hierarchical processing: lightweight integer kernels run on an embedded microcontroller to track real-time motion and detect heart-rate thresholds; intermediate biometric data synchronizes over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) to a paired smartphone, which uses mobile neural engines and gigabytes of DRAM to classify complex activity patterns; finally, the smartphone transmits periodic compressed summaries over Wi-Fi or cellular networks to cloud infrastructure for longitudinal health modeling.




Although the four deployment tiers differ by orders of magnitude in available energy, memory capacity, and compute throughput, they rest on identical systems foundations. Every tier moves data through a pipeline, manages a fixed budget of compute, memory, energy, and network capacity, and binds models to hardware through a software architecture. On those three shared foundations rest the same cross-cutting concerns of efficiency, monitoring, and trustworthy engineering (figure 12).






Figure 12: Convergence of ML Systems: Despite vast resource disparities across cloud, edge, mobile, and TinyML tiers, all deployments converge on three shared systems foundations: data pipelines, resource management, and hardware-software architecture. These shared pillars in turn support unified requirements for performance optimization, operational monitoring, and trustworthy engineering.



This architectural convergence explains why engineering optimizations transfer across hardware scales: they target the same underlying physical bottlenecks. In representative hardware, fetching operands from off-chip memory can cost orders of magnitude more energy than the arithmetic performed on them, as the memory-wall discussion established. Techniques that reduce those transfers help both an embedded microcontroller and a warehouse-scale accelerator. Lower-precision numerical representations (such as FP8, INT8, and INT4) reduce storage and transfer demands in both local devices and cloud clusters. Halving the bits per value can halve the bytes transferred for those values, and supported formats can also raise arithmetic throughput; prediction quality and complete memory traffic still determine the useful gain. Similarly, kernel fusion (executing a chain of operations in one pass so that intermediate results stay on chip) and static memory staging can reduce off-chip traffic on mobile SoCs and HBM traffic during cloud autoregressive decoding. Graph-partitioning techniques also help assign pipeline stages across the CPU, GPU, and neural processing units of a mobile SoC, just as they help divide work across cloud workers.
The shared systems foundation extends through data engineering, model compression, and operational lifecycles. These engineering principles apply whether the execution target is a multi-node TPU pod or an ultra-low-power ESP32 microcontroller. Because the foundational abstractions remain invariant, so do their vulnerabilities: data distribution drift, model staleness, and telemetry degradation recur at every tier, requiring uniform monitoring discipline across the entire hybrid hierarchy.

Checkpoint 2.3: Hybrid ML patterns
Hybrid architectures work when partitioning work across tiers, not when copying the same pipeline everywhere.
Integration patterns

Train-serve split: Can you explain why training in the cloud and serving on edge/mobile is often economically optimal, even when the model runs locally?
Hierarchical processing: Can you describe what each tier does in a sensor → edge → cloud pipeline, and why pushing some decisions down reduces both latency and bandwidth?
Progressive deployment: Can you explain why a shared task may require different model artifacts on different tiers, and which quality and resource measurements would establish their suitability?

Design sanity checks

Boundary choice: Given a concrete application, can you justify where the tier boundary should fall (latency, privacy, bandwidth, power), not just what model to use?
State synchronization: Can you identify which feature definitions, model versions, and preprocessing logic must remain synchronized across tiers?




Self-Check: Question

A smart agriculture system deploys soil moisture sensors on microcontrollers performing local anomaly detection, local gateway edge servers that aggregate sensor feeds across crop fields to trigger automated irrigation valves, and a central cloud system that aggregates regional data for seasonal crop yield forecasting. Which hybrid ML integration pattern does this architecture exemplify?

Pure Train-Serve Split
Monolithic Cloud Offload
Hierarchical Processing

Transistors in edge devices reverse polarity when receiving cloud RPC payloads.
The speed of light in optical fiber decreases proportionally with the number of connected edge clients.
Edge devices become unable to allocate floating-point registers during network handshakes.

Establish a reference model or artifact for that task

title: Deployment Paradigm Framework
text:
Across all four deployment tiers mapped into the convergence hierarchy of figure 12, correct execution does not establish reliable predictions on a changing population. A fixed model can return the same output for the same input while its accuracy over incoming inputs changes. Consider an unchanged deployment in which the algorithm (\(\text{A}\)) and machine (\(\text{M}\)) remain fixed: the model weights reside in memory, and the runtime executes the same compute graph on every forward pass. The operational data distribution (\(\text{D}\)), however, evolves as user behaviors change, sensor calibrations drift, and environments fluctuate. Because model parameters represent an empirical fit to a fixed training distribution \(\TrainingDistribution\), changes in the live distribution \(\CurrentDistribution\) can reduce prediction quality. The introduction called the result silent degradation and its cause data drift. Seen at the level of a whole deployed system, the risk of accumulating degradation is what this chapter calls system entropy, a metaphor for declining predictive reliability even when code, model weights, and execution environments remain byte-for-byte identical. It is not a thermodynamic law or a claim that every distribution shift reduces accuracy.
The degradation equation (equation 1.2) provides a local approximation to this decay: where outcome evidence supports the relationship, accuracy falls from its deployment value \(\InitialAccuracy\) in proportion to the statistical distance \(\StatisticalDivergence\) between the live and training distributions, scaled by the model’s sensitivity \(\FittedSensitivity\). Because inference engines report success as long as matrix multiplications finish without numeric exceptions or memory faults, statistical degradation remains invisible to traditional infrastructure monitoring. An unmonitored model can continue generating confident predictions while its operational utility erodes. Distribution drift alone does not establish that loss. Safeguarding system reliability therefore requires telemetry to trigger investigation, outcome evidence to confirm degradation, and diagnosis to determine whether pipeline repair or a model update is warranted, an operational discipline analyzed in ML Operations.


↩︎ The divergence between static code binaries and non-stationary production distributions is established in ML vs. Traditional Software.

↪ Drift detection that compares live feature distributions against the training baseline with statistical distance measures is operationalized in Feature distribution monitoring.

Zillow Group. 2021. Zillow Group Reports Third-Quarter 2021 Financial Results and Shares Plan to Wind down Zillow Offers Operations. Investor Relations Press Release.

When predictions drive automated actions, undetected errors can accumulate into physical or financial losses. In 2021 Zillow wrote down $304 million in housing inventory after its Zillow Offers home-buying business purchased houses at prices above its own revised estimates of their future selling prices (Zillow Group 2021). Zillow’s account does not attribute the losses to drift specifically, and it does not establish which operational safeguards were absent. The systems lesson is the exposure created when uncertain forecasts drive large purchase commitments: prediction error can become inventory loss rather than remain an evaluation metric.


↪ The full Zillow Offers case, read as a coupled-decision failure, is developed in Production debt patterns.
The Zillow Offers failure illustrates that a machine learning system encompasses both the predictive model and the operational feedback loop that acts on its outputs. Treating deployment as a terminal handoff, in which a trained model is frozen and left to execute unattended, leaves changes in prediction quality unchecked. Changes in data (\(\text{D}\)) can erode the value of an algorithm (\(\text{A}\)) that the machine (\(\text{M}\)) continues to execute flawlessly; outcome evidence establishes whether that loss has occurred. Protecting a production pipeline requires engineering safeguards across the entire architecture, from input drift telemetry and validation gates to automated circuit breakers.

Improving infrastructure health checks so failed containers are restarted before they miss prediction requests.

Explain the variables in the local degradation approximation \(\text{Accuracy}(t) \approx \text{Accuracy}_0 - \lambda \cdot \mathcal{D}(P_t \lVert P_0)\), and describe what drift telemetry establishes versus what additional evidence is still needed.
