Convolutional networks exploit spatial structure, where physical proximity governs statistical correlation. Many real-world signals exhibit temporal structure, where sequential order and historical context determine meaning. Recurrent networks process these signals by maintaining persistent state across time steps.

Definition 6.4: Recurrent neural networks
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are sequence-processing architectures that maintain a hidden state \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t = \LayerFunction(\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1}, \LayerInputVector_t)\) updated at each time step, encoding the assumption that the current output depends on all prior inputs through this fixed-size state vector.

Significance: The fixed-size state provides \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) inference state memory regardless of sequence length (processing a 10,000-token sequence requires the same state memory as a 10-token sequence), but the sequential update rule forces all \(\SequenceLength\) recurrent transitions to execute in order. Separate per-step kernels (compiled accelerator routines, a different sense of the word from a convolution kernel) add launch overhead \((\Latency)\); fusion can reduce those launches while preserving the serial dependency chain.
Distinction: Unlike MLPs, which require a fixed-dimensional input vector, or CNNs, which restrict context to a fixed spatial window, RNNs compress an unbounded history into a fixed-size bottleneck state, so they accept sequences of any length without widening the input layer. Gradient signals pass back through the recurrent steps, where repeated Jacobian products can attenuate or amplify them (derived below).
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that RNNs are obsolete. For streaming inference on resource-constrained hardware, such as keyword spotting on a microcontroller, a model that must keep every past input to see the whole stream needs memory that grows with stream length, which can be prohibitive. An RNN’s \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) state size makes it a candidate when a fixed state budget is required.






RNNs hold state memory fixed, but latency grows with sequence length.
Feedforward architectures and standard CNNs treat inputs independently or constrain context to a fixed spatial receptive field. In sequential domains, however, dependencies span variable and often unbounded temporal distances. Expanding a convolutional receptive field to cover long sequences requires either stacking dozens of layers or applying dilated kernels, both of which scale parameter count and intermediate activation storage regardless of whether the intervening tokens contain relevant information.
Recurrent architectures, from simple recurrent networks to gated variants such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks (Elman 1990; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997), address this constraint by introducing a temporal inductive bias: execution order encodes causal direction, and history compresses into a recurring state. Instead of processing each input vector in isolation, the network carries an internal state vector across successive time steps. This inductive bias establishes an explicit engineering trade-off: it provides variable-length temporal context within a fixed memory budget, but it introduces loop-carried data dependencies that serialize execution on parallel accelerator hardware.

Elman, Jeffrey L. 1990. “Finding Structure in Time.” Cognitive Science 14 (2): 179–211. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1402_1.


In sequential pattern processing, the interpretation of an incoming token depends on the preceding sequence. For example, polysemous words such as “bank” cannot be disambiguated in isolation: “river bank” specifies a geological shoreline, whereas “investment bank” specifies a financial institution. The word’s identity alone is insufficient; its semantic role is resolved by preceding context. Acoustic waveforms and telemetry time series exhibit identical properties: individual samples are ambiguous without historical context spanning multiple frequencies and timescales.
Data with this structure imposes three concrete requirements on the underlying model:

Variable-length ingestion: Sequences arrive with non-uniform lengths \(\SequenceLength\), precluding fixed-dimension weight tensors that require static input shapes.
Contextual persistence: The model must retain informative historical signals over arbitrary time lags without requiring explicit windowing.
Continuous state update: Internal representations must update dynamically as each new token arrives, integrating new evidence while discarding obsolete or noisy history.

A fixed-input MLP requires windowing, padding, or truncation to process variable-length sequences. CNNs see a bounded window per layer; covering long histories requires stacking layers (receptive field grows linearly with depth) or dilated kernels (exponentially), at a cost in activation storage. Recurrence addresses the streaming requirements above by making a persistent, fixed-size state part of its dataflow.



To meet the requirements of section 1.6.1, recurrent neural networks introduce directed cycles in their computational graph. Rather than mapping inputs directly to outputs through feedforward layers, an RNN maintains a persistent vector, the hidden state, that updates iteratively at each time step. The hidden state acts as an internal register, summarizing past observations to contextualize future predictions.
The fundamental state transition in equation 6 computes the current hidden state \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t\) by combining the incoming token vector \(\LayerInputVector_t\) with the preceding state \(\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1}\): \[
\RecurrentHiddenState_t = \LayerNonlinearity(\RecurrentStateWeights\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1} + \RecurrentInputWeights\LayerInputVector_t + \RecurrentHiddenBias)
\tag{6}\] where \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t\) denotes the hidden state at time \(\TimeStepIndex\), \(\LayerInputVector_t\) denotes the input at time \(\TimeStepIndex\), \(\RecurrentStateWeights\) contains the recurrent weights, \(\RecurrentInputWeights\) contains the input weights, \(\RecurrentHiddenBias\) is the hidden-state bias vector, and \(\LayerNonlinearity\) is the activation function. The equation uses column vectors; the later listings use row-major batched tensors, so their weight multiplications appear on the right. Figure 6 contrasts the compact recurrent loop (left) with its computational unrolling across consecutive time steps (right), sequencing the transitions \(\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1} \to \RecurrentHiddenState_t \to \RecurrentHiddenState_{t+1}\) and isolating the strict temporal serialization enforced by the shared recurrent weight matrix \(\RecurrentStateWeights\).






Figure 6: Recurrent Neural Network Unfolding: Left panel shows the compact recurrent loop; right panel unfolds this across time steps. Three weight matrices are shared across all steps: \(\RecurrentInputWeights\) (input-to-hidden), \(\RecurrentStateWeights\) (hidden-to-hidden), and \(\RecurrentOutputWeights\) (hidden-to-output). These matrices are reused at every step, so the parameter count is independent of sequence length. For a 128-dimensional hidden state and a 100-dimensional input, each time step requires 16,384 MACs for recurrent connections plus 12,800 for input projection.



Unfolding the recurrent loop across \(\SequenceLength\) steps reveals the algorithmic properties of recurrence. Parameter count remains independent of sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) because the weight matrices \(\RecurrentStateWeights\) and \(\RecurrentInputWeights\) are shared across all time steps. However, sharing weights across time establishes a loop-carried dependency: step \(\TimeStepIndex\) cannot evaluate \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t\) until step \(\TimeStepIndex-1\) finishes producing \(\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1}\). This dependency forms a critical path of length \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) serial operations that prevents hardware accelerators from parallelizing across the sequence dimension.
This sequential structure produces fundamentally different memory characteristics between inference and training. During streaming inference, an RNN evaluates one step at a time, discarding prior raw inputs and retaining only the current hidden state. State memory overhead remains strictly \(\mathcal{O}(\HiddenDimension)\) in the hidden dimension \(\HiddenDimension\), regardless of whether the sequence spans 10 or 10,000 steps. In contrast, training via backpropagation through time (BPTT) unrolls the graph across the entire sequence of length \(\SequenceLength\). Computing gradients via the chain rule requires evaluating the Jacobian product across all intermediate transitions: \[
\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \RecurrentHiddenState_0} = \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \FinalRecurrentHiddenState} \prod_{t=1}^{\SequenceLength} \frac{\partial \RecurrentHiddenState_t}{\partial \RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1}}
\] Ordinary BPTT retains the intermediate activations \(\RecurrentHiddenState_1, \RecurrentHiddenState_2, \dots, \FinalRecurrentHiddenState\) for these Jacobian products. This retained-state scheme converts an \(\mathcal{O}(\HiddenDimension)\) runtime state into an \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength \cdot \HiddenDimension)\) training footprint; recomputing saved intermediates trades additional work for memory. Repeated Jacobians combine activation derivatives with \(\RecurrentStateWeights\), and their products can attenuate or amplify gradients over long horizons, limiting the effective context window of simple RNNs. Gated variants such as the LSTM answer this with learned gates, elementwise valves that decide at each step how much of the stored state to keep, overwrite, or expose; a kept state passes to the next step without being multiplied by \(\RecurrentStateWeights\), which gives gradients a path that does not shrink at every step. Section 1.10.2.4 examines the gating mechanism and its price, roughly four affine transformations per step instead of one. The recurrent weight matrix often contains connections with minimal contribution to temporal dependencies, allowing significant compression through methods covered in Model Compression.



Translating recurrent equations into hardware execution reveals how mathematical abstractions map to accelerator kernels, memory hierarchies, and loop nests. Where convolutional layers exploit spatial locality and weight reuse across tiles (section 1.5.4.3), recurrent steps decompose into matrix-vector or matrix-matrix multiplications bound by dataflow serialization.
Listing 5 demonstrates the single-time-step mechanism using framework-level matrix operations: combine the previous hidden state with the current input, add the bias, and apply the activation to produce the next hidden state. The code is intentionally local to one step because the systems cost is not the step itself, but the dependency chain that prevents parallel execution across time.



Listing 5: RNN Layer Abstraction: Framework-level implementation combining two matrix multiplications, \(\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1}\RecurrentStateWeights\) and \(\LayerInputVector_t\RecurrentInputWeights\), per time step. For 128-dimensional hidden state and 100-dimensional input, each step requires 16,384 + 12,800 = 29,184 MACs, but sequential dependencies prevent parallelization across time.


def rnn_layer_step(x_t, h_prev, W_hh, W_hx, b):
    # x_t: input at time t (batch_size × input_dim)
    # h_prev: previous hidden state (batch_size × hidden_dim)
    # W_hh: recurrent weights (hidden_dim × hidden_dim)
    # W_hx: input weights (input_dim × hidden_dim)
    h_t = activation(matmul(h_prev, W_hh) + matmul(x_t, W_hx) + b)
    return h_t



At the framework level, rnn_layer_step hides the underlying loop structure and memory traffic behind high-level matrix multiplications (matmul). In hardware, evaluating this step requires moving weights and activations through the memory hierarchy. To see where execution serializes and where parallelism remains, listing 6 expands the matrix operations into explicit loop nests down to scalar multiply-accumulate operations.



Listing 6: RNN Layer Computation: Nested loops expose the sequential dependency structure. Loop 1 enables batch parallelism, but Loops 2-3 must complete before Loop 4’s activation; because each time step depends on the previous step’s output, the resulting \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) sequential depth prevents GPU parallelization across the time dimension.


def rnn_layer_compute(x_t, h_prev, W_hh, W_hx, b):
    # Initialize next hidden state
    h_t = np.zeros_like(h_prev)

    # Loop 1: Process each sequence in the batch
    for batch in range(batch_size):
        # Loop 2: Compute recurrent contribution (h_prev × W_hh)
        for i in range(hidden_dim):
            for j in range(hidden_dim):
                h_t[batch, i] += h_prev[batch, j] * W_hh[j, i]

        # Loop 3: Compute input contribution (x_t × W_hx)
        for i in range(hidden_dim):
            for j in range(input_dim):
                h_t[batch, i] += x_t[batch, j] * W_hx[j, i]

        # Loop 4: Add bias and apply activation
        for i in range(hidden_dim):
            h_t[batch, i] = activation(h_t[batch, i] + b[i])

    return h_t



The loop structure exposes the concurrency boundaries of recurrent execution. Loop 1 demonstrates that batch instances are completely independent: sequences within a batch parallelize across accelerator cores without cross-talk. Within each batch instance, Loops 2 and 3 execute the recurrent transformation (\(\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1}\RecurrentStateWeights\)) and input projection (\(\LayerInputVector_t\RecurrentInputWeights\)). Both reductions must accumulate fully before Loop 4 can apply the elementwise bias addition and activation function to produce \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t\).
For an input dimension of 100 and a hidden state dimension of 128, each step executes two matrix multiplications: a \(100{\times}128\) input projection and a \(128{\times}128\) recurrent transformation. When batch size is large (\(\BatchSize\gg 1\)), these operations execute as general matrix-matrix multiplications (GEMM), achieving high arithmetic intensity as weights loaded from memory are reused across all \(\BatchSize\) samples. When batch size is small (\(\BatchSize=1\), typical of real-time streaming inference), the operations collapse into matrix-vector multiplications (GEMV). In GEMV, every weight parameter must be fetched from memory to perform a single multiply-accumulate, dropping arithmetic intensity to \(\approx 1\) FLOP/byte in FP16 (0.5 in FP32) and starving accelerator compute units.



The hard physical constraint that recurrent architectures impose is sequential dependency. In the update \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t = \tanh(\RecurrentStateWeights\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1} + \RecurrentInputWeights\LayerInputVector_t)\), the recurrent transformation at time step \(\TimeStepIndex\) needs the state produced by step \(\TimeStepIndex-1\). An input sequence of length \(\SequenceLength= 1{,}000\) therefore requires \(1{,}000\) ordered state updates, even when a fused kernel executes several or all updates within one launch. Hardware can parallelize across batch instances and within each matrix operation; input projections can also be computed across time when the inputs are available. Faster arithmetic or memory shortens individual steps, while the recurrent dependency chain remains.
During inference, recurrent networks achieve exceptional memory efficiency. Because the recurrent state compresses history into a fixed-size vector \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t\), inference state memory scales as \(\mathcal{O}(\HiddenDimension)\) (for example, 2 KB for a 512-dimensional FP32 state), remaining completely flat whether sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) is 10 or 10,000 tokens. This constant memory footprint contrasts sharply with attention mechanisms (section 1.7), whose stored context grows with every token because generating each new token reuses the stored keys and values of every earlier token, an \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength\cdot \HiddenDimension)\) store called the key-value cache. For streaming deployments on memory-constrained edge hardware, such as microcontrollers, an RNN’s \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) runtime state eliminates the memory-capacity exhaustion that limits transformers.
Recurrent execution exhibits distinct memory-hierarchy behaviors: high temporal locality for parameters, but poor operational intensity under standard framework dispatch. Weight matrices \(\RecurrentStateWeights\) and \(\RecurrentInputWeights\) are reused at every time step, residing comfortably in SRAM or L2 cache if the model fits on-chip. However, naively launching separate kernels for input projection, recurrent projection, bias addition, and activation at each time step incurs severe kernel-launch overhead and forces intermediate tensors back and forth across HBM. To mitigate this memory-bandwidth bottleneck, production recurrent runtimes fuse the projections, bias addition, and activation into a single monolithic kernel that maintains \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t\) within GPU registers and shared memory throughout the sequence execution.


↪ Kernel fusion, which keeps intermediate tensors on-chip instead of round-tripping them through device memory, is developed in Why execution strategy matters: The memory wall.
This architectural tension between fixed-capacity state and serialized execution defined sequence processing before transformers. While recurrent networks maintain constant memory overhead regardless of sequence length, the sequential dependency prevents hardware from parallelizing across time steps, the fixed-capacity state becomes an information bottleneck in which early inputs fade over long spans, and gradients through long chains of recurrent steps vanish or explode (the vanishing gradient problem). Overcoming these constraints required an architecture capable of establishing direct, content-addressable links across arbitrary sequence positions without intervening recurrent steps: the attention mechanism (section 1.7).

Recurrent networks serialize execution along the sequence dimension and compress all historical context into a fixed-capacity hidden state vector (section 1.6.4). In a sentence such as “The cat, which was sitting by the window overlooking the garden, was sleeping,” the subject “cat” and predicate “sleeping” are separated by ten intervening words, yet they form the core syntactic and semantic relationship. An RNN must process all intervening tokens sequentially, risking information loss across intermediate recurrent transitions while preventing hardware from parallelizing across time steps. This constraint motivates an alternative computational pattern: an operation that directly computes relevance between any two positions regardless of distance.
Attention mechanisms17 address this limitation (Bahdanau et al. 2015) by introducing dynamic connectivity patterns that adapt to input content. The setting was sequence-to-sequence translation, built as an encoder-decoder pair. An encoder network reads the input sentence into one representation per input position, and a decoder network generates the output sentence one token at a time, carrying its own recurrent decoder state. Recurrent versions of that pair passed only the encoder’s final state to the decoder. Rather than forcing all context through that single fixed-capacity vector, encoder-decoder attention computes similarity scores between the decoder state at each output step and all encoder positions, routing information dynamically across the sequence. A single decoder step compares one query with every encoder position. In full-sequence self-attention, each position queries all positions in the same sequence, so the number of score interactions grows quadratically with sequence length.
17 Bahdanau attention: This approach broke the “fixed-length vector” bottleneck of prior sequence-to-sequence models by allowing a decoder to dynamically query all input elements at each output step, creating the adaptive connectivity described. This replaced the structural constraint of a fixed-capacity channel with a learned, content-based weighting system. The core trade-off was accepting a linear, \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) memory cost to store all input states in exchange for overcoming the information loss inherent in a single vector.
Definition 6.5: Attention mechanisms
Attention mechanisms are neural network operations that compute a weighted sum of value vectors, where the weights are derived from learned similarity scores between a query vector and a set of key vectors, enabling dynamic, content-dependent information routing between any two positions in a sequence.

Significance: Attention connects any two tokens in \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) depth but computes \(\SequenceLength^2\) score interactions. If those scores are materialized, a 4,096-token sequence with 16-bit scores consumes 33.6 MB per layer per head (about 16.8M scores at 2 bytes each), directly increasing the iron law’s \(\DataVolume\) term.
Distinction: Unlike RNNs, which compress all prior context into a single fixed-size state vector, attention mechanisms retain token representations and compute relevance scores directly. During training or full-sequence prefill, the initial pass that processes the whole prompt, score interactions grow quadratically with sequence length; during autoregressive serving, the stored key-value (KV) cache, the saved key and value vectors of prior tokens, grows as \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength \HiddenDimension)\). Generation applies a causal mask, so each token attends only to itself and earlier positions. Keys and values are kept because each new token’s query must attend over every earlier key and value; earlier queries are discarded because, under that mask, past tokens never attend forward.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that attention is a general-purpose weighting scheme that can be applied freely. Quadratic score computation is a hard scaling constraint: doubling the context quadruples score interactions. Naive implementations also quadruple score storage; tiled exact algorithms such as FlashAttention avoid the full matrix, while sparse variants reduce the scores computed.



While attention mechanisms were initially used as components within recurrent architectures, their ability to connect any position to any other made the recurrent structure unnecessary for many sequence tasks. The transformer18 (Vaswani et al. 2017) removed recurrence entirely, trading the RNN’s \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) sequential path for constant path length between positions within one attention layer and thereby enabling parallelization across sequence positions on high-throughput accelerators.
18 Transformer: The founding paper, “Attention Is All You Need,” made the explicit systems claim that a parallel attention mechanism could fully replace sequential recurrent processing. This architectural trade eliminates an RNN’s \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) path length constraint on parallelism but introduces \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) dense score computation, a quadratic cost that continues to shape context-window engineering.Attention functions as a computational primitive rather than an independent architecture family. The transformer (section 1.8), the family built around it, inherits its core systems properties directly from attention: content-dependent routing, parallel sequence execution, and quadratic score scaling. Evaluating those properties begins with the dynamic pattern-processing problem that attention addresses.


Dynamic pattern processing addresses scenarios where relationships between elements are not fixed by architecture but instead emerge from content. Language translation exemplifies this challenge: when translating “the bank by the river,” understanding “bank” requires attending to “river,” but in “the bank approved the loan,” the important relationship is with “approved” and “loan.” Unlike RNNs that process information sequentially or CNNs that use fixed spatial stencils, dynamic sequence processing requires an operation that evaluates relationships based on token identity. Figure 7 diagrams this dynamic routing for coreference resolution in a sample sentence, isolating how attention weights bridge non-adjacent words.






Figure 7: Illustrative Attention Pattern: A schematic attention pattern for the pronoun “they.” Line thickness represents hypothetical attention-weight magnitude, with stronger links to “student,” “finish,” and “homework.” One attention layer connects all positions directly and can compute their dense interactions in parallel.



The bipartite connection lines in figure 7 illustrate how the pronoun “they” could receive information from “student” and “finish.” The hypothetical weights demonstrate a direct routing path, not a measured coreference result. Pairwise connections can be evaluated in parallel, allowing a single layer to connect these positions without propagating intermediate state across intervening tokens.
Input-dependent processing extends well beyond language. In protein structure prediction, amino-acid interactions depend on chemical properties and spatial arrangement, not only chain position; in document analysis, connections between sections depend on semantic content rather than proximity. Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) (Kipf and Welling 2017) share attention’s input-dependent routing but gather features along the sparse edges of each input graph, producing irregular memory access that can bind execution on memory bandwidth and cache misses rather than compute throughput.

Kipf, Thomas N, and Max Welling. 2017. “Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
Input dependence does not imply all-to-all connectivity. Dense attention scores every pair of sequence elements, whereas a GCN restricts aggregation to edges in the observed graph. The common systems challenge is that the computation or memory-access pattern responds to the input rather than following a fixed stencil. Even when tensor dimensions stay fixed, content-dependent scores determine which information is emphasized. Attention provides one mechanism for learning such relationships, and dense self-attention forms the foundation of the transformer architecture.



Meeting the dynamic routing requirements of section 1.7.1 requires a formal operator that maps variable-length sequences to content-dependent affinity weights (Bahdanau et al. 2015). The transformer architecture implements this mapping via the scaled dot-product attention operator introduced by Vaswani et al. (2017): \[
\text{Attention}(\AttentionQueryMatrix, \AttentionKeyMatrix, \AttentionValuesMatrix) = \text{softmax}
\left(\frac{\AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T}{\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}}\right)\AttentionValuesMatrix\]
19 Query-key-value (QKV): The terminology is borrowed from information retrieval, explaining why the equation uses three distinct learned projections to calculate pairwise scores. Creating these projections requires three independent weight matrices, costing \(3 \times \HiddenDimension^2\) parameters per layer. The direct systems consequence is the “KV cache” for autoregressive inference: all prior key and value vectors must be stored for the next token, causing memory to grow linearly (\(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\)) with sequence length and potentially dominate serving memory at long contexts or high concurrency.For this self-attention case, the inputs \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\) (queries), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\) (keys), and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) (values)19 are learned linear projections of the token representations (\(\AttentionQueryMatrix= \LayerInputMatrix\QueryProjectionMatrix\), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix= \LayerInputMatrix\KeyProjectionMatrix\), \(\AttentionValuesMatrix= \LayerInputMatrix\AttentionValuesProjectionMatrix\)). Attention uses three separate projection matrices rather than computing dot-product affinities directly between raw tokens (\(\LayerInputMatrix\LayerInputMatrix^T\)) for two architectural reasons:

Asymmetric relationships: Direct token dot products \(\LayerInputVector_i \cdot \LayerInputVector_j\) are strictly commutative (\(\LayerInputVector_i \cdot \LayerInputVector_j = \LayerInputVector_j \cdot \LayerInputVector_i\)). However, linguistic and contextual relationships are fundamentally asymmetric. In “the chef cooked the meal,” read whole by an encoder that lets every token see every other, the verb “cooked” seeks its direct object (“meal”), while “meal” plays a receptive role. (A generating decoder adds a causal mask that blocks attention to later positions, so in generation only “meal” can look back at “cooked”; either way, the two directions of a token pair need different scores.) Decoupling into query (what information a token seeks) and key (what features a token advertises) allows \(\CookedTokenQueryVector\cdot \MealTokenKeyVector\) to be high while \(\MealTokenQueryVector\cdot \CookedTokenKeyVector\) remains low.
Decoupling routing from content: The dot products \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T\) determine where to look (routing coefficients), while the value projection \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) determines what information to retrieve. Without a separate value projection, a token acting as a strong structural signpost (such as a preposition or punctuation mark) would force its entire raw embedding into downstream layers. Projecting through \(\AttentionValuesProjectionMatrix\) allows the network to strip away irrelevant lexical identity and extract only task-relevant features.

For an input sequence of length \(\SequenceLength\) projected to a dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension\) (here the full width \(\HiddenDimension\); the transformer’s multi-head attention later splits that width across several parallel attention computations called heads), the dot product \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T\) computes all \(\SequenceLength^2\) pairwise token similarities. Scaling by \(1/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}\) prevents dot products from growing large in magnitude at high dimensions, which would push softmax into regions with vanishingly small gradients. The softmax operator20 normalizes each row of the score matrix into a probability distribution over key positions. Finally, multiplying these normalized weights by \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) produces output vectors formed as weighted combinations of the value representations.
20 Softmax: Named as a “soft” (differentiable) version of argmax, with mathematical roots in Boltzmann’s statistical mechanics, softmax normalizes each query row over all \(\SequenceLength\) scores and therefore requires a reduction over each row. Online softmax lets that reduction run over tiles with running statistics, which is why it need not force quadratic storage (section 1.7.4.1).

Figure 8 traces this dataflow for a sequence of length \(\SequenceLength= 6\): cyan query rows match against red key columns to populate the \(6{\times}6\) similarity matrix, whose rows subsequently weight the green value vectors to produce the contextualized output vectors on the right. Each row of the resulting \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) matrix determines how strongly an individual token attends to every token in the sequence. In a trained model, the largest affinity values reflect strong contextual dependencies, while near-zero entries suppress irrelevant positions.

While attention weights vary dynamically with the input tokens, generating the query, key, and value vectors requires static linear projections against learned parameter matrices. In accelerator implementations, these three operations are fused into a single batched matrix multiplication to maximize Tensor Core saturation and eliminate kernel launch overhead. Figure 9 diagrams this fused projection: multiplying the \(6{\times}768\) token embedding matrix by the packed \(768{\times}2304\) weight matrix and adding the bias vector produces a concatenated \(6{\times}2304\) output tensor in a single kernel pass.

The 2304 output dimension contains concatenated query, key, and value projections (each 768-dimensional). This single batched matrix multiplication, requiring \(6{\times}768{\times}2304\) = 10.6 million MACs, replaces 3 separate projection operations for efficiency. Lowering the attention operator \(\text{Attention}(\AttentionQueryMatrix, \AttentionKeyMatrix, \AttentionValuesMatrix) = \text{softmax}(\AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension})\AttentionValuesMatrix\) to physical execution exposes the system cost of data-dependent connectivity. Evaluating pairwise alignments requires two distinct matrix multiplications per attention head: the score GEMM (\(\AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T\)) and the context GEMM (\(\AttentionWeightMatrix\AttentionValuesMatrix\), where \(\AttentionWeightMatrix= \text{softmax}(\AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension})\)). For an input of sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) and head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension\), each phase executes \(\SequenceLength^2 \AttentionHeadDimension\) multiply-accumulate operations, yielding \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2 \AttentionHeadDimension)\) computational complexity per head.
Listing 7 contrasts the high-level matrix formulation with an explicit loop implementation that exposes this quadratic scaling. The matrix version lowers to optimized GEMM routines on accelerator Tensor Cores, whereas the loop version reveals the underlying physical execution structure: batch iterations, quadratic query-key inner products, row-wise softmax reductions, and the final value accumulation pass across all sequence positions.



Listing 7: Attention Computation: Two implementations showing the same \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2\times \AttentionHeadDimension)\) complexity. The matrix form (top) uses optimized GEMM, while the nested loops (bottom) expose the quadratic pairwise comparisons: for sequence length 512 and head dimension 64, computing attention scores requires \(512{\times}512{\times}64\) = 16.8M MACs per attention head, plus another 16.8M MACs for value aggregation.


def attention_layer_matrix(Q, K, V):
    # Q, K, V: (batch_size × seq_len × d_head)
    # Compute attention scores
    scores = matmul(Q, K.transpose(-2, -1)) / sqrt(d_head)
    weights = softmax(scores)  # Normalize scores
    output = matmul(weights, V)  # Combine values
    return output


def attention_layer_compute(Q, K, V):
    # Initialize outputs
    scores = np.zeros((batch_size, seq_len, seq_len))
    outputs = np.zeros_like(V)

    # Loop 1: Process each sequence in batch
    for b in range(batch_size):
        # Loop 2: Compute attention for each query position
        for i in range(seq_len):
            # Loop 3: Compare with each key position
            for j in range(seq_len):
                # Compute attention score
                for d in range(d_head):
                    scores[b, i, j] += Q[b, i, d] * K[b, j, d]
                scores[b, i, j] /= sqrt(d_head)

        # Apply softmax to scores
        for i in range(seq_len):
            scores[b, i] = softmax(scores[b, i])

        # Loop 4: Combine values using attention weights
        for i in range(seq_len):
            for j in range(seq_len):
                for d in range(d_head):
                    outputs[b, i, d] += scores[b, i, j] * V[b, j, d]

    return outputs






Attention mechanisms exhibit distinctive system-level patterns that break from fixed-stencil and recurrent architectures. In iron law terms, attention eliminates the latency-bound serial path of RNNs at the cost of quadratic score arithmetic and massive intermediate data movement. Evaluating these system demands requires distinguishing what physics makes mathematically unavoidable from what engineering can optimize away at runtime.


Attention mechanisms require storage for query-key-value projections and intermediate feature representations. A naive implementation also materializes an \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) attention-weight matrix for every sequence and head, creating a quadratic memory bottleneck alongside the \(\SequenceLength{\times}\HiddenDimension\) inputs and outputs. For long sequences, these transient scores can dominate accelerator memory even though the learned projection matrices remain fixed in size. Tiled exact-attention kernels such as FlashAttention stream score blocks through faster memory and avoid retaining the complete matrix in HBM, while still computing \(\SequenceLength^2\) dense interactions (FlashAttention Tiling & Online Softmax Recurrence Proof derives the online softmax recurrence and its I/O reduction). This distinction separates an unavoidable quadratic compute cost for dense attention from optional quadratic score storage. Without kernel tiling, materializing intermediate score matrices quickly exhausts accelerator high-bandwidth memory at production sequence lengths.



Doubling context quadruples score interactions and naive score storage.

Napkin Math 6.1: The quadratic bottleneckProblem: How much memory does a materialized attention matrix require at sequence length \(\SequenceLength =\) 100,000 (context window)?
Math:

Matrix size: The attention score matrix \((\AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T)\) has dimensions \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) per head, across \(\AttentionHeadCount\) heads (12 heads in this example).
Elements: 100,000 \(\times\) 100,000 \(\times\) 12 heads = 1.2 × 10¹¹ elements.
Memory: At FP16 (2 bytes/element): 1.2 × 10¹¹ \(\times\) 2 bytes = 240 GB.
Retained layers: 240 GB per layer \(\times\) 32 retained layers = 7,680 GB.

Systems insight: A materialized attention matrix consumes 240 GB per layer. Naive training that retains all 32 layers’ scores for backward would require 7,680 GB, far exceeding any single GPU’s capacity. This memory wall motivates two broad implementation strategies: avoid materializing the full matrix by tiling the computation, or reduce the number of scores computed in the first place.





Attention computation splits into two primary GEMM phases interleaved by a row-wise reduction: generating pairwise query-key scores and computing weighted sums over values. Query-key inner products require \(\BatchSize \times \AttentionHeadCount \times \SequenceLength^2 \times \AttentionHeadDimension\) MAC operations, mirrored symmetrically by the value-aggregation stage. The intervening softmax requires row-wise maximum finding, exponentiation, and summation. Unlike static weight convolutions where filter weights are reused across fixed grid positions, attention computes transient, input-dependent affinity matrices that must be refreshed for every token configuration.

Data movement in attention creates memory access patterns distinct from fixed-stencil operations. Evaluating attention requires projecting and streaming query, key, and value tensors, then routing value vectors according to dynamically evaluated scores. In naive implementations, staging the intermediate \(\SequenceLength \times \SequenceLength\) score matrix in global HBM/DRAM turns score materialization into the dominant bandwidth bottleneck. While static convolutions benefit from deterministic cache lines and RNNs reuse weights across time, naive attention generates massive, short-lived activation footprints that challenge standard on-chip cache capacities.

Example 6.4: The quadratic wallScenario: BERT was pretrained with 512 learned position embeddings, so its deployments enforced a hard 512-token input limit (Devlin et al. 2019).
Diagnosis: Inputs beyond the pretrained positions are undefined for the model, however much memory is available. The limit itself was chosen partly because attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Extending from 512 to 4,096 tokens would multiply materialized score memory by 64×.
Systems lesson: Super-linear scaling turns algorithmic complexity into a hardware constraint that becomes fixed in the model itself once pretraining chooses it. No serving-time memory fix extends BERT past 512 positions, so its longer inputs must be truncated or split into windows. A model meant for long inputs must be pretrained with longer positions, and tiled or sparse attention is what keeps that training and its serving within the HBM activation budget.

Attention replaces the serialized hidden-state bottleneck of recurrent models with dynamic, constant-depth routing, but shifts the system burden to quadratic arithmetic scaling and high memory bandwidth traffic. Built into a full architecture without recurrence, this primitive enables end-to-end parallel sequence processing on modern accelerators. The transformer architecture (section 1.8) builds directly on this foundation, establishing the dominant architectural paradigm for modern large-scale machine learning systems.

Attention provides the computational primitive of dynamic, content-dependent routing between positions, yet it was originally layered on top of recurrent architectures, inheriting their sequential bottleneck. The transformer architecture removes recurrence and makes attention the operation that mixes information between positions in every layer. This enables parallel computation across sequence positions during full-sequence processing while retaining dynamic connectivity. This architectural shift introduces distinct physical costs: quadratic dense-score computation during prefill, accumulating key-value state during serving, and severe memory-bandwidth pressure during autoregressive generation.

Definition 6.6: Transformers
Transformers are neural network architectures that combine self-attention, feed-forward layers, residual connections, normalization, and positional information without recurrence, enabling parallel processing across sequence positions during training and prefill.

Significance: Parallelism is the systems payoff. An RNN processing an \(\SequenceLength\)-token sequence executes \(\SequenceLength\) sequentially dependent steps. A transformer processes all positions of a sequence concurrently, mapping token interactions to large matrix multiplications (GEMMs) that maximize accelerator compute utilization. Dense self-attention still computes \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) pairwise score interactions (section 1.7.4.1).
Distinction: Unlike attention used inside a recurrent backbone, which inherits the host architecture’s \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) sequential path, transformers use attention as the primary mixing operation between positions, alternating it with position-wise feed-forward networks.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that transformers have “infinite context.” Two distinct memory footprints matter: the \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) attention-score activation matrix when materialized during training and prefill, and the \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) key-value (KV) cache that accumulates during autoregressive serving. Exact tiled attention avoids the full score matrix while retaining quadratic dense arithmetic. At long sequence lengths, the KV cache footprint can rival or exceed the static model weights, turning KV cache management and memory-bandwidth efficiency into dominant engineering constraints.





The recurrent sequence-to-sequence hybrids that first carried attention (Sutskever et al. 2014; Bahdanau et al. 2015) fixed the information bottleneck of section 1.6.4 but not its serialization. Step \(\TimeStepIndex\) still waited on step \(\TimeStepIndex-1\), so a 1,000-token input still paid 1,000 ordered state updates no matter how many execution units the accelerator offered. Removing that chain requires replacing sequential state propagation with all-to-all interactions among positions, giving up the RNN’s bounded per-step memory in exchange for parallel accelerator execution.

Sutskever, Ilya, Oriol Vinyals, and Quoc V. Le. 2014. “Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 27: 3104–12.
The transformer architecture (Vaswani et al. 2017) establishes self-attention as the primary mixing primitive across positions, paired with positional encodings to inject sequence order. This architectural choice trades the spatial parameter efficiency of CNNs and the bounded \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) step state of RNNs for unconstrained sequence parallelism during training and prefill.



The architectural shift in transformers centers on self-attention layers. Unlike encoder-decoder attention where queries originate from the target sequence and keys/values from the source, self-attention derives queries, keys, and values from the identical input sequence \(\LayerInputMatrix\). Making all three projections self-referential allows the model to resolve intra-sequence dependencies across arbitrary token distances without intermediate recurrent steps. Equation 7 formalizes this transformation: \[
\text{SelfAttention}(\LayerInputMatrix) = \text{softmax}
\left(\frac{\LayerInputMatrix\QueryProjectionMatrix(\LayerInputMatrix\KeyProjectionMatrix)^T}{\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}}\right)\LayerInputMatrix\AttentionValuesProjectionMatrix
\tag{7}\]
Here, \(\LayerInputMatrix\) is the input sequence, and \(\QueryProjectionMatrix\), \(\KeyProjectionMatrix\), and \(\AttentionValuesProjectionMatrix\) are learned weight matrices for queries, keys, and values respectively. This formulation highlights how self-attention derives all its components from the same input, creating a dynamic, content-dependent processing pattern. Without positional information or an attention mask, matrix multiplication and row-wise softmax operate symmetrically across the token dimension, making self-attention permutation-equivariant: shuffling the rows of \(\LayerInputMatrix\) merely shuffles the output rows identically, treating the sequence as an unordered set. Positional encodings, whether added as sinusoidal vectors or applied via rotary position embeddings, inject sequence order and relative distance.
For autoregressive models, the causal mask enforces directional dependency during both training and generation. It sets attention scores for future positions (\(\TimeStepIndex' > \TimeStepIndex\)) to negative infinity before the softmax, ensuring that each position attends only to preceding tokens and itself. During next-token training, the entire target sequence is already available in advance. Shifting the known sequence right by one position pairs each input token with its target successor (figure 10), while the causal mask guarantees that evaluation at position \(\TimeStepIndex\) cannot access tokens at \(\TimeStepIndex' > \TimeStepIndex\). Because all input tokens are known simultaneously, an accelerator evaluates every position in the sequence concurrently using dense matrix multiplications rather than stepping through a serial time loop as an RNN must. Autoregressive inference, in contrast, must generate token \(\TimeStepIndex\) before extending the context to predict token \(\TimeStepIndex+1\), though prompt prefill similarly evaluates the entire initial prompt in parallel.
Transformers extend single-head self-attention by executing multiple attention operations in parallel through multi-head attention. Instead of computing a single set of attention weights over \(\HiddenDimension\) dimensions, the architecture projects queries, keys, and values into \(\AttentionHeadCount\) distinct lower-dimensional subspaces of dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension = \HiddenDimension/ \AttentionHeadCount\). Each head attends to different representation patterns simultaneously. Their outputs are concatenated and projected through an output matrix \(\AttentionOutputProjectionMatrix\), as formalized in equation 8: \[
\text{MultiHead}(\QuerySourceMatrix, \KeySourceMatrix, \AttentionValuesSourceMatrix) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_{\AttentionHeadCount})\AttentionOutputProjectionMatrix
\tag{8}\] where each attention head is computed as follows. In this multi-head notation, \(\QuerySourceMatrix\), \(\KeySourceMatrix\), and \(\AttentionValuesSourceMatrix\) denote the source representations before the head-specific projections; for self-attention, all three are \(\LayerInputMatrix\). The head matrices apply the projections once: \[
\text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(\QuerySourceMatrix\HeadQueryProjectionMatrix, \KeySourceMatrix\HeadKeyProjectionMatrix, \AttentionValuesSourceMatrix\HeadValuesProjectionMatrix)
\]
The \(\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}\) scaling introduced with the attention operator follows from a variance argument. Assuming query and key components are independent random variables with zero mean and unit variance, their inner product \(\QueryVector_i \cdot \KeyVector_j = \sum_{\HeadComponentIndex=1}^{\AttentionHeadDimension} \QueryComponent \KeyComponent\) has zero mean and variance \(\AttentionHeadDimension\), so dividing by \(\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}\) restores unit variance and keeps softmax out of its saturated, near-zero-gradient region at large head dimensions.21
21 Attention scaling \((\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension})\): This normalization directly counteracts the linear growth in variance \((\AttentionHeadDimension)\) of the query-key dot product, preventing the softmax function from saturating where gradients would otherwise vanish. The systems consequence is most acute in mixed-precision training: when activations grow large, unscaled dot products can produce logits that overflow the 16-bit float range, destabilizing or halting learning entirely.Conceptually, attention implements a differentiable content-addressable memory. Whereas conventional memory architectures retrieve stored values at explicit addresses, self-attention uses the query vector \(\QueryVector_i\) to score similarity against all candidate keys \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \AttentionHeadDimension}\). The resulting softmax distribution generates a continuous interpolation over the value vectors \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \AttentionHeadDimension}\), functioning as a differentiable lookup operation.
Although individual attention heads often specialize in distinct syntactic or semantic patterns (Clark et al. 2019)—dynamically adapting the effective connectivity graph for each input sequence—empirical analyses reveal substantial head redundancy and acute numerical sensitivity in reduced-precision formats. These hardware-relevant behaviors motivate structural pruning, low-rank factorization, sparse attention patterns, and specialized quantization strategies.

To transform these dynamic projections into deep representations, the transformer architecture embeds self-attention within a standardized block topology. As diagrammed in figure 10, each block wraps multi-head attention and position-wise feed-forward sublayers with residual connections and layer normalization. Sinusoidal positional encodings combine with token embeddings at the base of both towers, feeding repeated multi-head attention and feed-forward stages before terminating in linear and softmax output heads. Because all positions can be processed in parallel rather than sequentially, the architecture trades recurrent state for large matrix operations that map well to accelerator training. The residual paths and normalization layers in this stack are shared building blocks rather than transformer inventions; section 1.10.2.2 and section 1.10.2.3 explain why they make deep stacks trainable and what each costs the machine.

Listing 8 presents a typical implementation, showing how self-attention derives queries, keys, and values from the same input sequence.



Listing 8: Self-Attention and Multi-Head Attention: Self-attention (top) derives \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\), and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) from the same input \(\LayerInputMatrix\) through three projections, then computes attention as before. Multi-head attention (bottom) runs \(\AttentionHeadCount\) parallel attention heads with dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension = \HiddenDimension/\AttentionHeadCount\), then concatenates and projects. For GPT-2 (768-dim, 12 heads), each head operates on 64 dimensions, partitioning the projected feature dimension across heads while enabling diverse relationship patterns.


def self_attention_layer(X, W_Q, W_K, W_V, d_head):
    # X: input tensor (batch_size × seq_len × d_model)
    # W_Q, W_K, W_V: weight matrices (d_model × d_head)

    Q = matmul(X, W_Q)
    K = matmul(X, W_K)
    V = matmul(X, W_V)

    scores = matmul(Q, K.transpose(-2, -1)) / sqrt(d_head)
    attention_weights = softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    output = matmul(attention_weights, V)

    return output

def multi_head_attention(X, W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O, num_heads, d_head):
    outputs = []
    for i in range(num_heads):
        head_output = self_attention_layer(
            X, W_Q[i], W_K[i], W_V[i], d_head
        )
        outputs.append(head_output)

    concat_output = concat(outputs, axis=-1)
    final_output = matmul(concat_output, W_O)

    return final_output



The attention listing accounts for information mixing across positions, but a complete block also transforms features within each position. An ordinary position-wise feed-forward network applies a dense projection from hidden width \(\HiddenDimension\) to an intermediate layer output width \(\LayerOutputWidth\), a nonlinear activation, and a second dense projection back to \(\HiddenDimension\). For a sequence of length \(\SequenceLength\), its tensor shapes follow \(\SequenceLength{\times}\HiddenDimension \to \SequenceLength{\times}\LayerOutputWidth \to \SequenceLength{\times}\HiddenDimension\). The same two weight matrices apply independently at every position, so the MLP accounting gives \(2\SequenceLength\HiddenDimension\LayerOutputWidth\) MACs and an intermediate tensor with \(\SequenceLength\LayerOutputWidth\) elements. This intermediate width is the feed-forward width in table 8.
For one full-sequence block at batch one, with one standard multi-head self-attention sublayer and that two-layer feed-forward network, the query, key, value, and output projections together require \(4\SequenceLength\HiddenDimension^2\) MACs. The two attention products add \(2\SequenceLength^2\HiddenDimension\) MACs across all heads, whose widths sum to \(\HiddenDimension\). Adding the feed-forward cost completes the block’s matrix-product account; these counts omit biases, softmax, normalization, nonlinear activations, and residual additions, and assume dense evaluation of all position pairs. At fixed widths, projections and the feed-forward network grow linearly with sequence length, while the pairwise products grow quadratically. Which part dominates therefore depends on both the sequence length and the chosen widths, even before memory traffic is measured.
During autoregressive inference, generating output tokens step-by-step reintroduces sequential serialization. At batch one, projection matrix multiplications become matrix-vector operations with less weight reuse, making off-chip bandwidth a likely limit when weights exceed cache capacity, as quantified in section 1.8.4 via the GPT-2 XL lighthouse.



The quadratic bottleneck analyzed in section 1.7.4 manifests differently across execution regimes. Because full-sequence training and prompt prefill operate on known token sequences under causal masking, accelerators evaluate all positions concurrently using dense matrix multiplications. Autoregressive decoding, by contrast, must generate each token before predicting the next. That loss of token concurrency reduces weight reuse and can shift the primary performance limit from arithmetic throughput to memory bandwidth and state retrieval; sequence length, batch size, and memory hierarchy limits determine whether that transition occurs.


During training and prompt prefill, all token positions are processed in parallel, allowing accelerator Tensor Cores to achieve high floating-point utilization, but dense attention’s score computation grows as \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) with sequence length \(\SequenceLength\). At 32k tokens, a materialized score matrix would occupy gigabytes per layer across multiple heads, and writing it to HBM and reading it back for softmax would make the layer bandwidth bound. I/O-aware tiling such as FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022) fuses the dot-product, softmax, and value-weighting steps into on-chip SRAM tiles (section 1.7.4.1), which removes that round-trip and leaves quadratic compute as the wall that remains.

Expanding sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) challenges accelerator memory hierarchies because full-sequence self-attention scales quadratically with context length. Autoregressive decoding generates one token at a time and often becomes memory-bandwidth bound at batch one (\(\BatchSize = 1\)) or small batch sizes when weights exceed on-chip memory. During prompt prefill or training, weight reuse across many token positions produces dense GEMMs with much higher arithmetic intensity. A large request batch (\(\BatchSize \gg 1\)) supplies many such positions, but prefill can obtain this reuse even for a single request with a long prompt.
During single-token generation (\(\BatchSize = 1\)), however, each projection layer collapses into a matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV). In the streamed-weight regime, the processor reads each projection weight from DRAM to multiply it by a single new token vector. This is the batch-one regime that equation 2 already derived for the MNIST layer at 0.5 FLOP/byte in FP32. Halving the weight width to 2 bytes in FP16, while still executing one multiply-accumulate operation (\(1\text{ MAC} = 2\text{ FLOPs}\)) per weight read, doubles that weight-only arithmetic intensity to exactly: \[\GemvArithmeticIntensity= \frac{2\text{ FLOPs}}{2\text{ bytes}} = 1.0\text{ FLOP/byte}\]


↩︎ The 1.0 FLOP/byte intensity of batch-one GEMV in 16-bit precision, and 0.5 FLOP/byte in FP32, is established in Performance enhancement techniques.
Because modern accelerators require tens to hundreds of FLOPs per byte to reach peak compute throughput, running at \(1.0\text{ FLOP/byte}\) leaves compute cores idling for the vast majority of execution time, waiting for weights to arrive across the memory bus. To generate each token, the system performs three operations:

Read model weights: Stream every parameter from off-chip memory to registers (for example, a 70-billion-parameter model streams 140 GB of FP16 weights per token; GPT-2 XL makes the cost of that first step concrete).
Perform matrix-vector operations: Compute projections with arithmetic intensity capped at \(1.0\text{ FLOP/byte}\).
Read and update the KV cache: Append new key and value vectors while streaming historical keys and values from memory.

The KV cache22 defined with the attention mechanism grows linearly with sequence length (\(\mathcal{O}(\LayerCount \times 2 \times \AttentionHeadCount \times \SequenceLength\times \AttentionHeadDimension)\) per request, distinct from the \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) attention score matrix during training), storing the key and value vectors for all previous tokens to avoid recomputing them (Pope et al. 2023; Kwon et al. 2023). Keys and values from past tokens are retained because the newly generated token’s query (\(\QueryVector_{t}\)) must attend across all historical context (\(\KeyVector_1 \dots \KeyVector_{t-1}\) and \(\AttentionValuesVector_1 \dots \AttentionValuesVector_{t-1}\)) to compute its next representation. Prior queries (\(\QueryVector_1 \dots \QueryVector_{t-1}\)) are safely discarded because past tokens never attend forward to future tokens, while caching past keys and values avoids re-running the entire model forward pass over the full prompt at every generated token. For long contexts, this cache can become massive (for example, 100+ GB), and each decoding step reads prior keys and values. The resulting bandwidth pressure depends on context length, batching, attention architecture, cache layout, and hardware.
22 KV cache memory scaling: For a 7-billion-parameter transformer in FP16, model weights consume ~14 GB; a single request’s cache requires 32 layers \(\times\) 2 (K,V) \(\times\) 32 heads \(\times\) 2,048 positions \(\times\) 128 dimensions \(\times\) 2 bytes, or about 1.07 GB. At 8 concurrent users, the cache is ~8.6 GB, a substantial addition to the weights. Because the cache grows linearly with context and concurrency, scaling throughput forces choices such as grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al. 2023), shorter contexts, or KV paging and offloading (Kwon et al. 2023). Paging and offloading preserve model outputs, whereas grouped-query attention changes the architecture and shorter contexts truncate historical context.

Across training and inference, transformers expose different opportunities for reuse: full-sequence processing parallelizes across token positions, dense attention computes quadratic score interactions, and small-batch autoregressive decoding stresses memory bandwidth when weights stream from off-chip memory.
Yet dense, spatial, and sequence models do not cover the full spectrum of production workloads. Large-scale recommendation systems depart from standard arithmetic-dominated pipelines by coupling sparse embedding lookups (where memory capacity and irregular access distributions govern throughput) with downstream dense interaction layers. This hybrid matters at production scale: Meta reported that recommendation models accounted for most of its AI inference cycles (Gupta et al. 2020), even though such workloads receive less academic attention than language or vision models. When a user opens a streaming service or e-commerce platform, the system must select a handful of recommendations from a catalog of millions within an end-to-end budget of tens of milliseconds. The engineering challenge requires mapping both users and items to dense vectors in a shared embedding space, then evaluating interaction probabilities at scale.
Large-table recommendation models expose a regime governed first by memory capacity. An accelerator engineered for dense matrix multiplication, such as an NVIDIA A100 providing hundreds of teraflops of arithmetic throughput alongside 80 GB of HBM, cannot hold terabytes of embeddings locally. The sparse stage gathers rows from these tables, placing different demands on the machine than the batched convolution and streamed-weight decoding regimes examined above.


The core challenge in recommendation systems is handling high-cardinality categorical features. A model must process user IDs across billions of accounts and item IDs across millions of products. Raw IDs carry no inherent geometry. User 1042 is not “near” user 1043 in any meaningful metric space, and a neural network cannot infer semantic relationships from integer values alone.
Embeddings solve the representation problem by mapping each discrete ID to a dense vector called an embedding23 (Mikolov et al. 2013). The system cost is that every lookup becomes an irregular read into a table spanning tens or hundreds of gigabytes. Recommendation models therefore encounter a capacity wall and a memory-bandwidth bottleneck before the first dense feedforward layer executes.
23 Embedding: Deriving from the mathematical embedding of one space into another, neural embeddings map discrete tokens (such as user IDs or vocabulary words) into continuous vector spaces where geometric proximity captures semantic similarity. Word2vec popularized neural word embeddings in 2013. For systems, embedding tables create a distinctive memory access pattern: each lookup is an irregular read into a potentially terabyte-scale table, producing a sparse, bandwidth-bound workload that makes DLRM fundamentally different from compute-bound architectures like ResNet.
Mikolov, Tomas, Kai Chen, Greg Corrado, and Jeffrey Dean. 2013. “Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space.” ICLR abs/1301.3781.



The DLRM architecture (Naumov et al. 2019) standardizes this workflow as a four-stage pipeline partitioned across dense and sparse regimes. Continuous features such as user age or time of day first flow through a bottom MLP, a compute-intensive but memory-light stage dominated by dense matrix multiplications. In parallel, categorical IDs index into dedicated embedding tables, which is where the memory capacity wall appears:

Naumov, Maxim, Dheevatsa Mudigere, Hao-Jun Michael Shi, Jianyu Huang, Narayanan Sundaraman, Jongsoo Park, Xiaodong Wang, et al. 2019. “Deep Learning Recommendation Model for Personalization and Recommendation Systems.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1906.00091.
For example, an embedding table for one billion users with 128-dimensional vectors requires \(10^9 \times 128 \times 4\) bytes \(\approx\) 512 GB of memory. This stage is memory-intensive but compute-light because each lookup is a memory copy with zero arithmetic reuse. The interaction layer then combines the dense activations from the bottom MLP with the gathered sparse embedding vectors through pairwise dot products that capture user-item correlations. Finally, a top MLP processes the concatenated interaction representations through feedforward layers to predict a target probability such as click-through rate. This combination of dense and sparse computation makes DLRM the chapter’s recommendation lighthouse; section 1.9.3 quantifies the capacity-bound profile that results.



DLRM’s computational mapping splits into two regimes that stress different hardware subsystems. The dense MLPs execute standard GEMM operations, identical to the MLP computational mapping discussed in section 1.4.4 and handled efficiently by Tensor Cores. The sparse embedding lookups, however, are qualitatively different. They are index-based memory gathers that copy parameter data with zero arithmetic reuse. An isolated lookup is bound by memory access latency; but when a batch executes hundreds of lookups across features and samples, aggregate throughput becomes memory-bandwidth bound as concurrent requests saturate the memory bus. This operational throughput limit is distinct from the capacity constraint: total table size dictates whether parameters fit in accelerator memory or must spill across PCIe to host DRAM, whereas available bandwidth governs how fast gathered rows arrive. Within each selected row, an embedding vector is contiguous (for instance, 128 FP32 elements spanning 512 bytes), allowing the downstream pooling loop to consume every transferred byte. Across rows, however, data-dependent categorical IDs lack predictable spatial locality, defeating hardware prefetchers between row accesses. Access popularity remains heavily skewed: a small set of hot rows (popular items, frequent users) exhibits strong temporal locality in on-chip caches, while the long tail of rarely touched rows misses to main memory. Listing 9 writes this sparse stage as a loop nest parallel to those of the other families.



Listing 9: Embedding-Bag Gather: Four nested loops expose DLRM’s sparse stage. Loops 1 and 2 parallelize across samples and features, but Loop 3 takes its addresses from the input IDs, so hardware cannot predict them, and Loop 4 performs one addition per 4-byte FP32 value loaded. Batching raises that intensity only when samples share hot rows.


def embedding_bag_compute(sparse_ids, tables):
    # Loop 1: Process each sample in the batch (parallelizable)
    for b in range(batch_size):
        # Loop 2: Each categorical feature has its own table
        for f in range(num_features):
            pooled[b, f, :] = 0
            # Loop 3: Multi-hot feature, one gather per active ID
            for idx in sparse_ids[b][f]:  # data-dependent address
                row = tables[f][idx]  # irregular read, little reuse
                # Loop 4: Pool (sum) the gathered rows
                for d in range(embed_dim):
                    pooled[b, f, d] += row[d]
    return pooled  # feeds the interaction layer

Once embedding tables exceed one device, capacity, not arithmetic, becomes the primary systems constraint. While a ResNet-50 (102.4 MB) fits on a single accelerator and a dense language model like GPT-3 (350 GB) fits within a single multi-GPU node, production recommendation models reach terabytes of embedding parameters. In iron law terms, capacity acts as a feasibility constraint that comes before either execution term. It decides where the tables live, and therefore which bandwidth the data term \(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\) must use: HBM when the tables fit, host DRAM over PCIe or a peer accelerator over NVLink when they do not.
The architecture therefore breaks the single-device assumption that holds for smaller dense models. Systems designers resolve this capacity wall through three distinct architectural strategies:

Shrink the tables: Compression, hashing, or pruning reduces capacity pressure, though these techniques risk information loss on long-tail users and items.
Move the tables: Embeddings can reside in host DRAM or external key-value stores, though remote lookups incur high data-movement latencies over PCIe or Ethernet.
Partition the tables: Tables can be sharded across multiple accelerators so that no single device stores the full model, though lookups then require cross-device communication.

Architecturally, DLRM turns recommendation into a capacity-management challenge before it becomes a compute-optimization task. Training-time model partitioning and hardware-accelerated interconnects address these distributed layouts, but the baseline sizing challenge begins with a single table.



One embedding table fits an 80 GB A100; a second breaches the capacity wall.

Math:

Table entries: 100M items.
Vector size: 128 elements.
Precision: FP32 (4 bytes per element).
Table size: 100M items \(\times\) 128 \(\times\) 4 bytes ≈ 51.2 GB.

Systems insight: A single embedding table for one feature (items) already consumes 64 percent of an 80 GB A100 GPU. Adding a user table of the same size means the embedding tables no longer fit on a single 80 GB accelerator, motivating table compression, off-device memory, or partitioning across devices. DLRM is capacity bound: the primary systems question is not how many FLOP/s the accelerator can deliver, but where the embedding state can physically reside.


Once the tables no longer fit on one device, sparse lookups cross memory and interconnect boundaries. A request may need rows owned by several accelerators, forcing the device executing the downstream MLP to wait while the system gathers them across PCIe or NVLink. Within a multi-accelerator server, gathering rows distributed across multiple GPUs turns memory routing into an interconnect bandwidth bottleneck. The architectural consequence is that a recommendation model’s memory layout directly determines its cross-accelerator data-transfer traffic, creating a coordination tax for both training and serving.

Three requests arrive at the same accelerator, one at a time. A single ResNet-50 frame performs about 8.2 GFLOP of arithmetic against 102.4 MB of FP32 weights, and each convolutional filter is reused across its feature map, creating opportunities to keep arithmetic units busy. A single GPT-2 token at batch size one performs about 3 GFLOP/token against 3 GB of FP16 weights. Streaming those weights once gives a weight-only arithmetic intensity of roughly 1 FLOP/byte, making bandwidth a likely limit. A DLRM request gathers a handful of embedding rows from tables totaling 100 GB, more than the accelerator’s 80 GB of memory, so before any question of speed arises the system must decide where those tables live.
The silicon is identical in all three cases, but the demands differ. Convolutional reuse favors arithmetic throughput, streamed token projections stress bandwidth, and oversized embedding tables impose a capacity constraint that decides which bandwidth their lookups pay. The iron law (Iron Law of ML Systems) turns these structural observations into predictions once execution conditions and machine balance are specified. The profiles below collect those conditions, shared building blocks explain costs that transfer between families, and deployment budgets screen the resulting candidates.

The parameter and activation columns decide how data reaches the arithmetic units, and the pattern of access matters as much as the volume. Three patterns cover the table. Sequential access, the streaming of contiguous weight rows in an MLP layer or a transformer projection, lets DRAM deliver long bursts and lets hardware prefetchers run ahead, so it approaches the interface’s peak bandwidth. Strided access, which a native convolution produces as it steps across the rows of a feature map, fetches whole cache lines to use a fraction of each; im2col lowering (section 1.5.3) converts it into sequential access at the price of up to \(\KernelSize^2\)-fold duplication (because overlapping sliding windows copy the same input pixels into multiple rows). Random access characterizes the DLRM row. Sparse IDs index arbitrary rows across multi-gigabyte tables; while each selected embedding vector is contiguous and fully consumed by pooling, row selection lacks predictable spatial locality between rows, which defeats hardware prefetchers and leaves sparse lookups exposed to memory latency unless many concurrent requests are in flight. Achieved bandwidth depends on vector width, alignment, and request concurrency, which is why caching popular rows is critical to reduce off-chip traffic. Attention is not random access despite its content-dependent weights, because its queries, keys, and values sit in contiguous tensors that tiled kernels stream through on-chip SRAM.
Whether an access pays DRAM prices at all depends on the working set, the data the execution units need at once. Small layers, such as the \(784{\times}100\) reference layer at 313.6 KB in FP32, fit in on-chip SRAM. Production-width layers of tens of megabytes do not, which is why unbatched MLP inference and transformer decode stream their weights from off-chip memory on every request. Accelerators answer both ends of the table with memory hierarchy rather than arithmetic. HBM stacks DRAM dies beside the processor to supply the streaming rows at more than an order of magnitude above standard DDR channels, and multi-megabyte on-chip SRAM, often an explicitly managed scratchpad, lets compilers stage tiles so that reuse happens on chip. The intensity column measures how much a family can profit from that staging, and it doubles as an energy column.



Moving a 32-bit value from DRAM costs far more energy than one FP32 multiply.

Systems Perspective 6.2: The energy cost of data movementA core systems principle: moving data costs more than computing on it. In the reference model of Horowitz (2014), an FP32 multiply costs about 3.7 pJ/FLOP, while fetching one 32-bit operand from off-chip DRAM costs 640 pJ, a gap of 173×. Low-intensity rows are therefore energy-dominated by DRAM traffic. An unbatched MLP or a decode step loads each weight once per request and spends most of its energy moving it. A CNN amortizes each filter load over \(\FeatureMapHeight\times \FeatureMapWidth\) applications, so the locality that makes it compute bound also makes it energy efficient, unless a fully materialized im2col buffer inflates temporary traffic by up to \(\KernelSize^2\). An RNN keeps its compact state in SRAM but idles execution units across serial steps, which raises energy per token. Tiled attention keeps score blocks on chip, so its energy tracks matrix multiplication rather than DRAM round-trips.
Later optimizations exploit this principle directly. Quantization reduces the bits moved per value; pruning removes unnecessary movement; and tiling keeps working sets in faster, lower-energy memory.


The parallel-axis column determines how data must move among processing elements once the work is spread out. Figure 12 schematizes the four fundamental data movement topologies (broadcast, scatter, gather, and reduction) that govern tensor routing among processing elements, whether those are units on one chip or several accelerators in one server. Batch parallelism in MLPs, CNNs, and prefill broadcasts stationary weight tiles to many units, each working on a different example or position, and compilers tile loops to reuse each broadcast value as often as possible. Spatial and model partitioning scatter a tensor across tiles or devices; mixture-of-experts models, which route each token to a few of many feedforward subnetworks, make the scatter input-dependent, so a popular expert can overload one accelerator while others idle. DLRM gathers embedding rows from wherever the sharded tables live, and each attention query gathers keys and values from every position in its sequence. Reductions combine values through sums or maxima (softmax denominators, normalization statistics, and the summing of gradients across accelerators that each trained on a different slice of the batch), and tree-structured reduction hardware finishes a reduction over \(\ReductionInputCount\) values in \(\mathcal{O}(\log \ReductionInputCount)\) stages rather than \(\mathcal{O}(\ReductionInputCount)\). The rows with a serial axis, RNNs and decode, are the rows these collectives cannot rescue, because no amount of broadcast or reduction bandwidth shortens a dependency chain.






Figure 12: Data Movement Primitives: Four fundamental patterns govern information flow in neural network computation. Broadcast (top-left) replicates a single value to all destinations, used when sharing weights across batch elements. Scatter (top-right) distributes distinct elements to different destinations, enabling work partitioning. Gather (bottom-left) collects distributed values to a single location, as in attention pooling. Reduction (bottom-right) combines multiple values through aggregation (sum, max), appearing in gradient synchronization and attention scoring. Because moving data costs more than computing on it, these patterns are primary optimization targets.



The last column applies the iron law under each row’s execution assumptions. When effective intensity exceeds the machine’s balance and parallel work is sufficient (batched CNNs, prefill), the compute term \(\Operations/(\PeakRate\,\EfficiencyHw)\) binds. Below that balance (streamed small-batch MLPs, decode), the data term \(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\) binds, favoring fewer transferred bytes, more reuse, or higher bandwidth. RNNs add a serial chain of state updates: faster arithmetic, memory, and reduced launch overhead \((\Latency)\) can shorten each step without removing the dependency. DLRM adds a constraint that sits in front of the equation. Capacity decides where the tables live and thus which bandwidth the data term pays. ResNet-50, GPT-2, and DLRM isolate these representative regimes. MobileNetV2 and KWS share the CNN row, with depthwise layers pulling their intensity down, because latency and power are deployment budgets that constrain the entire execution. No lighthouse occupies the RNN row, whose serial chain the recurrent family section analyzes directly.
