Mixed-precision training addresses two bottlenecks, compute throughput because Tensor Cores run faster on 16-bit operands, and memory capacity because each value uses fewer bytes. For transformer models, a third bottleneck often dominates, and the roofline analysis has already located it. Counting only its score-matrix traffic, materialized attention in GPT-2 Small reaches about 32 FLOP/byte, well left of the A100 ridge point in figure 1, because its quadratic intermediate matrices are written to HBM during the forward pass and read back during backpropagation. Halving the bytes per value does not change that quadratic traffic, so even with reduced precision the compute units can sit idle while the processor waits for data.
FlashAttention21 (Dao et al. 2022) addresses this bandwidth bottleneck by optimizing how data flows between memory hierarchies. Processing attention in SRAM-sized tiles avoids materializing the full \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) matrix in HBM and reduces traffic without changing the mathematical output, which is how the roofline preview moved attention rightward toward, and for favorable shapes past, the ridge.

FlashAttention-2 (Dao 2023) further improved parallelism and work partitioning, reporting 50–73 percent of theoretical peak on A100.

Standard self-attention computes relationships between all positions in a sequence. For an input sequence of length \(\SequenceLength\), the mechanism computes an \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) attention matrix according to equation 11:
\[ \text{Attention}(\AttentionQueryMatrix, \AttentionKeyMatrix, \AttentionValuesMatrix) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{\AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T}{\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}}\right)\AttentionValuesMatrix \tag{11}\]
Here, \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\), and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) are the query, key, and value matrices for the sequence, and \(\AttentionHeadDimension\) is the key-vector dimension used to scale the dot products before softmax. The \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T\) term is the source of the \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) score matrix, which is why attention becomes an I/O problem even when the arithmetic itself maps well to Tensor Cores.
The memory bottleneck emerges from materializing the \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) intermediate matrices for scores and probabilities. For a sequence length of 4,096 with head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension =\) 64 (typical for a single attention head), the attention score matrix alone requires \(4{,}096^2 \times 4\) bytes = 67.1 MB in FP32. This section counts FP32 scores throughout, since autocast policies commonly keep softmax in FP32; at FP16 every figure halves, as in the roofline estimate, while the quadratic growth stays the same. With 16 heads, this grows to 1.1 GB just for intermediate attention matrices, not including the keys, queries, values, or output tensors.
GPU memory hierarchy creates the opportunity for I/O-aware attention. HBM offers large off-chip capacity, while much smaller on-chip SRAM has substantially higher bandwidth and lower latency. Attention implementations that materialize the quadratic intermediates in HBM must write and later read them during backpropagation. Because that traffic grows with the square of sequence length, it takes a growing share of step time as sequences lengthen.
The backward pass requires the information represented by the attention probabilities, but an implementation may either save those intermediates or recompute them. For \(\AttentionWeightMatrix = \text{softmax}(\AttentionScoreMatrix)\) and \(\AttentionScoreMatrix = \AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}\), one gradient expression is: \[
\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \AttentionQueryMatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}} \cdot \text{dsoftmax}\!\left(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \AttentionWeightMatrix},\, \AttentionWeightMatrix\right) \cdot \AttentionKeyMatrix\] where \(\text{dsoftmax}\) denotes the softmax Jacobian-vector product. A conventional implementation may save the probability matrix for this computation; saving both probabilities and raw scores is not mathematically required. FlashAttention instead saves compact normalization statistics and recomputes tiled score and probability blocks during backward propagation, avoiding full quadratic intermediates in HBM.



FlashAttention eliminates the need to materialize full \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) attention matrices in HBM by computing attention incrementally through tiling. Instead of computing the entire attention matrix at once, the algorithm partitions \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\), and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) into tiles small enough to fit in fast SRAM, computes attention scores for these tiles, and incrementally accumulates results.
The key algorithmic insight relies on the structure of equation 11. Softmax normalizes each row of scores by a sum over the entire row, which seems to require the whole row before any output can be formed.
The online softmax algorithm removes that requirement. Ordinary softmax, \(\text{softmax}(\SoftmaxInputVector)_i = e^{\SoftmaxInputVector_i} / \sum_j e^{\SoftmaxInputVector_j}\), is computed stably by first subtracting the row maximum. The online form instead keeps two running statistics per row as blocks of scores arrive: the largest score seen so far, \(\SoftmaxRunningMaximum\), and the sum of exponentials taken relative to that maximum, \(\SoftmaxNormalizer\). When a new block raises the maximum from \(\SoftmaxRunningMaximum\) to \(\UpdatedSoftmaxRunningMaximum\), everything accumulated so far was exponentiated relative to the old maximum, and multiplying it by \(e^{\SoftmaxRunningMaximum-\UpdatedSoftmaxRunningMaximum}\) re-expresses it relative to the new one. The same factor rescales the partially accumulated output. After the last block, dividing the output by \(\SoftmaxNormalizer\) gives exactly the softmax-weighted result, as if the whole row had been seen at once.
Algorithm 3 decomposes this computation by partitioning the queries and the keys/values into tiles small enough to fit in SRAM, then streaming over the key/value tiles while maintaining the running softmax statistics needed to assemble each output tile, without ever forming the full score matrix.



FlashAttention swaps the full attention matrix for small SRAM tiles.
No full \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) score or probability matrix is written to HBM. A \(128{\times}128\) FP32 score tile, for example, occupies 65.5 KB compared with 67.1 MB for a \(4096{\times}4096\) matrix. Other inputs, outputs, and running statistics remain, so the tile is not necessarily the largest tensor in the entire kernel.

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{FlashAttention: tiled attention with online softmax}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require queries $\AttentionQueryMatrix$, keys $\AttentionKeyMatrix$, values $\AttentionValuesMatrix$ for a length-$\SequenceLength$ sequence; tile size $b_{\text{tile}}$
\Ensure attention output $\AttentionHeadOutput$, without materializing the $\SequenceLength\times \SequenceLength$ score matrix
\For{each query tile $\AttentionQueryMatrix_i$}
    \State in SRAM: $\AttentionHeadOutput_i^{\text{acc}} \gets \mathbf{0}$, $\SoftmaxRunningMaximum_i \gets -\infty$, $\SoftmaxNormalizer_i \gets 0$
    \For{each key/value tile $(\AttentionKeyMatrix_j, \AttentionValuesMatrix_j)$}
        \State load $\AttentionQueryMatrix_i, \AttentionKeyMatrix_j, \AttentionValuesMatrix_j$ into SRAM; $\AttentionScoreMatrix_{ij} \gets \AttentionQueryMatrix_i \AttentionKeyMatrix_j^T / \sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}$
        \State $\UpdatedSoftmaxRunningMaximum_i \gets \max(\SoftmaxRunningMaximum_i,\operatorname{rowmax}(\AttentionScoreMatrix_{ij}))$ \Comment{new stable max}
        \State $\AttentionHeadOutput_i^{\text{acc}} \gets \AttentionHeadOutput_i^{\text{acc}}\odot e^{\SoftmaxRunningMaximum_i-\UpdatedSoftmaxRunningMaximum_i} + e^{\AttentionScoreMatrix_{ij}-\UpdatedSoftmaxRunningMaximum_i}\AttentionValuesMatrix_j$
        \State $\SoftmaxNormalizer_i \gets \SoftmaxNormalizer_i\odot e^{\SoftmaxRunningMaximum_i-\UpdatedSoftmaxRunningMaximum_i} + \operatorname{rowsum}(e^{\AttentionScoreMatrix_{ij}-\UpdatedSoftmaxRunningMaximum_i})$; $\SoftmaxRunningMaximum_i \gets \UpdatedSoftmaxRunningMaximum_i$
        \State discard $\AttentionScoreMatrix_{ij}$ \Comment{never written to HBM}
    \EndFor
    \State $\AttentionHeadOutput_i \gets \AttentionHeadOutput_i^{\text{acc}} / \SoftmaxNormalizer_i$; write $\AttentionHeadOutput_i$ to HBM
\EndFor
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\(\AttentionQueryMatrix\)




FlashAttention improves both activation memory and memory IO, which are the limiting costs in bandwidth-bound attention. Standard attention requires \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) memory to store score matrices \(\AttentionScoreMatrix\) and attention-probability matrices \(\AttentionWeightMatrix\) across all sequence positions. FlashAttention reduces the stored activation footprint to \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) by keeping only input and output tensors \((\AttentionQueryMatrix, \AttentionKeyMatrix, \AttentionValuesMatrix, \AttentionHeadOutput)\) plus a small SRAM buffer for the current tile.
For \(\SequenceLength = 4096\), \(\AttentionHeadDimension = 64\), one materialized FP32 score matrix occupies \(4096^2 \times 4\) bytes = 67.1 MB per head. The three FP32 input tensors occupy \((3 \times 4096{\times}64) \times 4\) bytes ≈ 3.1 MB per head, a component-size ratio of 21.3× between one quadratic intermediate and the inputs. The comparison that decides memory is the whole per-head footprint each algorithm keeps for the backward pass. The conventional baseline assumed here stores the inputs, the output, and both the score and probability matrices, about 138.4 MB. FlashAttention stores the inputs, the output, and two numbers per row (the running maximum and sum), about 4.2 MB, roughly 32.7× smaller, and the gap widens as \(\SequenceLength\) grows because only the standard footprint is quadratic.
These stored-tensor totals exclude gradient buffers, temporary workspace, and the live SRAM tile, so they are not estimates of peak training memory. Implementations may also retain fewer quadratic intermediates than the conventional baseline assumed here.
The IO pattern changes for the same reason. Standard attention reads \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\), and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) from HBM, writes score, probability, and output matrices during the forward pass, then rereads those stored matrices during the backward pass before writing the gradients \(d\AttentionQueryMatrix\), \(d\AttentionKeyMatrix\), and \(d\AttentionValuesMatrix\) (shorthand for \(\partial \LossFunction/\partial \AttentionQueryMatrix\) and its counterparts). The resulting HBM traffic includes the same \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) term that made the activation footprint large. FlashAttention forms score and probability blocks in SRAM and never writes the full \(\SequenceLength \times \SequenceLength\) tensors to HBM. In the backward pass, it recomputes the needed blocks rather than reading stored full matrices. The exact HBM IO complexity depends on tile size and available SRAM because key and value blocks are streamed repeatedly across query blocks, so the bound is not simply \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength \cdot \HiddenDimension)\).
For large sequence lengths, FlashAttention reduces HBM traffic by avoiding writes and rereads of the \(\SequenceLength \times \SequenceLength\) score and probability matrices. With \(\SequenceLength = 4096\) and \(\AttentionHeadDimension = 64\), avoiding the stored attention matrices removes the quadratic component of the activation footprint, while the precise bandwidth reduction depends on hardware and kernel tiling.
Both approaches require \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2 \HiddenDimension)\) asymptotic FLOPs for dense attention. FlashAttention’s backward pass recomputes tiled attention intermediates from saved inputs and normalization statistics rather than storing full score and probability matrices. The resulting reduction in HBM traffic can shift the kernel toward compute-bound execution and produce a net speedup, but the final bottleneck remains shape- and hardware-dependent.



FlashAttention’s performance gains materialize through careful exploitation of GPU memory hierarchy. Modern frameworks can dispatch eligible attention operations among fused and fallback implementations based on hardware, inputs, and layouts; profiling verifies which path ran and whether it helped. Listing 6 contrasts standard and optimized attention implementations.



Listing 6: Attention Implementation Comparison: Standard attention materializes the full \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) matrix in HBM, while FlashAttention uses PyTorch’s optimized implementation or the dedicated flash-attn library.


import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


# Standard attention (materializes n-by-n matrix)
def standard_attention(q, k, v):
    # q, k, v: [batch, heads, seq_len, head_dim]
    scores = torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(-2, -1)) / (
        q.size(-1) ** 0.5
    )
    attn = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)  # n-by-n matrix in HBM
    output = torch.matmul(attn, v)
    return output


# FlashAttention (no n-by-n materialization)
def flash_attention(q, k, v):
    # Can use FlashAttention when inputs and hardware are eligible
    output = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)
    return output


# Explicit FlashAttention 2 (flash-attn library)
from flash_attn import flash_attn_func


def flash_attn_2(q, k, v):
    # q, k, v: [batch, seq_len, heads, head_dim]
    # Different layout for optimized memory access
    output = flash_attn_func(q, k, v)
    return output






Dao et al. (2022) reports end-to-end GPT-style training speedups and separate attention-kernel benchmarks showing that IO-aware attention reduces memory traffic and improves runtime. The mechanism established above is the important comparison: standard attention stores quadratic attention matrices for backward, while FlashAttention recomputes their tiles and avoids that off-chip materialization. Runtime and memory savings depend on batch size, head count, sequence length, precision, and the kernel implementation. A capacity threshold requires the complete training ledger, including the state outside attention.

Subsequent versions have continued improving performance: FlashAttention-2 (Dao 2023) achieved 1.5–2\(\times\) additional speedup through better parallelism and register allocation, while FlashAttention-3 (Shah et al. 2024) exploits asynchronous memory operations and FP8 tensor cores on Hopper GPUs; it reports about 740 TFLOP/s in FP16 on H100 (roughly 75 percent of peak), with its FP8 path reaching higher.



For transformer training with long sequences, FlashAttention is usually the first attention implementation to test. It often becomes essential once sequence length pushes standard attention into an HBM-capacity or HBM-bandwidth bottleneck, especially around the multi-thousand-token regime where the \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) attention matrices dominate memory. A100- and H100-class GPUs with fast on-chip SRAM benefit most. The returns diminish for short sequences where tiling overhead is not worthwhile, on older GPU architectures without comparable SRAM bandwidth, and for nonattention architectures such as convolutional neural networks and multilayer perceptrons.
In practice, deep learning frameworks handle much of FlashAttention’s integration, but the decision still depends on layout, precision, and memory budget. PyTorch’s scaled_dot_product_attention can dispatch to FlashAttention when hardware, inputs, and backend constraints permit; hand-written attention must use an eligible primitive. Three practical checks determine whether FlashAttention is appropriate:

Ensure tensor layouts match library expectations (contiguous memory, correct dimension ordering)
Use FP16 or BF16 for maximum speedup (FlashAttention optimized for mixed precision)
Combine with gradient checkpointing when additional activation-memory savings are needed.

The integration is often a single-line change—swapping a manual attention call for F.scaled_dot_product_attention, as listing 6 shows. The engineering decision is still the same one established by the roofline analysis: use the optimized primitive when the bottleneck is HBM traffic, and let the library manage the tiling and SRAM scheduling needed to remove it.



FlashAttention exemplifies a fundamental systems engineering principle: IO-aware algorithm design. Many accelerators are compute-abundant relative to memory bandwidth. For a bandwidth-bound kernel, traffic can govern runtime even when FLOPs do not change.
This principle extends beyond attention. In IO-aware matrix multiplication, tiling algorithms like those in CUTLASS minimize DRAM traffic by maximizing data reuse in fast caches. A naive \(\SquareGemmDimension{\times}\SquareGemmDimension\) matrix multiply performs \(\mathcal{O}(\SquareGemmDimension^3)\) FLOPs and, without reuse, \(\mathcal{O}(\SquareGemmDimension^3)\) memory traffic; blocking keeps tiles in fast memory and moves traffic toward the \(\mathcal{O}(\SquareGemmDimension^2)\) lower bound.
The same byte-movement principle reappears in communication-efficient distributed training, where gradient compression trades extra computation (compression/decompression) for reduced network bandwidth consumption. Low-power edge devices with limited memory bandwidth benefit even more from IO-aware algorithms. Trading 10 percent more arithmetic to halve memory traffic approaches a 2\(\times\) energy reduction in the limit where data movement accounts for the entire budget, and falls short of that bound whenever arithmetic carries a meaningful share, because halving one additive term of a sum cannot more than halve the sum. This section establishes the IO-aware heuristic; distributed and edge deployment settings reuse the same byte-movement logic.
Eliminating off-chip materialization of the \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) attention matrices reclaims accelerator memory across three architectural trade-offs. First, it enables longer sequence contexts on fixed hardware, with the workable context boundary determined by the complete training recipe. Second, freeing activation memory allows larger micro-batch sizes that improve hardware arithmetic saturation, provided gradient dynamics remain stable. Third, the contracted activation footprint permits deeper transformer stacks within a given memory budget, although end-to-end multi-billion-parameter feasibility continues to depend on parameter sharding, optimizer states, and remaining layer activations.
The technique demonstrates that systems-level algorithms can exploit memory hierarchy for large activation-memory reductions and workload-dependent speedups beyond hardware scaling alone. Treating memory bandwidth as the primary constraint and compute as abundant is a recurring pattern in ML performance optimization.
FlashAttention addresses memory bandwidth bottlenecks during computation, but another class of memory constraints exists: the sheer capacity required to store activations and optimizer states simultaneously. When models or batch sizes exceed GPU memory capacity, two complementary techniques trade computation for memory.




Both techniques have already appeared as tools. Gradient accumulation entered with mini-batch processing (section 1.3.2.1.2) as the way to build a large effective batch from micro-batches that fit, and checkpointing entered as algorithm 2, the schedule that discards activations and recomputes them during backward. This section supplies what using them correctly requires: the proof that accumulated gradients equal the large-batch gradient and the conditions under which that equivalence breaks, the per-update time cost and the synchronization boundary in multi-GPU training, the derivation of the \(\sqrt{\LayerCount}\) checkpoint placement, and the loss-normalization errors that most often break accumulation in practice.


Gradient accumulation and activation checkpointing operate on distinct principles, but both aim to optimize memory usage during training by modifying how forward and backward computations are handled. Gradient accumulation changes how many examples contribute to one update; checkpointing changes which activations remain resident between the forward and backward passes.


To execute large batch training on memory-constrained accelerators, systems split an effective logical batch across smaller sequential micro-batches. Figure 11 diagrams this reduction pathway: three consecutive micro-batches evaluate independent losses (\(\LossFunction_1, \LossFunction_2, \LossFunction_3\)) and gradients (\(\MicrobatchGradient_1, \MicrobatchGradient_2, \MicrobatchGradient_3\), where \(\MicrobatchGradient_j = \nabla_{\ModelParameters}\LossFunction_j\)), accumulating into a single unified tensor (\(\MicrobatchGradient_1 + \MicrobatchGradient_2 + \MicrobatchGradient_3\)) before triggering the optimizer step.






Figure 11: Gradient Accumulation: Three micro-batches each compute independent losses and gradients, which sum into a single combined gradient for one parameter update. This simulates training with a batch three times larger without requiring the memory to hold all samples simultaneously.



In PyTorch, gradient accumulation is usually implemented by dividing each micro-batch loss by the number of accumulation steps and calling optimizer.step() only after processing the entire effective batch. Under that averaging convention, no learning-rate adjustment is needed solely because of accumulation. The implementation follows five steps:

Perform the forward pass for a micro-batch.
Compute the gradients during the backward pass.
Accumulate the gradients into a buffer without updating the model parameters.
Repeat steps 1–3 for all micro-batches in the effective batch.
Update the model parameters using the accumulated gradients after all micro-batches are processed.

Gradient accumulation can reproduce the gradient of a larger batch under controlled assumptions. For an effective batch size \(\BatchSize= \AccumulationStepCount\times \MicrobatchSize\) where \(\AccumulationStepCount\) is the number of accumulation steps and \(\MicrobatchSize\) is the micro-batch size, equation 12 confirms that the accumulated gradient equals the true batch gradient: \[
\nabla \FullBatchLoss = \frac{1}{\BatchSize}\sum_{i=1}^{\BatchSize} \nabla \LossFunction_i = \frac{1}{\AccumulationStepCount}\sum_{j=1}^{\AccumulationStepCount}\left(\frac{1}{\MicrobatchSize}\sum_{i \in \MiniBatchSet_j} \nabla \LossFunction_i\right)
\tag{12}\]
This equivalence holds when each example’s computation is identical and the loss is averaged consistently. The right-hand side shows that averaging \(\AccumulationStepCount\) micro-batch gradients (each computed over \(\MicrobatchSize\) examples) produces the same result as computing the gradient over all \(\BatchSize= \AccumulationStepCount \MicrobatchSize\) examples at once. Stateful layers such as BatchNorm, stochastic operations such as dropout and data augmentation, finite-precision accumulation order, and step-indexed schedules can break exact equivalence, so large-batch accumulation still requires validation.
Gradient accumulation exchanges memory capacity for computation time. Table 14 separates the memory benefit from the compute and scheduling costs that remain.

Accumulation preserves the total example-level arithmetic but can change efficiency because smaller micro-batches use the accelerator differently and launch kernels more often. With distributed no_sync() accumulation, one gradient synchronization occurs after the \(\AccumulationStepCount\) local micro-batches rather than after each one. The wall-clock penalty relative to processing the effective batch at once is workload-dependent. It must be measured rather than inferred from the memory-reduction factor.
When gradient accumulation is combined with distributed data parallelism across multiple machines, additional considerations arise for gradient synchronization timing and effective batch size calculation across the cluster. Advanced distributed systems texts treat these patterns in depth.



Activation checkpointing reduces memory usage during the backward pass by discarding and selectively recomputing activations. In standard training, activations from the forward pass are stored in memory for use in gradient computations during backpropagation. However, these activations can consume gigabytes of memory, particularly in deep networks.
Activation memory can be reduced by trading additional FLOPs for reduced HBM occupancy during backpropagation. Figure 12 diagrams this recomputation cycle across forward and backward execution rows: only selected boundary tensors (solid green circles) are retained in device memory while intermediate activations (dashed gray circles) are dropped, then recomputed on demand (orange circles) as the backward pass traverses in reverse.






Figure 12: Activation Checkpointing: Trading memory usage for recomputation during backpropagation enables training deeper neural networks. By storing only a subset of activations from the forward pass and recomputing others on demand, this technique reduces peak memory requirements at the cost of increased training time.



The implementation keeps the capacity trade-off explicit. The system splits the model into segments, retains activations only at segment boundaries during the forward pass, and recomputes intermediate activations during the backward pass when needed.
Frameworks like PyTorch provide tools such as torch.utils.checkpoint to simplify this process, but the recompute cost remains. Checkpointing is most effective for deep architectures with dozens or hundreds of layers, such as transformers or large convolutional networks, where activation storage exceeds the GPU’s capacity before arithmetic throughput is exhausted.
The synergy between gradient accumulation and checkpointing enables training of larger, more complex models. Gradient accumulation manages memory constraints related to batch size, while checkpointing optimizes memory usage for intermediate activations. Together, these techniques expand the range of models that can be trained on available hardware.

Gradient accumulation produces an effective batch larger than the resident micro-batch without storing all of its activations simultaneously. A larger effective batch reduces sampling variance but does not guarantee faster convergence or better generalization. The technique is particularly valuable when the desired effective batch cannot fit in memory at once.
Activation checkpointing significantly reduces the memory footprint of intermediate activations during the forward pass, allowing training of deeper models. By discarding and recomputing activations as needed, checkpointing frees up memory for larger models, additional layers, or higher resolution data. This trade-off is critical in architectures like transformers that require substantial memory for intermediate computations.
Both techniques reduce activation-memory requirements without adding hardware. For lighthouse 8.1, accumulation provides a way to reach a chosen effective batch size while keeping the resident micro-batch within the conditional V100 memory budget.

Gradient accumulation is most valuable when optimal batch sizes exceed GPU memory capacity. Transformer language models often use effective batches of hundreds of thousands to millions of tokens; if memory only permits a smaller number of sequences per device, accumulation bridges the gap without requiring additional hardware. Activation checkpointing complements this by enabling deeper architectures and is commonly used in transformer-scale training, as well as in activation-heavy dual-network configurations such as generative adversarial networks.
Both techniques introduce explicit trade-offs. Activation checkpointing recomputes discarded activations during backward propagation; with ordinary segment checkpointing, each discarded activation is typically reconstructed once, while recursive schedules may behave differently. Gradient accumulation reduces parameter-update frequency because each update follows \(\AccumulationStepCount\) micro-batches. When each micro-batch loss is divided by \(\AccumulationStepCount\), the accumulated gradient follows the effective-batch mean convention. If losses are summed instead, the gradients must be rescaled before the optimizer step or the learning-rate convention changed accordingly. Framework and codebase conventions differ, making normalization a common source of subtle bugs.




Each training optimization targets a distinct physical bottleneck within the accelerator memory and compute hierarchy. Asynchronous prefetching pipelines host-to-device transfers across the PCIe bus with accelerator execution, preventing compute engines from idling on input data starvation. Mixed-precision training halves the bytes moved across the HBM bus for every 16-bit tensor and shrinks stored activations, while routing matrix arithmetic to specialized low-precision tensor units. FlashAttention complements these system-level interventions by resolving the quadratic memory-bandwidth bottleneck of self-attention; by tiling queries, keys, and values into on-chip SRAM, it reduces auxiliary attention memory from \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) to \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) and reports speedups of up to 3\(\times\) on evaluated workloads. Finally, activation checkpointing and gradient accumulation manage device memory capacity: checkpointing discards intermediate activations to reconstruct them via backward recomputation, while gradient accumulation partitions a large logical batch into temporal micro-batches to bound peak resident memory.
Because training throughput is governed by the system’s binding constraint, applying an optimization to a non-binding subsystem yields no end-to-end speedup. Accelerating tensor arithmetic with lower precision or FlashAttention cannot reduce step time if compute pipelines remain stalled waiting for batches from the host. Conversely, expanding prefetch buffers provides no benefit when execution is bound by HBM capacity or backward-pass recomputation. Profiling must therefore identify whether the workload is bound by I/O ingest, memory capacity, memory bandwidth, or arithmetic throughput before an intervention is selected.

Fitting the model into device memory resolves capacity, but does not guarantee efficient execution. Assume a profile of the newly executable model shows exposed input waits and the following breakdown of iteration time across subsystems:

Data loading: 40 percent of iteration time
Compute: 35 percent of iteration time

These assumed profile observations shift the diagnostic focus from machine memory capacity (M) to the data pipeline (D) in D·A·M terms. With 40 percent of iteration time spent waiting for host-prepared batches, reducing accelerator memory consumption alone does not address the dominant exposed delay. Improving input delivery is the next target in this scenario.
Step 5: Apply prefetching and data pipeline optimization.
Resolving input starvation requires overlapping host data preparation with accelerator computation. In this scenario, configuring the data loader with eight worker processes parallelizes CPU-side sample decoding, page-locked (pinned) host memory enables asynchronous DMA transfers across the PCIe bus, and a prefetch factor of 2 queues upcoming batches per worker in host memory. Device double buffering requires a separate copy-stream and buffer arrangement. Hiding host preprocessing and transfer latency behind kernel execution raises the accelerator’s busy-time fraction from 45 percent to 85 percent, reducing the assumed input starvation. A busy accelerator is not yet an efficient one; MFU measures how much of that busy time does useful model arithmetic. Re-profiling must establish whether memory bandwidth, arithmetic throughput, or another stage now limits execution.

\(90\text{ ms}\), because DMA transfers cannot overlap useful GPU computation.

Explain how FlashAttention computes exact self-attention with substantially lower memory footprint than standard attention, and describe what its backward pass does instead of reading a full stored score matrix from HBM.
Why does the chapter’s conventional FP16 mixed-precision recipe keep FP32 master weights and perform selected reductions in FP32 instead of forcing every part of training into 16-bit precision?

Tensor Cores cannot execute backpropagation unless gradients are stored in FP64.
FP16 allocations can lock the accelerator memory bus unless the master weights are moved to host RAM.
Automatic differentiation requires symbolic derivatives to be represented only in FP32.
Very small parameter updates can be rounded away when applied directly to FP16 weights, and selected reductions benefit from the wider range or precision of FP32 accumulation.

Gradient accumulation increases the memory footprint on the accelerator linearly with the accumulation factor \(K\) because all \(K\) micro-batches’ intermediate activations must remain in GPU memory simultaneously until the optimizer step.
In FP16 mixed-precision training, the loss is multiplied before backpropagation so the resulting gradients are shifted into a safer numeric range, then divided back down before the optimizer update. This technique is known as loss ____.
A team enables mixed precision on a transformer model and observes compute time drop by 45 percent, but total step time decreases by only 10 percent because the GPU now shows large idle gaps. Explain what likely happened in the system pipeline and what the team should do next.

title: Training Systems Fundamentals
text:
The GPT-2 walkthrough models how mixed precision and checkpointing reduce a batch-4 tensor budget to 28.6 GB, just under a V100’s 34.4 GB capacity before workspaces and allocator overhead. At batch 32, the modeled total falls from 597.8 GB to 60.7 GB but still exceeds that V100. Larger-memory accelerators may move the boundary. A 70-billion-parameter model, however, requires about 140 GB for FP16 weights alone and substantially more for full-parameter training state, motivating sharding, offload, or multiple devices.



GPT-2 at batch 4 fits just under one V100; batch 32 and a 70B model cross the wall.
When a chosen workload still exceeds one device’s memory or schedule, spreading it across devices provides aggregate memory and compute. Other responses include reducing the model, batch, sequence length, or training scope; offloading state; and parameter-efficient adaptation, which trains only a small set of added parameters on top of a frozen model. Scaling beyond one device begins with multi-GPU configurations inside one machine and may extend across nodes. The major parallelism strategies make different communication trade-offs; a full treatment of distributed-training implementation lies beyond this chapter.
Not all workloads benefit equally from adding GPUs. The relationship among useful computation, communication, imbalance, and synchronization determines scaling efficiency. Figure 13 charts this scaling decay on a log-log speedup plot up to 256 GPUs, contrasting ideal linear scaling against compute-bound (ResNet), balanced (a large language model (LLM) over NVLink), and bandwidth-bound regimes. The widening divergence between the ideal linear dashed reference and the plateauing modeled curves illustrates the communication tax paid as synchronization overhead compounds. In this fixed-fraction model, even unlimited parallel compute leaves the non-scaling fraction of the original runtime, so the limiting speedup is its reciprocal.














Figure 13: Communication Tax: An Amdahl-style model compares ideal linear scaling against workloads with varying non-scaling communication and synchronization fractions. Real communication overhead scales dynamically with device count, network topology, message size, and overlap efficiency.



The red curve’s widening gap from the dashed ideal is the communication tax made visible; shrinking that gap is what the distributed strategies in section 1.7.1 exist to do.


Multi-GPU training within a single node establishes the foundational architectural patterns for distributed execution. AlexNet22 (Krizhevsky et al. 2012) split its convolutional layers across two GTX 580 GPUs because the 3 GB device memory limit prevented single-chip execution, making cross-GPU connectivity an immediate architectural constraint. Confining multi-accelerator topologies to single-node interconnects (such as PCIe or NVLink) isolates the core parallelism strategies before introducing cross-rack network fabrics.
22 AlexNet (2012): The paper reports 60M parameters and a 3 GB single-GPU ceiling, but does not attribute the limit to one memory component. Its model-parallel design placed roughly half the kernels on each GPU and allowed communication only in selected layers, explicitly trading memory capacity against communication.
Krizhevsky, Alex, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey E. Hinton. 2012. “ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 25.
The two foundational strategies, data parallelism and model parallelism, represent fundamentally different partitioning choices: data parallelism replicates the model and partitions data, while model parallelism partitions model state or computation. This distinction determines memory requirements, communication patterns, and scaling behavior.


Data parallelism replicates the entire model on each GPU, with each processing different batches. After computing gradients locally, GPUs synchronize via gradient averaging. Figure 14 diagrams this distributed execution flow: input batches split across four parallel GPU workers for independent forward and backward passes, converge into an AllReduce collective for gradient synchronization, and apply identical parameter updates across all replicas.






Figure 14: Data Parallelism: Each GPU holds a complete model copy, processes a different data shard, and synchronizes gradients. Throughput can approach linear scaling only while computation dominates synchronization, input, and imbalance costs.



When a model and its optimizer state fit comfortably within single-device memory, data parallelism serves as the primary scaling baseline because local forward and backward kernels run at native memory bandwidth without inter-device synchronization. Gradient aggregation is the principal recurring communication cost; some implementations also synchronize buffers or other state. Historically, frameworks supported multi-GPU execution within a single node using multithreaded wrappers like PyTorch’s DataParallel (DP). However, this single-process design suffers from two severe architectural bottlenecks: the Python runtime remains throttled by the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), and a primary coordinator (GPU 0) must sequentially scatter mini-batches and gather outputs over PCIe, saturating host-device interconnect bandwidth and creating severe compute and memory imbalances. Modern systems commonly use PyTorch’s DistributedDataParallel (DDP); TensorFlow’s MirroredStrategy also provides replicated training but has a different execution model. With an independent Python process per accelerator, DDP avoids cross-replica contention for one Python GIL; each process maintains its own model replica and local optimizer, relying on decentralized collective AllReduce operations that bucket gradients into contiguous buffers and overlap synchronization directly with backward-pass computation.
Unsharded data parallelism has a hard constraint: every GPU holds a complete model replica and ordinarily its local optimizer state. A 7-billion-parameter model uses 14 GB for FP16 weights alone, before gradients, optimizer states, or activations. Sharded data parallelism (such as the Zero Redundancy Optimizer, or ZeRO) distributes that state across devices: ZeRO-1 shards optimizer states, ZeRO-2 shards gradients, and ZeRO-3 (or FSDP) shards model parameters; otherwise, a model that exceeds local memory requires pipeline or tensor partitioning.



Model parallelism partitions the model itself across GPUs, which becomes necessary when the model exceeds single-GPU memory. AlexNet adopted an early form of this strategy: selected convolutional layers split their kernels and channels across two GPUs, with communication at selected connections. Figure 15 illustrates a different, layerwise partition of the same broader model-parallel idea: Device 1 through Device 3 sequentially process layers 1–16, 17–32, and 33–48, streaming boundary activations forward during the forward pass and propagating loss gradients in reverse during backpropagation.






Figure 15: Model Parallelism: The model is partitioned across devices, with intermediate activations passing between them. This enables training models larger than single-GPU memory at the cost of sequential dependencies.




Systems Perspective 8.7: Data vs. model parallelismWhen a selected workload is partitioned across \(\AcceleratorCount\) devices, the split may divide examples, model state, layers, or tensor operations. For a model with parameters \(\Parameters\) and batch size \(\BatchSize\), data and model parallelism provide two starting points.
Data parallelism (split the batch): For a fixed global batch, each of \(\AcceleratorCount\) workers processes about \(1/\AcceleratorCount\) of the examples, but every worker holds a model replica and ordinarily its associated training state. Dense gradient communication is proportional to \(\Parameters\) per update. Scaling departs from the ideal as local batches shrink or synchronization and input costs grow.
Model parallelism (split model computation): Each accelerator stores and computes a portion of the model. An even partition may approach \(\Parameters/\AcceleratorCount\) parameters per worker, but embeddings, buffers, imbalance, and replicated state alter that estimate. Communication depends on the partition: layerwise pipeline parallelism exchanges activations at stage boundaries, while tensor parallelism performs collectives within partitioned layers.
Systems insight: Data parallelism is the simplest candidate when the complete training state fits per worker and more throughput is needed. Model-state, pipeline, or tensor partitioning becomes necessary when it does not, often in combination with data parallelism.


When a model exceeds the memory capacity of a single accelerator, its depth can be partitioned across sequential devices. Figure 16 stages this pipeline allocation across a four-accelerator execution chain, grouping 24 transformer blocks into contiguous six-block partitions (Blocks 1–6 through 19–24) that exchange boundary activations over the interconnect.






Figure 16: Layer-Wise Model Partitioning: Distributing consecutive transformer layers across sequential devices bounds network communication to intermediate activations (forward) and boundary gradients (backward). However, sequential layer dependencies leave downstream devices idle during forward passes unless micro-batches are pipelined.



The fundamental bottleneck in naive layer-wise partitioning is device serialization. Because layer evaluation is strictly sequential, Device 1 computes layers 1–6 while Devices 2–4 sit idle waiting for forward activations. During the backward pass, the dependency reverses: Device 4 computes first while upstream devices wait for returning gradients. This idle duration constitutes the pipeline bubble, which caps theoretical hardware utilization at \(1/\AcceleratorCount\) under naive sequential execution. It differs from the accelerator bubbles of the staged training pipeline, which arise when one device’s data-loading, transfer, and compute stages run at mismatched rates; a pipeline bubble arises even with perfectly fed devices, because each device must wait for another device’s layers. Mitigating this idle time requires either pipelining micro-batches across stages or partitioning tensor dimensions within layers so that all devices compute simultaneously.
Within a node, GPUs may communicate through high-bandwidth links such as NVLink23 (up to 900 GB/s aggregate bidirectional bandwidth for the represented H100 configuration). Effective collective bandwidth depends on topology and contention and is lower than a raw aggregate link specification. Data parallelism communicates gradients via collective AllReduce operations, while layerwise model parallelism communicates activations point-to-point at partition boundaries. Choosing a strategy requires balancing these communication patterns and memory footprints against the physical interconnect bandwidth of the node topology.
23 NVLink: NVIDIA’s high-bandwidth GPU interconnect. Its topology and generation determine the bandwidth available between a particular pair of GPUs and to collective operations. A parallelism strategy helps only when its communication and synchronization cost is smaller than the useful time it saves.



The cross-node analysis provides optional depth on the boundary beyond single-machine training. When a model’s parameter footprint, optimizer state, or training duration exceeds the capacity of an 8-accelerator node, distributed training extends across machines. This step introduces a fundamental bandwidth hierarchy: while accelerators within a node communicate across dense, high-bandwidth fabrics such as NVLink, distributed workers must synchronize over external network fabrics (such as Ethernet or InfiniBand) that offer substantially lower bandwidth, higher latency, and switch contention. The resulting bandwidth gap turns synchronous data-parallel gradient reduction into a recurring data-movement bottleneck on the critical path.

Systems Perspective 8.8: The physics of synchronizationRecall the energy cost of data movement quantified in Energy Cost of Moving vs. Computing on a 32-Bit Value, where a DRAM access, a local SSD read, and a network transfer each cost progressively more energy than the arithmetic performed on the value they deliver. In distributed training, this asymmetry establishes the communication tax.
Synchronizing gradients across accelerators moves megabytes to gigabytes across an interconnect on every training step. Uncovered communication time directly reduces hardware utilization, while transceiver and switch power inflates the cluster’s energy budget; these are distinct system costs. Mixed-precision execution (section 1.6.3) and gradient compression reduce transfer volumes through narrower numeric formats, sparsity, quantization, or delta encoding, relieving both bounds.


Within a node, high-bandwidth interconnects permit gradient synchronization to overlap with backward computation. Crossing node boundaries, however, transitions communication to a network fabric where available bandwidth is one to two orders of magnitude lower. In synchronous data parallelism, AllReduce24 aggregates gradients across workers; when network bandwidth fails to match accelerator compute throughput, uncovered communication time dominates the step and stalls arithmetic execution.
24 AllReduce: A collective communication primitive that sums data across all devices and distributes the result back to each device. Ring AllReduce is one common implementation: devices pass gradient shards around a logical ring so each participant sends and receives bounded chunks rather than a full copy of every gradient tensor at once. This is the communication primitive that makes large data-parallel training practical, but its detailed cost model belongs with distributed training.
Napkin Math 8.10: The network wallProblem: A team scales training to 8 GPUs, one per node, connected by a 100 Gbps fabric. Is the network the bottleneck?
Mechanism: For a 7B-parameter model with FP16 gradients:

Gradient size (FP16): 14 GB per step.
AllReduce cost: Ring AllReduce passes gradient shards around a logical ring, so each worker ends up sending nearly two full copies of the gradient: \(2(\AcceleratorCount-1)/\AcceleratorCount\), which equals 1.75× for 8 GPUs. That gives 1.75 \(\times\) 14 GB = 24.5 GB sent per worker, with the same amount received separately.
Bandwidth-only lower bound: At 12.5 GB/s per worker on the 100 Gbps fabric, synchronization latency for the \(\DataVolume\) bytes each worker sends is \(\CommunicationTime= \DataVolume / \NetworkBandwidth =\) 24.5 GB / 12.5 GB/s \(=\) 1.96 s.
Compute comparison: If the nonoverlapped forward and backward work takes \(\IronLawComputeTime \approx\) 1 s, communication latency \(\CommunicationTime\approx\) 1.96 s dominates.

Systems insight: The network becomes a wall when \(\CommunicationTime> \IronLawComputeTime\), reducing the fraction of this nonoverlapped step spent computing, given by \(\frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\IronLawComputeTime + \CommunicationTime}\) to about 33.8 percent. This fraction does not measure compute efficiency relative to peak FLOP/s. Ring AllReduce (Sergeev and Balso 2018) is already the baseline here. Further mitigations include gradient compression (reducing \(\DataVolume\)), overlap where dependencies permit, and hierarchical topologies that confine high-frequency transfers to fast intra-node links (NVLink at 900 GB/s vs. 12.5 GB/s inter-node).



Sergeev, Alexander, and Mike Del Balso. 2018. “Horovod: Fast and Easy Distributed Deep Learning in TensorFlow.” CoRR abs/1802.05799.
25 GPipe (2019): GPipe implements the described micro-batching strategy, staggering execution to fill the idle “bubbles” in naive model parallelism and thus boost utilization (Huang et al. 2019). The key trade-off it manages is increased memory for storing the activations of multiple in-flight micro-batches. It preserves large-batch training dynamics by accumulating gradients before the weight update; the paper reports almost linear Transformer throughput scaling when the micro-batch count is at least four times the number of partitions.
Huang, Y., Y. Cheng, A. Bapna, O. Firat, D. Chen, M. X. Chen, H. Lee, et al. 2019. “GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks Using Pipeline Parallelism.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 32: 103–12.
Because cross-node fabrics throttle frequent synchronization, scaling requires matching each communication pattern to the appropriate bandwidth tier. Pipeline parallelism partitions model layers across sequential devices, addressing the idle pipeline bubbles of naive model parallelism through micro-batching. Instead of processing an entire batch serially, the global batch is divided into smaller micro-batches that stream through the pipeline stages. While a downstream stage executes a forward pass on an early micro-batch, upstream stages concurrently process subsequent ones. The pipeline schedule controls this concurrency: retaining more in-flight micro-batches reduces accelerator idle time but requires each stage to store activations in memory until the corresponding backward pass completes. GPipe25 evaluates all forward micro-batches before draining the backward passes, whereas PipeDream interleaves one forward pass with one backward pass (1F1B) to bound resident activation memory (Huang et al. 2019; Narayanan et al. 2019).
Tensor parallelism operates at a finer granularity: rather than assigning whole layers to separate devices, it shards individual matrix operations across devices within a layer. (Sequence parallelism extends this principle by sharding activation tensors along the sequence dimension during long-context transformer training.) In a transformer feed-forward block, Megatron-LM splits the first weight projection column-wise and the second projection row-wise (Shoeybi et al. 2019). Each accelerator computes on a slice of the hidden dimension without intermediate communication; only a single AllReduce across the tensor-parallel group is required at the end of the block to sum the partial outputs. Because this pattern introduces frequent forward and backward collectives, tensor parallelism benefits from high-bandwidth links such as NVLink. Intra-node placement is a common choice; the actual communication pattern and topology determine whether crossing nodes is practical.

Shoeybi, Mohammad, Mostofa Patwary, Raul Puri, Patrick LeGresley, Jared Casper, and Bryan Catanzaro. 2019. “Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1909.08053.
Hybrid strategies combine tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism (3D parallelism) to scale large models across physical clusters. Table 20 summarizes the resulting placement heuristic: map the highest-frequency collective communication to the highest-bandwidth physical links, reserving lower-bandwidth tiers for coarser synchronization boundaries.



Table 20: Hybrid Parallelism Placement: A common heuristic places tensor parallelism within nodes, pipeline parallelism within racks, and data parallelism across racks. Actual placement depends on the model and topology.










Strategy
Typical placement
Communication pattern




Tensor parallelism
Within a node
Frequent communication that exploits NVLink’s high bandwidth


Pipeline parallelism
Across nodes within a rack
Moderate communication at layer boundaries


Data parallelism
Across racks
Gradient synchronization once per iteration






Partitioning computation across a cluster ultimately transforms training from a purely arithmetic problem into a multi-tier data-movement hierarchy. While collective communication algorithms, parameter servers, and fault-tolerant scheduling allow models to scale across thousands of accelerators, their sustained efficiency remains bound by the ratio of compute throughput to network transfer time. The remaining decision is whether the workload’s memory or schedule requires paying that communication cost.


↪ Empirical protocols for quantifying multi-accelerator scaling efficiency and communication loss are operationalized in Scalability and parallelism.



A run needs more devices only when its state or schedule exceeds what the chosen local configuration can provide. Knowing how to partition computation across devices does not answer when distributed execution is warranted. Distributing state introduces communication overhead, synchronization barriers, and operational failure modes, so the single-node optimizations come first, because they isolate whether the bottleneck is fundamentally algorithmic or capacity-driven. Profile-guided tuning should evaluate lower-precision execution paths (section 1.6.3) when numerical stability permits, gradient accumulation (section 1.6.5) to synthesize target batch sizes without activation blowup, activation checkpointing (section 1.6.5.1) to trade redundant forward compute for memory headroom, and overlapped data prefetching (section 1.6.2) when host ingestion limits the critical path.
Table 21 structures this progression as a resource lookup keyed to measured hardware bottlenecks rather than arbitrary parameter thresholds.



Table 21: Scaling Decision Guidelines: Choose the least distributed configuration that satisfies measured memory, throughput, and schedule requirements. Model architecture, training state, input pipeline, hardware, and topology all affect the boundary.










Observed constraint
Candidate approach
Rationale




Training state fits one device and time is acceptable
Single GPU
Minimizes communication and operational complexity


State or throughput exceeds one device but fits one node
Single multi-GPU node
Uses fast local interconnects before crossing the network


Required state or schedule exceeds one node
Multi-node cluster
Adds aggregate memory or compute at a communication cost


Input service rate is below accelerator demand
Parallel or distributed input pipeline
Adds input throughput where profiling shows it is needed






A measured single-device baseline guides scaling decisions, while a decisive capacity or compute-time lower bound can establish the need for additional resources before every local optimization is attempted. Every hardware device has a physical ceiling: a workload requiring \(10^{24}\) FLOPs cannot be completed on a single accelerator within a practical training schedule, no matter how carefully that accelerator is tuned. The resource expansion must match the hard limit that has been reached:

Memory exhaustion: The model weights, gradients, optimizer states, and activations exceed the VRAM of a single GPU. A 70-billion-parameter model requires approximately 140 GB in FP16 for weights alone, exceeding the 80 GB configurations of A100 and H100 SXM accelerators and leaving little or no headroom on higher-capacity variants like the H100 NVL (94 GB) and H200 (141 GB) once training state is included.
Training wall-clock time: The estimated time on one device exceeds the project’s actual deadline. At \(10^{15}\) FLOP/s sustained, a workload requiring \(10^{24}\) FLOPs would take about 32 years.
Input throughput: The input pipeline cannot sustain the aggregate accelerator consumption rate. This calls for more input-service capacity, not automatically more training accelerators. Dataset size alone does not determine this limit; reuse, compression, locality, transformation cost, and storage bandwidth matter.

These three limits are technical, but scaling carries a cost beyond complexity and capacity. Adding devices amplifies the energy consumption and environmental impact of training, so efficiency optimization becomes an environmental concern as much as a performance one.

Napkin Math 8.11: The carbon footprint of trainingContext: Training large models requires substantial energy and compute. The physical ceiling appears once training time is converted to energy, cluster power multiplied by training time (\(\TotalEnergy = \ClusterPower\cdot \TrainingTime\)), quantifying environmental scale:

Workload: Training a 7 billion-parameter model for 1 trillion tokens.
Compute: \(\Operations\approx\) \(4.2 \times 10^{22}\).
Efficiency: 156 TFLOP/s sustained on A100 (400 W thermal design power).
Execution time: \(\TrainingTime\approx\) 3.04 days on 1,024 GPUs.
Energy footprint: \(\TotalEnergy = \ClusterPower\cdot \TrainingTime= (\AcceleratorCount \cdot \DevicePower + \ClusterNodeCount \cdot \HostPower) \cdot \TrainingTime\) evaluates to (1,024 GPUs \(\times\) 400 W + 128 hosts \(\times\) 200 W) \(\times\) 73 hours \(\approx\) 31,784.2 kWh.

Impact: Under the assumed constant GPU and host-CPU power, this modeled subtotal equals 35.3 months of average household electricity use. GPU thermal design power is a scenario input rather than measured draw; memory, storage, network equipment, and facility overhead are not separately included, so the subtotal is not total facility energy.
Systems lesson: Doubling hardware utilization \(\EfficiencyHw\) at constant cluster power \(\ClusterPower\) halves execution time \(\TrainingTime\) and total energy \(\TotalEnergy\). Under average grid carbon intensity, doubling efficiency saves ~15,892.1 kWh of electricity and avoids 6.8 t of emissions. Environmental audits must measure \(\TotalEnergy = \int \ClusterPower(\TimeInstant)\,d\TimeInstant\) rather than relying on GPU utilization metrics alone.





The parallelism strategies in section 1.7.1 and section 1.7.2 represent the convergence of distinct architectural traditions. Modern training platforms integrate paradigms developed across four computing eras, each shaped by the physical constraints and dominant workloads of its time.
Neural network training combines requirements drawn simultaneously from high-performance computing (HPC) and warehouse-scale systems. From HPC, training inherits dense matrix multiplication (GEMM) kernels operating near accelerator compute limits, requiring tightly synchronized parallel execution across devices. From warehouse-scale computing, multi-day training jobs inherit the necessity of cluster-wide orchestration, asynchronous data ingestion, and automated fault recovery across failure-prone nodes. Figure 17 sequences this architectural lineage across four overlapping computing eras—from early mainframe mainstays (ENIAC, IBM System/360) and vector HPC supercomputers (CDC 6600, Cray-1) through warehouse-scale cloud clusters to modern GPU and TPU hypercomputing clusters.






Figure 17: Computing System Evolution: Four overlapping eras place representative system milestones against time. The overlap matters: AI hypercomputing builds on, rather than replaces, the parallel numerical methods of HPC and the distributed coordination of warehouse-scale computing.



The lineage explains why a training platform must support both tightly coupled numerical execution and reliable data supply over long runs. Table 22 contrasts the workload and execution patterns inherited from these architectural traditions.



Table 22: Computing Era Characteristics: Each computing era optimized for different workload patterns, and modern training systems inherit requirements from multiple predecessors. AI hypercomputing uniquely combines HPC’s parallel numerical computation with warehouse-scale distributed processing, while adding specialized support for the gradient-based optimization and massive parameter state management central to neural network training.

Scaling changes the binding constraint rather than removing it: data parallelism buys throughput, model parallelism buys memory capacity, pipeline parallelism buys utilization, and tensor parallelism buys layer-scale feasibility, but each adds communication and coordination cost. The implementation details of multi-node distributed training, including collective communication primitives, fault tolerance mechanisms, and elastic scheduling, build directly on the single-machine principles covered throughout this chapter and are treated in depth in advanced distributed systems texts.

Checkpoint 8.4: Scaling decisions
Scaling trades compute bottlenecks for communication bottlenecks.

Hard limits: Identify which resource limit binds a given training run: memory capacity, compute throughput, or input-service rate.
Single-node first: Explain how a single-node baseline and relevant local optimizations inform scaling, and when a physical lower bound can justify scaling before all tuning is exhausted.
Data vs. model parallelism: Justify why data parallelism fails when model states exceed single-accelerator memory, and identify what model parallelism must partition.
Communication tax: Explain why scaling efficiency degrades with accelerator count, and identify the communication metrics that dictate this ceiling.
Scaling ceiling: Estimate the theoretical speedup ceiling via Amdahl’s law when unparallelized synchronization accounts for 10 percent of step time, and determine where adding accelerators yields diminishing returns.




Self-Check: Question

A team trains a 1.5-billion-parameter model that already fits on one 80 GB GPU with batch size 16 and its Adam training state, but one epoch still takes 12 days. The team has an 8-GPU node available. Which strategy is the best first baseline, and why?

Tensor parallelism, because splitting every weight matrix across the 8 GPUs is always the fastest way to improve training throughput.
Pipeline parallelism, because dividing layers across devices is the default first step whenever a model is a transformer.
Data parallelism such as DDP, because the model already fits per device and replication avoids unnecessary pipeline bubbles or intra-layer communication as the initial throughput baseline.
Full parameter sharding first, because any multi-GPU run should avoid keeping complete replicas even when memory is sufficient.

In distributed data parallel training with \(N\) GPUs and a model with \(P\) parameters whose gradients use \(B_{\text{bytes}}\) bytes each, what is the number of bytes sent by each GPU during a Ring AllReduce?

\(2 \times \frac{N-1}{N} \times P \times B_{\text{bytes}}\), which approaches \(2 P B_{\text{bytes}}\) as \(N\) grows.
\(N \times P \times B_{\text{bytes}}\), because each GPU must broadcast the full gradient to every other GPU.
\(\frac{P \times B_{\text{bytes}}}{N^2}\), because the ring divides both the model and the communication quadratically.
Zero, because GPU replicas synchronize through shared CPU memory rather than explicit data movement.

Explain what the communication tax is in distributed training, and analyze why adding more GPUs can lead to diminishing throughput returns.
In pipeline model parallelism, partitioning a network linearly across \(K\) stages without micro-batching (naive pipeline parallelism) achieves 100 percent GPU utilization because downstream devices can compute backward gradients while upstream devices run forward passes.
Arrange the following engineering steps in the chapter’s preferred order for deciding whether to scale beyond one device, assuming the initial bounds do not already prove that single-device training is infeasible: (1) Re-evaluate whether memory or time limits still justify scaling. (2) Add distributed parallelism or sharding if the remaining limit still requires it. (3) Establish a single-device baseline and quantify the current bottleneck. (4) Apply relevant local optimizations such as mixed precision, prefetching, checkpointing, or accumulation.

title: Training Systems Fundamentals
text:
The progression from single-GPU optimization through multi-device parallelism shows that each technique introduces trade-offs and new constraints. The approach developed throughout this chapter quantifies costs through the iron law, diagnoses bottlenecks through profiling, applies targeted optimizations, and scales only when necessary. The following fallacies and pitfalls capture common errors that waste compute resources, delay research progress, or cause production training failures.

Fallacy: Larger models always yield better performance.
Teams sometimes treat scale as a monotonic lever: if a 7B-parameter model works well, a 20B-parameter model must work better. A 20B model requires approximately 320 GB of nonactivation training state in the stated mixed-precision Adam recipe (40 GB FP16 parameters + 40 GB FP16 gradients + 80 GB FP32 master weights + 160 GB Adam states). Whether it outperforms a 7B model depends on data quantity and quality, training compute, optimization, and evaluation, not on parameter count alone.


Pitfall: Assuming distributed training automatically accelerates development.
More accelerators do not guarantee faster training because communication, smaller local batches, input limits, and imbalance can consume the gain. In an illustrative 8 GPUs scenario, synchronization occupies 30–50 percent of step time and speedup reaches only 4–6× rather than the ideal 8×. The values are hypothetical; the decision requires measured end-to-end time and scaling efficiency.


Fallacy: Hyperparameters transfer directly from small-scale experiments to large-scale training.
A learning rate that works at batch size 512 may not transfer to batch size 4,096. The linear scaling rule (Goyal et al. 2017) would increase the rate from 0.1 to 0.8 for this eightfold change, often with warmup, but it is an empirical recipe rather than a requirement or convergence guarantee. Large-scale runs must validate the learning rate, schedule, optimizer state, and effective batch together.

Goyal, Priya, Piotr Dollár, Ross Girshick, Pieter Noordhuis, Lukasz Wesolowski, Aapo Kyrola, Andrew Tulloch, Yangqing Jia, and Kaiming He. 2017. “Accurate, Large Minibatch SGD: Training ImageNet in 1 Hour.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1706.02677 abs/1706.02677.


Pitfall: Treating mixed precision training as a simple toggle without validation.
The chapter’s illustrative V100 inputs imply a 2.4× speedup, but they are not a benchmark. FP16 commonly requires loss scaling (Micikevicius et al. 2017), while BF16 usually does not (Wang and Kanwar 2019; Kalamkar et al. 2019) (section 1.6.3 compares the two formats). Either recipe can change numerical behavior, so throughput and convergence must be validated on the target workload.

Kalamkar, Dhiraj, Dheevatsa Mudigere, Naveen Mellempudi, Dipankar Das, Kunal Banerjee, Sasikanth Avancha, Dharma Teja Vooturi, et al. 2019. A Study of BFLOAT16 for Deep Learning Training.


Fallacy: Memory and computation can be optimized independently.
Memory and compute are coupled: in this illustrative profile, accelerator utilization drops from 90 percent at batch 256 to 60–70 percent at batch 16. Gradient accumulation (effective batch 512, physical batch 64) shows a 5-percentage-point utilization gap for 8× activation-memory reduction. Tuning these parameters independently can therefore extend training time materially, because the utilization lost at the smaller physical batch applies to every step of the run (section 1.6.5 develops this trade-off).


Pitfall: Budgeting training memory as if it only contains model weights.
Sizing training memory from weights alone omits gradients, optimizer state, master weights when used, activations, temporary workspaces, and allocator overhead. In the chapter’s mixed-precision Adam recipe, FP16 weights (2 bytes), FP16 gradients (2), FP32 master weights (4), and two FP32 moments (8) total 16 bytes per parameter before activations. Other optimizers and sharding strategies change this budget. Activation memory then depends on batch size, sequence length, architecture, kernels, and checkpointing; no universal multiple of the weight footprint applies.


Fallacy: The accelerator is always the training bottleneck.
Data loading often creates idle time, yet teams optimize computation first. In this illustrative profile, prefetching with pipeline overlap reduces wall-clock time by 47.6 percent (105 min to 55 min) by overlapping data loading with computation (section 1.6.2 develops the overlap). Profile before assuming the GPU is the bottleneck.


Pitfall: Optimizing kernels before profiling the input pipeline.
Kernel-level tuning is attractive because GPU utilization is easy to inspect, but a starved accelerator can look like an inefficient accelerator. Before changing precision, rewriting kernels, or adding GPUs, measure dataloader throughput, host preprocessing time, storage wait, and host-to-device transfer overlap. If the accelerator is waiting for batches, the fastest optimization is to feed it reliably rather than make its kernels marginally faster.


Self-Check: Question

A team scales a dense model from 7 billion to 20 billion parameters while keeping the same training-token budget, precision recipe, and optimizer structure. Under the chapter’s fallacies discussion, what is the most defensible conclusion?

Validation accuracy must improve in proportion to parameter count because the larger model can represent more functions.
The run will necessarily move to CPU execution because 20B parameters cannot be trained on accelerators.
The larger model guarantees worse accuracy because fixed-token training always causes catastrophic interference at higher parameter counts.
The training-state and compute budgets rise substantially under the same dense-model accounting, but model quality is not guaranteed to improve because it still depends on data, optimization, and evaluation.

Explain why directly transferring hyperparameters such as learning rate and weight decay from a batch-size 512 baseline to a batch-size 4,096 distributed run can cause training to underperform, even when raw GPU busy time stays above 90 percent.
Which engineering mistake exemplifies “pipeline neglect” as described in the chapter’s pitfalls?

Using BF16 mixed precision instead of FP16 on NVIDIA Ampere GPUs.
Spending weeks hand-tuning custom CUDA attention kernels to achieve 95% peak arithmetic throughput, only to discover in production that the GPU sits idle 50% of the time waiting for single-threaded Python CPU tokenization.
Setting pin_memory=True and num_workers=8 in a PyTorch DataLoader.
Checkpointing activations every \(\sqrt{N_L}\) layers to reduce peak memory.

A team proposes moving a single-GPU training job to a 16-GPU cluster to achieve a \(16\times\) reduction in development cycle time. Explain two reasons why distributed training rarely delivers a linear \(16\times\) improvement in developer velocity.

title: Training Systems Fundamentals
text:
Training cost is governed by three accounts that this chapter first kept separate and then joined. The training-time law, \(\TrainingTime= \Operations/(\PeakRate \times \EfficiencyHw)\), prices time. The four-term memory budget decides what fits, and in a standard mixed-precision Adam recipe the static state alone reaches 8× the FP16 weights before a single activation is stored. The min-of-three pipeline model decides whether the accelerator is fed at all. GPT-2 tied the three together: its \(6\Parameters\DatasetSize\) operation count set the time, its weights, optimizer state, and activations overflowed a single V100 before any arithmetic began, and its single-threaded data loader could starve the device once the model fit.
Every intervention in the chapter changes one term of one account and pays in another, which is the conservation of complexity at work. Mixed precision raises \(\PeakRate\) and shrinks activation memory and traffic, but it leaves the static state at 16 bytes per parameter and requires loss scaling or a wider-exponent format. Checkpointing buys activation memory with extra forward arithmetic, accumulation buys batch size with update frequency, prefetching hides input time at the price of host memory, and FlashAttention removes quadratic HBM traffic by recomputing tiles. Scaling to more devices adds aggregate memory and compute but turns gradient synchronization into a new term on the critical path. The profile, not the menu of techniques, decides which trade is worth making.
The same pressures shaped the hardware. Dense matrix patterns drove Tensor Cores, frameworks exposed them through mixed-precision APIs, and reduced-precision training pushed later accelerators toward BF16 and FP8. Behind all of it sits the bitter lesson seen from inside the training loop. If capability grows with the computation a general method can absorb, every point of utilization lost to stalls is capability forgone at a fixed budget.

Key Takeaways: Why training costs millions

Training cost is an iron-law budget: \(\TrainingTime= \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \times \EfficiencyHw}\) makes every optimization accountable: reduce work, raise effective throughput, or improve utilization. A change that misses the dominant term only moves cost around the training loop.
Memory determines whether an optimizer fits: Standard mixed-precision Adam uses 8\(\times\) the FP16 inference-weight memory in the stated representation before activations. Optimizer state and batch-dependent activations—not weights alone—determine whether training fits.
Profiles choose the remedy: Profile, diagnose, fix, and re-profile. Compute-bound jobs need better arithmetic or algorithms; memory-bound jobs need less state or traffic; data- and communication-bound jobs need pipeline or parallelism changes.
Precision and IO-aware kernels shift bottlenecks: FP16 with FP32 accumulation can improve throughput and shrink activation memory (the static state stays at 16 bytes per parameter), while FlashAttention avoids materializing the full \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) matrix in HBM; realized gains depend on workload and hardware.
Checkpointing buys memory with recompute: The segment schedule counts retained boundaries and one live reconstructed segment, reducing the modeled activation allowance from 35.9 GB to 4.6 GB at batch 4. Use it when memory, not compute, binds.
Composed optimizations can postpone scale-out: Mixed precision and checkpointing turn 95.7 GB into a modeled 28.6 GB for batch-4 GPT-2, before temporary workspaces. Use relevant local levers before accepting distributed communication and operational overhead.



Training is where the iron law becomes a daily instrument. A profile read against the law names the dominant term, and the engineering task is to apply the least costly intervention that changes it before reaching for more hardware. The analysis took the model and training corpus as given, while changing how the system executed their work, including the extra arithmetic needed for recomputation. A further lever is which examples enter that workload in the first place.

What’s Next: From training to data selectionTraining produces learned parameters by spending compute on every example. Once the training loop is efficient, the next question is whether every example earns that cost. Repeated or low-information samples consume the same forward pass, backward pass, optimizer update, and communication as examples that add coverage or correct a weakness.
Data Selection therefore turns upstream from execution to workload composition, and in doing so opens the volume’s optimization sequence, which asks whether work is necessary before asking how to simplify or accelerate it. It starts from a supply imbalance. Accelerator fleets can grow usable compute faster than the stock of high-quality data, so extracting more learning from each example begins to matter more than collecting more examples. Its measure is the information-compute ratio, the learning an example returns per unit of training compute, and redundancy, representativeness, uncertainty, and class coverage all enter through it. A useful subset must reduce work without erasing rare cases or shifting the effective training distribution. When that balance holds, a carefully selected subset can approach full-dataset accuracy while lowering the cost of every epoch and making additional experiments affordable. The optimization target is no longer only how efficiently the system processes an example, but which examples the system should process at all.




Self-Check: Question

Which statement best summarizes the chapter’s recommended method for optimizing machine learning training systems?

Use the training-time law to structure the cost account, profile to identify the binding bottleneck, apply the relevant local optimizations first, and scale out only when measured or calculated physical bounds still require it.
Scale to a distributed cluster immediately, because more hardware is the fastest way to hide data, memory, and utilization problems.
Prefer SGD to Adam in every workload so memory stays low, and avoid checkpointing because recomputation always wastes time.
Maximize raw GPU busy percentage without worrying about whether the work being counted is useful model computation.

A cloud training run improves its MFU from 25 percent to 50 percent while holding the total useful model FLOP count fixed, along with the same peak-throughput convention, convergence target, hardware fleet, and hourly pricing. Explain how that change propagates through wall-clock time, and under what conditions similar reductions would or would not follow for energy, cost, and carbon.
Why does the chapter emphasize establishing a single-machine baseline and considering relevant local optimizations before accepting distributed complexity in multi-node training?

Distributed training systems cannot use mixed precision or optimized attention kernels.
