title: Data Selection
text:
Architecture stack focus for this chapter.
How can a carefully selected subset retain most of the value of a much larger dataset?
Training pays to acquire, label, score, move, and process examples even though their learning value differs. Large datasets contain redundant, noisy, or target-misaligned samples, while scarce regions may lack the cases a model needs, such as the rare conditions under which a deployed system is most likely to fail. Training on every example treats a near-duplicate and a rare failure case as equally worth paying for, and at scale much of the compute budget can go to relearning what the model already knows. Data selection turns that heterogeneity into a systems optimization. It can remove avoidable work before training, direct labels and training steps toward informative cases as learning proceeds, or create missing examples when scarcity is the binding constraint. It can also invest once in reusable representation learning when that cost can be amortized across downstream tasks. The objective is therefore not the smallest dataset but the lowest end-to-end cost of reaching target quality without losing rare cases, underrepresented groups, or deployment-relevant coverage. Every strategy adds its own overhead: examples must be scored, generated, shuffled, stored, or validated, and those costs can erase the savings they promise. That judgment must be made end to end, because gains in labeling or training can be erased by selection latency, storage access, or distributed coordination. A method earns its place only when the learning it preserves or creates exceeds the work required to apply it. This distinction matters across repeated experiments, where useful reductions compound, and across adaptation, where the value of an example changes with the model and target distribution. Data engineering established that data is the source code of ML systems; data selection asks which evidence is useful now and which is still missing. In D·A·M terms, it is data-algorithm co-design: shape the training signal so each unit of machine work buys more useful learning.

Learning Objectives

Explain data selection as data-algorithm co-design that controls sample value, training work, and labeling cost
Calculate information-compute ratio to decide whether additional examples improve learning per FLOP
Compare deduplication, coreset selection, and quality pruning for reducing redundant pretraining data
Design curriculum, active learning, or synthetic-data strategies for changing data value during training
Apply the selection inequality to test whether selection overhead beats full-dataset training cost
Evaluate distributed selection pipelines against storage locality, consistency, and accelerator utilization constraints
Select data-selection investments using ROI, amortization, and compute-optimal frontier diagnostics

title: Data Selection
text:
Training pays the iron-law cost for every example it processes, but not every example returns learning signal worth that cost. Data selection gives a clean, well-engineered dataset a systems objective: keep the examples that contribute the most learning per unit of compute. Data engineering makes the dataset reliable through correct labels, consistent schemas, and governed records. Data selection optimizes the dataset’s value by extracting maximum learning from minimum samples, shrinking the total operations \((\Operations)\) term in the iron law (principle \(\ref{pri-iron-law}\)) when it removes processing at matched quality. The distinction matters: quality asks whether data is correct, while value asks whether correct data is worth the compute spent processing it.



Compute outruns high-quality data supply; the widening gap is the data wall.
1 Scaling laws: Jared Kaplan and colleagues at Johns Hopkins and OpenAI empirically demonstrated in 2020 that language model loss follows power-law relationships with model size, dataset size, and compute budget over the regimes they studied (Kaplan et al. 2020). Their fitted data exponent was approximately \(\Glyph{\alpha} = 0.095\) in \(\LossFunction \propto \DataScalingLossFactor\). The value is not universal, but the diminishing-return shape makes it possible to reason about when selection becomes more cost-effective than collection.
Kaplan, Jared, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan, Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Chess, Rewon Child, Scott Gray, Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, and Dario Amodei. 2020. “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models.” ArXiv Preprint abs/2001.08361.
2 Data wall: Unlike compute (which scales with capital expenditure) or algorithms (which improve through research), the stock of high-quality human-generated text grows slowly; Epoch AI’s updated projections estimated that, under the paper’s modeled consumption assumptions, models could use datasets roughly equal in size to the stock of public human-generated text between 2026 and 2032 (Villalobos et al. 2022). The point for systems design is not a fixed calendar deadline; it is that data can become a supply constraint rather than merely an economic one. The wall does not change how many operations \((\Operations)\) a run performs. It lowers what each of those operations buys, because once quality data runs short, additional compute spent on repeated or weaker data yields diminishing accuracy regardless of hardware throughput.
Villalobos, Pablo, Anson Ho, Jaime Sevilla, Tamay Besiroglu, Lennart Heim, and Marius Hobbhahn. 2022. “Will We Run Out of Data? Limits of LLM Scaling Based on Human-Generated Data.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2211.04325.
Increasing the amount of training data has long been a standard way to improve models. Scaling laws1 (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022) quantify how model performance can improve with dataset size, and teams have responded by collecting and generating more examples. Accelerator fleets, however, can expand usable compute faster than the supply of novel, high-quality human-generated text and images. Much of the easily accessible public web has already been incorporated into large training corpora, and expert labeling capacity grows slowly. This asymmetry is the data wall,2 shifting engineering focus from indiscriminate data ingestion toward maximizing the learning signal extracted from every stored and processed sample.
Table 1 uses an illustrative growth scenario in which GPU compute rises 10× every 3 years while accessible high-quality data grows more slowly. These are scenario inputs, not measured universal rates.



Table 1: Scaling Asymmetry in ML Resources: In the illustrated scaling regime, compute grows faster than high-quality data supply, creating a compute-to-data imbalance that makes data selection valuable.

Growth Rate
Implication

Scaling dataset size eventually encounters the finite stock of high-quality human speech and text. Figure 1 charts the steep log-scale ascent of foundation model training sets from GPT-3 through Llama 3, showing the empirical trajectory converging toward the shaded ceiling of high-quality public text stock near \(10^{14}\) tokens.






Figure 1: Dataset Growth Approaching Limits: Several foundation-model datasets have grown toward estimates of the total stock of high-quality public text. The projection should be read as a dated constraint scenario rather than a fixed forecast: data selection, synthetic generation, multimodal learning, licensing, and filtering policy all change the usable supply.



When compute is abundant and quality data is scarce, the optimization priority inverts. Selection, not faster kernels, then extracts more learning per dollar, and for teams whose accelerator budget exceeds their curated corpus, the bottleneck shifts from accelerator access to the quality, legality, and diversity of the training data.
That inversion raises the bitter lesson’s question in data terms. General methods win by absorbing more computation, and scaling laws describe that absorption only while data grows alongside compute. Selection can look like the hand-built expertise the lesson warns against, and a filter written from human intuition about which examples matter is exactly that. Selection can also use the model’s own signals, such as loss, gradient norms, or embedding similarity. More compute can support stronger scoring models or more frequent score updates, but improved sample rankings must be established against downstream quality and coverage. Done that way, selection is how a compute-hungry general method stays fed once the supply of fresh, high-quality data stops keeping pace.


↩︎ The bitter lesson, that general methods using more computation outperform encoded human expertise, is established in The Bitter Lesson.
The engineering toolkit for intelligent data selection follows a deliberate optimization ordering: first ask whether a sample is worth processing, then ask how to process the remaining workload efficiently. Data selection sits first in the ordering that frames all of Part III, removing avoidable work before anything simplifies or accelerates the work that remains. Static pruning fixes the retained subset before target-model training; scoring may itself require proxy training. Dynamic selection adapts the data diet during training through curriculum learning and active learning. Synthetic generation creates high-value samples through augmentation, simulation, or examples labeled by a larger trained model (a teacher) when real data runs short.
Each stage can increase the information density of the data that reaches the model when measured quality gains justify its overhead, forming a complementary toolkit rather than a rigid execution sequence: pruning reduces what the pipeline contains, dynamic selection focuses how the training loop schedules it, and synthesis expands what the pipeline can access. Self-supervised pretraining complements these three levers by redefining what constitutes a supervision signal: rather than selecting among labeled examples, it derives learning targets directly from the intrinsic structure of unannotated data. Evaluating any of these techniques requires a systems definition of data selection and a quantitative account of its effectiveness.

Self-Check: Question

An I/O ingestion bottleneck where disk read bandwidth must be quadrupled to keep GPUs saturated
A compute-starved regime where synthetic data generation should be eliminated to avoid wasting accelerator cycles

It remains constant at \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) because additional compute scales proportionally with dataset size
It decays as \(\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{1}{O_{\text{sample}}D}\right)\), so under this illustrative model additional data eventually adds compute faster than marginal information
It grows logarithmically as \(\mathcal{O}(\log D / O_{\text{sample}})\) due to power-law parameter scaling
It decays exponentially as \(\mathcal{O}(\exp(-D))\) once the training corpus exceeds accelerator memory capacity

title: Data Selection
text:
A duplicated image, a mislabeled record, and a rare boundary case may all cost the same forward and backward pass, but they do not contribute the same learning signal. Data selection therefore starts by making sample value explicit relative to compute cost. The information-compute ratio measures that value as learning signal gained per unit of training compute, formalized in section 1.4.

Definition 9.1: Data selection
Data selection is the process of retaining, prioritizing, or generating training examples to minimize the end-to-end cost of reaching target quality while preserving required coverage.

Significance: It identifies data worth retaining, prioritizing, or generating for the target objective, reducing the total operations \((\Operations)\) when redundant or noisy samples can be excluded without losing required coverage.
Distinction: Unlike data engineering, which focuses on the cleanliness and consistency of data, data selection focuses on the informativeness and diversity of the samples.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that more data is always better. Additional low-quality data can yield less improvement than a much smaller, carefully selected set, so retained volume must be evaluated together with coverage and target quality.



To make this concrete, consider training an autoregressive language model in the GPT-2/Llama lighthouse family at frontier scale. The scenario deliberately steps outside this book’s one-machine scope, to a 70-billion-parameter model on a cluster of thousands of accelerators, because that is where the data wall binds first. The GPT-2 model trained in Running example: Training GPT-2 sits far below this point, but the same arithmetic applies to any team whose compute can traverse its curated corpus many times over.


↩︎ GPT-2, the bandwidth-bound lighthouse for decoder-only language models, is established in Lighthouse Roster: Model Biographies.
The compute budget (10,000 H100 GPUs for 3 months) represents roughly $86.4M at a cloud rental price of $4/GPU-hour and can process about 73.2T tokens at 40 percent sustained model FLOPs utilization (MFU), the fraction of peak arithmetic a training run actually delivers (definition \(\ref{dfn-training-model-flops-utilization-mfu}\)). Estimates of quality- and repetition-adjusted public human-generated text are on the order of 300T tokens, far larger than a single curated web corpus. The practical bottleneck is narrower: how much of that stock is accessible, legally usable, high quality, deduplicated, and useful for the target distribution. If a team has only a 5T filtered corpus ready for use, the compute budget can already process it roughly 14.6× over. At that point, the cluster outstrips the available unique signal. An engineering team can repeat epochs over the same corpus, but gradient updates on familiar tokens yield diminishing loss reductions. It can lower quality thresholds to admit uncurated web text, but noisy and misaligned tokens degrade downstream evaluation. Or it can invest in data selection (refining quality filters, constructing difficulty curricula, and synthesizing missing edge cases) to raise the learning return per FLOP. When compute capacity outpaces high-signal data, selection delivers higher return on capital than provisioning additional accelerators.
The opportunity applies across the lighthouse models, from ResNet-50 to GPT-2/Llama, although the safe reduction differs by task. Whenever a validated method removes examples or tokens without adding compensating steps, training FLOPs fall. The appropriate framing is therefore systemic rather than purely statistical.

title: Data Selection
text:
The data wall dictates the physical limits of scaling uncurated datasets; a systems perspective determines how to manage that constraint across the hardware stack. The conventional ML framing evaluates data selection through statistical sample complexity and generalization theory, asking how many samples are required to achieve a given test error. That formulation treats every sample as a zero-cost mathematical abstraction, ignoring the physical resource cost of data ingestion, transport, and execution.
A data-selection systems framing asks instead how to minimize the total resource cost of achieving target accuracy across the entire ML lifecycle. This framing shifts attention from theoretical sample efficiency to concrete resource consumption, as table 2 illustrates.



Table 2: ML vs. Systems Perspectives on Data Selection: The ML framing optimizes sample complexity; the systems framing optimizes total resource cost across the pipeline.









ML Framing
Systems Framing




“Fewer samples for same accuracy”
“Fewer FLOPs for same accuracy”


“Better generalization”
“Lower training cost (time, money, energy)”


“Sample complexity bounds”
“End-to-end resource efficiency”


“Learning theory”
“Cost engineering”






This framing reveals optimization leverage across the execution stack. In the D·A·M taxonomy, data selection operates at the data layer to eliminate physical work before algorithmic and hardware optimizations execute it, as formalized by the iron law of ML systems.


↩︎ The D·A·M taxonomy and its three diagnostic axes are established in Defining ML Systems.
Read as an optimization map (figure 2), the taxonomy assigns each vertex its own governing question, positioning data selection as an input optimization that prunes the total workload before algorithmic and physical execution take place. The model vertex determines how many operations each forward and backward pass requires; the machine vertex determines how rapidly the hardware executes that arithmetic; and the data vertex determines whether an example warrants processing at all. The connecting edges demarcate the primary operational bottlenecks: compute-bound arithmetic throughput between algorithms and hardware, I/O-bound bandwidth between storage and accelerators, and sample efficiency between data curation and model capacity. Sample efficiency governs the Data–Algorithm boundary (what to learn from), the I/O bound governs the Data–Machine boundary (how information moves), and the compute bound governs the Algorithm–Machine boundary (how to execute arithmetic efficiently). By optimizing at the data vertex, data selection eliminates work across both adjacent boundaries—reducing storage ingestion traffic along the machine edge and raising effective learning return along the algorithm edge.






Figure 2: The D·A·M Taxonomy as an Optimization Map: Machine learning performance is organized around Algorithms (Model), Data Selection, and Machine (Hardware). The triangle’s edges label the compute-bound, I/O-bound, and sample-efficiency relationships, while data selection reduces workload before model or hardware execution.




Systems Perspective 9.1: Data selection and the iron lawIn the iron law of ML systems \((\Time= \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency)\), data selection reduces the number of examples or tokens that enter the workload. Later model-level optimizations reduce operations per forward/backward pass, and machine-level optimizations increase \(\PeakRate\) (peak throughput) and \(\EfficiencyHw\) (utilization). Selection removes work before those downstream optimizations execute it.
Within the compute term \(\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)\), data selection is multiplicatively valuable. Data selection and model-level optimization shrink the numerator while machine-level optimization enlarges the denominator, so when a compute-bound run applies all three, a 2× reduction in dataset size with 2× fewer operations per sample and 2× higher effective throughput yields an 8× reduction in compute time because the factors multiply; each layer divides the work the next layer sees. The iron law itself remains the sum of equation 1.3, so a run bound by data movement \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)\) or fixed overhead \((\Latency)\) sees less than the full product.


Holding epoch count, batch size, and per-sample work fixed, a 50 percent reduction in dataset size directly halves the required forward passes, backward passes, and gradient updates. For the $100M scenario, this reduction yields $50M in direct compute savings, provided the training schedule does not compensate by adding optimization steps.
These compute savings propagate throughout the hardware hierarchy. By decreasing total data volume (\(\DataVolume\)), deduplication and coreset selection alleviate storage bandwidth demands, network fabric ingress, and host-to-accelerator PCIe transfers that otherwise leave the accelerator’s arithmetic units waiting on input. Upstream, active learning curbs annotation budgets by directing human labeling to samples chosen for uncertainty, diversity, or other task-relevant query criteria.
Yet selection is not free: every selection strategy incurs its own runtime overhead to score, filter, shuffle, or coordinate samples. An online selection algorithm that executes additional forward passes to rank sample difficulty can easily consume more accelerator cycles than it saves if its selection overhead exceeds the subsequent reduction in training time. A pipeline claiming a training-time saving must make filtering plus subset training faster than full-data training at the same target quality. Labeling savings and reusable representations require the broader cost accounting developed later in the chapter.

title: Data Selection
text:
The systems framing established in section 1.3 calls for a quantitative metric. Data selection moves along a Pareto frontier (principle \(\ref{pri-pareto-frontier}\)) between accuracy and cost: retaining every example preserves coverage but expends compute on redundant signal, whereas over-aggressive pruning saves FLOPs at the expense of rare-slice recall. Navigating that trade-off requires quantifying the marginal learning signal each sample yields per unit of hardware execution. Data engineering already priced task-relevant signal against one cost, the data gravity of moving bytes, in the data selection gain of equation 4.1. Selection needs the same ratio with training compute in the denominator, because a sample that is cheap to move can still cost a full forward and backward pass. That ratio is the information-compute ratio (ICR).
Let \(\FiniteChange\DataInformationContent\) be the learning signal a sample or batch adds and \(\FiniteChange\Operations\) the training operations spent processing it. In practice \(\FiniteChange\DataInformationContent\) is measured as the gain in a fixed evaluation metric, such as percentage points of validation accuracy, so ICR carries units of metric gain per FLOP. The ratio relates the two: \[\text{ICR} = \frac{\FiniteChange\DataInformationContent}{\FiniteChange\Operations}\]
A higher ICR indicates that each FLOP of training buys more measured learning signal over the stated interval. Validation gain and training FLOPs can be observed for a specified experiment with a fixed evaluation protocol; the causal contribution of an individual example generally cannot. Uncertainty and gradient-based scores instead rank candidate examples before their downstream benefit is known. Those rankings require validation against measured quality, compute cost, and deployment-critical slice coverage. The core metrics in section 1.6.1 supply complementary evidence for that evaluation rather than interchangeable measurements of per-example information.

title: Data Selection
text:
The information-compute ratio falls as increasingly redundant examples enter the dataset. The ICR frontier is the dataset size beyond which the marginal ICR, the learning bought by the next FLOP spent on more data, drops below what that FLOP could buy elsewhere: a larger model, a different data source, or an earlier stop.
To illustrate diminishing returns, let \(\DataInformationContent(\DatasetSize)\) be the information content of a dataset of size \(\DatasetSize\) and assume \(\DataInformationContent(\DatasetSize) \propto \log \DatasetSize\). This is a simplified analytical model rather than a universal law. If compute cost scales linearly with the per-sample operation count \(\OperationsPerSample\), then total operations are \(\Operations = \OperationsPerSample \cdot \DatasetSize\), and the resulting marginal ICR follows equation 1: \[\text{ICR}(\DatasetSize) = \frac{\DerivativeOperator\DataInformationContent/d\DatasetSize}{d\Operations/d\DatasetSize} \approx \frac{1/\DatasetSize}{\OperationsPerSample} = \frac{1}{\OperationsPerSample\cdot \DatasetSize} \tag{1}\]
The derivative ratio describes the return on an infinitesimal increase in dataset size. For two controlled finite allocations, the corresponding incremental ratio divides the additional evaluation gain by the additional training FLOPs, using the same evaluation metric and protocol. The coreset comparison that follows instead averages gain over one epoch of each dataset; that average does not establish the return on the next increment.
Under this illustrative model, marginal ICR falls as \(1/(\OperationsPerSample \cdot \DatasetSize)\), so doubling the dataset halves the learning each additional FLOP buys. Inverted, the compute spent per unit of learning grows linearly with \(\DatasetSize\). ICR never reaches zero in this model and the curve has no knee of its own, so the frontier is located by comparing marginal ICR with the threshold the engineer sets, not read off the curve. That saturation is distinct from the data wall (a limit on how much new, high-quality data exists), but the two compound. When new data is scarce and marginal data is weak, selection becomes the main lever. Beyond the frontier, additional data still adds compute but buys less learning than the threshold demands. In this regime, data becomes a data tax that inflates the \(\Operations\) term of the iron law without a commensurate gain in ICR. Priced in dollars rather than FLOPs, the same tax lowers the return on compute (RoC) of equation 1.6, the accuracy gained per added dollar of infrastructure.


↩︎ Return on compute, the economic lens that prices accuracy gains against infrastructure spending, is established in Return on compute (RoC) as an economic lens.
Data selection turns the total operations \((\Operations)\) term in the iron law from a fixed constant into a variable. A 2\(\times\) improvement in measured ICR halves the FLOPs required to reach the same measured gain. It produces the same ideal time reduction as a 2\(\times\) throughput increase only when the workload is compute-bound and the saved work lies on the critical path. ICR focuses specifically on compute; the cost-modeling framework in section 1.13 extends the same reasoning to acquisition, labeling, and storage costs.
A random batch of raw data can have low ICR when it contains redundant, noisy, or already-mastered examples. To systematically raise ICR, figure 3 organizes three intervention points: offline static pruning before target training, dynamic selection during training loops, and on-demand synthetic generation. Their use and ordering depend on the workload.






Figure 3: An Example Data Selection Pipeline: One possible combination of interventions for increasing data value. The three intervention points are Static Pruning before target training, Dynamic Selection during training, and Synthetic Generation on demand. The sequence is illustrative rather than required: synthetic data can enter independently and can itself be pruned or dynamically selected. The final evaluation determines whether the quality gain justifies the compute cost through the Information-Compute Ratio (ICR).



The ratio becomes concrete on a coreset, a deliberately selected subset intended to preserve the full dataset’s learning signal. Computing ICR for an ImageNet coreset used to train the ResNet-50 lighthouse shows how large the efficiency gap could become once dataset size, per-sample model cost, and selection strategy meet concrete FLOP budgets. The scenario uses assumed accuracy gains to illustrate the arithmetic; it is not a reported result for the scoring method (EL2N) that section 1.7.4 develops.

Napkin Math 9.1: Computing ICR: CoresetsProblem: Training the ResNet-50 lighthouse model on ImageNet for one epoch costs 3.15 × 10¹⁶ FLOPs. Under the scenario’s assumed accuracy gains, how would retaining 50 percent of the data change the information-compute ratio? The calculation holds the per-sample work fixed and does not include selection overhead.
Setup:

Dataset: ImageNet (1.28M)
Model: ResNet-50 lighthouse (~8.2 GFLOP per forward pass, roughly 24.6 GFLOP for a forward plus backward training step, depending on implementation)
One epoch: 1.28M \(\times\) 24.6 GFLOP = 3.15 × 10¹⁶ FLOPs
Assumed accuracy improvement per epoch (early training): 5 percentage points

Random selection (baseline):

Process all 1.28M samples uniformly
Accuracy gain: 5 percentage points
\(\text{ICR}_{\text{random}}\) = 5 percentage points / (3.15 × 10¹⁶ FLOPs) = \(1.6 \times 10^{-16}\) per FLOP

Difficulty-scored coreset (EL2N, a training-dynamics score defined in section 1.7.4; 50 percent of data):

Process 640.6K selected samples
Assumed accuracy gain: 4.5 percentage points (90 percent of the full-data gain)
Compute: 640.6K \(\times\) 24.6 GFLOP = 1.6 × 10¹⁶ FLOPs
\(\text{ICR}_{\text{coreset}}\) = 4.5 percentage points / (1.6 × 10¹⁶ FLOPs) = \(2.9 \times 10^{-16}\) per FLOP

Systems insight: Under these assumptions, the selected subset achieves 1.8× higher ICR with a 0.5 percentage points smaller accuracy gain. The comparison is learning per FLOP over one epoch of each dataset. It does not show that the coreset reaches the full-data run’s final accuracy, which must be checked separately at equal quality, and a real decision also requires measured gains, selection overhead, and coverage checks.



Checkpoint 9.1: Data selection efficiency
The goal is to improve ICR subject to target quality and required coverage, then verify that the resulting pipeline reduces the cost it is intended to address.
Metric checks

ICR application: Given two training runs with identical accuracy gains but different compute budgets, determine which achieved higher ICR.
Data efficiency: The coreset notebook reports 1.8× higher ICR but a smaller per-epoch gain. Explain what would have to change for a 50 percent subset to match the full-data gain, which would give it 2\(\times\) higher ICR and so deliver the same measured gain for half the training FLOPs.

Pipeline checks

The three stages: Map static pruning, dynamic selection, and synthetic generation to the training lifecycle.



A reduction in sample count remains a claim until it is shown to translate into end-to-end efficiency without silently compromising generalization. Notebook 9.1 holds per-sample work fixed and assumes its accuracy gains; testing the claim on a real workload requires measured metrics that weigh arithmetic savings, data movement overhead, and task quality across the complete pipeline.

title: Data Selection
text:
Deploying a model trained on an aggressively filtered dataset can yield unexpected regressions in production: an autonomous vehicle perception model might maintain high aggregate precision while failing on rare pedestrian crossings pruned as low-density noise. Failures of this kind make a disciplined measurement framework essential. Every data selection technique claims to improve efficiency, but only rigorous measurement separates genuine training savings from shifted computational debt or degradation on safety-critical tail distributions. Three kinds of evidence judge a smaller dataset by what it preserves under production stress rather than by the volume it discards: efficiency metrics that tie sample reduction to accuracy, a diagnostic that tests whether the training run is data-limited at all, and validation that deployment-critical slices survive the reduction.


Three core metrics connect sample reduction to model quality instead of reporting accuracy alone. Performance-per-data measures accuracy gain per sample, the area under the learning curve measures cumulative learning efficiency across dataset scales, and the data compression ratio measures dataset reduction at a target accuracy. Together they complement the measured information-compute ratio (section 1.4). PPD measures average gain per sample, which becomes gain per FLOP once per-sample cost is fixed. AULC summarizes performance across a common dataset-size range, while DCR measures retained sample reduction at fixed quality. None establishes the causal value of an individual example.


The most direct metric, performance-per-data (PPD), measures accuracy gain per sample: \[
\text{PPD}(\LearningCurveSampleCount) = \frac{\text{Accuracy}(\LearningCurveSampleCount) - \text{Accuracy}(0)}{\LearningCurveSampleCount}
\] where \(\LearningCurveSampleCount\) is the number of training samples. A higher PPD indicates greater average improvement per sample over the stated interval. Its shape must be measured because diminishing returns and their onset are workload-dependent.



Rather than comparing at a single point, the area under the learning curve (AULC) integrates performance across all dataset sizes: \[
\text{AULC} = \int_0^\DatasetSize\text{Accuracy}(\LearningCurveSampleCount) \, d\LearningCurveSampleCount\] where \(\LearningCurveSampleCount\) is the dataset size and \(\DatasetSize\) is the total dataset size.
For the same metric and integration range, a higher AULC means stronger integrated performance across dataset sizes, though one strategy need not outperform the other at every size. Comparisons must use the same upper limit \(\DatasetSize\) or normalize the integral. Measuring AULC requires training at several dataset sizes, so the metric itself spends compute, and when it guides a selection decision that cost belongs to the selection overhead.



For coreset methods, the data compression ratio (DCR) measures how much data reduction is achieved at a target accuracy: \[
\text{DCR} = \frac{\FullDatasetSize}{\SubsetDatasetSize} \text{ at } \text{Accuracy}_{\text{target}}
\]
A DCR of 5\(\times\) means the coreset achieves target accuracy with 20 percent of the data.
Applied to the coreset notebook, the three metrics behave differently. Over one epoch, the full ImageNet set gains 5 percentage points while the half-size coreset gains 4.5 percentage points, so the coreset’s PPD is higher by the same 1.8× as its ICR, because per-sample work is fixed. DCR cannot be computed from that notebook at all, because the two runs never reach a common target accuracy. Exposing that missing equal-quality check is exactly the job DCR is designed for.




While the core metrics in section 1.6.1 measure individual techniques, a higher-level diagnostic is also needed to test whether the overall training strategy is data-limited or compute-limited. Neural scaling-law experiments (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022) fit power-law relationships over particular model families, datasets, and compute ranges. Controlled sweeps can use those fitted relationships to compare model and data allocations, but no single ratio diagnoses every training run.
3 Chinchilla: Chinchilla is a 70-billion-parameter language model trained on 1.4 trillion tokens. In the experiments reported by Hoffmann et al. (2022), it outperformed the larger GPT-3 on most evaluated tasks under a similar training-compute budget. The fitted compute-optimal allocation scaled parameters and tokens at roughly equal rates within the study’s experimental regime; it is not a universal prescription for every architecture, dataset, or training recipe.
Hoffmann, Jordan, Sebastian Borgeaud, Arthur Mensch, Elena Buchatskaya, Trevor Cai, Eliza Rutherford, Diego de Las Casas, et al. 2022. “Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 30016–30. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-2176.
The Chinchilla study3 (Hoffmann et al. 2022) fit a compute-optimal balance between model size and training data within its experimental regime. Allocations on either side of that fitted balance used the study’s compute budget less effectively.
The optimal balance defines a compute-optimal frontier: the best achievable performance at each compute budget when data and model size are properly balanced. Figure 4 plots this diagnostic curve over normalized training compute, isolating the optimal operating envelope on the green frontier from the compute-starved and data-starved allocations charted in the suboptimal region below.














Figure 4: Illustrative Compute-Optimal Frontier: The green curve is a conceptual frontier over normalized compute, not a fitted result from Chinchilla. Points below it illustrate allocations that a controlled model-size and token-count sweep might identify as data- or compute-limited.



The frontier answers one allocation question, whether the next unit of compute at a given budget should go to more parameters or to more training tokens. A run is data-starved when it trains on too few unique, useful tokens for its parameter count, so its tokens-per-parameter ratio sits well under the fitted balance, and the same compute would buy more accuracy with more or better data. Against a frontier fitted from controlled sweeps, an operating point’s location motivates further experiments. The directional vectors charted in figure 4 illustrate two candidate interventions: additional training compute and improved data selection at fixed compute. Controlled changes to model size, data, and training allocation determine which intervention helps; a point below the frontier does not identify a unique remedy. Points near a fitted frontier remain specific to the model family, dataset, objective, and compute range used to estimate it.


Within the fitted Chinchilla regime, compute-optimal model parameters and training tokens grew at roughly equal rates.4 Training a dense transformer costs approximately \(6\Parameters\DatasetSize\) FLOPs for \(\Parameters\) parameters and \(\DatasetSize\) tokens, the forward-plus-backward accounting derived for the GPT-2 lighthouse in Running example: Training GPT-2. Under an equal scaling regime where parameters and tokens grow proportionally (\(\Parameters \propto \DatasetSize\)), total compute scales quadratically (\(\Operations \propto \DatasetSize^2\)), directly implying that optimal token count scales as the square root of the compute budget (\(\ComputeOptimalTokenCount \propto \sqrt{\Operations}\)). Doubling compute therefore corresponds to about \(\sqrt{2} - 1\), or 41.4 percent, more tokens under those assumptions. The commonly quoted 20 tokens per parameter is a useful reference point from that study, not a universal optimum.
4 Tokens per parameter: The ratio \(\DatasetSize/\Parameters\) compares training tokens with model parameters; GPT-3 used approximately 1.7 tokens per parameter (Brown et al. 2020), while Llama 2 70B used approximately 28.6 (Touvron et al. 2023). These descriptive ratios do not establish whether either run is compute-optimal under a different architecture, corpus, objective, or hardware budget. Controlled model-size and token-count sweeps are required for that diagnosis.
Brown, Tom B., Benjamin Mann, Nick Ryder, Melanie Subbiah, Jared Kaplan, Prafulla Dhariwal, Arvind Neelakantan, et al. 2020. “Language Models Are Few-Shot Learners.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33: 1877–901. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2005.14165.

Touvron, Hugo, Louis Martin, Kevin Stone, Peter Albert, Amjad Almahairi, Yasmine Babaei, Nikolay Bashlykov, et al. 2023. “Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2307.09288.



If a training run underperforms expectations, extending one run can reveal whether additional optimization steps still help, but a plateau does not identify data starvation by itself. Learning-rate schedules, optimization limits, model capacity, and data quality can all produce a plateau. A reliable diagnosis compares controlled runs that vary model size, token count, and compute allocation while holding the evaluation protocol fixed.
When controlled runs do point to the data, the remedy that keeps compute fixed is better selection, which changes the shape of the learning curve itself. Seeing that change requires switching axes, from the frontier’s training compute to the core metrics’ dataset size, where the area under each curve is the AULC defined in section 1.6.1. In the illustrative curves of figure 5, efficient selection bends into an accuracy plateau near 25 percent of the data while uniform random sampling climbs gradually across the entire budget. The horizontal separation between the curves is the reduction in required samples, and at an identical 20 percent data budget the vertical gap is the accuracy that selection buys without any additional compute.














Figure 5: Illustrative Diminishing Returns of Data: The synthetic data-efficient curve (blue) reaches the same plateau with fewer samples than random sampling (gray). The vertical red arrow marks the modeled performance gap at a fixed dataset size; measured curves need not have this shape.



These evaluation metrics govern the transition point where indiscriminate data collection yields to targeted curation, identifying when marginal samples waste training compute rather than improving generalization. Yet algorithmic efficiency does not guarantee that a reduced dataset preserves model quality across operational edge cases.
Data selection techniques implicitly rank sample value, and validating that a curated dataset preserves model quality requires systematic benchmarking across three dimensions. Coverage metrics validate that coreset selection preserved representation across classes and demographic groups. Distribution alignment metrics (such as KL divergence and population stability index, which Measuring drift (divergence) defines) detect whether the curated training set drifted from the deployment distribution. Label quality metrics (inter-annotator agreement, and confident learning, which flags examples whose given label disagrees with a model’s confident out-of-sample prediction) validate that active learning did not introduce systematic labeling errors. A 50 percent dataset reduction is only valuable if benchmarking confirms the model maintains target accuracy, calibration, and robustness.


↪ Coverage, label-quality, and distribution-alignment checks are developed into a full data-benchmarking protocol in Data benchmarking.
The validation target can itself be unreliable. Benchmark accuracy can overstate generalization when test sets fail to capture operational distribution shifts, demanding the same scrutiny for evaluation benchmarks as for curated training sets.

Example 9.1: The benchmark replication gapScenario: Classifiers evaluated on newly collected test sets experienced 3 to 15 percentage-point accuracy drops on CIFAR-10 and 11 to 14 points on ImageNet (Recht et al. 2019).
Diagnosis: The replicated collection produced slightly harder images than the original test sets. The study found that benchmark adaptivity did not explain the gap, even though repeated use of a fixed test set remains a general evaluation risk.
Systems lesson: Evaluation-set construction affects measured generalization. Data-selection pipelines should validate curated subsets on independently collected and deployment-relevant test sets rather than trusting one long-reused benchmark.



Recht, Benjamin, Rebecca Roelofs, Ludwig Schmidt, and Vaishaal Shankar. 2019. “Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?” Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 5389–400.
An efficiency gain measured against a single benchmark can evaporate under distribution shift; a curated subset must demonstrate consistent quality across multiple held-out distributions before its reported reduction ratio is trusted.
Disciplined metrics separate genuine compute savings from deferred computational debt: a selection strategy must be evaluated against its stated objective, counting the overhead of scoring, filtering, and staging samples alongside training, labeling, or reuse savings at target quality. When teams optimize selection algorithms against isolated benchmarks rather than end-to-end pipeline constraints, intuitive heuristics frequently backfire. They waste cluster cycles on scoring overhead, destabilize optimization trajectories, or silently corrupt downstream generalization.
These metrics apply to three complementary levers, taken in order of when they act: prune static waste upfront, steer dynamic batches during execution, and synthesize missing coverage on demand. Static pruning comes first because it fixes the subset before target-model training, though its scoring process may use a trained proxy.

A team wants one metric for how much smaller a selected dataset is at a target accuracy, and another for how much learning is gained per sample over a measured interval. Which pair of chapter metrics matches that need?

Data Curation Rate and Accuracy Reduction Ratio
Data Compression Ratio and Performance-Per-Data
Dynamic Checkpoint Rate and Active Retention Rate
Data Convergence Ratio and Amortized Risk Ratio

An ML systems diagnostic plot maps normalized training compute on the horizontal axis against model performance on the vertical axis. A 10M-parameter run sits well below a fitted frontier under a fixed evaluation protocol and fixed total budget. A controlled sweep then shows that reallocating the same budget toward a larger model improves performance. What is the most defensible diagnosis of the original operating point?

Data-starved regime
I/O bandwidth-saturated regime
The model/data allocation was suboptimal under the tested budget
Over-echoing regime

Why is Area Under the Learning Curve (AULC) a more informative metric than single-point final validation accuracy when comparing data selection methods across dataset sizes?
True or False: If two training runs reach the same validation plateau, they must have processed identical amounts of informative signal.
The Pareto frontier that defines the maximum achievable model accuracy or minimum loss for every given training compute budget (FLOPs) under balanced parameter and token allocation is known as the compute-____ frontier.

title: Data Selection
text:
Web-scale scraping routinely gathers terabytes of boilerplate text, duplicate images, and malformed records that waste cluster compute before a single valid gradient is calculated. Static pruning and pretraining filtration eliminate this uninformative volume upstream of the training loop. By purging redundant and corrupt records before target-model training, static filtration shrinks the operation count \((\Operations)\) without modifying model architectures or execution kernels.


Empirical scaling studies show that dataset volume alone does not dictate model accuracy: large-scale corpora harbor substantial redundancy. In many regimes, a significant fraction of training examples contributes negligible gradient signal while consuming full forward-backward compute.
On CIFAR-10, Paul et al. (2021) report that EL2N pruning (which scores each example by its prediction error early in training) removed half of the training data without reducing accuracy. On ImageNet-1K, Sorscher et al. (2022) report that a self-supervised prototype metric discarded 20 percent of the data without sacrificing performance. The pattern extends to language modeling, where web-scraped corpora like The Pile5 and C46 contain enough duplicate and templated content to make deduplication a systems issue. In datasets studied by Lee et al. (2022), approximate near-duplicate removal affected 3.04 percent of C4 and 13.63 percent of RealNews, and deduplicated training reduced memorization while preserving or improving perplexity.

Sorscher, Ben, Robert Geirhos, Shashank Shekhar, Surya Ganguli, and Ari S. Morcos. 2022. “Beyond Neural Scaling Laws: Beating Power Law Scaling via Data Pruning.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 19523–36. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-1419.
5 The Pile: An approximately 886 GB English text corpus (reported as 825 gibibytes by the source) aggregating twenty-two sub-datasets, including PubMed, ArXiv, GitHub, Project Gutenberg, Common Crawl, Stack Exchange, Wikipedia, and USPTO patents (Gao et al. 2020). Its multi-source design makes it a useful example of data diversity: each source family has a different duplication, quality, and domain-coverage profile, so selection pipelines must preserve coverage while removing redundant text.
Gao, Leo, Stella Biderman, Sid Black, Laurence Golding, Travis Hoppe, Charles Foster, Jason Phang, et al. 2020. “The Pile: An 800GB Dataset of Diverse Text for Language Modeling.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2101.00027.
6 C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus): C4 applies filtering to Common Crawl data, including language detection, deduplication of repeated three-sentence spans, and removal of pages that fail heuristic quality checks, producing approximately 750 GB of cleaned English text (Raffel et al. 2020). Filtering has its own compute cost and can remove useful material, so its ROI and quality effects must be measured rather than inferred from corpus size alone.
Raffel, C., N. Shazeer, A. Roberts, K. Lee, S. Narang, M. Matena, Y. Zhou, W. Li, and P. J. Liu. 2020. “Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer.” Journal of Machine Learning Research 21 (140): 1–67.
The reported gains are benchmark-specific. Pruning effectiveness depends on intrinsic dataset redundancy, the selection algorithm, and target model capacity; production deployments require task-specific validation before committing to aggressive filtration.
Individual data points need not provide equal value for training. This heterogeneity follows in part from how classifiers learn decision boundaries. Many samples fall far from a boundary: a picture of a dog in good lighting may become easy once the model has learned its dominant features, while ambiguous and underrepresented cases can remain informative. Label quality also affects data requirements. Conflicting labels can push updates in opposing directions, so reaching a target error may require more examples or more passes over them. The size of that penalty depends on the task and training procedure. A data quality multiplier therefore comes from comparing learning curves at the same held-out error, rather than assigning a universal convergence rate to all noisy data.

Napkin Math 9.2: The data quality multiplierProblem: Two hypothetical pilot learning curves reach the same held-out error using different amounts of clean and noisy data. With epoch count and per-sample work held fixed, what training-work multiplier do these sample counts imply?
Setup: Consider a representative evaluation where a fixed model architecture and training recipe reach target error \(\TargetError\) = 0.01 (1 percent) under clean versus noisy training partitions:

Clean data: \(\CleanLabelSampleCount\) = 10,000
Noisy data: \(\NoisyLabelSampleCount\) = 16,000

Result: Dividing the noisy-data count by the clean-data count gives 1.6×. Under the fixed training recipe, the noisy dataset therefore requires 1.6× as much training work to reach the same error.
Systems insight: The avoided training work sets a budget for cleaning. Cleaning pays for itself only when correction or review costs less than the work it removes, with required coverage preserved. If the two learning curves require different epoch counts, compare total examples processed to the target instead of unique sample counts. The decision depends on measured learning curves and pipeline costs, not on the presence of noise alone.





The cheapest samples to remove are the ones that repeat what the dataset already contains. Repeated content costs a full forward and backward pass on every presentation, even when that repetition adds little useful learning signal. Exact hashing and shingle-based near-duplicate detection can identify candidates for removal without training a scoring model. Deduplication therefore comes first among the static levers and can provide immediate efficiency gains. This makes it one of the most accessible optimizations in data selection, but near-duplicate thresholds must be validated so the pipeline does not remove useful distributional signal.
The simplest form of deduplication uses hash-based methods for exact matches. By computing a cryptographic hash (MD5 or SHA-256) for each sample and removing those with identical hashes, practitioners can eliminate byte-for-byte duplicates that inevitably accumulate in large web-scraped corpora. This process is computationally cheap, scaling linearly with dataset size, and can be parallelized trivially.


↩︎ Deduplication as a deterministic data-cleaning step that keeps training and serving pipelines consistent is established in Training-serving consistency.
7 MinHash: Invented by Broder (1997) to detect duplicate web pages for AltaVista, the algorithm creates compact signatures using random hash functions such that similar documents produce similar signatures with high probability. Each signature compresses a document to a fixed-size sketch, enabling pairwise similarity estimation in \(\mathcal{O}(\MinHashSketchSize)\) time for sketch size \(\MinHashSketchSize\).
Broder, A. Z. 1997. “On the Resemblance and Containment of Documents.” Proceedings. Compression and Complexity of SEQUENCES 1997 (Cat. No.97TB100171), 21–29. https://doi.org/10.1109/sequen.1997.666900.
8 Locality-sensitive hashing (LSH): LSH hashes MinHash signatures into buckets so that similar signatures are more likely to collide. Candidate generation avoids an exhaustive all-pairs comparison, while runtime and memory depend on signature width, banding, bucket sizes, and the number of candidates that require verification.9 Jaccard similarity: Defined as \(|\FirstJaccardSet\cap \SecondJaccardSet| / |\FirstJaccardSet\cup \SecondJaccardSet|\) for two sets \(\FirstJaccardSet\) and \(\SecondJaccardSet\), ranging from 0 (disjoint) to 1 (identical). For deduplication, the metric compares sets of shingles across documents of different lengths. The threshold must be calibrated for the shingle definition, corpus, and downstream quality because no universal cutoff separates duplicates from legitimately related documents.Near-duplicate detection addresses content that differs at the byte level while retaining substantial token- or character-shingle overlap. For text, MinHash7 with Locality-Sensitive Hashing8 (LSH) approximates Jaccard similarity9 efficiently. In practice, the pipeline converts each document into a set of overlapping character or word \(\ShingleLength\)-shingles, compresses these sets into fixed-length MinHash signatures where the probability of hash collision equals Jaccard similarity, and partitions the signatures into \(\LshBandCount\) bands of \(\LshRowsPerBand\) rows using LSH. Documents matching across all rows in any single band collide in the same bucket, restricting expensive similarity verification to likely candidates and avoiding an impossible \(\mathcal{O}(\DatasetSize^2)\) all-pairs comparison across a corpus of \(\DatasetSize\) web documents numbering in the billions. It can detect lightly edited content with high overlap, but it does not establish semantic paraphrase equivalence.
For images, perceptual hashing produces signatures robust to minor transformations like resizing and compression, identifying visually similar candidates stored in different formats. Embedding-based similarity can retrieve semantic near-neighbor candidates by computing dense representations (CLIP10 (Radford et al. 2021) for images, sentence transformers for text), though proximity does not itself prove duplication and the approach incurs higher computational overhead.
10 CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining): Pretrained on 400 million image-text pairs, CLIP maps semantically related images and text into a shared embedding space (Radford et al. 2021). Embeddings can retrieve candidates for review, but semantic proximity is not proof that two samples are duplicates. Generating embeddings also costs substantially more than computing perceptual hashes, with the ratio depending on model and hardware.
Radford, Alec, Jong Wook Kim, Chris Hallacy, Aditya Ramesh, Gabriel Goh, Sandhini Agarwal, Girish Sastry, et al. 2021. “Learning Transferable Visual Models from Natural Language Supervision.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 8748–63.
Deduplication can reduce repeated-content memorization and avoid spending FLOPs on exact or near duplicates. It can also alter the corpus’s intentional empirical weighting, so thresholds and downstream quality must be validated rather than assuming that every duplicate is harmful.
The systems impact of deduplication shifts when input examples index persistent model state rather than streaming through stateless compute layers.

Lighthouse 9.1: DLRM and embedding deduplicationThe DLRM lighthouse model is memory capacity-bound, and at production scale its embedding tables reach terabytes of storage for billions of user/item IDs. Much of this capacity is wasted on cold embeddings, IDs that appear rarely in training data.
Data selection for DLRM can include interaction deduplication and embedding pruning for cold IDs. Removing repeated interactions reduces training examples but shrinks an embedding table only when IDs disappear or the allocation, hashing, or sharing policy changes.





Deduplication removes samples that repeat information; quality pruning targets samples whose information is wrong or absent. Quality-based pruning eliminates samples that either contribute no meaningful signal or introduce contradictory information that confuses the optimization process.
Label error detection can be a high-impact form of quality pruning. Tools like Cleanlab identify samples where the assigned label may be incorrect based on model confidence patterns across training. A sample that the model consistently predicts as class A but is labeled class B may be a hard boundary case, a distribution shift, a model blind spot, or an annotation mistake. The score should trigger review rather than automatic deletion; confirmed errors can then be corrected or removed.
Outlier removal addresses a different pathology: samples far from any cluster center in feature space. Such points can indicate noise, annotation errors, or corruption, but they can also be the rare edge cases that define deployment risk. The key is distinguishing informative outliers from invalid samples, with conservative thresholds and slice-level review before removal.
Low-information filtering applies domain-specific heuristics to remove samples that lack sufficient signal for learning. For text corpora, this often means removing high-perplexity garbled text (perplexity is a language model’s measure of how surprising a text is, so high values can flag incoherent strings but also valid specialist or rare-language text) and, in some pipelines, low-perplexity boilerplate or repetitive text. For image datasets, filtering targets blurry, corrupted, or near-uniform samples that provide little visual information.
Beyond heuristics and perplexity, industrial pretraining pipelines rely heavily on classifier-based filtering: training a lightweight, high-throughput linear classifier (such as fastText) using curated, high-quality reference text (e.g., Wikipedia, books, and scientific papers) as positive examples and uncurated web dumps as negative examples. This classifier assigns each scraped document a continuous quality score, allowing pipelines to filter out millions of low-quality web pages at gigabyte-per-second ingestion speeds without the heavy computational burden of evaluating a full neural language model.



Once duplicates and defective records are gone, the remaining samples are unique and valid but still unequal in value, which is the heterogeneity that opened this section. Ranking them requires systematic selection criteria. Coreset selection11 turns the static pruning decision into a coverage problem: keep the smallest subset that preserves the statistical properties of the entire dataset.
11 Coreset (core set): In computational geometry, a small subset can approximate a specified geometric objective within a controlled error factor (Agarwal et al. 2005). Machine learning adapts this idea as a selection principle, but a guarantee for an embedding and distance objective does not by itself guarantee neural-network accuracy. The retained subset must still be validated on the target task.
Agarwal, Pankaj K., Sariel Har-Peled, and Kasturi R. Varadarajan. 2005. “Geometric Approximation via Coresets.” In Combinatorial and Computational Geometry, edited by Jacob E. Goodman, János Pach, and Emo Welzl, vol. 52. MSRI Publications. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009701259.002.
The systems decision is where to spend the selection budget: on cheap coverage metrics that preserve distributional structure, or on costlier training-dynamics scores that better target the decision boundary. The decision also needs a guardrail before any score is applied: classes, demographic groups, time windows, and rare failure modes that matter at deployment require minimum representation, because the highest-average-ICR subset can still remove the examples that define production risk.
Geometry-based methods select samples that cover a chosen representation without requiring target-model training. The \(\CenterCount\)-Center algorithm,12 a facility-location-style objective, selects samples that reduce the maximum distance from any point to its nearest selected center under the chosen embedding and metric.
12 k-center algorithm: Its greedy strategy iteratively picks the point farthest from the existing centers under a chosen embedding and metric. Sener and Savarese use this core-set framing for convolutional-neural-network active learning (Sener and Savarese 2018). The resulting coverage bound applies to that geometric objective, not directly to downstream accuracy or rare-class preservation.
Sener, Ozan, and Silvio Savarese. 2018. “Active Learning for Convolutional Neural Networks: A Core-Set Approach.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Welling, Max. 2009. “Herding Dynamical Weights to Learn.” Proceedings of the 26th Annual International Conference on Machine Learning, 1121–28. https://doi.org/10.1145/1553374.1553517.
Herding takes a different approach. Welling’s original procedure iteratively constructs representative pseudo-samples whose feature statistics approximate observed moments (Welling 2009). Related moment-matching objectives can guide subset selection from a fixed pool. These methods are computationally attractive because they operate on feature representations, but their scores are not inherently label-aware.
Training-dynamics methods use a proxy model to identify examples that may be important. GraNd (Gradient Normed) and EL2N (error L2-norm)13 score samples by gradient magnitude or prediction error early in training (Paul et al. 2021). Theoretically, sample valuation can be framed via influence functions (Koh and Liang 2017), which measure how removing a sample changes validation loss. Evaluating true sample influence requires calculating an inverse empirical Hessian (\(\LossHessian^{-1} \nabla_\ModelParameters\LossFunction\)), where the Hessian matrix \(\LossHessian\) captures the local curvature of the loss surface across all parameter interactions. For a model with \(\Parameters\) parameters, storing the \(\Parameters \times \Parameters\) Hessian demands \(\mathcal{O}(\Parameters^2)\) memory, and computing its inverse requires \(\mathcal{O}(\Parameters^3)\) arithmetic operations. Exact second-order influence is therefore intractable for models with millions or billions of parameters.
13 EL2N (error L2-norm) and GraNd (gradient normed): These methods score samples based on their error or gradient norm early in training, identifying samples the model finds most difficult. The practicality of this approach relies on transferability, where scores from a small proxy model can guide data selection for a much larger target model. For instance, a proxy trained for five epochs can generate scores to curate a dataset for a full 90-epoch production training run (Paul et al. 2021).
Paul, Mansheej, Surya Ganguli, and Gintare Karolina Dziugaite. 2021. “Deep Learning on a Data Diet: Finding Important Examples Early in Training.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 34: 20596–607.

Koh, Pang Wei, and Percy Liang. 2017. “Understanding Black-Box Predictions via Influence Functions.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 70: 1885–94.
14 Forgetting events: This method identifies valuable examples by tracking when the model “forgets” them, transitioning from a correct to an incorrect classification during training. The central trade-off is the high cost of this analysis, which requires a full training run. However, the resulting importance scores can transfer from small proxy models to larger target models (for example, ResNet-18 to ResNet-50), enabling inexpensive proxy-based selection when ranking quality holds for the target task (Toneva et al. 2019).
Toneva, Mariya, Alessandro Sordoni, Remi Tachet des Combes, Adam Trischler, Yoshua Bengio, and Geoffrey J Gordon. 2019. “An Empirical Study of Example Forgetting During Deep Neural Network Learning.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
Systems methods circumvent this barrier by relying on lightweight first-order approximations: GraNd scores samples using expected gradient norm (\(\|\nabla_\ModelParameters\LossFunction\|_2\)), while EL2N observes that early in training, the gradient norm with respect to linear layers is strongly correlated with output prediction error (\(\|\PredictedOutput - \LabelVector\|_2\), the distance between the predicted probability vector \(\PredictedOutput\) and the one-hot label \(\LabelVector\)). This enables practitioners to score prediction error using a single forward pass without computing backward-pass gradients. Error and uncertainty differ: a confident prediction of the wrong class can have high EL2N despite low predictive uncertainty. High scores identify examples the proxy finds difficult, but they can also identify noise or unrepresentative samples and therefore need coverage and quality checks. The same work reports useful score transfer across several architectures, which can enable less expensive proxy-based selection. A third training-dynamics signal, forgetting events,14 tracks how often a sample is correctly classified and later misclassified during training (Toneva et al. 2019).
Each algorithm in table 3 balances upfront scoring computation against downstream training reduction. Because geometry-based and training-dynamics methods optimize different proxies, their relative ranking depends on dataset scale, feature representations, target model capacity, and scoring budgets; a score is computationally justified only when downstream training savings exceed evaluation overhead.

Geometry-based methods prioritize coverage in a chosen feature representation, while training-dynamics methods use signals such as error or forgetting. Uncertainty sampling, which active learning uses as a query rule (section 1.8.2), concentrates the budget near the current decision boundary; EL2N instead ranks prediction error, which can also be high for confidently wrong examples away from the boundary. Figure 6 contrasts that boundary-focused allocation with uniform random sampling of the same five-point budget. It illustrates one family of selection rules; a geometry-based method such as \(\CenterCount\)-center would instead spread its picks to cover the feature space.






Figure 6: Illustrative Boundary-Focused Selection: Both panels select five samples, isolating allocation rather than budget. Random sampling distributes those choices across the feature space; a boundary-focused rule such as uncertainty sampling concentrates them in the shaded band around the current decision boundary.



EL2N with a small proxy model offers one practical balance between scoring cost and selection quality. The approach trains a lightweight model for a few epochs, computes EL2N scores, and selects a subset subject to coverage and quality checks. The proxy must provide rankings that transfer to the target model, and the investment pays off only when downstream training savings exceed selection overhead. A concrete scenario shows the workflow; whether its 10 percent subset preserves accuracy is exactly what validation must establish.

Example 9.2: Coreset selection in practiceScenario: An engineering team aims to select a 100,000 coreset (10 percent) from 1 million training images for faster model iteration.
Diagnosis: Naive random subsampling can miss rare classes and boundary examples. Training a lightweight proxy model for 5 epochs calculates EL2N error scores, prioritizing high-error examples while checking rare-class coverage.
Systems lesson: Proxy-based coreset selection replaces some full-data passes with targeted scoring compute. It accelerates full-model training only when the proxy ranking transfers and coverage checks preserve rare classes and edge cases.


Listing 1 turns proxy prediction error into reusable selected indices. The compute_el2n_scores function spends a small amount of probe compute to measure which samples still confuse a briefly trained model, and select_coreset retains the highest-scoring examples. This top-\(\Glyph{k}\) sketch needs quality and coverage checks before its subset replaces the full training pool. The scoring pass requires an unshuffled dataloader so each score position remains aligned with its dataset index.



Listing 1: EL2N-Based Coreset Selection: The compute_el2n_scores function trains a proxy model for a few epochs, then measures prediction error via L2 distance from one-hot labels. High scores identify samples the proxy finds difficult, including potentially noisy examples. The select_coreset function illustrates ranking by this score; production use also requires coverage, noise, and target-quality validation.


def compute_el2n_scores(model, dataloader, num_epochs=5):
    """Compute EL2N scores.

    Returns L2 norm of (prediction - one_hot_label).
    """
    # Train proxy model for a few epochs to get meaningful predictions
    train_proxy(model, dataloader, num_epochs)

    scores = []
    model.eval()
    for x, y in dataloader:
        logits = model(x)
        probs = softmax(logits, dim=1)
        # One-hot encode labels
        one_hot = zeros_like(probs).scatter_(1, y.unsqueeze(1), 1)
        # EL2N score = L2 distance between probabilities and one-hot target
        el2n = (probs - one_hot).norm(dim=1)  # High = large prediction error
        scores.extend(el2n.tolist())
    return scores


def select_coreset(scores, dataset, fraction=0.1):
    """Select top-k samples with the largest prediction errors."""
    k = int(len(dataset) * fraction)
    # Sort by score descending (largest prediction error first)
    indices = argsort(scores, descending=True)[:k]
    return Subset(dataset, indices)


# Illustrative 10% subset; validate accuracy and coverage before use
scores = compute_el2n_scores(proxy_model, full_loader)
coreset = select_coreset(scores, full_dataset, fraction=0.1)
train_full_model(model, coreset)



A coverage floor changes the indices retained by the score ranking. Consider disjoint classes A and B, a total coreset budget \(\CoresetBudget\) as in table 3, and task-validated minimum counts \(\FirstClassCoverageFloor\) and \(\SecondClassCoverageFloor\) for the respective classes. First reserve the highest-scoring \(\FirstClassCoverageFloor\) eligible examples from A and the highest-scoring \(\SecondClassCoverageFloor\) from B. Fill the remaining \(\CoresetBudget-\FirstClassCoverageFloor-\SecondClassCoverageFloor\) slots from the global ranking, skipping indices already reserved. The allocation is infeasible if \(\CoresetBudget<\FirstClassCoverageFloor+\SecondClassCoverageFloor\), if either class lacks enough eligible examples to meet its floor, or if the eligible pool is smaller than \(\CoresetBudget\); the pipeline must revise the budget or acquire missing coverage before training.
Suppose the unconstrained top-\(\CoresetBudget\) ranking contains only A examples and the budget can meet both floors. Reserving B’s floor replaces the lowest-scoring \(\SecondClassCoverageFloor\) members of that all-A subset with the highest-scoring eligible B examples, while the remaining slots still follow the score order. Coverage thus has an explicit opportunity cost in the selection score. Overlapping demographic or operational slices require joint constraint handling because one example may satisfy several floors; summing those floors as if the slices were disjoint can reject a feasible budget. Even a feasible allocation establishes only retained counts. Independent evaluation must still establish target quality and performance on the required slices.
Together, these three static pruning techniques (deduplication, quality filtering, and coreset selection) shrink \(\Operations\) before training begins, subject to the same fixed-schedule caveat as before. A schedule that adds compensating epochs or steps gives back part of the saving.
Static pruning answers a question about what to keep, but it treats the answer as fixed. Once the pruned dataset is set, every epoch trains on the same subset. A sample’s usefulness, however, can change as the model learns: examples that challenge an undertrained model may become easy after sufficient gradient updates. Dynamic selection techniques address this limitation by adapting the training data at each stage based on what the model has already mastered.

Self-Check: Question

A team wants to score a dataset cheaply before training a large production model. They plan to train a small proxy for a few epochs and rank examples by prediction error, knowing that confidently wrong predictions can still score highly. Which method best matches that plan and its trade-off?

\(k\)-Center clustering on raw pixel inputs, because it guarantees zero-cost label-aware boundary identification
Forgetting Events scoring on the full production model, because it requires no proxy architecture and computes in \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) time
EL2N (Error L2-Norm) scoring with a briefly trained proxy model, accepting that high error can reflect hard examples or noise
Herding on Gaussian-distributed features, because it completely avoids computing feature representations

Why is Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) with MinHash preferred over exhaustive pairwise Jaccard similarity comparison for large-scale text deduplication?

MinHash LSH guarantees \(100\%\) precision in detecting semantic paraphrases across different natural languages
