title: Data Selection
text:
Data sharding dissolves the single-process abstraction even on one machine with two to eight accelerators. In a centralized pipeline, coreset algorithms sort a single global ranking, curricula enforce a uniform sequence, and active-learning loops evaluate a shared candidate pool. Parallel worker processes divide the corpus into local shards and may score them using different model checkpoints. Selection must reconstruct a representative global subset from these local views and keep rankings coherent as the model changes. The workers still share host memory capacity, storage bandwidth, and host-to-device links.
Whether distributed selection stays faithful to the global dataset or collapses into local shard heuristics depends on how much cross-worker coordination each technique requires against the bandwidth available to sustain it. On one host, score gathering and index dispatch compete for CPU time and memory bandwidth with decoding and batch preparation. Evaluating selection therefore requires analyzing statistical fidelity alongside these shared resources.
These are independent requirements. A coreset can remain representative yet cost too much to coordinate, while a cheap shard-local method can scale but systematically miss rare groups visible only in the global corpus. A distributed design therefore needs two acceptance tests: compare selected-data quality with a centralized or otherwise auditable reference, and compare selection overhead with the end-to-end training time it saves. Passing only one test is insufficient.


In a basic data-parallel layout, each worker processes a distinct shard and model synchronization is handled separately. Data selection can add dependencies across those shards (table 8).



Table 8: Selection Dependencies in Distributed Training: The table starts from a common centralized formulation of each technique and identifies the coordination problem introduced by sharding. Distributed variants may relax rather than reproduce the centralized result exactly.










Technique
Single-Process Assumption
Distributed Challenge




Coreset Selection
Global view of dataset
Each worker sees only its shard


Active Learning
Centralized uncertainty scoring
Scoring requires model synchronization


Curriculum Learning
Global difficulty ordering
Workers may have different “hardest” samples


Deduplication
One shared duplicate map
Shard-local hashes miss cross-shard duplicates






The selection dependencies admit several architectural solutions, each navigating a different point in the consistency-scalability trade-off space. The most straightforward approach centralizes selection while distributing training. A coordinator process performs selection on the full dataset, then distributes selected indices to workers. This preserves selection quality but introduces a single bottleneck:
Coordinator: score_all_samples() → selected_indices
Broadcast: selected_indices → all workers
Workers: train on subset(local_shard, selected_indices)
The semantics remain clean, but the coordinator can serialize scoring or index dispatch. Whether that overhead is acceptable depends on the selection payload, refresh rate, worker count, and copies through shared host memory. Adding accelerator workers does not increase the host memory available to the coordinator.
Hierarchical selection addresses this scalability limitation by distributing the selection computation itself. Each worker performs local selection on its shard, then a coordinator merges results:
Workers: local_selected = select_top_k(local_shard)
Coordinator: global_selected = merge_and_rerank(all local_selected)
Broadcast: final_indices → all workers
Shard-local selection reduces coordinator load but introduces a quality trade-off: local quotas and score distributions may not preserve the global ranking or rare groups spread unevenly across shards. The merge step therefore needs normalization, coverage constraints, or a second global pass.
Cross-shard deduplication has the same visibility requirement. Workers can compute MinHash signatures locally, but a shared merge must compare candidates across shard boundaries. Independent local hash tables cannot detect a duplicate whose counterpart belongs to another worker. The merge must fit the host’s memory budget or operate in bounded batches, rather than assuming that more workers supply more host capacity.



Shard-local selection already needs a coherent score scale, but active learning introduces an additional complication because the model changes during selection. Consider what happens when Worker A scores samples using the model at step \(\OptimizerStepIndex\) while Worker B simultaneously updates the model to step \(\OptimizerStepIndex+1\). Worker A’s scores are now stale and may select samples that the updated model would rank differently.
The scoring schedule therefore defines the meaning of a query, not merely its cost. A reproducible system versions the model checkpoint, candidate-pool snapshot, scoring rule, and selected indices together. It can then measure how much ranking agreement decays with checkpoint age and choose a refresh interval from that evidence rather than from an arbitrary number of steps.
Several strategies mitigate this staleness problem, each with distinct overhead characteristics:

Synchronous scoring: All workers pause training and score simultaneously, guaranteeing consistency but at substantial cost in GPU utilization.
Periodic score refresh: Workers re-score every \(\ScoreRefreshInterval\) epochs rather than every batch, trading freshness for reduced overhead.
Checkpoint-robust selection: The system selects samples that exhibit high uncertainty under multiple model checkpoints, favoring decisions that are less sensitive to checkpoint choice. Agreement across past checkpoints is a robustness heuristic; ranking quality still needs validation as the model evolves.

An illustrative one-host scenario with eight accelerator workers prices the shard-local scoring and centralized merge of a one-time coreset selection. Repeated refreshes incur this cost again; the assumed phase times include parallel execution and host coordination rather than promising linear speedup from the worker count.

Example 9.7: Distributed coreset selectionScenario: One host with 8 A100 accelerator workers selects a 10 percent coreset from ImageNet (1.3M images) across local worker processes.
Diagnosis: Scoring on one accelerator leaves the other devices unused. Shard-local embedding, parallel signature generation with cross-shard deduplication, local EL2N scoring, and a centralized candidate merge distribute that work. Under the assumed phase times, dataset selection takes 67 minutes.
Systems lesson: Parallel scoring reduces work per accelerator, while embeddings, score arrays, and the global index must still fit within the machine’s memory budget. In figure 11, “Coordinator Node” names the logical selection role on this same host; the worker boxes represent accelerator processes, not additional machines. Workers return candidate scores and indices to the coordinator, which maintains the global FAISS index for embedding-based checks, merges local candidates, and dispatches the final coreset indices. The merge must enforce coverage floors and compare its result with the centralized reference, because candidates discarded locally cannot be recovered from their scores alone.








Figure 11: Distributed Coreset Selection Architecture: Parallel shard-local scoring reduces the work assigned to a centralized rank-merging coordinator. Workers send local EL2N scores upward; the coordinator merges them and broadcasts final coreset indices. The design is beneficial only when this coordination overhead remains below the training time saved by the coreset.



Positive ROI can erode quickly when workers coordinate frequently during training. Distributed selection introduces a coordination tax whose size depends on what is synchronized and how often. That tax must remain smaller than the training time saved; if it approaches the limit, simplify the strategy or increase the refresh interval.
The communication path adds a further constraint. Gradient synchronization may use accelerator collectives over local interconnects, while embedding vectors, score arrays, and coreset indices may pass through host memory and CPU dispatch. Selection can therefore expose host-memory, PCIe, storage, or process-synchronization bottlenecks that the training profile alone does not reveal. Extending the design to independent machines adds network topology and remote-storage constraints; those are a further scaling problem beyond the one-host design developed here.
Yet operational feasibility does not guarantee economic viability. A deduplication pipeline that costs $50K to engineer and saves $10K per training run loses money on a single run and pays off only if enough runs reuse it. Deploying selection techniques requires rigorous financial accounting of capital, compute, and human annotation budgets.

Self-Check: Question

On one host with two to eight accelerator workers, how can centralized coreset selection become a bottleneck, and what trade-off does hierarchical selection introduce?

Centralized selection requires all workers to share a single GPU; hierarchical selection distributes weights across SSDs
Centralized selection fails because sharding prevents network cards from transmitting floating-point values
Centralized selection can bottleneck host memory and coordinator dispatch; hierarchical selection prunes locally per shard, risking loss of globally rare samples across shards
Centralized selection eliminates gradient synchronization; hierarchical selection disables local backpropagation

In distributed active learning, Worker A scores candidate samples using checkpoint step \(t\), while Worker B has already advanced the shared model to step \(t+100\). What consistency challenge arises, and what is the best response?

Worker A encounters deadlock in CUDA streams; disable autograd during scoring
Worker B overwrites Worker A’s local storage; mount the dataset read-only
Worker A’s GPU runs out of memory; reduce batch size to 1
Worker A may produce stale rankings that differ from fresher ones; version checkpoints and choose the score-refresh interval from measured ranking agreement

Explain why performing independent, shard-local coreset pruning on an unstratified, partitioned dataset can cause minority class collapse during distributed training.
Order the execution phases of the distributed coreset-selection example in this chapter: (1) Local EL2N scoring on each shard, (2) Central aggregation and top-\(k\) merge of candidate scores, (3) Broadcast final coreset indices to workers, (4) Shard-local embedding and deduplication.

title: Data Selection
text:
The hospital team in notebook 9.3 could not label every scan, because doing so would have cost $5,000,000, 10× over its budget. Allocating capital between human annotation and accelerator compute is a primary systems decision, and a team under a fixed budget must determine whether the next dollar buys more downstream accuracy as specialist annotations or as additional accelerator hours. Systematic cost modeling establishes the quantitative framework required to navigate these trade-offs, calculating break-even points for active learning pipelines and determining how many training runs are required to amortize custom data curation tooling.


The total cost of training data spans acquisition, labeling, storage retention, and accelerator compute, extending well beyond object-storage invoices: \[
\TotalDataCost= \DataAcquisitionCost+ \DataLabelingCost+ \DataStorageCost+ \DataProcessingCost\] Labeling (\(\DataLabelingCost\)) represents the expenditure that data selection targets most directly, whereas storage (\(\DataStorageCost\)) and processing (\(\DataProcessingCost\)) scale mechanically with retained byte volume and the number of accelerator passes. Table 9 itemizes these four cost components alongside their operational drivers.



Table 9: Total Cost of Training Data: The four cost components span the full data lifecycle. Here \(\DatasetSize\) is the total sample count, \(\LabeledSampleCount\) is the labeled subset, \(\StoredDataVolume\) is stored byte volume, \(\StorageRetentionTime\) is retention time, \(\EpochCount\) is the number of training passes, and \(\OperationsPerSample\) is per-sample training work. The ranges are scenario anchors rather than universal market prices.










Component
Formula
Illustrative Range




\(\DataAcquisitionCost\)
\(\DatasetSize\times \SampleAcquisitionPrice\)
$0.001–$10/sample (web scrape vs. licensed)


\(\DataLabelingCost\)
\(\LabeledSampleCount\times \SampleLabelingPrice\)
$0.01–$200/sample (crowd vs. expert)


\(\DataStorageCost\)
\(\StoredDataVolume\times \StoragePrice\times \StorageRetentionTime\)
$0.02–$0.10/GB/month


\(\DataProcessingCost\)
\(\DatasetSize\times \EpochCount\times \OperationsPerSample\times \FlopPrice\)
Proportional to training FLOPs






The interplay of these four cost terms becomes concrete when evaluating an ImageNet-scale vision model training run.

Napkin Math 9.5: Cost breakdown: ImageNet-scale trainingTable 10 itemizes one illustrative acquisition, labeling, storage, and compute scenario at ImageNet scale. The resulting ratio follows from the stated licensing, annotation, storage, runtime, and compute-cost assumptions; it is not a typical ratio for every supervised workload.



Table 10: Illustrative ImageNet-Scale Cost Breakdown: Itemized acquisition, labeling, storage, and compute costs under the stated scenario assumptions. Each amount follows from the rate shown beside it, using the book’s published crowd-labeling, object-storage, and cloud-GPU rates. Data costs dominate this particular calculation because licensing and annotation are included while the training run itself is short.










Cost Component
Calculation
Amount




Raw data (1.2M images)
Licensed dataset, flat fee
$50,000


Labels (crowd annotation)
1.2M \(\times\) $0.05/label
$60,000


Storage (cloud object store)
150 GB \(\times\) $0.02/GB/month \(\times\) 12 months
$36


Training campaign (30 runs, each 100 epochs in 24 h on 8 A100s)
5,760 GPU-hours \(\times\) $4/GPU-hour
$23,040


Total

$133,076


Data vs. Compute ratio

82.7% data, 17.3% compute






Systems insight: Acquisition and labeling can dwarf compute cost in supervised vision workloads, as they do under these assumptions. The compute figure prices the whole training campaign, not one run: a published model is the survivor of sweeps, restarts, and ablations, and costing a single run would understate compute roughly thirtyfold. Even so, acquisition and labeling remain the larger share. The run count is an assumption like any other, so a complete ROI calculation must state it and price both categories rather than assuming which one dominates.





Data selection techniques insert algorithmic filtering into the training pipeline to reduce downstream costs. However, evaluating sample importance is not free: scoring consumes accelerator cycles, generates host-device memory traffic, or requires engineering custom pipeline stages. Evaluating whether a selection strategy is economically justified requires balancing these upfront overheads against downstream savings through Return on Investment (ROI): \[
\text{ROI} = \frac{\text{Savings} - \text{Investment}}{\text{Investment}} \times 100\%
\]
The balance between investment and savings varies across selection strategies. Table 11 maps the primary cost drivers and benefit mechanisms across four standard techniques; their net return depends on corpus volume, model scale, and existing pipeline infrastructure.



Table 11: ROI Profiles for Data Selection Techniques: The table identifies costs and possible savings. No technique guarantees positive ROI. A training-time claim must satisfy the selection inequality; labeling savings or reusable data investments require their corresponding total-cost comparison at target quality.










Technique
Investment (Cost)
Savings (Benefit)




Deduplication
One-time compute for hashing + infrastructure
Reduced storage and repeated-sample processing


Coreset Selection
Proxy model training + selection compute
Fewer retained samples if target quality and coverage hold


Active Learning
Inference on unlabeled pool + human-in-the-loop latency
Lower labeling demand when query selection transfers


Data Augmentation
CPU/GPU cycles for transforms
Effective dataset size increase without new data acquisition






The profiles in table 11 demonstrate that data savings never come for free. Deduplication requires an upfront investment in hashing or embedding infrastructure, but can pay off across many epochs and runs by eliminating redundant storage and compute. Coreset selection demands training a proxy model to score the dataset; it only breaks even if the compute saved by dropping samples exceeds the cost of that proxy training. Active learning shifts the cost from human labelers to machine inference, generating high ROI when human time is expensive, though it introduces human-in-the-loop latency that can stall automated pipelines. Finally, data augmentation requires zero new data acquisition but shifts the burden to the CPU or GPU, trading compute cycles for effective dataset expansion. In all cases, a technique earns its place only when its specific benefit outweighs its structural investment.



Selection algorithms expend compute and pipeline latency to reduce downstream labeling or training work. The break-even point marks the operating boundary where the financial savings from omitted samples exactly equal the computational and operational overhead of selecting them. If candidate scoring is computationally intensive or candidate pools are massive, a selection policy can easily consume more resources than it recovers.
Suppose labeling costs $10/sample, active learning starts from 1,000 labeled samples ($10,000), issues 100 queries per round at $50 inference cost (the expense of scoring the candidate pool \(\UnlabeledPool\) with the active model), and the random-labeling baseline requires 5,000 samples for target accuracy. If active learning reaches target accuracy with only 2,000 labeled samples, the following comparison reports net savings relative to the stated labels-plus-scoring cost. This calculation includes labels and pool scoring only, assumes both methods reach the same target accuracy, and excludes retraining, engineering, storage, and annotation-delay costs. It reports net savings per dollar of that stated active-learning budget, using a different denominator from the incremental-investment ROI of section 1.13.2: \[\begin{gather*}
\text{Random labeling cost} = \text{5,000} \times \text{\$10/sample} = \text{\$50,000}
\\
\text{Active learning cost} = \text{2,000} \times \text{\$10/sample} + \text{10 rounds} \times \text{\$50} = \text{\$20,500}
\\
\text{ROI} = \frac{\text{\$50,000} - \text{\$20,500}}{\text{\$20,500}}= \text{$143.9\%$}
\end{gather*}\]
Within this labels-plus-scoring boundary, break-even occurs when avoided labeling costs equal selection overhead. A complete dollar comparison must also deduct any additional retraining, engineering, storage, and delay-related expense relative to the random-labeling baseline. When an unlabeled candidate pool \(\UnlabeledPool\) contains millions of uncurated examples, repeatedly scoring it across multiple rounds scales scoring cost with \(|\UnlabeledPool| \times \CandidateScoringCost\), meaning an algorithmic reduction in labeled samples can be erased if proxy inference costs are not carefully bounded.



Static data selection techniques decouple dataset curation from the model training loop. Computational filters such as MinHash deduplication, exact \(\NgramLength\)-gram indexing, or embedding clustering require substantial upfront engineering and preprocessing compute. However, production model development is inherently iterative: hyperparameter search, neural architecture search, ablation studies, and seed sweeps repeatedly train on the identical curated corpus. Evaluating these techniques on a single isolated run misrepresents their economics. Amortized return on investment (ROI) accounts for how upfront curation investments spread across an entire training campaign: \[
\text{Amortized ROI} = \frac{\TrainingRunCount\times \text{Per-Run Savings} - \text{One-Time Investment}}{\text{One-Time Investment}} \times 100\%
\]
Table 12 itemizes the upfront capital and compute expenditures against per-run savings for an illustrative MinHash deduplication pipeline.



Table 12: Deduplication Infrastructure Cost Components: The one-time investment covers engineering effort and initial compute; the per-run savings accrue with every subsequent training run on the deduplicated data.









Component
Cost




Build deduplication pipeline
$50,000 (engineering time)


Compute MinHash signatures (one-time)
$5,000


Per-run savings
$10,000/run






Because the initial infrastructure and signature-generation costs are fixed, each subsequent training run compounds the net financial return. Three operational factors govern whether curation infrastructure reaches break-even:

Repeated training runs: Hyperparameter search, model iterations, and scheduled retraining reuse the same selection infrastructure many times.
Shared datasets: A cleaned or deduplicated corpus can support multiple teams or model architectures.
Broadly reusable techniques: Methods such as deduplication transfer across models, whereas task-specific coresets may not.

Table 13 tracks how amortized return scales with campaign run count under these cost parameters.



Table 13: Amortized ROI over Multiple Training Runs: Under this scenario’s costs and savings, a deduplication pipeline that loses money on its first use becomes profitable when reused across enough runs. Infrastructure investments should be evaluated over their expected lifetime rather than from one use.









Number of Runs
Amortized ROI




1 run
-81.8% (net loss)


5 runs
-9.1% (near break-even)


10 runs
+81.8% (positive)


50 runs
+809.1% (highly profitable)






Deduplication achieves high investment leverage because eliminating redundant sequences reduces host-storage footprint and avoids wasted gradient updates across every downstream architecture. Sample-selection methods conditioned on proxy gradients or uncertainty scores transfer within a model family or between related architectures, but their rankings must be revalidated when the target model, task, or data changes, which narrows their amortization window relative to deduplication. For exploratory or one-off training runs, low-overhead methods like uniform random sampling or basic augmentation may offer better ROI. A static scoring pass can still pay for itself in one run if its measured savings exceed its cost at target quality.



The centrality of self-supervised learning to foundation-model workflows stems directly from cost amortization. A foundation model is a broadly pretrained reusable base model adapted to downstream tasks through fine-tuning. This architecture divides costs into two phases: an expensive upfront pretraining investment executed once on unlabeled data, and lightweight task-specific adaptations reused across many applications (table 14).



Table 14: Illustrative Foundation-Model Amortization: The label and compute ranges are scenario assumptions. They illustrate why reuse can lower marginal task cost when representations transfer, not a universal fine-tuning ratio.











Approach
Labels per Task
Compute per Task
Data Acquisition




Train from scratch
100K–1M labeled
100% full training
Task-specific collection


Fine-tune foundation model
100–1K labeled
1–5% of full training
Reuse pretraining corpus






To illustrate this economic transformation, consider a company building 10 specialized classifiers. Under the scenario assumptions, each task trained from scratch needs 100,000 labels at $1 per label, for $1M across all tasks. The modeled compute burden is 10,000 GPU-hours.
The fine-tuning scenario pays 10,000 GPU-hours once, then assigns 1,000 labels and 50 GPU-hours of compute to each task. Across all 10 tasks, the modeled fine-tuning labels cost $10K.
Assuming both approaches reach the same target quality on every downstream task, labeling cost drops by 100× and per-task marginal compute by 20×. These are consequences of the chosen scenario values, while total compute becomes favorable only after enough downstream tasks amortize pretraining.
The compute-only crossover occurs when enough downstream tasks share the pretraining cost, provided the representations transfer at the required quality. A dollar crossover also depends on labeling savings, compute prices, and other costs that differ between the approaches. The side-by-side bar charts in figure 12 contrast the cost structures across ten downstream tasks: training from scratch expends a constant 1,000 GPU-hours per task (totaling 10,000 GPU-hours), whereas the foundation model approach absorbs a 10,000 GPU-hour pretraining bar upfront but collapses subsequent task fine-tuning to just 50 GPU-hours per bar.














Figure 12: Cost Amortization in Foundation Models: Training from scratch (left) requires 1,000 GPU-hours per task (10,000 GPU-hours total for 10 tasks). The foundation model approach (right) pays 10,000 GPU-hours upfront for pretraining but reduces each subsequent task to just 50 GPU-hours. At 10 tasks the totals are comparable (10,000 GPU-hours vs. 10,500 GPU-hours), but the per-task marginal cost drops by 20×, and the compute-only crossover favoring the foundation model occurs around 10.5 tasks. The plotted 10-task snapshot therefore remains just below that break-even point.




Checkpoint 9.3: Accepting a data intervention
A smaller training pool is one observation in the acceptance decision. Connect the measurements to the constraint the intervention was meant to relieve.

Time savings: Identify the scoring, coordination, and training times needed to compare a selected subset with full-data training at the same target quality.
Cost objective: Explain how an active-learning pipeline could reduce total expenditure even if it takes longer to train, and identify the costs that must enter that comparison.
Coverage: Decide whether unchanged aggregate accuracy is sufficient when a deployment-critical rare slice regresses, and name the additional validation evidence needed. For the disjoint-class allocation in section 1.7.4, explain why reducing \(\CoresetBudget\) below \(\FirstClassCoverageFloor+\SecondClassCoverageFloor\) requires revising the selection plan before training, even if every remaining example has a high score.



With time, labeling, and amortized costs expressed in one accounting, every technique in the chapter can now be priced against the claim it makes. A training-time saving must satisfy the selection inequality, a labeling saving must beat the random-labeling baseline after scoring and any other differing costs, and a reusable investment must recover its one-time cost across the runs or tasks that share it. Pricing each technique separately, however, does not say which one to reach for first when several of them compete for the same budget.

Self-Check: Question

A company invests \(\$30{,}000\) to compute a high-quality coreset. Training on the full dataset costs \(\$10{,}000\) per run, whereas training on the coreset costs \(\$4{,}000\) per run. What is the break-even number of training runs, and what is the ROI after 10 runs?

Break-even is 5 runs, and ROI after 10 runs is \(100\%\)
Break-even is 3 runs, and ROI after 10 runs is \(300\%\)
Break-even is 8 runs, and ROI after 10 runs is \(50\%\)
Break-even is 10 runs, and ROI after 10 runs is \(0\%\)

Using the chapter’s cost model \(C_{\text{total}} = C_{\text{acquire}} + C_{\text{label}} + C_{\text{store}} + C_{\text{process}}\), which scenario best justifies an upstream filtering investment?

Skip filtering so that maximum raw volume reaches training, regardless of downstream processing and labeling cost
Spend \(\$5{,}000\) on automated filtering only if measured avoided labeling, storage, and processing costs exceed that amount while task coverage and target quality still hold
Double human labeling effort to manually review every raw sample before filtering, because filtering cost is always worse than labeling cost
Cut evaluation entirely to offset the cost of training on unfiltered data

Explain why calculating Return on Investment (ROI) for data selection requires tracking engineering implementation and pipeline maintenance costs in addition to raw accelerator compute hours.
True or False: If GPU time costs the same hourly price in both cases, target quality is unchanged, and there are no other cost benefits, then in a production setting where a single model will be trained exactly once (\(N=1\)) with no hyperparameter tuning or future refreshes, spending 50 GPU-hours to compute static EL2N coreset scores that save 30 GPU-hours of training time is an economically sound decision.
The metric defined as \(\text{ROI} = \frac{N \cdot \Delta C_{\text{train}} - C_{\text{select}}}{C_{\text{select}}}\), which measures the net financial or compute return generated by a data selection technique over \(N\) training runs, is known as Return on ____.

title: Data Selection
text:
When labeling budget, redundancy, rare classes, privacy, and convergence speed conflict, systems engineering requires identifying the primary binding constraint. Table 15 collects the three levers with order-of-magnitude ranges drawn from scenarios like those worked in this chapter; each must reduce the cost it targets after counting its overhead and preserving target quality and required coverage. Self-supervised pretraining, which changes the training signal rather than the sample set, enters the decision through the labeling-cost branch of the tree that follows.



Table 15: Three-Stage Data Selection Pipeline: The ranges illustrate possible outcomes rather than portable expectations. Actual gains depend on the dataset, model, selection method, and target metric.

When Applied
Techniques

On-demand

Once the dominant constraint is named, table 16 compares which technique changes that constraint and why. The same mapping recurs across the five lighthouse workloads, because each is bound by a different resource.

Constraint

Lighthouse 9.3: Lighthouse data selectionData selection principles apply to all five lighthouse models, though the dominant constraint determines the technique. Table 17 maps each workload to a priority. Compute-bound ResNet-50 training benefits from coreset selection, while GPT-2/Llama training relies on deduplication and quality filtering to cut the raw tokens it must process. MobileNetV2’s binding constraints, latency and power, apply at inference, where no choice of training data changes the cost of a prediction. The data lever that matters is therefore the one that helps a small model generalize, augmentation matched to its capacity, and the work is validating that the augmentation preserves the invariances the deployment environment requires. DLRM, bound by memory capacity, uses interaction deduplication to cut redundant examples and embedding pruning to shrink massive embedding tables by dropping or rehashing cold IDs. Finally, the tiny Keyword Spotting model is bound as much by a scarce, costly seed set as by its memory budget, and it overcomes that scarcity by using augmentation and synthesis to build robust datasets from minimal seed samples.



Table 17: Data Selection Priorities by Lighthouse: Primary bottleneck and candidate data-selection priority for each lighthouse workload. The pairing suggests a hypothesis to test; the dominant resource constraint alone does not guarantee that a technique pays off.










Lighthouse
Primary Bottleneck
Data Selection Priority




ResNet-50
Compute

GPT-2/Llama
Training compute (tokens \(\times\) FLOPs/token)

MobileNetV2
Latency/Power
Validate augmentation against the target model and deployment invariances


DLRM

Keyword Spotting
Data scarcity (small seed set)
Augmentation and synthesis create datasets from minimal seeds






Across these workloads, data selection functions as a systems optimization tailored to relieve whichever physical resource binds the pipeline.


Both table 16 and the lighthouse mapping assume a single dominant constraint, but real projects face several at once. The triage flowchart in figure 13 therefore routes candidate strategies hierarchically from the root bottleneck (labeling expense, compute limits, or data scarcity) through operational checks on oracle availability, dataset redundancy, teacher or simulator support, and unlabeled-pool size to isolate actionable techniques.






Figure 13: Data Selection Decision Tree: The tree begins with the primary bottleneck (labeling cost, compute cost, or data scarcity) and narrows each branch using available pools, oracles, redundancy, teachers, or simulators. Its leaves identify candidate techniques; projects with multiple binding constraints may require more than one branch.



The tree identifies candidates; an engineering decision must still test their cost and quality. The vision workload in example 9.6 provides a concrete comparison. Its target-model and proxy scorers retain the same fraction of data, but they need not retain the same examples. A cheaper ranking can therefore win the time comparison and lose the deployment-quality comparison.




The vision team’s stated objective is shorter training turnaround at the existing quality target. The full-data baseline takes 277.8 h, and both candidates retain 10 percent of the images. This places the decision in the compute-cost branch. The retained fraction alone does not settle it; selection time and training time to the target must both be included, and the selected data must preserve the required slices.
A different binding constraint would change the comparison. If labels were the limiting expense, fewer annotations could justify additional training time. If controlled sweeps instead diagnosed a shortage of useful tokens, the data-scarcity branch would be relevant even with idle accelerators. Naming the objective determines which saving the candidate must actually deliver.



Both vision candidates require access to the full image pool, a scoring model, and stable sample indices. The proxy additionally needs a ranking that transfers to the target model; its lower execution cost does not establish that prerequisite. Table 18 places these requirements alongside those of the alternative branches.



Table 18: Technique Prerequisites: Each technique carries specific infrastructure and data requirements that must be verified before implementation. A technique with excellent theoretical gains but unmet prerequisites will fail in practice, making this checklist the first step in technique selection.









Technique
Prerequisites




Active Learning
Access to oracle, unlabeled pool, retraining infrastructure


Coreset selection
Proxy model or embedding extractor, full dataset accessible


Curriculum Learning
Difficulty scoring method, pacing schedule


Semi-Supervised
Some labeled data, unlabeled data from same distribution


Self-Supervised
Large unlabeled corpus, pretraining compute budget


Augmentation
Domain knowledge of invariances, augmentation library


Synthetic Generation
Generative model or simulator, domain gap mitigation









For the stated vision scenario, target-model scoring plus subset training takes 30.6 h (Option A), while proxy scoring plus subset training takes 28.3 h (Option B). These figures evaluate the marginal scoring pass using existing checkpoints. Both options beat the full-data baseline in the cost model. The proxy reduces only the scoring term; the retained training work is identical.
Suppose pilot validation in this hypothetical decision confirms that both runs reach the aggregate target under the modeled schedule, but only Option A meets every deployment-critical slice threshold. Option B regresses on a rare class. Option A is then the acceptable choice despite its more expensive scoring pass, saving 247.2 h against the baseline. Option B remains a candidate for repair, not deployment: enforce the coverage floor from section 1.7.4, rescore or enlarge the subset as needed, and repeat the time-to-quality comparison. Additional examples or passes change its cost, so the original proxy saving cannot simply be carried forward. If both candidates passed all quality gates at the stated times, Option B would win this time comparison.
A time saving must still justify any engineering investment. If the proxy checkpoint is not pre-existing and its training must be charged entirely to a single run rather than amortized across a campaign (section 1.13.4), that preparatory training will erase Option B’s modest time advantage over Option A. Section 1.13.2 prices that investment, and section 1.13.4 spreads one-time costs across the planned experiments \(\TrainingRunCount\). Reusing the proxy is economically useful only while its ranking continues to pass the same quality checks.



Data selection techniques are not mutually exclusive, but combining them does not guarantee additive gains. A representative workflow deduplicates the raw corpus, applies a coverage-aware coreset filter, orders retained batches through an empirical curriculum, and applies runtime augmentations during batch collation. Pretrained representations alter the baseline trajectory further. Every additional stage must justify its compute overhead, because cascading filters frequently discard overlapping subsets while their scoring latencies accumulate.
Stages can compound efficiency gains when their effects do not overlap and their overhead remains small; combined savings must be measured rather than assumed.
A choice made at the data layer does not stay there. This decision process prices a technique by its own scoring cost and the training work it removes, but a smaller or reordered corpus also changes what the model learns to represent, which hardware resource binds once compute pressure falls, and how much synchronization a multi-accelerator run performs. A selection that looks optimal in isolation can therefore move cost into compression, the input pipeline, or communication, so the chosen strategy must be checked against the layers it feeds.

title: Data Selection
text:
Halving a training corpus halves the forward and backward passes, yet the resulting model may be no cheaper to compress or serve, and a selection policy that balanced work on one accelerator can leave eight workers idle at a synchronization barrier. Real ML systems combine data selection with model-level efficiency, machine-level throughput, and distributed training, and these optimizations amplify or undermine each other in ways no single layer reveals.
In the D·A·M taxonomy, data selection operates on the data dimension to change the examples processed and the learning signal they provide. Yet execution time under the iron law of ML systems depends on how input pruning alters the algorithm (model representations, loss landscapes, and compressibility) and the machine (memory bandwidth, kernel arithmetic intensity, and inter-accelerator communication). These cross-layer interactions can amplify efficiency gains across the stack or introduce unexpected bottlenecks that negate upstream savings. System efficiency requires co-designing data curation alongside model compression and hardware scheduling rather than optimizing each component in isolation.


Model-level efficiency reduces parameter counts and arithmetic operations in the trained network through post-training weight pruning, lower-precision representation, and distillation. The composition of the training corpus shapes internal representations, altering how susceptible the resulting network is to downstream compression. However, arithmetic operation reductions do not automatically reduce serving latency; unless the target execution substrate and runtime kernels support the resulting sparsity or precision patterns, wall-clock inference time can remain unchanged despite substantial parameter elimination (Hoefler et al. 2021).

Hoefler, Torsten, Dan Alistarh, Tal Ben-Nun, Nikoli Dryden, and Alexandra Peste. 2021. “Sparsity in Deep Learning: Pruning and Growth for Efficient Inference and Training in Neural Networks.” Journal of Machine Learning Research 22 (241): 1–124.

↪ Why accelerators turn structured sparsity patterns into wall-clock speedup while unstructured sparsity rarely pays off is developed in N:M structured sparsity mechanics.

This cross-layer interaction traces back to how networks allocate capacity during training. A model trained on an uncurated, repetitive corpus frequently assigns representational capacity to redundant features that post-training pruning subsequently discards, wasting the training compute expended to learn them. Conversely, training on a curated corpus of diverse, informative examples can produce more compact internal representations from the start. That initial efficiency can simplify subsequent pruning or quantization, although this remains an empirical hypothesis to verify through profiling rather than an invariant property of every selected dataset. Data selection and model compression remain distinct levers within the D·A·M taxonomy: data selection reduces training work and shapes learned representations, whereas model compression shrinks the trained deployment artifact. Their combined impact must be measured by benchmarking serving latency and task accuracy directly rather than assuming that an upstream dataset reduction automatically guarantees downstream model efficiency.


↪ Co-designing post-training pruning and quantization under the silicon contract is developed in Optimization Framework.



While model-level efficiency determines the computational work remaining after training, machine-level throughput determines how efficiently hardware executes the training loop itself. Under the iron law of ML systems, training runtime depends on whether execution is bound by input data transfer (\(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\)), arithmetic execution (\(\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)\)), or scheduling latency (\(\Latency\)). Pruning samples reduces total floating-point operations, but non-uniform sampling and dynamic filtering alter data-loader access patterns and expose new hardware limits. Table 19 outlines how selection strategies shift the dominant system bottleneck.



Table 19: Diagnosing Bottlenecks after Data Selection: Dataset and access-pattern changes can expose a different bottleneck, but dataset size alone does not determine the limiting resource. Re-profile the pipeline and match the response to the measured condition.










Observed Condition
Possible Bottleneck
Candidate Response




Input rate below accelerator demand
Storage, decode, or host link
Sharding, prefetching, parallel decode


Low-intensity training kernels
Accelerator memory bandwidth
Fusion, reduced traffic, lower precision


Dynamic scoring dominates iteration
Selection compute or index I/O
Proxy models, cached scores or embeddings






Data selection can therefore shift the hardware execution regime. A technique that reduces sample count by 80 percent may relieve pressure on the accelerator’s arithmetic units, only to expose random-access storage latency, host-to-device PCIe bandwidth, or scoring overhead as the new critical path. Relieving that subsequent bottleneck requires matching the engineering response to the active constraint: caching selection scores, fusing memory-bound operations, or pre-staging contiguous shards into host memory before accelerator dispatch. Before applying aggressive data reduction, engineers must profile the full pipeline to verify which bottleneck actually binds execution.



The hardware bottleneck analysis in section 1.15.2 focuses on execution on a single accelerator. When training scales to several accelerators in one node (two to eight devices in this book’s scope), data selection alters both communication volume and memory synchronization.
In data-parallel training across accelerators, each device computes forward and backward passes on a local micro-batch before synchronizing parameter gradients via an all-reduce collective. With per-device batch size and epoch count held fixed, pruning the training corpus reduces the total number of parameter updates across a run, directly eliminating collective communication rounds over PCIe or NVLink interconnects. Furthermore, smaller per-worker shards can increase the proportion of the dataset that fits into local host RAM or accelerator cache, reducing repetitive storage streaming.
These communication savings must be balanced against the coordination overhead analyzed in section 1.12. While gradient synchronization exploits dedicated high-bandwidth interconnects, dynamic sample scoring and index exchanges often route through host memory and CPU dispatch threads. A selection policy that scales efficiently on a single accelerator can introduce serialization bottlenecks or imbalanced shard workloads when partitioned across eight parallel workers, stalling devices at synchronization barriers and eroding the compute time saved by pruning.



Pairwise interactions expose localized bottlenecks, but production deployments execute these techniques as an integrated pipeline. Figure 14 diagrams the complete optimization stack across two stages, tracing how data selection and training curate raw inputs into a trained model before post-training compression and hardware acceleration deploy the artifact to production. Every stage along this end-to-end path amplifies or attenuates downstream efficiency.






Figure 14: The Optimization Stack: Data artifacts flow through selection and training before the resulting model enters compression and deployment. Upstream changes propagate quality and cost effects downstream, but reducing training data does not automatically simplify the model or deployment hardware.



Tracing artifacts through the pipeline in figure 14 reveals why data selection occupies an asymmetric position at the head of the optimization stack: pruning raw inputs reduces upstream training FLOPs, but does not automatically shrink parameter footprint, improve quantization headroom, or relax serving latency constraints in the downstream compression and hardware stages. Each downstream tier inherits both the computational savings and any representational deficits created upstream; an aggressive filter that discards rare but critical edge cases can force downstream engineers to train longer or abandon aggressive quantization to preserve task accuracy. The same asymmetry underlies the recurrent failure modes that follow, which show how data selection breaks down in production and how systems engineers diagnose them before launching expensive training runs.

title: Data Selection
text:
Data selection involves counterintuitive diminishing returns that contradict the “more is better” intuition from traditional machine learning. The following errors fall into three groups: conceptual fallacies about what data selection can achieve, implementation pitfalls that arise when correct strategies meet engineering realities, and transfer errors that occur when benchmark results are applied uncritically to new domains.

Fallacy: Data is the new oil, so more is always better.
More data does not imply proportional accuracy gains because learning curves exhibit power-law diminishing returns. Test loss diminishes sub-linearly with dataset size (\(\LossFunction(\DatasetSize) \propto \DataScalingLossFactor\) for a fitted exponent \(\DataScalingExponent\)), meaning each successive error reduction demands a multiplicatively larger corpus. In an illustrative learning-curve scenario, scaling a dataset tenfold from 1M to 10M samples yields only 4 percentage points of accuracy gain. In systems terms, that 10\(\times\) volume expansion requires a tenfold increase in storage I/O, host-to-device transfers, and accelerator FLOPs, expending massive cluster energy to process redundant, low-gradient examples that contribute negligible information to parameter updates. Engineering teams must measure the empirical learning curve and marginal compute cost of their specific workload rather than assuming uncurated data scaling will deliver proportional value.


Pitfall: Replacing real-data validation with synthetic-only training data.
Engineers often assume generative models can replace empirical data collection with inexhaustible synthetic samples at zero marginal acquisition cost. Synthetic-only training faces two primary failure modes. First, as examined in section 1.10.3, synthetic data can differ from the deployment distribution, allowing a model to learn features that fail to transfer (figure 9). The resulting effect on classification must be checked with real-data labels; marginal feature densities alone do not determine the decision boundary. Second, recursive training on model-generated data can trigger model collapse (Shumailov et al. 2024). Feeding synthetic outputs back into subsequent training cycles progressively erodes distribution tails: in this scenario, evaluation accuracy degrades from 95 percent to 78 percent across five recursive generations, suffering a 17 percentage-point collapse. Although synthetic augmentation provides valuable coverage for scarce tail classes, synthetic mixtures must always be validated and anchored against curated real-world distributions.




Illustrative model collapse: accuracy erodes with each recursive synthetic generation.

Fallacy: Data selection is merely data cleaning.
Engineers often conflate data quality (correcting malformed schemas, corrupted labels, and noisy tokens) with data value under a specific training procedure. A dataset can be completely clean, correctly labeled, and grammatically impeccable, yet mathematically redundant: if the model has already minimized loss on a feature cluster, processing additional identical samples yields zero gradient signal while burning memory bandwidth and accelerator FLOPs. Data cleaning addresses intrinsic data defects, whereas data selection actively maximizes the learning return per FLOP spent. By selecting examples for task-relevant information and coverage (figure 6; see algorithmic objectives in section 1.7.4), coreset algorithms can elevate the ICR, as in the worked coreset scenario of notebook 9.1, where the selected subset reached 1.8× higher ICR. Cleaning ensures data correctness; selection optimizes training compute efficiency.


Pitfall: Treating data selection as a budget-only tactic.
Practitioners often view data selection as a technique reserved for resource-constrained edge deployments or budget-limited teams, assuming that frontier foundation models can simply brute-force convergence by scaling cluster size. In reality, large-scale training is bounded by the public data wall charted in figure 1, where exponential token consumption rapidly converges toward the finite ceiling of high-quality human text stock. Furthermore, the economic return of selection scales with cluster expenditure: a 10 percent efficiency gain on a $100M frontier training run saves $10M under our baseline assumptions. When selection infrastructure, pre-computed importance scores, and cached embeddings are amortized across repeated training runs and downstream adaptations (section 1.13.4), intelligent filtering becomes a foundational economic lever for large-scale engineering systems.


Fallacy: Selection overhead is too small to change training economics.
A data selection strategy claiming a training-time saving must spend less time scoring and filtering than it saves in training at matched quality. As formalized by the selection inequality in equation 2, that time-saving claim requires \(\SelectionTime+ \TrainingTime(\SubsetDatasetSize) < \TrainingTime(\FullDatasetSize)\). Consider a baseline training run requiring 8 hours, where training on an optimized coreset takes 2-hour. If a complex selection algorithm requires 10 hours to compute sample importance, the selection step alone consumes 5× the duration of the accelerated training run and exceeds the full training baseline itself, generating a net wall-clock penalty. Cached embeddings or lightweight proxy networks can reduce scoring time enough to satisfy equation 2, provided selection quality transfers. In our illustrative comparison, proxy-based EL2N scoring completes in 30 minutes, just 6.2 percent of the full-training baseline, satisfying the inequality and delivering tangible wall-clock savings.


Pitfall: Pruning rare classes into oblivion.
Standard selection objectives minimize aggregate empirical loss, giving tail slices minimal influence over global sampling probabilities. In a 1M dataset where rare classes comprise 0.1 percent of the data (1,000 examples), an unstratified 10 percent coreset retains only 100 rare-class examples in expectation, far below the illustrative 150-sample retention floor assumed here. An appropriate floor must be validated from task-specific learning curves and critical-slice performance. While importance sampling can theoretically compensate by weighting loss contributions by inverse selection probabilities, extreme sampling weights inflate gradient variance. This gradient variance destabilizes optimizer momentum trajectories, forcing smaller learning rates that slow cluster convergence. As recommended in section 1.7.4, production coreset pipelines must enforce hard stratification floors per class or deployment-critical slice before optimizing the remaining selection budget.


Fallacy: Deduplicating training data is enough to make evaluation reliable.
Engineers often assume that eliminating duplicate sequences within the training partition prevents memorization and ensures clean evaluation. However, web-scale ingestion pipelines scrape training, validation, and benchmark test splits from common web crawls, introducing silent cross-split leakage. When evaluation sets contain duplicates or near-duplicates of training documents, validation metrics measure memorization rather than out-of-distribution generalization. A comprehensive deduplication study revealed that train-test overlap affects over 4 percent of validation examples across standard language-modeling benchmarks (Lee et al. 2022). Deduplicating training data in isolation leaves this evaluation contamination untouched. Rigorous pipeline hygiene requires cross-partition deduplication using \(\NgramLength\)-gram matching or MinHash LSH (section 1.7.2), calibrating near-duplicate similarity thresholds against the declared split policy. For a frozen evaluation set, remove overlapping training records while preserving the evaluation set and its provenance; rebuilding evaluation splits requires a new documented benchmark version.

Lee, Katherine, Daphne Ippolito, Andrew Nystrom, Chiyuan Zhang, Douglas Eck, Chris Callison-Burch, and Nicholas Carlini. 2022. “Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better.” Proceedings of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), 8424–45. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2022.acl-long.577.


Pitfall: Active learning without considering annotation latency.
Theoretical formulations of active learning assume a zero-latency oracle that labels queried samples instantaneously, allowing the model to incorporate new gradients immediately before selecting the subsequent query batch. In production systems, human annotation queues introduce substantial turnaround delays, such as the illustrative 14-day latency between sample dispatch and label return assumed here. This latency breaks the active learning feedback loop in two ways. If accelerator clusters halt training while awaiting labels, expensive hardware sits idle, destroying cluster compute utilization. Conversely, if training continues asynchronously on background data while annotations are pending, model weights drift across training steps; by the time the labels arrive, the uncertainty scores that justified querying those samples are obsolete. Furthermore, dispatching massive batches to amortize labeling turnaround causes information redundancy within the query batch unless diversity penalties are applied. The return on investment for active learning depends on both label pricing and the ratio of annotation turnaround latency to the model retraining cycle.


Fallacy: If a technique works on ImageNet, it will work on my dataset.
Data-selection pruning ratios derived from standard vision benchmarks cannot be blindly transferred to domain-specific workloads. Benchmark datasets like CIFAR-10 and ImageNet exhibit high semantic redundancy across canonical object classes, allowing aggressive coreset pruning (often 30 to 50 percent) without measurable accuracy degradation. In contrast, specialized domains such as histopathology, satellite remote sensing, or industrial defect detection exhibit heavy-tailed feature distributions where safety-critical patterns appear in only a few rare samples. Discarding 50 percent of examples based on an ImageNet heuristic can eliminate the sole boundary examples that separate subtle pathologies, triggering catastrophic domain degradation. Furthermore, geometric coreset algorithms rely on embedding spaces: if the feature extractor was pretrained on natural images, its representations lack the inductive bias needed to resolve fine-grained domain distinctions. Engineering teams must measure the redundancy of their own data, evaluate representations against target downstream tasks, and validate retention fractions across safety-critical slices before applying pruning.


Pitfall: Optimizing data selection metrics instead of deployment metrics.
Selection algorithms optimize surrogate objectives such as overall loss reduction, area under the learning curve (AULC), or performance-per-data (PPD, section 1.6.1), each evaluated as an aggregate scalar over the validation corpus. A selection policy retaining a 10 percent coreset can achieve superior aggregate PPD by prioritizing dense clusters of common, easy samples that accelerate average convergence, while discarding ambiguous edge cases and rare slices. In production, however, system failures occur on tail slices, edge cases, and protected sub-populations rather than dataset averages. Maximizing aggregate selection efficiency without subgroup constraints produces models that pass global validation gates but fail catastrophically in deployment. As mandated by the measurement framework in section 1.6, selection policies must be evaluated using stratified, slice-level benchmarks that enforce coverage across demographic groups, rare categories, and operational edge cases, even when doing so slightly lowers average PPD.


Self-Check: Question

Violating the smoothness assumption in semi-supervised consistency regularization

title: Data Selection
text:
Data selection treats training volume as an engineering variable rather than an unchangeable constraint. Where traditional machine learning asks how many samples are required to reach target accuracy, systems engineering optimizes total cost across compute, storage, labeling, energy, and wall-clock time. Curated datasets can match or outperform massive uncurated corpora because marginal learning signal varies by orders of magnitude across raw examples. Within the optimization ordering, selection addresses the first question: which examples are worth processing, prioritizing, or generating for the target task.
This systems perspective becomes actionable through three quantitative tools: the ICR, the selection inequality, and the total data cost model. The information-compute ratio quantifies learning gained per floating-point operation, providing a proxy for sample value that must be evaluated alongside coverage and target quality. The selection inequality tests a training-time claim by requiring scoring plus subset training to take less time than full-data training at matched quality. Together with return-on-investment and break-even analysis, these formulations determine whether a proposed selection mechanism saves resources or merely shifts expenditure between stages.
The three complementary intervention points address different parts of this cost equation: static pruning removes redundancy before training through coreset selection and deduplication; dynamic selection prioritizes informative examples during training through curriculum and active learning; and synthetic generation creates data where none exists through augmentation, simulation, and distillation. Together, these strategies address the data wall, the structural asymmetry between rapidly growing compute capacity and slowly growing high-quality data.
Self-supervised learning sits beside these levers rather than within them. Pretraining moves the bulk of representation learning into an unannotated upstream phase, so downstream tasks can reach target quality with far fewer task-specific labels; the worked amortization scenario assumes 100× fewer. The compute-only crossover occurs at roughly 10.5 tasks under the scenario assumptions. Labeling savings enter a separate dollar comparison that also requires compute prices and other differing costs.
In production, the difficult part is rarely the scoring rule itself. It is keeping selection from becoming the next bottleneck. Proxy models and cached embeddings bound scoring time, shard-based loaders keep storage access sequential, and data echoing recovers accelerator cycles when ingestion lags. Controlled model-size and data sweeps diagnose whether a run is data-limited or compute-limited in the first place, and PPD, AULC, and DCR then show whether a reduction bought what it promised at the binding resource.

Key Takeaways: Curate, do not accumulate

Selection optimizes system cost: The objective is minimizing total cost across compute, storage, labeling, and energy rather than reducing sample counts alone. The information-compute ratio measures learning gained per FLOP spent; total-cost accounting and pipeline measurements establish whether that gain serves the system objective.
Start with deduplication: Exact deduplication is often the lowest-risk first technique because it removes repeated bytes without a learned scoring pass. Apply near-duplicate and semantic deduplication only after validating thresholds against downstream quality metrics.
Training-time savings must exceed selection overhead: At matched quality, \(\SelectionTime+ \TrainingTime(\SubsetDatasetSize) < \TrainingTime(\FullDatasetSize)\). Lightweight proxy models and cached embeddings keep \(\SelectionTime\) low, whereas unoptimized selection algorithms can consume all the compute they save.
Dynamic selection adapts the data diet: Curriculum learning changes presentation order, while active learning changes which samples receive labels. Either improves efficiency when its scoring rule, coverage, and refresh overhead are validated.
Self-supervised pretraining can amortize adaptation cost: Pretraining once and fine-tuning many times spreads pretraining cost across downstream tasks. The worked scenario assumes a 100× label reduction and a 20× marginal-compute reduction; realized savings depend on transfer quality and reuse.
Synthetic data is a supplement, not a replacement: Synthetic samples augment scarce tail cases effectively, but cannot substitute entirely for empirical data. Unanchored synthetic training introduces domain-gap degradation, and recursive synthetic loops trigger catastrophic model collapse.
Validated workload reduction compounds downstream: When selection safely eliminates examples or tokens without adding compensating steps, that work never reaches later model or machine optimizations. Dynamic scoring and synthesis add their own costs, so the combined saving must be measured rather than assumed.



The governing invariant of data selection is that training examples provide vastly unequal marginal learning signal per byte transferred and FLOP executed. Within the D·A·M taxonomy, selection operates at the head of the system: every redundant sample or uninformative token safely eliminated directly reduces operation count (\(\Operations\)) in the iron law of ML systems (principle \(\ref{pri-iron-law}\)) and can avoid downstream training reads. Scoring may still read the entire pool, and shard streaming may read discarded records, so reductions in data volume (\(\DataVolume\)) must count scoring and shard-read traffic separately. When fewer examples are actually processed and selection overhead satisfies the time-saving comparison at matched quality, that upstream reduction removes work before downstream compression or hardware acceleration ever sees it. Model-based scoring offers a way to invest additional compute in selection, consistent with the bitter lesson, but a stronger scorer earns that investment only if its improved rankings save more downstream work than it costs. The Pareto frontier (principle \(\ref{pri-pareto-frontier}\)) applies upstream of the model as well. Each retained fraction is an operating point that trades coverage and rare-slice accuracy against compute, and no single fraction is optimal for every workload.

What’s Next: From data to algorithmsData selection changes what the system learns from, and its savings end where the trained model begins. A model trained on a carefully curated subset has the same parameter count, numerical precision, and memory footprint as one trained on the full corpus, so it can still overflow a phone’s memory or leave inference bound by memory bandwidth. Model Compression turns to how the model represents what it has learned. It starts from the deployment envelope the model must fit and renegotiates three things against it: the model’s structure through pruning and distillation, its numerical precision through quantization, and the way the remaining operations map onto the hardware that executes them.

title: Data Selection
text:
Self-Check: Answer

In an ML infrastructure scaling scenario where available GPU compute grows by approximately \(10\times\) every 3 years while high-quality web data grows by only \(2\times\) every 5 years, what primary systems regime emerges, and what is the appropriate systems response?

A compute-rich, data-constrained Data Wall regime where intelligent data selection and curation must maximize the learning signal extracted per token
A memory bandwidth-bound regime where model parallel sharding must replace data parallelism across all training clusters
An I/O ingestion bottleneck where disk read bandwidth must be quadrupled to keep GPUs saturated
A compute-starved regime where synthetic data generation should be eliminated to avoid wasting accelerator cycles

Answer: The correct answer is A. Compute throughput growing faster than accessible high-quality human data creates a compute-to-data imbalance known as the Data Wall. In this regime, additional raw compute yields diminishing returns on uncurated corpora, making data selection essential to maximize the Information-Compute Ratio (ICR). Shifting model parallelism addresses parameter memory limits rather than data scarcity, scaling disk bandwidth solves I/O stalls rather than token information quality, and eliminating synthetic generation ignores a key strategy for expanding scarce data pools.
Learning Objective: Analyze the systems implications of the compute-to-data scaling asymmetry and diagnose the Data Wall regime.
Under the illustrative analytical model where dataset information content scales as \(\mathcal{I}(D) \propto \log D\) and training compute scales linearly as \(O = O_{\text{sample}} \cdot D\), how does the marginal Information-Compute Ratio \(\mathrm{ICR}(D)\) scale with dataset size \(D\)?

It remains constant at \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) because additional compute scales proportionally with dataset size
It decays as \(\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{1}{O_{\text{sample}}D}\right)\), so under this illustrative model additional data eventually adds compute faster than marginal information
It grows logarithmically as \(\mathcal{O}(\log D / O_{\text{sample}})\) due to power-law parameter scaling
It decays exponentially as \(\mathcal{O}(\exp(-D))\) once the training corpus exceeds accelerator memory capacity

Answer: The correct answer is B. Under the chapter’s illustrative model, \(d\mathcal{I}/dD \propto 1/D\) and \(dO/dD = O_{\text{sample}}\), so their ratio is \(\mathrm{ICR}(D) \approx 1/(O_{\text{sample}}D)\). This captures diminishing marginal learning signal under the stated log-information and linear-compute assumptions. A constant or growing answer ignores the derivative of \(\log D\), while the exponential-decay choice introduces a memory-capacity mechanism that is not part of this model.
Learning Objective: Calculate the scaling behavior of the Information-Compute Ratio under the section’s illustrative logarithmic-information model.
Explain why a dataset where \(100\%\) of the sample labels are verifiably correct can still exhibit a very low Information-Compute Ratio (ICR).
Answer: Label correctness measures ground-truth accuracy, whereas ICR measures evaluation gain per unit of training compute over a stated interval. A dataset of completely correct examples will have near-zero ICR if the samples are redundant, easily classified by the current model state, or already mastered, because processing them consumes forward and backward FLOPs without producing a corresponding evaluation gain; parameter updates alone do not establish learning value.
Learning Objective: Compare data correctness with data value in the Information-Compute Ratio framework.
True or False: Doubling the amount of raw, deduplicated web data will always double the total information learned by the model.

Order the following stages as they are presented in this chapter’s conceptual map of the data-selection pipeline: (1) Dynamic Selection, (2) Static Pruning, (3) Synthetic Data Generation.

The sequence is a conceptual map rather than a mandatory runtime chronology, because synthetic data can also be created earlier and then pruned or selected before final training.
Learning Objective: Identify the chapter’s conceptual ordering of the three main data-selection intervention points.

Herding on Gaussian-distributed features, because it completely avoids computing feature representations

Why is Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) with MinHash preferred over exhaustive pairwise Jaccard similarity comparison for large-scale text deduplication?

MinHash LSH guarantees \(100\%\) precision in detecting semantic paraphrases across different natural languages
MinHash eliminates the need to tokenize or shingle input documents before hashing
Exhaustive pairwise Jaccard comparison requires training a deep neural network, whereas LSH is purely rule-based
Exhaustive pairwise comparison requires \(\mathcal{O}(D^2)\) document comparisons, whereas MinHash LSH hashes compact signatures into sublinear candidate collision buckets

Answer: The correct answer is D. Comparing all pairs in a dataset of \(D\) documents requires \(\mathcal{O}(D^2)\) comparisons, which is computationally intractable for web-scale datasets (\(D \ge 10^7\)). MinHash compresses documents into fixed-size sketches where collision probability equals Jaccard similarity, and LSH bands these sketches into hash buckets so only candidate pairs colliding in a bucket are compared. MinHash LSH does not detect cross-lingual semantic paraphrases, still requires shingling/tokenization, and pairwise Jaccard comparison is an exact set operation rather than a deep learning method.
Learning Objective: Analyze the computational scaling benefits of MinHash and Locality-Sensitive Hashing for web-scale deduplication.
In recommendation systems like DLRM where embedding tables consume terabytes of memory, how does interaction deduplication differ in systems impact from cold embedding pruning?
Answer: Interaction deduplication removes repeated user-item examples, so under a fixed epoch count and fixed per-sample work it means fewer examples are actually processed, reducing total traffic and total training work. Cold-ID pruning or reindexing reduces allocated embedding capacity only when IDs disappear from the table design, but that alone does not guarantee lower realized memory traffic or bandwidth cost. A useful deployment check is whether removing rare IDs hurts recommendation quality on sparse users or items.
Learning Objective: Compare how interaction deduplication and cold-ID pruning affect training work, embedding capacity, and quality risk in recommendation systems.
True or False: Removing near-duplicate documents with MinHash LSH always improves model accuracy because duplicate data has zero statistical value in all training regimes.
Answer: False. While deduplication reduces redundant computation and memorization risk, in some domains duplicate frequency reflects natural empirical data distributions or intentional weighting. Aggressive deduplication with miscalibrated thresholds can prune legitimate variations or distort class priors, necessitating empirical validation on downstream accuracy.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the systems and statistical trade-offs of aggressive near-duplicate filtering.

Least-confidence sampling, because it strictly selects the lowest top-1 probability prediction

Random undersampling of the entire unlabeled pool to reduce dataset size before scoring
Uniform zero-shot pseudo-labeling without confidence thresholds

Answer: The correct answer is B. Pure uncertainty sampling often suffers from sampling bias by selecting clustered points near a single ambiguous boundary region. Explain the mechanism of confirmation bias in semi-supervised pseudo-labeling, and specify how confidence thresholding mitigates it.
Answer: Confirmation bias arises when the model trains on its own wrong pseudo-labels and reinforces those mistakes in later rounds. A high confidence threshold filters out low-confidence predictions, but confidently wrong pseudo-labels can still survive, so thresholding is only a partial defense. The practical check is to compare the model’s confidence against held-out labeled validation evidence before trusting the expanded training set.
Learning Objective: Explain confirmation bias in pseudo-labeling and evaluate what confidence thresholding can and cannot fix.

The key caveat is that closeness in raw input space alone is not enough—rotations, crops, or other perturbations can change the true label on some tasks.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the task-dependent assumption behind consistency regularization.

How does the MoCo (Momentum Contrast) framework reduce the hardware and memory constraints of contrastive self-supervised learning compared to naive SimCLR?

By replacing convolutional backbones with rule-based lookup tables to avoid backpropagation
By requiring fully supervised class labels to filter out false negative pairs
By using a dynamic queue of negative keys and a slowly updating momentum encoder, decoupling negative dictionary size from mini-batch size
By computing exact pairwise Jaccard similarities on raw byte sequences rather than latent embeddings

Answer: The correct answer is C. Contrastive learning requires large sets of negative examples for effective representation learning. While SimCLR scales the mini-batch size (requiring massive GPU memory across many accelerators, e.g. batch size 4096), MoCo decouples the dictionary size from the mini-batch size by maintaining a memory queue of negative keys updated with a momentum-averaged teacher encoder. MoCo still uses neural backbones and backpropagation, operates in an unsupervised manner without human labels, and computes cosine similarities in latent space rather than raw byte Jaccard comparisons.
Learning Objective: Compare contrastive self-supervised learning architectures and their memory-compute scaling trade-offs.
What is the systems-level ‘homogenization risk’ (or blast radius) of pretraining a shared foundation model on an uncurated dataset?
Answer: A shared base model can propagate the same upstream defect into many downstream tasks, so a bad pretraining-data choice has a much larger blast radius than in train-from-scratch workflows. For example, a memorized private pattern or systematic bias in the base model may affect many adaptations built on top of it. The actual impact is not universal, because downstream fine-tuning and validation can reduce or expose some defects.
Learning Objective: Analyze why pretraining-data defects in a shared foundation model can affect many downstream adaptations.
True or False: Because self-supervised pretraining learns general representations from unlabeled data, it completely eliminates the need for data selection or quality filtering during the pretraining stage.

Learning Objective: Explain the concept and role of pretext tasks in self-supervised learning.

A failure of the I/O storage subsystem to deliver synthetic batches at line rate

In knowledge distillation, what is the primary role of the temperature parameter \(T\) when computing soft targets from a teacher model’s logits \(z_i\) (\(p_i = \frac{\exp(z_i / T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j / T)}\))?

To soften the output probability distribution, exposing the relative probability structure (‘dark knowledge’) over non-target classes to the student
To clamp gradients to prevent numerical overflow in the student’s backward pass
To dynamically increase learning rate when the student loss plateaus
To randomly drop connections in the student network like dropout

Answer: The correct answer is A. Higher temperature \(T > 1\) softens the softmax distribution over logits, revealing the rich relative similarities between incorrect classes (the teacher’s ‘dark knowledge’) that are hidden by standard hard argmax or sharp low-temperature one-hot predictions. Why do naive random sample lookups across non-contiguous indices in large un-sharded dataset files severely degrade I/O throughput on storage hardware, and how do shuffle buffers mitigate this?

Random lookups bypass host CPU caches, forcing floating-point registers to re-encode all labels
Random lookups violate PCIe parity checks, causing GPU kernel timeouts during backward passes
Random lookups trigger hash collisions in the Python garbage collector, halting dataloading threads
Random 4 KB reads achieve only a tiny fraction of peak sequential storage bandwidth due to IOPS limits, whereas shuffle buffers read large sequential chunks and randomize locally in memory

Answer: The correct answer is D. Storage devices (HDDs, SATA SSDs, NVMe SSDs, and cloud object stores) provide peak throughput under large, contiguous sequential reads. Shuffle buffers co-design data loading by reading large sequential shards into host RAM and performing pseudo-random shuffling locally within memory, preserving peak sequential disk bandwidth. Contrast upstream data echoing (echoing before data augmentation) with downstream data echoing (echoing after augmentation) in terms of computational overhead and sample diversity.

Downstream echoing amortizes earlier work through augmentation, but repeats the same already-augmented tensors rather than creating new views. The practical implication is to place the echo point after the bottleneck stage whose work you want to amortize, then check whether the repeated data still preserves target quality.
