\(\mathcal{O}(\BatchSize\times \SequenceLength\times \HiddenDimension)\)









A tensor is a view over an underlying storage buffer, described by shape, stride, dtype, and offset metadata. Its shape specifies the dimensions of the tensor (for example, (3, 4)), while its stride defines the number of elements to skip in memory to move to the next element along each dimension. Only contiguous tensors lay their logical elements out as one adjacent block.
Operations like transpose() or view() often just change the strides, not the data in memory. This is fast (\(\mathcal{O}(1)\)) but can lead to noncontiguous tensors that fail in kernels requiring contiguous data. In such cases, calling contiguous() on a tensor of \(\TensorElementCount\) elements forces an \(\mathcal{O}(\TensorElementCount)\) memory copy that can dominate runtime if triggered repeatedly inside a loop.



Broadcasting allows arithmetic operations on tensors of different shapes by comparing dimensions from right to left. Two dimensions are compatible when they are equal or when one of them is 1.
Figure 1 diagrams this virtual expansion across complementary singleton dimensions, adding a \((3, 1)\) column tensor (\(\BroadcastColumnTensor\)) to a \((1, 4)\) row tensor (\(\BroadcastRowTensor\)) to generate a \((3, 4)\) matrix of pairwise sums (\(\BroadcastColumnElement_i + \BroadcastRowElement_j\)). Dashed cell boundaries mark result elements whose operands are read through stride-0 views, so neither input is copied; only the \((3, 4)\) output is allocated, and hardware repeatedly accesses identical input buffer addresses.






Figure 1: Tensor Broadcasting Rules: A (3,1) column and a (1,4) row broadcast across complementary dimensions, producing the pairwise sums in a (3,4) result.



Consider a concrete case: tensor A has shape (32, 1, 64) and tensor B has shape (1, 128, 64). Comparing dimensions right to left, 64 matches 64, then 1 stretches to 128, then 1 stretches to 32, yielding result shape (32, 128, 64). Visualizing this expansion prevents silent logic bugs that accidentally allocate a large tensor (for example, a (Batch, Batch) matrix instead of an element-wise (Batch) vector).
Shapes, strides, and broadcasting govern how tensors flow through a model’s forward pass. Training adds a second requirement: learning from errors. Backpropagation makes that learning possible and imposes the memory costs developed below.

title: Algorithm Foundations
text:
Valid tensor programs make training loops possible. Backpropagation orchestrates these tensors to compute gradients, transforming a forward prediction into a backward learning signal.

Systems Perspective 1.2: Why this mattersWhen training fails—loss goes to NaN, gradients explode, or memory runs out—understanding what backpropagation actually does is essential for diagnosing the problem. The backward graph supplies the mental model for reasoning about gradient flow and memory usage during training.




For a composed function \(\ComposedFunctionOutput= \LayerFunction(\InnerLayerFunction(\ComposedFunctionInput))\), the derivative is \(\frac{d\ComposedFunctionOutput}{d\ComposedFunctionInput} = \frac{d\ComposedFunctionOutput}{d\InnerLayerFunction} \cdot \frac{d\InnerLayerFunction}{d\ComposedFunctionInput}\). In a neural network, \(\LayerFunction\) and \(\InnerLayerFunction\) are layers, and the composition can be many levels deep. For a three-layer network \(\ComposedFunctionOutput= \LayerFunction_3(\LayerFunction_2(\LayerFunction_1(\ComposedFunctionInput)))\), the chain rule extends to: \[ \frac{\partial \ComposedFunctionOutput}{\partial \ComposedFunctionInput} = \frac{\partial \LayerFunction_3}{\partial \LayerFunction_2} \cdot \frac{\partial \LayerFunction_2}{\partial \LayerFunction_1} \cdot \frac{\partial \LayerFunction_1}{\partial \ComposedFunctionInput} \]
Each factor in this product is a local derivative—computed at one layer using only that layer’s inputs and outputs. This locality is what makes the algorithm tractable: the entire network never needs to be differentiated as a monolithic function. Instead, each layer computes its own local derivative during the backward pass and multiplies it by the gradient flowing in from the layer above.
Modern frameworks use reverse-mode automatic differentiation, which computes gradients for all \(\Parameters\) parameters in a single backward pass. The key insight is that starting from the output and working backward (reverse mode) requires one pass regardless of the number of parameters, whereas starting from each input and working forward (forward mode) would require \(\Parameters\) passes—one per parameter. This is why a training step is a small constant multiple of inference, commonly about 2–3\(\times\) a forward pass for dense networks, rather than \(\Parameters\) passes.



Backpropagation3 implements the chain rule efficiently through two passes: forward to compute outputs, backward to compute gradients. The gradient edges retrace forward dependencies, meaning each backward step requires intermediate activations retained from the corresponding forward operation. Figure 2 traces these dual dataflow passes across a two-layer network: solid gray arrows stage forward activations (\(\InputFeatureVector\to \HiddenActivation\to \PredictedOutput\)) through weight parameters \(\WeightMatrix_1\) and \(\WeightMatrix_2\) to evaluate loss \(\LossFunction\), while curved dashed red arrows propagate intermediate adjoints (\(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \PredictedOutput}, \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \HiddenActivation}, \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \InputFeatureVector}\)) in reverse order.
3 Backpropagation: Short for “backward propagation of errors.” The algorithm was independently discovered multiple times—by Werbos (1974) and Linnainmaa (1970) for reverse-mode differentiation and by Rumelhart et al. (1986) for neural network training. Its key insight is that computing gradients for all parameters requires one backward pass through the graph rather than one pass per parameter. Section 1.4 derives the constant-factor work bound and a representative dense-layer cost.
Werbos, Paul. 1974. “Beyond Regression: New Tools for Prediction and Analysis in the Behavioral Sciences.” PhD thesis, Harvard University.

Linnainmaa, Seppo. 1970. “The Representation of the Cumulative Rounding Error of an Algorithm as a Taylor Expansion of the Local Rounding Errors.” Master's thesis, University of Helsinki.

Rumelhart, David E., Geoffrey E. Hinton, and Ronald J. Williams. 1986. “Learning Representations by Back-Propagating Errors.” Nature 323 (6088): 533–36. https://doi.org/10.1038/323533a0.






Figure 2: Backpropagation Computational Graph: Solid gray arrows carry the forward computation from input \(\InputFeatureVector\) to loss \(\LossFunction\), while dashed red arrows carry gradients backward along the same dependencies.





Using row-vector activations, omitting biases, and retaining intermediate activations for backward execution, computation begins at input \(\InputFeatureVector\). Multiplying \(\InputFeatureVector\) by weight matrix \(\WeightMatrix_1\) yields hidden activation \(\HiddenActivation\), which the execution runtime caches for backward differentiation. Multiplying \(\HiddenActivation\) by \(\WeightMatrix_2\) produces network output \(\PredictedOutput\), which is similarly cached. Finally, comparing \(\PredictedOutput\) to the target label produces scalar loss \(\LossFunction\).
At this point, forward evaluation is complete, and memory holds input \(\InputFeatureVector\), cached activation \(\HiddenActivation\), cached prediction \(\PredictedOutput\), and loss \(\LossFunction\). For large models, these retained activation tensors frequently dominate overall memory consumption.



Gradient propagation begins backward from scalar loss \(\LossFunction\). The loss function evaluates \(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \PredictedOutput}\), the error gradient with respect to network prediction, introducing the external learning signal.
Because \(\PredictedOutput = \HiddenActivation\cdot \WeightMatrix_2\), the matrix chain rule yields two gradients at this layer: \[ \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \WeightMatrix_2} = \HiddenActivation^T \cdot \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \PredictedOutput} \qquad \text{(weight gradient—used to update } \WeightMatrix_2\text{)} \] \[ \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \HiddenActivation} = \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \PredictedOutput} \cdot \WeightMatrix_2^T \qquad \text{(input gradient—passed backward to the previous layer)} \]
Computing \(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \WeightMatrix_2}\) requires cached activation \(\HiddenActivation\) from the forward pass. Activations must remain resident in memory because every layer’s weight gradient depends directly on that layer’s input.
Continuing backward to the first layer, the linear relationship \(\HiddenActivation= \InputFeatureVector\cdot \WeightMatrix_1\) produces: \[ \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \WeightMatrix_1} = \InputFeatureVector^T \cdot \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \HiddenActivation} \]
Each backward step requires two operands: the gradient flowing in from downstream layers \(\left(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \HiddenActivation}\right)\) and that layer’s cached input (\(\InputFeatureVector\)). Consequently, the backward pass requires roughly 2\(\times\) the forward pass FLOPs: each layer executes two matrix multiplications (one for the parameter gradient, one for the upstream activation gradient) rather than one.




A common mistake is to assume that training memory equals model size. This assumption leads to immediate OOM errors because weights are only one of four components. Training memory comprises weights, gradients, optimizer state, and retained activations: \[ \TotalMemoryFootprint = \WeightMemory + \GradientMemory + \OptimizerStateMemory + \ActivationMemory \]
For a standard Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) optimizer (Kingma and Ba 2015) in mixed precision (Micikevicius et al. 2017):

Kingma, Diederik P., and Jimmy Ba. 2015. “Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization.” 3rd International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Micikevicius, Paulius, Sharan Narang, Jonah Alben, Gregory Diamos, Erich Elsen, David Garcia, Boris Ginsburg, et al. 2017. “Mixed Precision Training.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1710.03740.

Weights: 2 bytes (FP16/BF16) or 4 bytes (FP32).
Gradients: Same size as weights.
Optimizer State: Adam moments require 8 bytes per parameter; an FP32 master copy adds another 4 bytes, giving 8–12 bytes per parameter.
Activations: Activations typically dominate the dynamic memory footprint during training. A recomputation- or tiled-attention-friendly estimate scales as \(\mathcal{O}(\BatchSize\times \SequenceLength\times \LayerCount \times \HiddenDimension)\); a full no-recompute attention implementation also materializes attention-score tensors that scale with \(\SequenceLength^2\).

To see how these components interact in practice, consider a concrete model.

Napkin Math 1.1: Worked example: GPT-2 (1.5B) training memoryThe model: GPT-2 XL has \(\Parameters=\) \(1.5 \times 10^{9}\) parameters, 48 layers, hidden dimension \(\HiddenDimension=\) 1600.
Model state (fixed per step):

Weights (BF16): \(1.5 \times 10^{9}\) \(\times\) 2 bytes = 3 GB
Gradients (BF16): \(1.5 \times 10^{9}\) \(\times\) 2 bytes = 3 GB
Optimizer (FP32 master + momentum + variance): \(1.5 \times 10^{9}\) \(\times\) 12 bytes = 18 GB
Total model state: 24 GB—fits on an 80 GB-class A100/H100 (85.9 GB in decimal units), but leaves only 61.9 GB for activations.

Activations (scale with batch):
Per-layer retained activations for this quick estimate are approximately \(12 \times \BatchSize\times \SequenceLength\times \HiddenDimension\) BF16 elements, or \(12 \times \BatchSize\times \SequenceLength\times \HiddenDimension\times 2\) bytes, where \(\BatchSize\) is batch size and \(\SequenceLength\) is sequence length. The factor twelve accounts for the major intermediate tensors retained for backpropagation: input activations, QKV projections (\(3\HiddenDimension\)), attention output, FFN intermediate (\(4\HiddenDimension\)), and layer norm/dropout masks. This estimate assumes the implementation does not retain the full \(\BatchSize\times \AttentionHeadCount \times \SequenceLength^2\) attention-score tensor, as in recomputation- or tiled-attention-friendly accounting. With 48 layers, batch size 8, and sequence length 1024:
\[48 \times 12 \times 8 \times 1024 \times 1600 \times 2\text{ bytes } \approx 15.1\text{ GB}\]
Systems insight: Total memory reaches ~39.1 GB under this activation-accounting convention, which fits on one 85.9 GB accelerator. However, increase the batch to 64 and activations grow to ~120.8 GB, exceeding the remaining capacity. This is the threshold where gradient checkpointing or another memory-saving method becomes necessary; its savings and recomputation overhead depend on checkpoint placement and implementation.




While weights are fixed (\(\mathcal{O}(\Parameters)\)), activations grow linearly with batch size and at least linearly with sequence length; implementations that materialize attention scores add an \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) component. As the worked example shows, activation memory can quickly exceed the room left after model state. Gradient checkpointing4 reduces this pressure by storing only selected activations and recomputing the rest during backpropagation (Chen et al. 2016); techniques such as FlashAttention address related attention-memory bottlenecks by tiling attention to reduce memory round-trips (Dao et al. 2022). The same decomposition provides a quick feasibility check: sum the per-parameter model state, add the activation term implied by batch size and sequence length, and compare the total against the accelerator’s capacity.
4 Gradient checkpointing: Trades compute for memory. Instead of storing all activations, only a subset (checkpoints) is kept, and the missing ones are recomputed during the backward pass. This reduces memory usage from storing every layer activation to roughly the square root of the layer count at the cost of ~33 percent more compute (Chen et al. 2016).
Chen, Tianqi, Bing Xu, Chiyuan Zhang, and Carlos Guestrin. 2016. “Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1604.06174.




The dependency structure exposed by backpropagation also gives compilers something to optimize. ML compilers represent models as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), and that representation enables hardware-independent transformations.


Compilers transform graphs into static single-assignment (SSA) form, where each variable is assigned exactly once. This makes data dependencies explicit, enabling safe optimizations—most notably, operator fusion.



Without fusion, each operation in a chain like MatMul → Add (bias) → ReLU produces an intermediate tensor that is written to HBM and then read back for the next operation. For elementwise operations like Add and ReLU, the compute is trivial (one FLOP per element) but the memory traffic is not (read the tensor, write it back). The arithmetic intensity of unfused elementwise operations is therefore close to zero—deeply memory bound.
Fusion combines consecutive operations into a single kernel that reads the input once, applies all operations in registers or shared memory, and writes the final result once. For a sequence of \(\ChainedOperationCount\) elementwise operations on a tensor of \(\TensorElementCount\) elements of \(\ElementStorageSize\) bytes each, fusion reduces memory traffic from \(2\ChainedOperationCount \TensorElementCount\ElementStorageSize\) bytes (each operation reads and writes) to \(2\TensorElementCount\ElementStorageSize\) bytes (one read, one write)—a \(\ChainedOperationCount\times\) reduction.
FlashAttention is an I/O-aware tiled attention algorithm: it computes the score, softmax, and value-product stages in SRAM tiles without materializing the full attention matrix in HBM, reducing auxiliary attention memory from \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) to \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) for a fixed head dimension. HBM traffic also falls, with its reduction depending on head dimension and available SRAM capacity. The original work reports up to 3\(\times\) wall-clock speedups on its evaluated workloads (Dao et al. 2022); realized gains depend on shape and hardware (see section 1.5 for the step-by-step derivation). Together, the linear algebra foundations, tensor programming mechanics, and training memory model covered in this appendix form the algorithmic substrate on which all ML systems are built.

title: Algorithm Foundations
text:
Modern deep learning scales to hundreds of billions of parameters because evaluating the full gradient vector \(\nabla \ScalarGraphFunction(\FunctionInputVector)\) of a scalar loss function \(\ScalarGraphFunction: \mathbb{R}^\FunctionInputDimension\to \mathbb{R}\) requires compute proportional to evaluating \(\ScalarGraphFunction(\FunctionInputVector)\) itself, with a constant-factor bound independent of the input dimension \(\FunctionInputDimension\). Baur and Strassen proved this complexity result in 1983 (Baur and Strassen 1983).

Baur, Walter, and Volker Strassen. 1983. “The Complexity of Partial Derivatives.” Theoretical Computer Science 22 (3): 317–30. https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3975(83)90110-x.


Let \(\ScalarGraphFunction: \mathbb{R}^\FunctionInputDimension\to \mathbb{R}\) be a multivariate scalar-valued function represented as a computational graph \(\ComputationalGraph= (\GraphNodeSet, \GraphEdgeSet)\) consisting of \(\ElementaryOperationCount(\ScalarGraphFunction)\) elementary operations (additions, subtractions, multiplications, divisions, and unary functions such as \(\exp, \ln, \sin, \sqrt{\cdot}\)).

Theorem 1.1: Baur–Strassen complexity theoremIf a scalar function \(\ScalarGraphFunction: \mathbb{R}^\FunctionInputDimension\to \mathbb{R}\) can be computed in \(\ElementaryOperationCount(\ScalarGraphFunction)\) elementary operations, then the full gradient vector \(\nabla \ScalarGraphFunction(\FunctionInputVector) = \left(\frac{\partial \ScalarGraphFunction}{\partial \FunctionInputElement_1}, \frac{\partial \ScalarGraphFunction}{\partial \FunctionInputElement_2}, \dots, \frac{\partial \ScalarGraphFunction}{\partial \LastFunctionInputComponent}\right)^T \in \mathbb{R}^\FunctionInputDimension\) can be evaluated in total work \(\text{Work}_{\text{Reverse}}(\ScalarGraphFunction, \nabla \ScalarGraphFunction)\) satisfying: \[ \text{Work}_{\text{Reverse}}(\ScalarGraphFunction, \nabla \ScalarGraphFunction) \le \ReverseModeWorkConstant\cdot \ElementaryOperationCount(\ScalarGraphFunction) \] where \(\ReverseModeWorkConstant\le 5\) is a universal constant independent of the input dimension \(\FunctionInputDimension\). Furthermore, the backward pass alone requires work \(\text{Work}_{\text{Backward}}(\nabla \ScalarGraphFunction) \le 4 \cdot \ElementaryOperationCount(\ScalarGraphFunction)\).





Let the computational graph \(\ComputationalGraph= (\GraphNodeSet, \GraphEdgeSet)\) be topologically ordered with nodes \(\FirstInputNodePrimal, \dots, \TraceIntermediateVariable_0, \TraceIntermediateVariable_1\), \(\TraceIntermediateVariable_2, \dots, \OutputNodePrimal\), where input variables are \(\FunctionInputElement_{\InputVariableIndex} = \InputNodePrimal\) for \(\InputVariableIndex\in \{1, \dots, \FunctionInputDimension\}\) and the final output is \(\ScalarGraphFunction(\FunctionInputVector) = \OutputNodePrimal\). Each intermediate node \(\TraceIntermediateVariable_j\) is evaluated via a primitive operation: \[ \TraceIntermediateVariable_j = \PrimitiveOperation_j\left( \{ \TraceIntermediateVariable_k \mid \ParentNodeIndex\in \text{Parents}(\CurrentNodeIndex) \} \right) \]
Define the adjoint variable \(\TraceIntermediateAdjoint_i\) for every node \(\TraceIntermediateVariable_i\) as the partial derivative of the scalar output \(\OutputNodePrimal\) with respect to \(\TraceIntermediateVariable_i\): \[ \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_i \triangleq \frac{\partial \ScalarGraphFunction}{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_i} = \frac{\partial \OutputNodePrimal}{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_i} \]
By the multivariate chain rule, the adjoint \(\TraceIntermediateAdjoint_i\) is the sum of partial derivatives propagated from all successor nodes (children) that consume \(\TraceIntermediateVariable_i\): \[ \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_i = \sum_{j \in \text{Children}(i)} \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_j \cdot \frac{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_j}{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_i} \]
Reverse-mode automatic differentiation initializes \(\OutputNodeAdjoint = 1\) and \(\TraceIntermediateAdjoint_i = 0\) for all \(\GraphNodeIndex< \ElementaryOperationCount\), then traverses the nodes in reverse topological order from \(\OutputNodePrimal\) down to \(\TraceIntermediateVariable_1\). For each primitive node \(\TraceIntermediateVariable_j\), its fully accumulated adjoint \(\TraceIntermediateAdjoint_j\) propagates error signals to its parent nodes \(\TraceIntermediateVariable_k\) (\(\ParentNodeIndex\in \text{Parents}(\CurrentNodeIndex)\)) via: \[ \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_k \gets \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_k + \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_j \cdot \frac{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_j}{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_k} \]
We now perform operation-by-operation micro-cost accounting for all primitive nodes to bound the backward work:

Addition/Subtraction (\(\TraceIntermediateVariable_j = \TraceIntermediateVariable_i \pm \TraceIntermediateVariable_k\)):

Local derivatives: \(\frac{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_j}{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_i} = 1\), \(\frac{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_j}{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_k} = \pm 1\).
Backward updates: \(\TraceIntermediateAdjoint_i \gets \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_i + \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_j\) and \(\TraceIntermediateAdjoint_k \gets \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_k \pm \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_j\).
Cost: 2 additions in backward pass for 1 forward operation. Work ratio: \(\text{Fwd}(1) + \text{Bwd}(2) = 3 \text{ OPs} \le 5 \cdot 1\).

Multiplication (\(\TraceIntermediateVariable_j = \TraceIntermediateVariable_i \cdot \TraceIntermediateVariable_k\)):

Local derivatives: \(\frac{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_j}{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_i} = \TraceIntermediateVariable_k\), \(\frac{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_j}{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_k} = \TraceIntermediateVariable_i\).
Backward updates: \(\TraceIntermediateAdjoint_i \gets \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_i + \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_j \cdot \TraceIntermediateVariable_k\) and \(\TraceIntermediateAdjoint_k \gets \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_k + \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_j \cdot \TraceIntermediateVariable_i\).
Cost: 2 multiplications + 2 additions = 4 operations in backward pass for 1 forward operation. Work ratio: \(\text{Fwd}(1) + \text{Bwd}(4) = 5 \text{ OPs} \le 5 \cdot 1\).

Division (\(\TraceIntermediateVariable_j = \TraceIntermediateVariable_i/\TraceIntermediateVariable_k\)):

Local derivatives: \(\frac{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_j}{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_i} = \frac{1}{\TraceIntermediateVariable_k}\), \(\frac{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_j}{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_k} = -\frac{\TraceIntermediateVariable_i}{\TraceIntermediateVariable_k^2} = -\frac{\TraceIntermediateVariable_j}{\TraceIntermediateVariable_k}\).
Backward updates: \(\TraceIntermediateAdjoint_i \gets \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_i + \frac{\TraceIntermediateAdjoint_j}{\TraceIntermediateVariable_k}\) and \(\TraceIntermediateAdjoint_k \gets \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_k - \frac{\TraceIntermediateAdjoint_j \cdot \TraceIntermediateVariable_j}{\TraceIntermediateVariable_k}\).
Cost: Compute the quotient of the incoming adjoint and the denominator once, then reuse it in both updates: add it to the numerator adjoint, and multiply it by the cached forward output before subtracting from the denominator adjoint. This requires 2 multiplications/divisions + 2 additions = 4 operations in backward pass for 1 forward operation. Work ratio: \(\text{Fwd}(1) + \text{Bwd}(4) = 5 \text{ OPs} \le 5 \cdot 1\).

Unary transcendental operations (\(\TraceIntermediateVariable_j = \PrimitiveOperation(\TraceIntermediateVariable_i)\)):

Local derivative: \(\frac{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_j}{\partial \TraceIntermediateVariable_i} = \PrimitiveOperation'(\TraceIntermediateVariable_i)\).
Backward update: \(\TraceIntermediateAdjoint_i \gets \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_i + \TraceIntermediateAdjoint_j \cdot \PrimitiveOperation'(\TraceIntermediateVariable_i)\).
For \(\TraceIntermediateVariable_j = \exp(\TraceIntermediateVariable_i)\), \(\PrimitiveOperation'(\TraceIntermediateVariable_i) = \TraceIntermediateVariable_j\), requiring 1 multiplication + 1 addition = 2 OPs.
For \(\TraceIntermediateVariable_j = \ln(\TraceIntermediateVariable_i)\), \(\PrimitiveOperation'(\TraceIntermediateVariable_i) = 1/\TraceIntermediateVariable_i\), requiring 1 division + 1 addition = 2 OPs.


Summing across all primitive nodes in \(\ComputationalGraph\), every forward operation generates at most 4 backward operations: \[ \text{Work}_{\text{Backward}}(\nabla \ScalarGraphFunction) \le 4 \cdot \ElementaryOperationCount(\ScalarGraphFunction) \]
Adding the forward pass work \(\ElementaryOperationCount(\ScalarGraphFunction)\) yields the total work bound: \[ \text{Work}_{\text{Reverse}}(\ScalarGraphFunction, \nabla \ScalarGraphFunction) = \ElementaryOperationCount(\ScalarGraphFunction) + \text{Work}_{\text{Backward}}(\nabla \ScalarGraphFunction) \le 5 \cdot \ElementaryOperationCount(\ScalarGraphFunction) \qquad\blacksquare\]

Systems Perspective 1.3: Why 175B-parameter large language models can be trainedThe independence of \(\ReverseModeWorkConstant\le 5\) from input dimension \(\FunctionInputDimension\) is the mathematical reason deep learning works. Consider training a transformer model with \(\Parameters= 175 \times 10^9\) parameters:

Forward pass: Matrix multiplications \(\LayerOutputMatrix= \LayerInputMatrix\WeightMatrix\) require \(2\Parameters\) FLOPs per token.
Reverse-mode backward pass: Computes both weight gradients \(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \WeightMatrix} = \LayerInputMatrix^T \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \LayerOutputMatrix}\) (\(2\Parameters\) FLOPs) and input activation gradients \(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \LayerInputMatrix} = \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \LayerOutputMatrix} \WeightMatrix^T\) (\(2\Parameters\) FLOPs), totaling \(4\Parameters\) FLOPs per token.
Total training work: \(2\Parameters(\text{fwd}) + 4\Parameters(\text{bwd}) = 6\Parameters\) FLOPs per token. The backward compute factor is exactly \(\frac{4\Parameters}{2\Parameters} = 2\), well within the Baur–Strassen theoretical bound of \(\ReverseModeWorkConstant\le 5\).

If we instead used forward-mode AD or finite differences to compute \(\nabla \ScalarGraphFunction\in \mathbb{R}^\Parameters\), evaluating each partial derivative separately would require \(\Parameters\) forward passes: \(\text{Work}_{\text{ForwardMode}}(\nabla \ScalarGraphFunction) = \mathcal{O}(\Parameters\cdot \ElementaryOperationCount) = \mathcal{O}(\Parameters^2)\) FLOPs. For \(\Parameters= 175 \times 10^9\), that method would require \(2 \times (175 \times 10^9)^2 \approx 6.1 \times 10^{22}\) FLOPs per token—\(\Parameters\) times the forward-pass work and therefore prohibitive at this scale. Reverse-mode AD collapses this \(\mathcal{O}(\Parameters)\) factor into a constant multiplier of 2 for the dense-layer accounting above.

title: Algorithm Foundations
text:
Standard self-attention in transformers requires materializing an \(\SequenceLength\times \SequenceLength\) attention score matrix in HBM, creating an \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) memory bandwidth bottleneck. FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022) eliminates this bottleneck by tiling query, key, and value matrices and recomputing attention using an online softmax recurrence without materializing intermediate scores to HBM.


Given queries \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \AttentionHeadDimension}\), keys \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \AttentionHeadDimension}\), and values \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \AttentionHeadDimension}\) for sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) and head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension\), standard attention evaluates: \[ \AttentionScoreMatrix= \AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T \in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \SequenceLength}, \qquad \AttentionWeightMatrix= \text{softmax}(\AttentionScoreMatrix) \in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \SequenceLength}, \qquad \AttentionHeadOutput= \AttentionWeightMatrix\AttentionValuesMatrix\in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \AttentionHeadDimension} \]
To prevent numerical overflow, row-wise softmax subtracts the row maximum \(\SoftmaxRowMaximum_i = \max_{1 \le j \le \SequenceLength} \AttentionScoreEntry\): \[ \AttentionWeightEntry = \frac{\exp(\AttentionScoreEntry - \SoftmaxRowMaximum_i)}{\sum_{k=1}^\SequenceLength\exp(\AttentionScoreSummand - \SoftmaxRowMaximum_i)} \]
Standard GPU implementations execute this in three discrete kernel launches:

Compute \(\AttentionScoreMatrix= \AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T\) in SRAM, then write \(\AttentionScoreMatrix\in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \SequenceLength}\) to HBM (\(\AsymptoticTightBound(\SequenceLength^2)\) writes).
Read \(\AttentionScoreMatrix\) from HBM, compute row max \(\SoftmaxRowMaximum\) and row sum \(\SoftmaxNormalizer\), compute \(\AttentionWeightMatrix= \text{softmax}(\AttentionScoreMatrix)\), write \(\AttentionWeightMatrix\in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \SequenceLength}\) to HBM (\(\AsymptoticTightBound(\SequenceLength^2)\) reads + writes).
Read \(\AttentionWeightMatrix\) and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) from HBM, compute \(\AttentionHeadOutput= \AttentionWeightMatrix\AttentionValuesMatrix\), write \(\AttentionHeadOutput\in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \AttentionHeadDimension}\) to HBM (\(\AsymptoticTightBound(\SequenceLength^2 + \SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension)\) reads + writes).

Total HBM memory traffic is \(\AsymptoticTightBound(\SequenceLength^2 + \SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension)\) elements. For \(\SequenceLength= 8192\), \(\AttentionHeadDimension = 128\) in FP16, \(\AttentionScoreMatrix\) requires \(8192^2 \times 2 \text{ B} = 134 \text{ MB}\) per head per layer. Because modern GPUs feature massive compute throughput relative to HBM bandwidth, repeatedly reading and writing intermediate matrices \(\AttentionScoreMatrix\) and \(\AttentionWeightMatrix\) leaves GPU execution units memory-bound.



Tiling softmax is difficult because computing \(\SoftmaxNormalizer_i = \sum_{k=1}^{\SequenceLength} \exp(\AttentionScoreSummand - \SoftmaxRowMaximum_i)\) requires the global maximum \(\SoftmaxRowMaximum_i\) across all \(\SequenceLength\) keys. The online softmax recurrence solves this by incrementally updating normalization statistics as sub-blocks arrive.

Theorem 1.2: Online softmax recurrence theoremLet a vector \(\SoftmaxInputVector\in \mathbb{R}^\SoftmaxVectorLength\) be partitioned into two sub-vectors \(\SoftmaxInputVector^{(1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_1}\) and \(\SoftmaxInputVector^{(2)} \in \mathbb{R}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_2}\) with \(\SoftmaxVectorLength= \SoftmaxVectorLength_1 + \SoftmaxVectorLength_2\). Let the local statistics for block 1 be: \[ \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)} = \max_{1 \le j \le \SoftmaxVectorLength_1} \SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(1)}, \qquad \SoftmaxNormalizer^{(1)} = \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_1} \exp\left(\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(1)} - \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)}\right) \] and for block 2 be: \[ \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)} = \max_{1 \le j \le \SoftmaxVectorLength_2} \SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(2)}, \qquad \SoftmaxNormalizer^{(2)} = \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_2} \exp\left(\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(2)} - \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)}\right) \]
Then the combined maximum \(\MergedSoftmaxMaximum\), normalization sum \(\MergedSoftmaxNormalizer\), and accumulated output vector \(\MergedAttentionOutput\) satisfy the exact recurrence relations: \[ \begin{aligned}
\MergedSoftmaxMaximum &= \max\left(\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)}, \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)}\right), \\
\MergedSoftmaxNormalizer &= \SoftmaxNormalizer^{(1)} e^{\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum} + \SoftmaxNormalizer^{(2)} e^{\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum}, \\
\MergedAttentionOutput &= \frac{\SoftmaxNormalizer^{(1)} e^{\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum}}{\MergedSoftmaxNormalizer} \AttentionHeadOutput^{(1)} + \frac{e^{\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum}}{\MergedSoftmaxNormalizer} \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_2} e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(2)} - \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)}} \AttentionValuesMatrix_j^{(2)},
\end{aligned} \] where \(\AttentionHeadOutput^{(1)} = \frac{1}{\SoftmaxNormalizer^{(1)}} \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_1} e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(1)} - \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)}} \AttentionValuesMatrix_j^{(1)}\) is the partial output accumulated from block 1.




Expanding the combined sum \(\MergedSoftmaxNormalizer = \sum_{j=1}^\SoftmaxVectorLength e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum}\): \[ \begin{aligned} \MergedSoftmaxNormalizer &= \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_1} e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(1)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum} + \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_2} e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(2)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum} \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_1} e^{\left(\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(1)} - \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)}\right) + \left(\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum\right)} + \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_2} e^{\left(\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(2)} - \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)}\right) + \left(\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum\right)} \\ &= e^{\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum} \underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_1} e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(1)} - \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)}}}_{\SoftmaxNormalizer^{(1)}} + e^{\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum} \underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_2} e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(2)} - \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)}}}_{\SoftmaxNormalizer^{(2)}} \\ &= \SoftmaxNormalizer^{(1)} e^{\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum} + \SoftmaxNormalizer^{(2)} e^{\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum}. \quad \blacksquare \end{aligned} \]



The true normalized output over the concatenated sequence is \(\MergedAttentionOutput = \frac{1}{\MergedSoftmaxNormalizer} \sum_{j=1}^\SoftmaxVectorLength e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum} \AttentionValuesMatrix_j\): \[ \begin{aligned} \MergedAttentionOutput &= \frac{1}{\MergedSoftmaxNormalizer} \left[ \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_1} e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(1)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum} \AttentionValuesMatrix_j^{(1)} + \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_2} e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(2)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum} \AttentionValuesMatrix_j^{(2)} \right] \\ &= \frac{1}{\MergedSoftmaxNormalizer} \left[ e^{\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum} \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_1} e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(1)} - \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)}} \AttentionValuesMatrix_j^{(1)} + e^{\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum} \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_2} e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(2)} - \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)}} \AttentionValuesMatrix_j^{(2)} \right] \end{aligned} \]
Noting that \(\SoftmaxNormalizer^{(1)} \AttentionHeadOutput^{(1)} = \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_1} e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(1)} - \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)}} \AttentionValuesMatrix_j^{(1)}\), we substitute this directly: \[ \MergedAttentionOutput = \frac{\SoftmaxNormalizer^{(1)} e^{\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(1)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum}}{\MergedSoftmaxNormalizer} \AttentionHeadOutput^{(1)} + \frac{e^{\SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)} - \MergedSoftmaxMaximum}}{\MergedSoftmaxNormalizer} \sum_{j=1}^{\SoftmaxVectorLength_2} e^{\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(2)} - \SoftmaxRowMaximum^{(2)}} \AttentionValuesMatrix_j^{(2)}. \quad \blacksquare \]




Let \(\SramCapacity\) be the fast SRAM capacity (in words). Following Algorithm 1 of Dao et al. (2022), FlashAttention sets \(\KvTileSize = \lfloor \SramCapacity/(4\AttentionHeadDimension) \rfloor\) and \(\QueryBlockSize = \min(\lfloor \SramCapacity/(4\AttentionHeadDimension) \rfloor,\AttentionHeadDimension)\). The proof abstracts constant factors and buffer reuse, using \(\KvTileSize=\AsymptoticTightBound(\SramCapacity/\AttentionHeadDimension)\), \(\QueryBlockSize=\AsymptoticTightBound(\min(\SramCapacity/\AttentionHeadDimension,\AttentionHeadDimension))\), and \(\QueryBlockSize\KvTileSize=\mathcal{O}(\SramCapacity)\) for the on-chip working set.
The algorithm partitions \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\) into \(\QueryBlockCount = \lceil \SequenceLength/\QueryBlockSize \rceil\) blocks of size \(\QueryBlockSize \times \AttentionHeadDimension\), and partitions \(\AttentionKeyMatrix, \AttentionValuesMatrix\) into \(\KvTileCount = \lceil \SequenceLength/\KvTileSize \rceil\) blocks of size \(\KvTileSize \times \AttentionHeadDimension\). It executes two nested loops:

Outer loop over \(\KvTileIndex= 1, \dots, \KvTileCount\): Load \(\AttentionKeyMatrix_j\) and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix_j\) into SRAM.
Inner loop over \(\QueryBlockIndex= 1, \dots, \QueryBlockCount\): Load \(\AttentionQueryMatrix_i\), \(\AttentionHeadOutput_i\), and its softmax statistics; compute \(\AttentionScoreTile = \AttentionQueryMatrix_i \AttentionKeyMatrix_j^T\) in SRAM; then update and write \(\AttentionHeadOutput_i\) and the statistics without materializing \(\AttentionScoreTile\) in HBM.

This loop order is the source of the I/O reduction. A key-value tile remains resident while the algorithm visits every query tile, so each element of \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\) and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) crosses the HBM boundary once. The query and output tiles must be revisited for each key-value block, but the \(\QueryBlockSize\times \KvTileSize\) score tile is consumed on chip and discarded. Standard attention instead writes and rereads the full \(\SequenceLength\times \SequenceLength\) score and probability matrices.


Total HBM accesses comprise two components: key and value reads, where each element of \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\) and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) is loaded once (contributing \(2\SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension\) accesses); and query, output, and statistics passes, where each of the \(\KvTileCount\) column blocks reads all of \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), reads and writes \(\AttentionHeadOutput\), and updates \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) softmax statistics. The matrices dominate the statistics for head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension\geq 1\), so each pass contributes \(\AsymptoticTightBound(\SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension)\) accesses and all passes contribute \(\AsymptoticTightBound(\SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension \KvTileCount)\).
Because \(\KvTileCount=\lceil \SequenceLength/\KvTileSize\rceil=\AsymptoticTightBound(\SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension/\SramCapacity)\), the total is \[ \text{HBM}_{\text{Flash}} = \AsymptoticTightBound\left(\SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension + \SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension \KvTileCount\right) = \AsymptoticTightBound\left(\SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension + \frac{\SequenceLength^2 \AttentionHeadDimension^2}{\SramCapacity}\right) = \AsymptoticTightBound\left(\frac{\SequenceLength^2 \AttentionHeadDimension^2}{\SramCapacity}\right), \] where the final equality follows for \(\AttentionHeadDimension \leq \SramCapacity\leq \SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension\).
The bound counts communication rather than arithmetic. FlashAttention still evaluates the same dense score blocks and may recompute intermediate quantities during backpropagation; its advantage comes from keeping those intermediates out of HBM.



Comparing standard attention I/O to FlashAttention I/O: \[ \frac{\text{HBM}_{\text{Standard}}}{\text{HBM}_{\text{Flash}}} = \frac{\AsymptoticTightBound(\SequenceLength^2 + \SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension)}{\AsymptoticTightBound\left(\SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension + \frac{\SequenceLength^2 \AttentionHeadDimension^2}{\SramCapacity}\right)} = \AsymptoticTightBound\left(\frac{\SramCapacity}{\AttentionHeadDimension^2}\right) \quad \text{for } \SequenceLength\gg \max\left(\AttentionHeadDimension,\frac{\SramCapacity}{\AttentionHeadDimension}\right) \]

Systems Perspective 1.4: A100 I/O reductionThe asymptotic ratio \(\SramCapacity/\AttentionHeadDimension^2\) predicts how greater SRAM capacity can reduce HBM traffic, but hidden constants and kernel details prevent it from serving as an exact transfer count. In an NVIDIA A100 measurement, Dao et al. (2022) report the effect for a forward-and-backward attention workload with sequence length 1,024, head dimension 64, 16 heads, batch size 64, a key-padding mask, and no dropout:

Standard attention: 35.3 GB of HBM reads and writes; 35.1 ms runtime.
FlashAttention: 4.4 GB of HBM reads and writes; 11.7 ms runtime.

The measurements show the systems consequence of the I/O bound: substantially less HBM traffic coincides with lower runtime even though FlashAttention performs additional recomputation. They do not imply that every configuration becomes compute bound; tile size, sequence length, and kernel implementation determine the realized regime.



Dao, T., D. Y. Fu, S. Ermon, A. Rudra, and C. Ré. 2022. “FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 16344–59. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-1189.

title: Algorithm Foundations
text:
Determining the compute-optimal allocation between model parameters and training dataset tokens for a given floating-point budget \(\Operations\) is a central decision in large language model system design. This section provides the rigorous mathematical derivation of compute-optimal scaling laws using Lagrange multipliers, contrasting the original findings of Kaplan et al. (2020) with the compute-optimal corrections of Hoffmann et al. (2022).
Notation note: This derivation writes model parameters as \(\Parameters\), dataset size in tokens as \(\DatasetSize\), and the training compute budget as \(\Operations\) total FLOPs; Kaplan et al. (2020) and Hoffmann et al. (2022) write \(\Glyph{N}\) for parameters and \(\Glyph{C}\) for compute. The fitted constants \(\ChinchillaIrreducibleLoss\), \(\ParameterScaleCoefficient\), \(\DataScaleCoefficient\), \(\ParameterScalingExponent\), and \(\DataScalingExponent\) and the Lagrange multiplier \(\ComputeConstraintMultiplier\) keep the papers’ letters and are local to this section, so \(\ChinchillaIrreducibleLoss\) is a loss rather than an energy and \(\DataScaleCoefficient\) is a fitted constant rather than batch size.


The cross-entropy evaluation loss \(\LossFunction(\Parameters, \DatasetSize)\) of an autoregressive transformer language model trained with \(\Parameters\) non-embedding parameters on \(\DatasetSize\) tokens is modeled by the power-law formulation: \[ \LossFunction(\Parameters, \DatasetSize) = \ChinchillaIrreducibleLoss+ \frac{\ParameterScaleCoefficient}{\Parameters^\ParameterScalingExponent} + \frac{\DataScaleCoefficient}{\DatasetSize^\DataScalingExponent} \] where:

\(\ChinchillaIrreducibleLoss\): Irreducible loss representing the entropy of natural language data.
\(\frac{\ParameterScaleCoefficient}{\Parameters^\ParameterScalingExponent}\): Capacity bottleneck loss resulting from finite model parameters \(\Parameters\).
\(\frac{\DataScaleCoefficient}{\DatasetSize^\DataScalingExponent}\): Dataset size bottleneck loss resulting from finite training tokens \(\DatasetSize\).
\(\ParameterScaleCoefficient, \DataScaleCoefficient> 0\): Empirical scaling constants.
\(\ParameterScalingExponent, \DataScalingExponent> 0\): Power-law scaling exponents for model size and dataset size, respectively.




The total floating-point operations required to train a transformer with \(\Parameters\) non-embedding parameters for \(\DatasetSize\) tokens is given by \[ \Operations= 6 \Parameters \DatasetSize\text{ FLOPs}, \] where \(2 \Parameters \DatasetSize\) accounts for the forward pass and \(4 \Parameters \DatasetSize\) accounts for the backward pass.
Given a fixed training compute budget \(\Operations_0\), we formulate the constrained optimization problem to minimize the reducible loss \(\ReducibleLoss(\Parameters, \DatasetSize) = \frac{\ParameterScaleCoefficient}{\Parameters^\ParameterScalingExponent} + \frac{\DataScaleCoefficient}{\DatasetSize^\DataScalingExponent}\): \[ \min_{\Parameters, \DatasetSize} \left( \frac{\ParameterScaleCoefficient}{\Parameters^\ParameterScalingExponent} + \frac{\DataScaleCoefficient}{\DatasetSize^\DataScalingExponent} \right) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \ComputeBudgetConstraint(\Parameters, \DatasetSize) = 6 \Parameters \DatasetSize- \Operations_0 = 0 \]
We construct the Lagrangian function \(\ComputeConstrainedLagrangian(\Parameters, \DatasetSize, \ComputeConstraintMultiplier)\): \[ \ComputeConstrainedLagrangian(\Parameters, \DatasetSize, \ComputeConstraintMultiplier) = \frac{\ParameterScaleCoefficient}{\Parameters^\ParameterScalingExponent} + \frac{\DataScaleCoefficient}{\DatasetSize^\DataScalingExponent} + \ComputeConstraintMultiplier(6 \Parameters \DatasetSize- \Operations_0) \]
Taking partial derivatives with respect to \(\Parameters, \DatasetSize\), and \(\ComputeConstraintMultiplier\) and setting them to zero yields: \[ \frac{\partial \ComputeConstrainedLagrangian}{\partial \Parameters} = -\ParameterScalingExponent \ParameterScaleCoefficient \Parameters^{-\ParameterScalingExponent- 1} + 6 \ComputeConstraintMultiplier \DatasetSize= 0 \implies \ParameterScalingExponent \ParameterScaleCoefficient \Parameters^{-\ParameterScalingExponent- 1} = 6 \ComputeConstraintMultiplier \DatasetSize, \tag{1} \] \[ \frac{\partial \ComputeConstrainedLagrangian}{\partial \DatasetSize} = -\DataScalingExponent \DataScaleCoefficient \DatasetSize^{-\DataScalingExponent- 1} + 6 \ComputeConstraintMultiplier \Parameters= 0 \implies \DataScalingExponent \DataScaleCoefficient \DatasetSize^{-\DataScalingExponent- 1} = 6 \ComputeConstraintMultiplier \Parameters, \tag{2} \] \[ \frac{\partial \ComputeConstrainedLagrangian}{\partial \ComputeConstraintMultiplier} = 6 \Parameters \DatasetSize- \Operations_0 = 0. \tag{3} \]
Multiplying Equation (1) by \(\Parameters\) and Equation (2) by \(\DatasetSize\) gives: \[ \ParameterScalingExponent \ParameterScaleCoefficient \Parameters^{-\ParameterScalingExponent} = 6 \ComputeConstraintMultiplier \Parameters \DatasetSize, \] \[ \DataScalingExponent \DataScaleCoefficient \DatasetSize^{-\DataScalingExponent} = 6 \ComputeConstraintMultiplier \Parameters \DatasetSize. \]
Equating these expressions yields the fundamental power-law optimality condition: \[ \ParameterScalingExponent \ParameterScaleCoefficient \Parameters^{-\ParameterScalingExponent} = \DataScalingExponent \DataScaleCoefficient \DatasetSize^{-\DataScalingExponent}. \]
This condition proves that at the compute-optimal allocation, the marginal loss reduction per fractional increase in parameter count must equal the marginal loss reduction per fractional increase in dataset tokens.



From \(\ParameterScalingExponent \ParameterScaleCoefficient \Parameters^{-\ParameterScalingExponent} = \DataScalingExponent \DataScaleCoefficient \DatasetSize^{-\DataScalingExponent}\), solving for \(\DatasetSize\) in terms of \(\Parameters\) yields: \[ \DatasetSize^\DataScalingExponent= \left(\frac{\DataScalingExponent \DataScaleCoefficient}{\ParameterScalingExponent \ParameterScaleCoefficient}\right) \Parameters^\ParameterScalingExponent\implies \DatasetSize= \left(\frac{\DataScalingExponent \DataScaleCoefficient}{\ParameterScalingExponent \ParameterScaleCoefficient}\right)^{1/\DataScalingExponent} \Parameters^{\ParameterScalingExponent/\DataScalingExponent}. \]
Substituting \(\DatasetSize\) into the compute constraint \(\Operations= 6 \Parameters \DatasetSize\) gives: \[ \Operations= 6 \Parameters\left(\frac{\DataScalingExponent \DataScaleCoefficient}{\ParameterScalingExponent \ParameterScaleCoefficient}\right)^{1/\DataScalingExponent} \Parameters^{\ParameterScalingExponent/\DataScalingExponent} = 6 \left(\frac{\DataScalingExponent \DataScaleCoefficient}{\ParameterScalingExponent \ParameterScaleCoefficient}\right)^{1/\DataScalingExponent} \Parameters^{\frac{\ParameterScalingExponent+ \DataScalingExponent}{\DataScalingExponent}}. \]
Solving explicitly for the compute-optimal parameter count \(\Parameters^*(\Operations)\): \[ \Parameters^*(\Operations) = \left( \frac{\ParameterScalingExponent \ParameterScaleCoefficient}{\DataScalingExponent \DataScaleCoefficient} \right)^{\frac{1}{\ParameterScalingExponent+ \DataScalingExponent}} \left( \frac{\Operations}{6} \right)^{\frac{\DataScalingExponent}{\ParameterScalingExponent+ \DataScalingExponent}} \propto \Operations^{\frac{\DataScalingExponent}{\ParameterScalingExponent+ \DataScalingExponent}}. \]
By symmetry, solving for the compute-optimal token count \(\DatasetSize^*(\Operations)\) yields: \[ \DatasetSize^*(\Operations) = \left( \frac{\DataScalingExponent \DataScaleCoefficient}{\ParameterScalingExponent \ParameterScaleCoefficient} \right)^{\frac{1}{\ParameterScalingExponent+ \DataScalingExponent}} \left( \frac{\Operations}{6} \right)^{\frac{\ParameterScalingExponent}{\ParameterScalingExponent+ \DataScalingExponent}} \propto \Operations^{\frac{\ParameterScalingExponent}{\ParameterScalingExponent+ \DataScalingExponent}}. \]


Fitting the parametric loss surface to over 400 experimental runs, Hoffmann et al. (2022) estimated \(\ParameterScalingExponent\approx 0.34\) and \(\DataScalingExponent\approx 0.28\). Substituting these values gives exponents close to the paper’s parametric-model result:
\[ \frac{\DataScalingExponent}{\ParameterScalingExponent+ \DataScalingExponent} \approx 0.45, \qquad \frac{\ParameterScalingExponent}{\ParameterScalingExponent+ \DataScalingExponent} \approx 0.55 \]
Thus the parametric model predicts: \[ \Parameters^*(\Operations) \propto \Operations^{0.45}, \qquad \DatasetSize^*(\Operations) \propto \Operations^{0.55} \]
The paper’s two direct empirical approaches report near-balanced exponents of \((0.50, 0.50)\) and \((0.49, 0.51)\), which motivate the common square-root shorthand. Under the parametric fit, however, \(\DatasetSize^*/\Parameters^*\) grows slowly with compute rather than remaining strictly constant. Across the regime studied, roughly 20 training tokens per parameter is a useful Chinchilla heuristic, not a universal invariant.

Systems Perspective 1.5: Kaplan vs. Chinchilla scaling
The difference between Kaplan et al. (2020) and Hoffmann et al. (2022) highlights how hyperparameter choices in empirical benchmarking can alter system design conclusions:

Kaplan scaling model: Kaplan et al. (2020) fit a different loss form with its own exponents and reported compute-optimal growth of \(\Parameters\propto \Operations^{0.73}\) and \(\DatasetSize\propto \Operations^{0.27}\); this split does not follow from substituting exponents into the two-term surface above. This led the field to scale model sizes aggressively while holding training dataset sizes relatively small (e.g., GPT-3 175B trained on 300B tokens, giving \(\DatasetSize/\Parameters= 1.71\)).
Methodological divergence: Kaplan et al. (2020) used a fixed token budget and learning-rate schedule across models. Hoffmann et al. (2022) matched the schedule to each training horizon and found that the earlier setup understated the value of training smaller models on more data.
Chinchilla revision: Hoffmann et al. (2022) found near-balanced parameter and token scaling: its three approaches report exponent pairs of \((0.50, 0.50)\), \((0.49, 0.51)\), and \((0.46, 0.54)\) rather than one exact universal ratio.
Practical impact: Chinchilla (70B parameters trained on 1.4T tokens, \(\DatasetSize/\Parameters= 20\)) outperformed GPT-3 (175B parameters trained on 300B tokens) across downstream benchmarks while requiring \(2.5\times\) less compute during inference and \(2.5\times\) lower weight memory at the same precision (Hoffmann et al. 2022).




Hoffmann, Jordan, Sebastian Borgeaud, Arthur Mensch, Elena Buchatskaya, Trevor Cai, Eliza Rutherford, Diego de Las Casas, et al. 2022. “Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 30016–30. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-2176.

Kaplan, Jared, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan, Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Chess, Rewon Child, Scott Gray, Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, and Dario Amodei. 2020. “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models.” ArXiv Preprint abs/2001.08361.

title: Algorithm Foundations
text:
An algorithm becomes a systems workload through its shapes, operation graph, data dependencies, and numerical representation. Linear-algebra primitives, memory layouts, broadcasting, and sparse formats determine work, traffic, locality, and usable parallelism. Automatic differentiation and backpropagation add saved activations and backward computation; computational graphs then expose opportunities for fusion and recomputation. The Baur–Strassen result bounds reverse-mode overhead, while FlashAttention shows how tiling and an online recurrence can reduce HBM traffic without changing attention semantics.
The same accounting connects kernels to scaling decisions. Compute-optimal scaling turns a fixed budget into a model-data allocation, but the fitted exponents remain empirical rather than universal. Across these models, the reusable method is to expose operations, bytes, saved state, dependencies, and asymptotic constraints before selecting an optimization.

title: System Assumptions
text:
A napkin calculation is only as trustworthy as the inputs behind it, and those inputs are easy to lose track of: an accelerator’s peak rate, a model’s parameter count, an electricity price, an energy cost per operation. This appendix gathers those canonical values and unit conventions into a single reference sheet, allowing any quantitative estimate in the book to be audited, updated with newer figures, or checked across chapters. It also fixes the unit conventions those estimates depend on. The chapters can then argue from numbers without restating where each one came from.


When a chapter says an H100 delivers a certain ridge point, or that training a 7B model needs a certain amount of memory, the underlying bandwidths, capacities, and model sizes are listed here. A local estimate can use the relevant Value and Unit entries. The tables are grouped by topic: accelerators, reference models, energy per access, interconnect bandwidth, economics, production-scale anchors, and unit conventions. Assumptions come from vendor datasheet peaks, published studies or industry reports, illustrative market or grid statistics, and book conventions; section 1.1 lists the provenance in one place.
The calculations below expose which assumptions dominate each estimate, so a changed hardware specification or price can propagate without changing the method.
The constants in this appendix support quick, reproducible calculations. The three examples below apply them to performance, capacity, and cost.

Napkin Math 1.1: Classify a roofline regimeProblem: For the stated H100 and workload intensities, which operations are compute bound and which are memory bound?
Variables: For an H100 at FP16/BF16 peak, use 989 TFLOP/s peak compute and 3.35 TB/s memory bandwidth.
Math: Divide peak FLOP/s by memory bandwidth to get the roofline ridge point: 989 TFLOP/s/3.35 TB/s \(\approx\) 295.2 FLOP/byte. A large general matrix multiply (GEMM) with \(\SquareGemmDimension=\) 4,096 has intensity \(\SquareGemmDimension/3 \approx\) 1,365.3 FLOP/byte.
Result: Operations above 295.2 FLOP/byte are compute bound; operations below it are memory bound. The GEMM example is compute bound, while a single-token autoregressive decode with intensity \(\approx 1\) FLOP/byte is deeply memory bound.
Systems insight: The same accelerator can be compute rich and memory constrained. Arithmetic intensity determines which resource the workload actually consumes.


Throughput is only one constraint. Training also requires enough capacity for weights, gradients, and optimizer state.

Napkin Math 1.2: Estimate training-state memoryProblem: How much model-state memory is required to train a 7B model with mixed-precision Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam)?
Variables: Mixed-precision Adam stores BF16 weights, gradients, FP32 master weights, momentum, and variance. The model-state budget is 16 bytes per parameter.
Math: For 7B parameters, model state is 7 \(\times 10^9 \times\) 16 bytes = 112 GB.
Result: An H100 has 80 GB of high-bandwidth memory (HBM), so the model state alone exceeds a single accelerator before accounting for activations.
Systems insight: Optimizer state, not weights alone, sets the floor for training memory. Capacity planning that starts from parameter bytes underestimates the real requirement.


Fitting the model in memory establishes feasibility, but not operating cost. Power and elapsed time provide the remaining quantities for a first electricity estimate.

Napkin Math 1.3: Estimate accelerator electricity costProblem: What is the accelerator-only electricity cost of the GPT-3 training run?
Variables: Use 10,000 V100s, 300 W per accelerator, ~14.8 days wall-clock, and $0.12/kWh electricity (Patterson et al. 2021).
Math: The run requires roughly \(3.14 \times 10^{23}\) FLOPs. The accelerator-only electricity-cost estimate is ~14.8 days wall-clock \(\times\) 10,000 V100s \(\times\) 24 h/day \(\times\) 0.3 kW \(\times\) $0.12/kWh = ~$127,872.
Result: The accelerator-only electricity cost is roughly $128,000. This thermal design power (TDP)-only estimate excludes host CPUs, networking, storage, cooling, and facility overhead. The 1,066 MWh of accelerator energy behind it covers about 83 percent of the 1,287 MWh reported for the run, which also counts host power and data center overhead. The GPU count and duration are a published reconstruction from measured per-GPU throughput, so only their product is firm (Patterson et al. 2021).
Systems insight: Energy is measurable from power and time, but full cost accounting must also include capital utilization, networking, storage, staffing, and failed or repeated runs.





These are the accelerator assumptions used in the book’s roofline, training-memory, energy, and cost examples: peak throughput, memory bandwidth, memory capacity, and TDP for each generation the chapters cite. Values are vendor datasheet peaks—ceilings for napkin math, not sustained utilization—drawn from NVIDIA product documentation and IEEE Micro architecture articles (NVIDIA Corporation 2017, 2020b, 2020a, 2021, 2018, 2024; Choquette et al. 2021; Choquette 2023), AMD MI300X documentation (AMD 2023), Google Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) publications (Jouppi et al. 2020; Jouppi et al. 2023), and Google Cloud’s current TPU v6e specification page (Google Cloud 2026). Capacity rows preserve official capacity nameplates. Tables progress from table 2 (Volta) and table 3 (Turing) through current and forward-looking generations.

The assumptions above use shared unit conventions: decimal data prefixes, distinct FLOPs and FLOP/s quantities, and the aliases defined below. Table 18 fixes the unit conventions used in every quantitative example in this book. Each row gives the multiplier \(\UnitAliasMultiplier\) in 1 alias \(=\) \(\UnitAliasMultiplier\) base. Data prefixes use decimal SI (\(\text{KB} = 10^3\) bytes, not 1024). Binary IEC prefixes do not appear in the book’s prose. Throughput quantities (FLOP/s, GB/s) combine these aliases with time; adding incompatible dimensions (bytes to FLOP/s) is a category error in napkin math, not a unit conversion.
Hardware capacity labels are the one deliberate exception. The reference tables retain vendor nameplate numbers and labels; the byte budgets used in calculations follow the device assumptions stored in the book’s hardware registry. For example, the book models an 80 GB accelerator with \(80 \times 2^{30}\) bytes and assigns \(512 \times 2^{10}\) bytes to a microcontroller with 512 KB of SRAM. These are modeled capacity assumptions, not universal guarantees inferred from the labels. Every other data quantity, including model footprints, activation sizes, and transfer volumes, uses the decimal prefixes above. Where a worked example subtracts a computed footprint from a device capacity, the stored capacity byte budget is converted to decimal units alongside the footprint so that the arithmetic printed on the page is the arithmetic a reader can reproduce.

This appendix is the reference catalog for the quantitative inputs used throughout the book. It gathers accelerator and model specifications, training-memory conventions, energy constants, interconnect bandwidths, economic and scale references, unit conventions, and provenance. The values come from vendor peaks, published measurements, standards, and editorial scenarios, so they carry different evidentiary weight and age at different rates.
Use these tables as starting inputs, not universal constants. For each estimate, record the table row, unit convention, and provenance; replace time-sensitive peaks, prices, and rates with local values; distinguish a physical ceiling from a measured operating point and a scenario assumption; and report which assumptions dominate the result. This keeps napkin math reproducible and makes clear which input controls the conclusion.

title: System Assumptions
text:
When a chapter says an H100 delivers a certain ridge point, or that training a 7B model needs a certain amount of memory, the underlying bandwidths, capacities, and model sizes are listed here. A local estimate can use the relevant Value and Unit entries. The tables are grouped by topic: accelerators, reference models, energy per access, interconnect bandwidth, economics, production-scale anchors, and unit conventions. Assumptions come from vendor datasheet peaks, published studies or industry reports, illustrative market or grid statistics, and book conventions; section 1.1 lists the provenance in one place.
The calculations below expose which assumptions dominate each estimate, so a changed hardware specification or price can propagate without changing the method.
The constants in this appendix support quick, reproducible calculations. The three examples below apply them to performance, capacity, and cost.

Napkin Math 1.1: Classify a roofline regimeProblem: For the stated H100 and workload intensities, which operations are compute bound and which are memory bound?
Variables: For an H100 at FP16/BF16 peak, use 989 TFLOP/s peak compute and 3.35 TB/s memory bandwidth.
Math: Divide peak FLOP/s by memory bandwidth to get the roofline ridge point: 989 TFLOP/s/3.35 TB/s \(\approx\) 295.2 FLOP/byte. A large general matrix multiply (GEMM) with \(\SquareGemmDimension=\) 4,096 has intensity \(\SquareGemmDimension/3 \approx\) 1,365.3 FLOP/byte.
Result: Operations above 295.2 FLOP/byte are compute bound; operations below it are memory bound. The GEMM example is compute bound, while a single-token autoregressive decode with intensity \(\approx 1\) FLOP/byte is deeply memory bound.
Systems insight: The same accelerator can be compute rich and memory constrained. Arithmetic intensity determines which resource the workload actually consumes.


Throughput is only one constraint. Training also requires enough capacity for weights, gradients, and optimizer state.

Napkin Math 1.2: Estimate training-state memoryProblem: How much model-state memory is required to train a 7B model with mixed-precision Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam)?
Variables: Mixed-precision Adam stores BF16 weights, gradients, FP32 master weights, momentum, and variance. The model-state budget is 16 bytes per parameter.
Math: For 7B parameters, model state is 7 \(\times 10^9 \times\) 16 bytes = 112 GB.
Result: An H100 has 80 GB of high-bandwidth memory (HBM), so the model state alone exceeds a single accelerator before accounting for activations.
Systems insight: Optimizer state, not weights alone, sets the floor for training memory. Capacity planning that starts from parameter bytes underestimates the real requirement.


Fitting the model in memory establishes feasibility, but not operating cost. Power and elapsed time provide the remaining quantities for a first electricity estimate.

Napkin Math 1.3: Estimate accelerator electricity costProblem: What is the accelerator-only electricity cost of the GPT-3 training run?
Variables: Use 10,000 V100s, 300 W per accelerator, ~14.8 days wall-clock, and $0.12/kWh electricity (Patterson et al. 2021).
Math: The run requires roughly \(3.14 \times 10^{23}\) FLOPs. The accelerator-only electricity-cost estimate is ~14.8 days wall-clock \(\times\) 10,000 V100s \(\times\) 24 h/day \(\times\) 0.3 kW \(\times\) $0.12/kWh = ~$127,872.
Result: The accelerator-only electricity cost is roughly $128,000. This thermal design power (TDP)-only estimate excludes host CPUs, networking, storage, cooling, and facility overhead. The 1,066 MWh of accelerator energy behind it covers about 83 percent of the 1,287 MWh reported for the run, which also counts host power and data center overhead. The GPU count and duration are a published reconstruction from measured per-GPU throughput, so only their product is firm (Patterson et al. 2021).
Systems insight: Energy is measurable from power and time, but full cost accounting must also include capital utilization, networking, storage, staffing, and failed or repeated runs.

These are the reference model assumptions behind training-cost, memory-footprint, and inference-workload examples: parameter counts, per-inference FLOP budgets, and published training-scale anchors. The assumptions above use shared unit conventions: decimal data prefixes, distinct FLOPs and FLOP/s quantities, and the aliases defined below. Table 18 fixes the unit conventions used in every quantitative example in this book. Each row gives the multiplier \(\UnitAliasMultiplier\) in 1 alias \(=\) \(\UnitAliasMultiplier\) base. Data prefixes use decimal SI (\(\text{KB} = 10^3\) bytes, not 1024). Binary IEC prefixes do not appear in the book’s prose. Throughput quantities (FLOP/s, GB/s) combine these aliases with time; adding incompatible dimensions (bytes to FLOP/s) is a category error in napkin math, not a unit conversion.
Hardware capacity labels are the one deliberate exception. The reference tables retain vendor nameplate numbers and labels; the byte budgets used in calculations follow the device assumptions stored in the book’s hardware registry. For example, the book models an 80 GB accelerator with \(80 \times 2^{30}\) bytes and assigns \(512 \times 2^{10}\) bytes to a microcontroller with 512 KB of SRAM. These are modeled capacity assumptions, not universal guarantees inferred from the labels. Every other data quantity, including model footprints, activation sizes, and transfer volumes, uses the decimal prefixes above. Where a worked example subtracts a computed footprint from a device capacity, the stored capacity byte budget is converted to decimal units alongside the footprint so that the arithmetic printed on the page is the arithmetic a reader can reproduce.

Each assumption has a provenance record that lets readers trace the number back to its primary source. Table 19 groups the appendix’s quantitative inputs by evidence class and identifies the primary references behind each group. Vendor specifications and standards define published limits, peer-reviewed measurements provide empirical anchors, and explicitly marked editorial scenarios supply illustrative values where no durable universal constant exists. This distinction lets readers judge the evidentiary weight of an input, update time-sensitive values, and reproduce an estimate with an appropriate local substitute.

title: System Assumptions
text:
This appendix is the reference catalog for the quantitative inputs used throughout the book. It gathers accelerator and model specifications, training-memory conventions, energy constants, interconnect bandwidths, economic and scale references, unit conventions, and provenance. The values come from vendor peaks, published measurements, standards, and editorial scenarios, so they carry different evidentiary weight and age at different rates.
Use these tables as starting inputs, not universal constants. For each estimate, record the table row, unit convention, and provenance; replace time-sensitive peaks, prices, and rates with local values; distinguish a physical ceiling from a measured operating point and a scenario assumption; and report which assumptions dominate the result. This keeps napkin math reproducible and makes clear which input controls the conclusion.
